## Chapter 1: Fragile Flames

### Text

When Sokka was ten, his world came apart like rotten ice. He knelt in the snow, body cold and numb except for the sickening red warmth seeping through his pants, Katara screaming and screaming and screaming in his arms louder than he ever thought someone her size could scream. He stared into his mother’s blank eyes and clutched Katara close and vowed that he wouldn’t let the Fire Nation take anything else from him ever, ever again.

Now, coaxing Katara into a few minutes of rest in between healing sessions, half-delirious himself from watching over Aang’s barely-responsive form, Sokka wonders if some vows are best left unmade lest the universe takes it as a challenge.

&#45;-

Sokka never wants to see another spot of rust for the rest of his life. He’s spent weeks scrubbing at it and picking it away and figuring out how to patch it and paint it to stop it spreading because the last thing anyone needs right now is to go down because a rogue wave hit a weak patch in the hull of their *stupid metal ship*. It only took a few days to realize that saltwater and dampness and steel means that the ocean is constantly trying to eat away at your mode of transportation, but that was a few days they could ill afford to lose. Sokka’s been obsessively tracking the progress of the rust ever since, spending his days waging war against its spread.

The men weren’t entirely sold on spending their time maintaining an enemy vessel—at least not until Tulok put his foot right through the deck, and good thing Katara hadn’t totally exhausted herself for the day yet—and they want to do it even less in full armor, especially the Fire Nation kind. Which Sokka doesn’t disagree with, even if he’s the one shouting about the necessity. When Sokka thinks armor, he thinks some nice vambraces, a dramatic helmet, maybe some heavy shin guards if you’re a strong swimmer.

This is not that.

And somehow, even after spending so much time dodging Fire Nation soldiers and thinking about peeling one in particular out of all his literal and figurative defenses, Sokka never quite appreciated how *much* of this Fire Nation armor there is until he’s scrubbing at the steel deck of their captured Fire Nation ship under the full sun in a complete set of it.

He doesn’t know how the Fire Nation soldiers do it without boiling themselves. The deck is fucking *hot*—its metal and painted black and the fucking tropics. And how do they even *find* all the rust, which seems to get everywhere except this fucking armor, without having Toph around metalbending her way into permanent rust-finding duty? Which she took with remarkably good graces, but then, no one wants to sink into the Mo Ce Sea because a dolphin piranha decided to take a bite out of a rotten hull.

Sokka never wants to see even a single fleck of rust ever again, after this. But he’s grimly grateful for each and every bit of it now, because donning Fire Nation armor and putting his head down and scrubbing the deck is a thankless task, which means it’s a task he can do alone, and a necessary one, which means no one is going to tell him to stop.

Sokka may have lost his ability to pretend that everything is normal and fine and good right around the second Aang finally woke up. And since Sokka *isn’t* feeling normal, or fine, or good, and also does *not* want to talk about it, he’s been hiding out on the open deck behind full Fire Nation paraphernalia ever since.

There’s something kind of nice to being so thoroughly concealed behind stiff leather and plates of metal and layers of tough fabric, so long as no one gets a good look at his face. Which probably says something about Zuko that Sokka will think about when thinking about Zuko isn’t quite so hard.

The other benefit of everyone needing to wear full Fire Nation regalia on deck is that no one can sneak up on anyone, which Sokka very much appreciates as someone begins clanking their way over to his corner of the stern. It gives Sokka just enough time to wrestle himself his thoughts toward something marginally less volatile before Panuk plops down next to him in a clatter of metal plates on steel decking.

“I don’t know how they do this all day,” Panuk says cheerfully as he begins to scrub at the far side of Sokka’s rust patch, face already flushed with exertion and heat. “They must just melt their brains right out of their skulls. Nothing but ash left behind in there.”

“I don’t think melting things leave ash behind,” Sokka says, eyeing the deck critically. It’s looking a *little* better—right?

“You know what I mean. This stuff is ridiculous to have on all the time.”

Sokka glances up. “You’re wearing it wrong.”

“What? But I got the sleeves all puffy this time like you said they should be.”

Sokka sighs, leaning over to reposition and re-buckle straps until it looks how Zuko used to wear it. Somehow none of them can ever get it wholly right.

“That is,” Panuk mutters, “Somehow even *less* comfortable than before.”

Sokka shrugs, grabbing his brush again and leaning his weight behind his scrubbing. Maybe if he does it hard enough, he can also scrub all the thoughts right out of his brain for a few hours.

“You know,” Panuk muses as he contemplates his new, more restrictive armor. “I had a really rough time of it, in one of our second or third battles. It wasn’t my first fight or anything, but it was the first time someone actually almost got killed. Yura.”

Sokka snorts. Yura has to be first at everything. He would be the first to almost die, too.

Panuk’s grin flashes quick and bright in the sun. “It’s a miracle we’ve gotten however long it’s been—”

“Three years,” Sokka murmurs.

“—with as few casualties as we’ve had. And those are hard. Will always be hard.” Panuk purses his lips for a moment. “But it’s still hard even when it doesn’t happen, you know? And that can be weird, because it’s like you’re upset about something that didn’t even happen. But sometimes it’s not easy to get over what could have happened.”

Sokka holds back a sigh. There’s a reason he’s been hiding out on the deck in full armor, and dealing with everyone’s concern over his lack of joking and cheerfulness is at the top of the list. Still, he appreciates the sentiment and general effort behind what Panuk is trying to do.

If only lingering fear over Aang’s near-death were the only thing Sokka is dealing with.

“It can be really easy to get stuck in imaging all the ways it could have gone worse, you know? And that can make it hard to stop being afraid even though the battle’s over.” Panuk glances over and Sokka gives him a tiny nod to show he’s listening. “Some people get mad. Kolo is never as angry as when he’s afraid for you. And Tinrak can’t stand feeling like you’re smothering him.”

Well. That answers the question of whether the Water Tribe warriors noticed the tension between Sokka and everyone else. Clearly, they could see the strain between him and Katara and Aang and Toph just fine, even if they couldn’t see the shape of it.

“It’s all normal, even if it sucks. But it *does* get better.” Panuk nudges his shoulder, his expression one of reassurance. “People’s fear lessens when they realize the danger is gone. It just sometimes takes your body time to catch up.”

“I’m not sure if the danger is ever gone,” Sokka mutters, aware that he sounds more broody and pissy than his usual state of being. And aware that even a few weeks ago he would have probably tried to project cheer and unbotheredness and a good healthy focus on planning. But Spirits, it would be a thin veneer right now that he is sure his dad and Bato and Panuk and everyone else would see right through anyway. Not really worth the effort.

“You know what I mean,” Panuk rolls his eyes. “I’m just trying to say—scary things are scary, and it’s okay to be scared by them. And it won’t always be like this. They’ll get over it, and so will you.”

That, Sokka needs to be true. He desperately needs to know that at some point in the future Sokka will be past this, and so will the others, that the way he feels right now isn’t going to be how he feels forever. But Spirits, no matter how much he thinks about it—or doesn’t think about it—while scrubbing rust under the blazing sun, or staring at the ceiling as Yue travels across the sky, Sokka can’t figure out how they’re ever going to get there from where they’re standing now.

&#45;-

Sokka is a silent presence at Katara’s side, handing her bandages and bowls of broth and fresh water. He lets her work, doing his best to have everything she needs at hand as she needs it, only interrupting to echo an order for Aang to rest, or to be a new voice trying to make Aang appreciate the mere fact that he is conscious again and functional.

They need Aang to recover and regain his strength, not fret himself back until illness in his increasing distress over the idea of being thought dead. And maybe, separate from that, *Sokka* needs Aang to recover. Needs to see him breathing evenly and moving easily and always finding a reason to smile.

Sokka tries to explain that it’s a tactical advantage, for their enemies to think the Avatar is dead. That it’s something they can use, something that will make their journey less dangerous, that will give them a critical element of surprise. But he’s pretty sure all Aang hears is that it’s a Fire Nation lie they’ve decided to accept.

In the past, Sokka might have said ‘trust me’ or ‘believe that I know when I’m being lied to.’ But that doesn’t really feel like a thing he can ask for anymore, so he just makes himself useful to Katara, and bites his tongue, and hopes.

&#45;-

Sokka glances at the little square of mirror bolted to the wall of his bunk and freezes in the middle of shaking out a fresh shirt. He stares at his reflection, feeling like his heart is trying to crawl up into his throat before he explodes into frantic motion, turning and twisting and contorting, hiking down his waistband and craning his neck to try to look at himself in the little bit of mirror and wrenching his arms to try to run his hands over the parts of himself he can’t manage to see.

His skin looks like it always does, maybe a bit darker in places from the sun, unblemished outside of the thin bright lines of old scars. All the damage he picked up in Ba Sing Se has finally healed over. No more healing scrapes or fading bruises or barely-there echoes of firebender-hot hands over his skin.

It takes Sokka a long moment to register that the expression staring back at him from the mirror is…bereft. He knew this would happen. Obviously, the signs of Zuko’s touch would fade along with everything else. Logically, putting off Katara’s offer of healing by pointing out that she needed to save her energy for Aang—which wasn’t wrong—was only going to delay the inevitable so much.

But Sokka still feels hollowed out inside, collapsing around something he didn’t even realize how completely he was clinging to until it’s gone, to be down to only the burn scar on his left forearm to be able to prove that the thing between him and Zuko was ever anything more than a dream. And that one has never been the same, anyway.

Sokka forces himself to breathe, pressing his right hand over his ribs, just to the side of and under his heart. One of Zuko’s favorite places, and Sokka loved the way he could casually brush his upper arm against that spot during the day and feel Zuko’s handprint come to life, warm, beating in time with Sokka’s heart. Like the embers of a campfire in the morning, cold until you prod them open, quiet but ready to be stirred back to life.

Sokka is trying to swallow back something that feels dangerously close to mourning when Katara shoves the door open with a resounding clang that has then both flinching in surprise. He jumps, spinning around to see her wincing in the doorway, arm still extended. “Katara, what the fuck? Why are you just barging in?”

“…Why are you checking yourself out in the mirror?”

“I’m not,” Sokka mutters, casting around for his shirt. “I was just…” checking himself out in the mirror.

“…Sure,” she says with that special little sister humoring-you-because-you’re-an-idiot tone even as she gives him a quick, automatic check over for injury.

“What’s up,” Sokka sighs, grabbing up his shirt and turning it right-side out. It’s one of the dark Fire Nation ones that the ship’s stores were full of, the ones that somehow have far more fabric than they have a right to.

Katara watches him trying to sort himself out, worrying at her lip, fingers restless on her necklace. Not a good sign, when it’s both those things. “Have you talked to Aang?”

“In general?” Sokka gives up and just tugs the shirt over his head. He’ll find his way through the billowing fabric from the inside. “Sure.” In particular? Not really. There’s too much that Sokka doesn’t know how to talk about yet. So much that went unsaid, shoved aside and pushed down and pinned for later while Aang was in dire straits, that now the weight of it all feels impossible to move on his own.

“I think you should.”

Sokka finally pops his head back into the light, frowning as he works to get his arms free now. “Why?”

“He’s going to do something.”

Sokka pauses, one arm half-extended as he searches for the sleeve. “He *is* the Avatar. That’s kind of his job.”

“Not like that,” Katara huffs, rolling her eyes. “Like—he just has this look. All—” She flaps her hand. “Like he’s going to go out on his own and try to take the Fire Nation down by himself, or something ridiculous like that.”

Sokka digests that a moment, finally shoving his hand free. “That would be suicide.”

“Yeah. That’s why you should talk to him.”

Sokka takes his time getting his other arm where it’s supposed to be in this ridiculous tent of a shirt. Were there no perfectly normal-sized men in the Fire Nation navy? Were they all giants? “Why do you think he’ll listen to me?”

“You guys have your whole…talking thing. That you do. You know, where you go off together and be all broody and come back all…unbroody.”

Sokka snorts, hefting up the heavy quilted skirt-guard, which goes *under* the curaiss not on top of it, not that anyone but him ever seemed to remember that. Spirits, they’re in trouble if another Fire Nation ship gets too close. “What, you think I can show him the right path? You trust me to tell him how to find it?” Sokka winces as soon as he says it, the words coming significantly more acid than Sokka meant to let slip.

Katara scowls, shifting on her feet as she sets her jaw. “We don’t have time for this.”

“Well then when *is* the time for this,” Sokka demands, bouncing a little to settle all his underlayers before he starts strapping down metal plates. Because Sokka isn’t the only one who’s been dodging conversations for days now, ever since Aang woke up.

“I don’t—What do you want me to say, Sokka?” Katara snaps. “Because you’ve already made it clear you don’t want to hear what I think.”

“You haven’t exactly been listening to me, either,” Sokka bites back, yanking a strap so hard he nearly drives the air out of his own lungs, coughing in surprise. “What do you need to say,” he grunts as he loosens the strap a bit. “Let’s start there.”

“You look ridiculous,” she throws out, glaring at his half-put-together armor.

“Okay, one—it looks fine when it’s all buckled down,” Sokka says, ignoring her sarcastic ‘sure.’ “Two—it’s not my fault all of the soldiers on this ship had abnormally wide shoulders. And three—stop changing the subject. That’s not the point and you know it.”

He meets her glare for glare before sighing, glancing away to finish strapping on his armor. Of course this finally happens when he’s literally putting himself into a Fire Nation uniform. “Katara. Do you still trust me?”

“…Yes.”

“You didn’t sound sure,” Sokka points out, striving for a neutral tone because contrary to how all this is starting, he doesn’t actually want this conversation to be a fight.

Katara sighs, looking up at the steel ceiling a moment before relenting. “I don’t understand how you can still trust Zuko after what he did. And I don’t like not understanding.”

“You haven’t seen him like I have,” Sokka says quietly.

“*You* haven’t seen him like *I* have,” Katara pushes back, eyes snapping back down into glare. “Is it really so far outside the realm of possibility that he was just pretending with you? Because his firebending sure felt real when he was *fighting* me.”

Sokka glances away, giving more attention than he needs to tugging the last of his buckles into place. It’s not that he can’t *conceptualize* a world in which Zuko was leading him on the whole time. It’s just…

“Or do you just need it to not be an option?”

Sokka can’t meet her eyes.

“Sokka—I don’t know what you want us to think,” says sighs, shoving a hand through her hair and scowling when it immediately gets tangled. She hasn’t had much time for anything but healing, even now, and neither of them has been feeling relaxed enough for Sokka to try workout out the knots for her. “You won’t answer Toph’s questions, or mine. You want to hear all about everything I can remember but then you won’t tell us anything back. What are we supposed to do with that?”

“I don’t *have* answers,” Sokka says, for the two hundredth time, not that anyone’s counting...

“But you have *ideas*. And guesses, and suspicions. And you never used to hold those back before.”

She’s…not wrong. Sokka has always done his best thinking when he can make his thoughts tangible somehow, through words or writing or sketching to make some kind of sense of his crowded mind. But it’s different to talk through ways to travel across the Fire Nation without being seen than it is to let the others in on the morass of tangled worry and fear and hope that Sokka has bundled up inside himself over what Zuko *might* be doing.

Katara’s shoulders slump, her exhaustion suddenly visible in every line of her body. “How can you ask me to trust you when you don’t even act like you trust yourself?”

That's...Sokka finds that he doesn’t have anything to say in response to that, fiddling with the edge of his vambrace since his wrist wraps are buried under all these layers.

“Will you talk to Aang?” Katara finally asks, straightening and seeming to forcibly inject briskness and energy into her spine.

Sokka eyes her sidelong. “If you want me to.”

“Please?” She searches his face, expression softening in a way that makes him want to squirm. “I never doubted your commitment to what we’re trying to do, Sokka. I know you want to end the war.”

“Just my judgment, then?”

She sighs. “Talk to Aang.”

Sokka nods his agreement, trying to swallow back the part of himself that feels plaintive and mad and sharp, because Katara is doing…so much, right now, and she doesn’t need this on top of it.

Sokka doesn’t follow right after her as she leaves, though, just turns back to the mirror, running his fingers along the spot on his forearm where Zuko’s burn mark sits. This whole conversation, the realization that the last evidence of Zuko is gone from his skin—it’s all making Sokka feel more unsteady than he wants to be.

He needs to gather his thoughts, to get himself in some semblance of order if he’s going to do a bit of good for Aang. Spirits, he needs to do that just to leave the room. Dad doesn’t need Sokka walking around the ship like a mobile vat of emotional blasting jelly when Katara is already staking out her place as an emotional trebuchet. She’s been lobbing enough pointed comments across the bow for both of them.

&#45;-

The thing about trying to get himself into some semblance of order is that Sokka has been trying to do that ever since they left Ba Sing Se.

The thing about trying to get himself into some semblance of order is that to do that a person generally has to have some idea of the semblance they’re trying to order themselves around.

The thing about trying to get himself into some semblance of order is that Sokka has no idea which way is up anymore, torn between the facts as he knows them and the facts that others tell him, between the things he can say aloud and the things he can’t articulate but knows down to his bones are true.

The thing about it all is that Sokka wishes Katara was wrong. Or fuck, he’d even take feeling certain that she was wrong about what happened underneath the Earth King’s palace, even if she’s actually right. Zuko thoroughly and completely yanked the sled out from under Sokka back in Ba Sing Se, and now he feels like he’s divided within himself, torn between the picture Katara paints and the one Sokka holds in his mind. There’s the Zuko of stolen afternoons together and the Zuko who fights Katara and the Zuko who might have a grand secret plan that he never once hinted at.

And sure, all of those versions could coexist—it’s not like Sokka hasn’t become excellent at compartmentalizing—but…isn’t it a huge omission to not even suggest that one of those versions was even *there*? So huge it feels dangerously close to a lie. Something that Sokka thought Zuko couldn’t do at all, and if Zuko can…well, doesn’t that just throw a heaping mountain of uncertainty onto everything else Sokka thought he knew.

&#45;-

Sokka finds Aang sitting on top of the command tower or lookout tower or whatever this is, which isn’t exactly the most concealed location the Avatar could choose to hide in for their infiltration of the Fire Nation. Not to mention that it isn’t the easiest to haul himself up to in full armor—Spirits, how did Zuko *do* this all day. At least Aang hasn’t followed through on his threat to shave his head again, and his glider is folded into a staff, which Sokka takes to mean that Aang isn’t quite ready to go off into parts unknown by himself just yet, regardless of how determined his expression looks as Sokka settles beside him at the railing.

“It’s a long way up, but the view might be worth it,” Sokka pants, looking out over the endless ocean all around them. Spirits, the water is so *blue* around here.

“I guess,” Aang mutters, leaning out against the railing to consider the water beneath with an airbender’s regard for falling.

Sokka resists the urge to tug him back by the tunic. Aang is generally more than happy to expound on the natural wonders of the world around him, but he isn’t biting at this. This… might take longer than Sokka anticipated to gently guide the conversation in the direction he wants it to go.

Fuck gentle, then.

“So,” Sokka says conversationally, contemplating how the dark metal plates on his armor seem to suck in the sun without getting hot. They should figure that out for the decks, too. “You aren’t planning anything, are you?”

Aang doesn’t react, just going more broody and silent, which is as good as screaming to Sokka after months of interpreting Zuko’s particular brand of sullen nonreaction.

“Cause to be honest,” Sokka says, letting just a bit of his tight frustration out. “I’m pretty fucking done with secret plans.”

*That* gets Aang’s attention, enough to startle him into responding. “You—? Oh. Yeah. That… isn’t great.”

“That it certainly is not,” Sokka sighs, rubbing at his eyes and laughing a little at the understatement. “So. Let’s get it all out there. What’s on your mind, buddy?”

Aang sets his jaw and manages to hold back for all of five seconds before the words burst free. “People think I’m *dead*.”

“And?”

Aang gives him an incredulous look, mouth working in outraged silence.

“People think you’re dead,” Sokka shrugs. “You aren’t. What does it matter what they think?”

“People will think I failed them! *Again.* I’m supposed to be inspiring people and giving them hope and beating the Fire Nation and instead, I’m hiding on some ship!”

“But you haven’t failed them, and you’re working to beat the Fire Nation, and you’re not hiding out, we’re infiltrating,” Sokka says. “So who cares what they think. Especially if it gives us a better shot at winning.”

Aang stares. “*You* care what people think,” he bursts out. “You get mad at Toph all the time for what she thinks about you. All the way to the North you were caring what people thought!”

“Okay, first off—not *all* the way to the North—”

“Most of it, then!”

“—and second—then take it from someone with experience.” He flicks Aang’s shoulder harder than is strictly necessary to grab his attention. “Caring too much about what other people think gets you in trouble. You can’t just do whatever makes other people happy, you need to look out for yourself.” *Especially* the Avatar.

“Well, I don’t *want* to pretend to be dead,” Aang grumbles. “I don’t want the Fire Nation to think it won!”

“Even if letting them think that makes it easier to actually beat them?”

“I *can’t* let them think that! It’s not just about them,” Aang says, fingers going white-knuckled around the railing. “People need a symbol! *I’m* supposed to be a symbol!”

“Aang, no,” Sokka protests, straightening around a sudden burst of alarm. “You’re not just some empty symbol. It’s not like anyone could take your place if people thought they were the Avatar. You’re—”

“The Avatar, and the last airbender, and one of the last people who remembers what the world was like *before*, the way it’s supposed to be! I need to stop the Fire Nation, and end the war, and restore balance to the world, and revive the Air Nomad culture, and preserve our traditions, and I didn’t even *know* all of them I didn’t have *time,* and every day more and more could be lost, and I need to prove myself so that—”

“Aang,” Sokka breaks in as Aang’s words start to trip over themselves. “Hey, deep breaths. Just—deep breaths, okay?” He waits until he sees Aang actually inhale. “There’s only one thing you need to think about right now, okay? All that other stuff—that all comes after.”

Aang glares. “And how does not thinking about what comes next work out for you?”

“…Wow,” Sokka says, sitting back and watching frustration and instant regret fight across Aang’s face. “Ouch. Shots fired, huh?”

“I’m sorry,” Aang mutters, hunching his shoulders like he can hide behind them. “That wasn’t…”

“No, no, it’s fine,” Sokka says, shaking his head. It’s not like Aang is saying something Sokka hasn’t been kicking himself for every night ever since they left Ba Sing Se and Zuko wasn’t with them. “And here I thought Katara was the one to look out for.”

Aang cuts him a quick, guilty look. “I didn’t mean to imply that you…”

Sokka raises his eyebrows. “That I…Focus on the present to the point of blindly committing to enormously questionable courses of action with significant long-term ramifications because they’re gratifying in the immediate moment, which is particularly concerning as our chief Maker of Plans?”

“Uh—That’s basically…Yeah.”

“It would be a fair statement,” Sokka says, forcing his voice to stay easy, forcing himself to breathe through the way his chest tightens with familiar self-recrimination. “I *do* think a lot about the future and what comes next, just…” He gropes for a way to describe the careful tightrope he and Zuko walked, of sharing themselves and opening to each other while still holding back.

“Not about everything?”

“Apparently.”

Aang stacks his chin on top of his fists on the railing, peeking at Sokka out of the corner of his eye. “Katara said that you think he didn’t defect.”

Sokka sighs, absently scanning the horizon as he searches for words. It feels like all Sokka has are nuances, when all anyone needs are clear, blunt lines. “I don’t know if you can really call it a defection if he was never on our side to begin with.”

Aang shrugs away the difference. “Katara said you don’t think he betrayed us, then.” *Betrayed you*, are the words Sokka hears tacked on to the end. He doesn’t need Aang to say them to know they’re there.

“I think he has a plan,” Sokka clarifies, watching out of the corner of his eye as Aang digests the distinction. One that Sokka is almost positive Zuko intended to signal to Sokka, even if that conviction feels like it only spawns more uncertainty. Did Zuko just want to give him a heads up? Does he need Sokka to do something specific? Was he warning Sokka off? Or maybe he was just messing with Katara’s head, like she thinks, and Sokka is reading far, far too much into an actually disconnected series of events and offhand comments.

“Down there, when we were fighting,” Aang finally says, worrying at a fleck of paint on the railing in front of him. Sokka immediately and absently notes it as a source of new rust. “It felt like he wanted to be the one fighting Katara, instead of letting his sister do it.”

“Or he wanted Azula fighting you,” Sokka says, because there are so many ‘what-ifs’ and can Sokka really afford to continue ignoring the ones he doesn’t want to be true?

“Maybe,” Aang shrugs, absently reaching toward the new scar on his back that looked like it was in that raw, itchy stage the last time Sokka saw it. “If it even matters.”

“It probably does,” Sokka sighs, trying to rein in his bitterness. “But it’s not like I know why.” Every new piece of information about what happened is like this, something Sokka seizes with both hands and then freezes in the face of. Everything can’t be important, but he doesn’t know what *is*, which means Sokka is left with nothing but endless possibilities for why Zuko might have wanted to be the one fighting Katara. Why Zuko might have done anything. Fuck, *if* Zuko did anything, or if each new fact is just a thing that happened rather than a thing Zuko chose.

Sokka scrubs at his face, feeling the beginnings of a fruitless-thoughts-and-sunlight-off-water induced headache beginning to settle behind his eyes. “Nice job changing the subject, by the way.”

Aang freezes like a puffin seal sensing a polar orca in the waters, then slumps forward, all the breath seeming to gust out of him as he stares down toward the deck. Sokka feels like he could paint a picture of Aang right now and call it ‘dejection.’

“The Fire Nation not knowing that you’re alive is a huge tactical advantage,” Sokka says, which just makes Aang look frustrated and angry and something that would definitely qualify as pissy on Zuko’s face. Sokka sighs, slumping forward with him. “Talk to me here, buddy.” He can’t have a one-sided heart to heart.

“…I’m the last airbender because I failed my people,” Aang says, face twisting like the words are bitter leaving his mouth. “I failed the whole *world* the first time. And now people are going to think I failed them again.”

Sokka waits, watching Aang’s knuckles turn more and more white around the railing as the silence yawns between them.

“I *did* fail them again,” Aang finally bursts out. “I didn’t *almost* die back there, I *did* die. Azula *won*. And—what would that have meant for the Water Tribes? And there’s so much that I need to *do*. I need to make the world right again! And how can I do that when I couldn’t even beat *one* firebender? It wasn’t even the Fire Lord! And I still wasn’t good enough.”

Sokka refrains from pointing out that Aang is twelve and shouldn’t have to feel like the world will collapse without him for a few weeks, because age has never mattered all that much in war as far as Sokka can tell, especially if you’re an Air Nomad. “This isn’t over yet,” Sokka says, taking a deep breath and making his voice firm. “I know what happened in Ba Sing Se feels like it was huge, but the plan didn’t change. We can still defeat the Fire Lord. We still have the advantage on the Day of the Black Sun. We’re still going to attack when he’s at his weakest.”

“Because I failed when Azula had her fire,” Aang says darkly. “So let’s make sure I don’t have to face that again.”

“*Because* this isn’t some kind of symbolic one on one showdown,” Sokka says, kicking at Aang’s dangling ankle to grab his attention. “The Avatar might be a symbol, but *you* aren’t in this alone. This is a war, and it sucks but wars aren’t settled in single combat, no matter how much we might want them to be. I’m not going to say you don’t have a role to play, but so does everyone else. And we’re all going to set aside our pride and our ego and do what needs to be done because that’s what war *is.*”

“But the world already thinks I abandoned them,” Aang says, voice aching in a way that makes Sokka wish Momo were around for a good cuddle.

“People will survive feeling abandoned if it means we win,” Sokka says, wincing at the pain that flashes over Aang’s face.

“It feels like I’m giving up part of who I am,” Aang admits quietly, hand brushing over his dark, spiky hair. “Like I’m ashamed to be an airbender.”

“War takes,” Sokka says softly, “It will take everything it can. If a few weeks of this is all you have to give it? And then it’s done? I can think of worse things to have to give up than that.”

“No one should have to give up anything in the first place.”

“Yeah, well. War doesn’t care about that either.” It never has and it never will, which is why it’s no use indulging his clamoring thoughts about all that’s already been given up, about what he might still need to sacrifice. “I get that this isn’t easy, that we’re asking a lot,” Sokka says, fiddling with the edge of his shirtsleeve. “But do you think you can still have faith in us to do it with you? I know its…hard, after I—after I failed to see it coming. In Ba Sing Se. I know we—I—let you down—”

“You didn’t,” Aang protests, head snapping up and face looking shocked that part of Sokka actually believes him. “No one expected you to see that coming, Sokka. No one could have known that Azula would be there.”

“I should have, though.”. Because Zuko knew. Zuko told him, and Sokka just…didn’t understand what Zuko was trying to say, didn’t understand where Zuko was coming from. Spirits, what else has Sokka misunderstood, that he thought he heard clearly?

“And I should have beat Azula,” Aang says tightly. “So I guess we both fucked up.”

Sokka startles, eyeing the way Aang’s expression is daring him to disagree and feeling the protest fighting to work its way free. “I don’t know if I’ve ever heard you curse like that before,” Sokka finally says, throwing out a bracing hand when Aang suddenly sighs and slumps against his side.

“This sucks,” Aang mutters, and Sokka doesn’t know if he means the hair he is tugging on again or what has to be the hard edge of Sokka’s shoulder guard.

“It does,” Sokka agrees anyway, because it really, really does. All of it. “But we can still do this if, you have still believe that we can. We can still win.”

“If we all have faith in each other,” Aang corrects, voice an odd mix of glum and resolute. “You said everyone has a part to play. That means you can’t do it alone, either.”

&#45;-

The hard thing about faith is that it’s all about belief, and Sokka doesn’t know what to believe anymore.

He knows what he *wants* to believe, just like he knows what he wants to be true, just like he knows he wants to feel the absolute certainty in his convictions that Katara seems to hold.

But it feels like nothing in his life is certain anymore, that all the things Sokka barely even realized he was taking on trust and faith and gut-level instinct are now thin and fragile and tenuous in the harsh light of day.

Even the fact that Zuko has a plan—being sure of that fact is barely anything, once other people start wanting details. When people want reasons and understanding and interpretation and all Sokka has are plain facts loosely connected to context. Zuko was so insistently alarmed when he thought Azula was in the city, wanted Sokka to take her seriously before the threat of her felt remotely real. Was that because Zuko already knew that Azula was infiltrating Ba Sing Se’s power structures? Because there was already a plan in place, then? Zuko’s plan? Or did Zuko just suspect what was going on, because even after so many years in exile he could still predict the way his sister would operate? And if he could, does that means she could predict him back?

The cold hard facts don’t feel like they’re worth nearly as much as they used to be, these days. But they’re all that Sokka has, so they’re somehow going to need to be enough, because it’s his own fault he doesn’t have anything more. That all he has are suddenly thin, sparse facts and not the reasons why.

If Sokka had just been more willing to push harder on the things Zuko didn’t want to talk about, or to offer up the things he himself cringed from sharing, then even if Sokka didn’t know exactly what Zuko’s plan is, he might be able to guess at the goal, or the purpose. Fuck, at this point Sokka would even take being able to look at the details gleaned from Katara and Aang and Toph and being able to tell which parts are the signals and which parts are the noise.

&#45;-

Sokka hovers at Toph’s back, not daring to offer an arm in support unless she asks but ready to catch her if she lists as the ship heaves against the waves. Her hands are braced on her knees, hair clinging damply to her face as she stares in the direction of the Fire Nation ship behind them, like if she tries hard enough she can somehow make her earth sense work through the water.

“More?” She pants, straightening like her joints ache.

“No, Katara has it from here,” Sokka says, grabbing onto the railing as a surge of waterbending rocks the ocean below them. The ship pursuing them is still more functional than Sokka would like, considering the state of their own vessel, but trying to metalbend across the expanse of water is taking more out of Toph than Sokka wants to risk when Katara is in her element.

Toph grunts, stamping on the deck and cocking her head as the echoes come back to her. “We took damage.”

“Yeah,” Sokka agrees, leaning out over the water to try to assess. Nothing seems to be riding too low, or leaning where it shouldn’t, but there was already so much rust…he doesn’t know how long they can hold up if Katara’s waves get stronger. “Can you fix it?” Toph can repair what’s broken, but she can’t make metal from nothing.

“Eh, probably,” Toph frowns, with an alarming lack of confidence. “Got to get closer.”

“Make it fast, if you can,” Sokka sighs. “We’re going to need to split up soon.” They’re too visible on their captured ship like this, too trapped, which Sokka never quite thought he would think about being on a ship with the open sea around him. But Aang has always been best protected by their ability to be mobile, and the Water Tribe can only do so much with a Fire Nation ship.

“You don’t sound happy about it,” Toph says, grabbing for the railing as Katara launches another wave. “Wasn’t that the plan all along?”

“Fuck plans,” Sokka mutters, scowling at the reality of separating—*again—*from his dad so soon after reuniting with him, at the idea of just…everything.

Toph perks up. “Come again?”

“Nothing.”

She wrinkles her nose. “Just get it out, Snoozles. Don’t be all mumbly and cryptic. You worried we’re going to sink? That another ship is going to show up and attack? That Sparrowkeet will be on it?”

“Well, I wasn’t *before—”*

“You’re welcome.”

“—and I don’t even know if he’s out of Ba Sing Se,” Sokka grumbles. Part of him hopes Zuko isn’t, even though he doesn’t know what that would mean with Azula. A larger part desperately wants to see him again, to talk to him, to *understand*. Though opposite sides of a naval battle wouldn’t be the ideal setting, for understanding. For anyone, but from what Sokka’s picked out from Zuko’s muttered dreaming, he doesn’t think Zuko in particular would handle it well.

“You don’t know much of anything,” Toph agrees cheerfully. “You must feel like an idiot, huh?”

“It’s not—he didn’t *tell me* he was planning anything!”

Toph waves that away. “Did you tell him everything?”

“No, but—”

“But you’re both idiots,” Toph cuts in, utterly without sympathy. “You want to know what I learned in the Earth Rumble, Snoozles?”

Sokka eyes her warily. “…How to be the best earthbender in the world?”

Toph scoffs, crossing her arms. “I already knew that. I learned that people can’t read your mind! *You* didn’t tell *him, he* didn’t tell *you*—sounds like you both did the exact same thing to each other and you’re both probably pissed about it.”

“Uh.” Sokka…doesn’t love that he can’t protest against the parallels Toph is drawing. He doesn’t like thinking of making Zuko feel the way he’s feeling himself right now.

Toph’s expression makes it clear what she thinks of that. “Look, if you’re right about him having some plan? Then you’ll have the chance to yell at him all you want. And if you’re wrong, then you can do more than yell.” Said with pure pragmatism and casual unconcern, as if Sokka doesn’t want to do far more than just yell at Zuko for springing this whole thing on him. As if Zuko isn’t going to feel the exact same way when Sokka springs an invasion on him.

Fuck.

How can everyone else seem to see to the heart of this tangle, when Sokka’s stuck mired in the details? It’s like all those little glimpses of who Zuko is when everyone isn’t watching are suddenly working against him. Aang and Toph and Katara know Zuko filtered through Sokka’s eyes, but Sokka doesn’t wholly trust that he can see Zuko clearly anymore, even if he also can’t accept that the Zuko he knew was just a mirage.

Toph lets out an explosive, exaggerated sigh. “Stop beating yourself up for not reading his mind and beat yourself up over being so drowning stupid that you expected yourself to. And go tell people we’re leaving. Tomorrow?”

“In the morning,” Sokka confirms, wondering who she picked that curse up from. Bato, probably. “What are you going to do?”

Toph cracks her knuckles, shaking out her arms and glaring out over the deck. “I’m going to fix this rust bucket so it doesn’t go down the minute I’m gone.”

&#45;-

Maybe part of Sokka’s whole state of never quite feeling like he has his feet under him— which *sucks,* at sea—is that being on a Fire Nation ship is just *weird*. Beyond the rust and the echoing and the oddness of seeing Water Tribe faces aged past his memories of what they should be, there are too many thoughts of Zuko that he can’t escape. The past, back when it was full of ‘maybe’ and ‘what if,’ feels too close here. His day-to-day reality slides too close to memory even though Sokka has never been on this particular ship before.

Fucking Fire Nation standardized production.

It’s too easy to lie in his bunk at night and feel that cell back around him, too easy to open his eyes and expect to find Zuko sitting across a set of bars, too easy to feel firebender heat and lean strength at his back every time he scales a ladder to the surface. Sokka can’t compartmentalize like he’s used to doing until he has the space to process, and he can’t process when it feels like his present and his past are sharing the same space. Sokka tries to fall back on irrefutable facts and instead finds himself swirling through that sense of breathless, pent-up possibility that burned beneath the surface of every minute on Zuko’s ship.

It all leaves Sokka mentally tangled and emotionally short, tired and overfull of inconvenient things that he really doesn’t have the privacy to deal with, with the way sound carries through the metal structure of the ship. He feels an intense sympathy for Zuko, going through his teen years in a room like this. And in a communal bathing environment, to top it all off.

Sokka finally breaks that last night before they part ways. Aang is on his way toward recovering, the ship isn’t going to fall apart underneath them, Katara seems less tense now that their departure is in sight, the eclipse plan is on track, and as each anxiety drops away thoughts of Zuko loom larger and larger. The metal ceiling here looks exactly like every ceiling in every bunk on the ship, exactly like the ceiling in his cell on Zuko’s ship, and Sokka can only hold out against the mess of worry and wanting inside himself for so long with nothing else to buffer against it.

He’s just so *tired* of stressing over Ba Sing Se and getting nowhere. But shoving it forcefully aside to sort through later gives breathing room for the desire that’s been persistently simmering low in his gut finally kindle to life, and Sokka just…finally decides not to feel guilty about it, because that kind of guilt is one particular piece of the past Sokka refuses to let creep into his present.

Sokka takes a half-second to remember that he did, in fact, lock the door on his way in tonight before letting his legs splay open. He fists one hand into the blankets and skims the other over his chest, down his stomach, wondering if he’d be torturing himself or not to imagine firebender heat trailing behind.

He presses the heel of his hands to the base of the hardening bulge in his pants, a puff of air shuddering out of him as he instinctively pushes up into the pressure. It’s going to be a challenge to be quiet, something Sokka has never been particularly good at and is distinctly out of practice with after the luxury of his own room in Ba Sing Se. But maybe the need for silence can be like a gentle, self-imposed restraint, one that he can test himself against as hard as he likes.

Sokka gasps as he thought sends his pulse surging, and apparently he’s deciding on self-inflicting some torture for himself, because as he raises his hand to lick his own palm he can’t stop remembering the half-lidded way Zuko would always catch Sokka’s eyes when doing that.

Sokka shoves his hand beneath his waistband, palming himself and biting his pillow and sinking into memories. He works himself to the echo of weight pressing him down into a thin mattress, to the almost-there sensation of strong thighs bracketing his hips. He teases the head of his cock while remembering the taste of Zuko’s mouth, traces the vein from top to bottom while picturing the boneless way Zuko could slide to his knees. He slowly strokes with almost-too-much pressure to memories of sparks breathed over his chest and hot fingers sinking inside him.

Sokka’s breaths come harsh through his nose, borderline too loud even with the constant noises of the ship and the water. His pace quickens as pre-come begins to bead at the head of his cock, adding slickness as his mind bounces from the way Zuko’s body would yield beneath him to the heady sensation of being tossed over Zuko’s shoulder to the way Zuko always hid his face against Sokka’s chest after he came, like he needed space from his own vulnerability but couldn’t bear to pull away.

Pleasure and fire and electricity build at the base of his spine and in his balls, coiling tighter with every stroke until Sokka tumbles over the edge with a barely swallowed cry that feels dangerously close to the shape of Zuko’s name. He clenches and shudders as his release rolls through him in wave after wave until Sokka pulls the last tremor out of his body, collapsing back onto the mattress and turning his face out of the pillow with a heaving gasp for air.

Sokka slowly releases himself, fumbling with his non-sticky hand over the edge of the futon. He snags some pile of fabric, silently hoping it isn’t an article of clothing he actually needs to wear tomorrow as he goes through the motions of cleaning himself up. His breaths are just a touch too loud still, and in the metal-walled room he could almost imagine that there’s another body here matching him breath for breath.

Spirits, Sokka wishes that were true. He wants Zuko to be here so badly, so he can…what? Demand an explanation? Ask for details that he himself isn’t sure he could easily provide if Zuko asked about his own plans? Finally try to pin down the strange relationship Zuko seems to have with his sister? Push for a level of transparency and honestly that he’s almost too afraid to offer back, because what if he *is* wrong, what if he *doesn’t* know Zuko like he thinks he does?

Sokka sighs, mind racing again even as his body settles into a languid bonelessness. He can’t stop sorting through observations and facts and trying to grasp onto something that feels strong and steady enough to stand on. There’s Zuko at the teashop and out dancing and alone with Sokka, Zuko in armor and with a sword in his hand and fire around his fists. There’s Iroh and pai sho and nearly four years away from a home that almost killed him. There’s an uncle, a little sister, a mother who’s gone, a father who’s all too present even from a distance. Tense, prickling anger and muted brooding and sun-soaked contentment and lightning highs and growing restlessness with every successive day in the Upper Ring. Because the expectations surrounding Zuko started to feel confining, maybe. Except that’s a supposition, not a fact, so Sokka sets it aside in a separate corner of his mind for later.

What *is* a fact, though, and an uncomfortable one, is that Sokka can see the ways he might have started to become one more set of expectations. He scowled at Iroh’s heavy hand in Zuko’s life, but wasn’t Sokka just another person wanting Zuko to fit his idea of how—who —Zuko should be?

Another uncomfortable fact that Sokka can’t avoid: A Crown Prince, even a former one, can never just be one thing to one person. For Sokka to think—to act?—even for a moment that someone as kinetic and driven as Zuko could be content to wait at home for Sokka to be ready for him is almost as outrageous as thinking Zuko would be happy serving tea to Earth Kingdom nobles for the rest of his life.

And the worst part is that it’s not like Sokka even *wanted* that of Zuko, not really. It’s just… what they never bothered to question, lest it upset the careful balance that let them see each other. What would have happened if Sokka actually asked, genuinely and without the pressure of ongoing battle around them, for Zuko to join them? Would Zuko still have been held back by all the things weighing him down in the North? Or would it be different now?

Does it even matter, if Sokka was too scared to find out?

Sokka curls onto his side, tugging his pillow to his chest and then immediately shoving it away as a poor substitute. He could chase down hypotheticals and suppositions for the rest of his life. None of them ever felt particularly urgent when Zuko was only an afternoon away, but now that Zuko’s out in the world again, location unknown, the things Sokka *doesn’t* know are clamoring louder than the things he does.

There are so many bits and pieces and half-known half-inferred things that sketch out a version of the truth that Sokka feels more in his heart and his gut than in his head. And Katara seems so sure, and Aang doesn’t refute her story when if he seems apologetic about it, and Sokka doesn’t quite trust his own intuition and instincts like he did before Ba Sing Se fell for those things alone to be enough.

Which is a problem, because Sokka can’t feel sure, but he also can’t make a Zuko who could do that—who could deliberately seduce Sokka while plotting with his sister to capture Sokka’s friend—make sense alongside the Zuko who can’t even insist he’s fine without giving away the lie. And even if Zuko *could*, it feels like a knife to the gut to think that he *would*. That the Zuko who missed an ostrich horse so much he never spoke about her, who has unreasonably strong opinions about local theater, who wrote back before he ever knew who he was writing to, would smile all shy and flustered at Sokka while planting a knife in his back.

Fuck. Sokka could twist in these tangled thoughts forever if he lets himself, because there are just too many unknowns. He and Zuko both mutually skirted around one too many things, together avoided thinking too far ahead, for Sokka to feel the kind of conviction he needs to refute Katara with anything other than his own need for her to be wrong. Maybe that’s why it cuts so precisely, this time, when Katara and Toph and Aang doubt. Because Sokka is just as guilty in creating this situation as Zuko is.

Sokka could hypothetical himself to death, so with a soundless groan he picks up all the potential reasons *why* and tosses them aside to focus just on the *what*. What did Sokka observe. What are the incontrovertible things Sokka knows occurred, the ones he can line up and examine, because one thing he is still sure of is that when it comes to Zuko, actions always speak more clearly than words, anyway.

Zuko made Sokka happy—not passively, but actively and attentively and honestly a little too determinedly, sometimes. He trained with Sokka, made him a more effective fighter. He let Sokka see him asleep and defenseless, let Sokka share the same orbit as Iroh. Zuko made himself vulnerable to Sokka in so many ways, over and over, and treated everything Sokka offered like it was something to cherish.

And somehow in the chaos of Ba Sing Se’s fall, Zuko went from escaping Azula’s trap to fighting alongside side her. Somehow Zuko found himself with an opportunity to turn the tide of the war, even if it was just in one city, and turned it in a direction Sokka doesn’t understand. Somehow Zuko chose to pit himself against Aang and then Katara, and made a point to give Katara a message to bring to Sokka so that Sokka would know that what Zuko was doing was part of a larger plan, was something *intentional*, something goal-driven*.*

Maybe. That last bit is more like a hope, than a fact.

Still, Sokka could rely on all that that, if it were just Zuko doing those things. The scientist in him could be content with the volume of observations on the ‘probably at the very least still a pseudo-good guy’ side of things. But it’s not *just* Zuko, is the problem. It’s also Azula. And believing that Zuko has a plan, and that Sokka won’t entirely hate the outcome of it, is one thing—Sokka has months of history and observation to fall back on for that. But relying on anything involving Azula? All Sokka has to work from is the hazy idea that Zuko might feel some sense of loyalty or familial duty toward her, woven in with a healthy dose of trepidation and a heap of anxiety.

Azula might be the biggest ‘what if’ in this whole thing, one that Sokka doesn’t know he can set aside because he just doesn’t know enough about her, plain and simple. He doesn’t even know if she’s part of Zuko’s plan, or acting against it, or fuck, if she’s the one leading it. Sokka doesn’t know if she’s an active antagonist or just a passive opponent if they get in her way, and he doesn’t know if there will ever be a way to make himself comfortable with how much uncertainty that introduces into…everything, really.

But can Azula’s mere existence really be enough to tip Zuko from ‘pseudo-good guy’ to ‘astonishingly manipulative Fire Nation imperialist?’ Or can Sokka stack enough in Zuko’s favor—in his *own* favor—to allow himself to hold onto a tentative kind of faith, at least until new facts come into play.

Sokka will have to shore up the walls around the fragile flames of that faith strong, to proceed with caution and not suspicion in the face of all he doesn’t know and all that everyone else seems so sure is true. He’s going to have to build those walls tall and deep with every soft memory and shy smile and incontrovertible fact of Zuko’s care as shelter against the onslaught of conjecture and speculation from his own anxious thoughts, the hypotheses he has no means of testing.

It could be disastrous if Sokka bets wrong. And he can’t help but wonder if this is how Zuko felt all those months in Ba Sing Se, knowing that Sokka was planning something to end the war, which meant something against the Fire Nation, but never knowing what.

## Chapter 2: Where It All Began

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular chapter warnings for this one!

### Text

When Zuko was ten years old, he woke from a nightmare to find that it had become real. The dark shadows of night were gone, Agni’s gaze was sharp upon his skin, but his mother wasn’t at breakfast, his grandfather’s rigid firebending wasn’t wrapped around the torches in the family wing, and suddenly Zuko was ‘Your Highness’ not ‘Your Grace.’ Overnight, he’d risen in Agni’s eyes, which meant that overnight, so many others had fallen.

Zuko fixed himself into a perfect seiza so the muscle memory would stop the trembling that no one, and especially not servants, could be allowed to see, and fixed his face to blankness because he gave up years ago on anything like Azula’s cool disinterest. When Father summoned them to the throne room instead of his office, Zuko’s steps were as steady as Azula’s, his breathing matched to hers as he listened to the Fire Lord explain from behind a curtain of freshly lit flame how the world would be now.

Zuko stood at his sister’s side and knew with a piercing kind of clarity that things would never be the same ever again, that more had changed than just half his family—more, maybe, Uncle Iroh was *gone* with that extra emphasis to the word that meant more than Zuko could figure out—disappearing in the space of a night.

Nearly seven years later, standing at his sister’s side again, it feels pretty much the same. Though this time, Zuko worries that he could be the only one who realizes just how much things have changed outside of Agni’s watchful eye.

&#45;-

The vibration of steps through the steel deck shifts in a way that means someone is peeling away from the usual flow of traffic toward Zuko, and he’s so at the edge of his control being back on a ship, being back on the water, that he has nothing left for stopping himself from snapping up and toward the threat of someone at his back.

The servant flinches from the movement, barely visible before regaining his bland composure, which…doesn’t feel good but is probably deserved, considering who else is on the ship. “My sincere apologies for interrupting your mediation,” the man murmurs, gaze fixed somewhere around Zuko’s boots. “Her Highness sends her regards on this—auspicious day.”

Zuko wants to laugh at that. No one enjoys the shortest day of the year, when Agni is most absent from the world and her touch is weakest in a firebender's blood.

The man’s eyes flicker up when Zuko doesn’t reply. “The Lightning Princess requests your presence at the breakfast table, if it pleases you.”

Zuko mulls over the titles there. Is ‘Lightning Princess’ what they’re calling her these days, then? Or is it just what they’ve started using as they all mutually dance around the fact that no one is quite sure what to call Zuko. He was never formally removed from his position as Crown Prince, but everyone knows that Crown Princes don’t generally come back from indefinite exile.

Zuko glances up to see the man still there, unmoving in his half-bow. The “Thanks” Zuko offers is belated, as is the realization that ‘thanks’ isn’t what he was supposed to say. The man stares a moment before catching himself meeting the eyes of one of Agni’s line and hastily redirecting his gaze back to the deck, backing away with the bit too much haste of someone politely trying to avoid something unpleasant.

Zuko sighs, watching him go. He’s going to need to remember how to act, the motions of deference and authority that let everyone believe that the system is working the way it should. Or maybe Zuko can get away with having acquired a few quirky eccentricities in his travels, if he can manage to stop being so visibly jumpy about it…

And Zuko is stalling, which is also not something a Child of Agni does, regardless of their position in the line of succession. Azula’s request wasn’t actually a question, and he is aware he wouldn’t be able to get away with not making an appearance today of all days anyway. He checks the line of his armor—the weight is a familiar comfort, even if he keeps trying to move in ways it doesn’t allow—and resettles the visible weapons on his back and the much less decorative ones concealed at his wrists and boot. Zuko needs to seem like a casual threat without seeming threatened, which is a fine line to walk depending on the audience and the venue and whether there will be chopsticks or forks on the table.

And he is stalling again, so Zuko stops fiddling with his dao—new ones, good ones, already in his room on the ship when he came on board. Zuko had stared at them for a long time, that first night—and sets out to join the others in the more public areas of the ship.

He’s cautiously surprised to see that it’s just Azula at the pretentious little table at the front of the ship, cutting quite the…not exactly jarring, but notable figure in her precise armor against the delicate chairs. The whole setup is more delicate and fussy than her typical style, but then it’s visible to the entire deck, practically a stage for her to tug strings on. That part is how she likes it.

“Where are Mai and Ty Lee,” Zuko asks, glancing automatically to the east. It’s well past sunrise, and even with the days so short at this longitude it's firmly within the realm of mid-morning.

Azula waves the question away with a flick of her fingers. “Congratulations, Brother, on reaching seventeen.”

Zuko grunts as he takes his seat, eyeing the shocking amount of food managing to fit on such a small table. It’s an almost overwhelming amount to choose from after so long with so little. Maybe he should just do what Sokka would do and eat everything.

“It wasn’t looking so good for a while there,” she adds, sounding more interested in daintily selecting a jam-filled pastry without getting filling on her fingers. “I didn’t think you would manage it.”

Neither did Zuko. “What did you do for Mai’s birthday?” That would have been the most recent one, and Ty Lee always insisted on sticking to a theme for the year. It had left him plenty of time to prepare to endure whatever was coming, and he can only hope that she’ll be more restrained given they’re at still sea. Zuko didn’t think anything could make him appreciate being back on the water, but he can silently thank Agni that he can dodge the travesty of whatever would have happened in Caldera if the ocean currents were more in their favor.

Azula hums, shrugging and neatly breaking off a bite of pastry. “You’ll have to ask her.”

Zuko pauses halfway through reaching for a plain-looking rice cake. “What?”

Another careless shrug, her face flickering with boredom. “I haven’t seen Mai and Ty Lee in years, Brother, before a few months ago. She would have been in Omashu for her birthday, I suppose, so probably some horrid Earth Kingdom thing.”

It’s dangerous to reveal so much ignorance by staring so long, but Zuko can’t drag his eyes away from her face, searching for any hint of a reaction. “…Oh.”

Azula’s tawny gaze flashes with annoyance before she makes a show of finding an imperfection in her pastry and examining the offending piece of crust. Zuko jerks his eyes away, looking out over the deck instead and trying to rapidly figure out when, exactly, their absence would have occurred. Azula never mentioned it in her letters—not that she would have—but…Zuko can guess now that he knows. Fuck.

As if summoned by his thoughts, Zuko’s gaze catches on a familiar pair of pink and black figures as Mai and Ty Lee finally make their way out onto deck. Azula must have purposefully timed it for Zuko to be at the table first, and he swallows back his anger and turns back to the food, unsurprised to find Azula watching him.

“I have something for you, Brother,” Azula calls when Mai and Ty Lee are close enough to hear, and Zuko’s chest begins to thrum with adrenaline as he catches the way Azula’s expression is already starting to curl around the edges with self-satisfaction.

Zuko carefully finishes his bite, wary of the sudden theater and anything that makes her look like that. “What is it?”

“Really, Zuzu, so suspicious,” Azula chides. “It’s a gift, to mark this auspicious occasion.”

“Stop saying that,” Zuko mutters. *Auspicious*, when everyone knows the words used up until seventeen years ago would have been ill-omened, unfortunate, unlucky. When Zuko and Azula both know those are the words still used when Zuko isn’t in anyone’s line of sight, and sometimes when he is.

“But it’s your special day,” Ty Lee chirps as she joins them, completely earnest and thoroughly ignoring Mai’s put-upon sigh. “Everyone should know!”

Azula smiles, eyes flat, and beckons with an imperious wave that could put every Upper Ring aristocrat to tears. A servant hurries over, from behind Zuko of course, because it’s a surprise and because Azula would never turn down an opportunity to demonstrate her awareness of his weak spots. Zuko refuses to twist around and look, so he barely has a breath to hide his shock when the servant steps into view to deposit a messenger hawk on Azula’s armor-clad arm.

“I believe,” Azula says, stroking a gentle finger over Gao’s breast and holding him up so the sun makes his feathers shine, “That this belongs to you.”

“…Yes,” Zuko manages, clearing his throat and barely keeping himself from gaping. “He does.” Gao would have been trained to go back, that’s not entirely unexpected. But here? She *brought* him?

“Then aren’t you lucky that I was there for him to find, Zuzu?” Her eyes are remarkably similar to Gao’s unblinking stare. “Best not lose sight of him again.”

“No,” Zuko agrees, finally reaching over to take the offered hawk, something in his chest lurching at the familiar weight. Agni, only Azula would gift a means of extended, low-level psychological torture on a birthday. Does she even know she's doing it? Fuck, can he afford to risk that she doesn't? “I guess I better not.”

&#45;-

Zuko’s body remembers how to be on a ship even if his mind is still unused to being so constantly around this many people. It’s not the same as in the teashop. He had to deal with crowds all day, sure, but there he could retreat to the back, hold distance between himself and the patrons in the form of the counter or an order pad, could withhold eye contact unless he wanted to give it. He was supposed to be invisible.

Here he’s supposed to be seen, distant and on display and untouchable in a whole different way, constantly in front of an *audience*. And if Zuko doesn’t get with the picture quick, doesn’t learn how to deal with this, it’s going to be an even bigger problem in the palace.

Zuko isn’t unused to forcing himself to endure unpleasant things. He knows how to do that. It would be easier now, though, if he wasn’t also having to remind himself that the feeling of numb limbs, of biting cold, is only in his head. If the weight of armor didn’t feel like a danger instead of a comfort, if the sound of feet moving across metal decking didn’t slide so easily into the sound of metal rending.

Zuko might think this whole journey back to Caldera was designed specifically to get into his head if he wasn’t also tightly aware of Azula’s eyes always on him, narrowed and assessing as she drums her nails against the metal tabletop, as she pours tea, as she lingers over the growing circles beneath his eyes from yet another sleepless night.

Zuko *tries*, he might not be used to any of this anymore but that doesn’t mean he’s forgotten how to reach for the shields of anger and armor and regulation and etiquette. But those weren’t his only old habits, and it’s a constant temptation to seek out a quiet corner of the ship when things start to feel like too much. This cruiser might be three times bigger and five generations newer than the *Wani*, but Fire Nation standardization means it follows the same basic design. Zuko knows exactly where to go looking for a place to not be found.

Zuko is forcing himself through pure determination and will to meditate to the rhythm of waves against the hull—he doesn’t feel like he’s going to vomit from the sound of it anymore, and he’s been able to close his eyes for days now, and he *will* get this back—when he feels a body of heat at his back. His ever-extended heat sense wraps around it, and it’s not a firebender, which leaves just about everyone else. But there are only so many people who would seek him out with quite so much surety of where to look.

His scowl is already firmly in place as Mai turns the corner. She looks as unimpressed by it as ever.

“Hiding away again?” She asks, disinterested as she takes in the corner of the ship Zuko found for himself, with its low visibility from most of the deck and access to the railing that theoretically should be all the assurance he needs against slipping into the water.

“I’m not hiding.” He’s just…trying to be by himself. And not be found.

“Sure.”

He glares, feeling himself already edging toward the border of hostility. “What do you want?”

She gives him a bland stare. “Azula is going to come looking for you if you keep hiding.”

Zuko grunts. She isn’t wrong. “So you’re her messenger now?”

Mai gives the shadow of a shrug, glancing vaguely over the water, hands hidden in her sleeves in a way that Zuko is sure still means she is playing with her knives, and that bit of normalcy, that bit of enduring sameness, is enough for his inner fire to spark against his frustration.

“That must be a change,” he bites out, his fire crawling through his veins when Mai glances over, head tilted in the equivalent of a surprised question, and he sees that that is unchanged, too. “Caring about what she wants again.”

“Ugh,” Mai mutters, flicking her own glare his way. “Not you too. You don’t know how it was, Zuko. You weren’t there.”

“And apparently neither were you.”

Her pale brown eyes finally snap up to his face. “Do you think I had a choice about it?”

Zuko nearly barks out a laugh at that. “There’s always a choice,” he says, tasting the bitterness of the words as his inner flame twists around the kinds of choices they all had to make—that Azula would have made for them—that resulted in this.

“Oh, Zuko,” Mai sighs, shaking her head and turning back to the water. “Keep telling yourself that if it makes you feel better.”

Zuko opens his mouth to snap out a reply, then hesitates as he takes in the fixed avoidance of her posture. He can recognize that as easily on someone else as on himself, and he isn’t in the mood to waste his breath today when it’s still so hard to consistently come by on this ship.

“Don’t hide too long Azula comes looking,” Zuko finally says, words quiet as he moves past her to make his way back toward the public parts of the ship. He doesn’t want to get into this when there are still so many unknowns, when both of them being gone might send Azula hunting. Better to leave Mai to hide away until she builds back her composure and go find Azula before she decides to find him, and give himself time to settle before he burns down another bridge on her behalf.

&#45;-

“Agni’s *balls*,” Zuko breathes, the words tripping out in his shock.

“Really, Zuzu,” Azula says as she steps up to the railing, taking in the fanfare laid out before them as they come into port. And this is just for the *docking*. Fuck, what is Caldera going to be like? “You sound like a cheap dockside whore.”

Zuko flicks her a habitually annoyed glance. “Have a lot of experience with those?”

“Oh, tons!” Ty Li enthuses as she skips over. “Such interesting people, their auras are so vibrant.” Azula looks faintly pained. “And they have the best information!”

…Yes, they do, don’t they. Zuko eyes Azula again, wondering what exactly this says about their upbringing. She notices his interest and waves it away with a huff. “Clean it up, Brother,” she snaps, redirecting the focus back toward him. “We wouldn’t want Father to think your tastes have grown…uncouth.”

Zuko lets the comment pass with only a quick flare of warning. “I doubt he’ll think much of anything about me,” he says, eyeing the tapestries and hanging of the eternal flame suddenly unfurling around the port in impressive synchronization.

“Oh, Zuzu.” Azula gives him a sharp, glittering smile. “I’m sure he can’t wait to see you again.”

&#45;-

Zuko can’t bring himself to leave his cabin. What little he had in here is already packed up and whisked away, and he thought he might actually come to blows for a moment with a servant over holding onto his swords and the packet of tea leaves tucked into his armor, his inner fire keyed up and tight enough to snap.

He's breathing deep, braced against the desk, trying to settle himself, center himself, anything himself for what’s coming. He can’t go out there like this, with his composure so visibly fractured, but Agni, he is hyperaware of the odd way his new armor sits—in that it fits, for the first time in…well, four years—and the tension of his hair pulled up into a topknot again, the stiffness of his new boots. Everything feels simultaneously exactly the same and entirely different, and none of it feels *right*, which Zuko expected, braced himself for, but still. It would have been nice if at least some things didn’t feel that way.

“You’ll be fine.”

Zuko glances up into the mirror to see Mai standing in the doorway. He’s slipping, not to have noticed her hovering there, but then he’s had to pull his heat sense in so much more than he’s used to with so many servants and soldiers always scurrying around and Azula’s grip stretched over every flame on the ship. “Has anything changed?”

“I don’t know. I wasn’t there,” she reminds him, with what could be a bare hint of rebuke, or maybe sadness.

Zuko straightens with a sigh, reaching up to run a hand through his hair before remembering that he can’t do that anymore. “*I’ve* changed.” It feels dangerous to say out loud, even though they all have to know it.

Mai flicks the words away. “Don’t worry about it, Zuko. That's never helped anyone.”

No, Zuko supposes. It never did, did it? But it feels just as impossible to stop now as it did back then. Harder, even, now that he has so much more to worry about, and understands so much more clearly all the ways it can go wrong.

&#45;-

“Stop fidgeting,” Azula hisses.

“I’m *not—”*

“You’re wiggling like a toddler with a spider snake down its pants.” That’s…a horrifying image. “Stand. Still.”

Zuko glares, but takes a deep breath and locks himself into a military precise parade rest to match Azula’s, just a heartbeat before the arching, ornate doors sweep open. He turns sharply on his heel in time with Azula—old habits die hard—to greet Lo and Li as they make their stately way into the antechamber. The twins are somehow even more bent and wizened than before, but their eyes are as sharp and expressions as pinched as Zuko remembers.

“Your Highness—es.” Lo adds the plural with a deliberate, judgmental flick of her eyes that somehow seems to take in Zuko’s entire being and find him thoroughly lacking.

Azula bends her head in the barest of acknowledgments to her two longest-lasting firebending mentors. “You will be announcing the victory?”

“Yes, Princess,” Li says with her own withering dismissal for Zuko. “And Prince.”

“Good.” Azula settles back onto her heels, allowing herself the shadow of a smile. “Proceed, then.”

Lo and Li nod, as if they needed the instruction, and walk past through the towering glass doors onto the raised terrace. A roar of excited cheering greets them from the crowd gathered below and Zuko lets out a breath he didn’t realize he was holding. It’s not good that he’s feeling this distinctly picked apart with just a few looks, even if the twins have always had a particular talent for finding problems, and a particularly low tolerance for anything less than perfection.

Zuko has never been their favorite person. But he wonders what they see when they look at him now. He didn’t think anything would grant him that title until the Fire Lord used it publicly first.

“Relaxing already, Zuzu?” Azula is facing the terrace now, breathing deep like the roar of the crowd and Lo and Li’s ringing narration is feeding her energy and life. “Do try to remember that you aren’t some teashop drudge anymore.”

As if he could ever forget.

“You need to impress the peasants, not take orders from them.” She pauses before she steps out on her cue, letting the anticipation outside build as she rakes him with her own scathing glance. “Though I suppose you have a talent for both, these days.”

Zuko scowls after her before smoothing out his face and brushing aside her barbs to listen for his own cue to step forward. He hovers on the edge of daylight and shadow, Agni’s touch just across his boots, the blaze of the ceremonial fire tugging him ahead as he finally steps forward.

The crowd cheers at the sight of him, a sound Zuko honestly never expected to hear again, at least not full of adulation instead of some gleeful anticipation over his pending execution. Hearing it does things to his inner flame that he can’t entirely articulate, and he is…grateful, almost, for Azula’s sharp-edged constancy at his side as the screaming washes over him.

&#45;-

They’re set loose in the palace afterward with the kind of casual disregard for their whereabouts that Zuko’s entirely comfortable and familiar with.

Zuko wanders around his old rooms to start, wondering how fast the servants had to work to air out the linens and clean off the dust, or if the space is always kept as if he could return at any moment. He runs his fingers over dressers that are shorter than they used to be, crosses the width of the room in fewer strides than it used to take, tests whether he can still curl up in the window seat that’s smaller than he remembers, looks at the expanse of the bed that used to be so huge and now…actually, it’s still huge, and after so long sleeping on futons and berths and on the ground, Zuko can’t quite wrap his head around how excessively large it is.

He’s tempted to flop down and see if the mattress is as soft, the sheets as silky, as he remembers. Maybe just hide his face in the pillows and see if they can still muffle a scream as well as they used to. He can do that later, though. He’s far too restless for anything so still, and he can’t afford to let go of the tense, taut feeling of his inner flame, not when being left so suddenly to his own devices after weeks of being under someone else’s eye has made him so acutely aware that it’s only his own determination giving him anything solid to stand on.

But it doesn’t take Zuko all that long to run out of places to explore between the bedroom and sitting room and washroom, and it doesn’t take him much longer to decide that he can’t stay cooped up in here just waiting for whatever is coming next. Which means he better be allowed to leave.

Zuko braces himself for the possibility of finding out otherwise, straightening his spine and pulling on his scowl and checking his hair and striding into the hallway, relying on almost entirely on bravado and nearly dropping the facade when the guards barely react. Something in Zuko relaxes a little at that, the scales tipping even closer toward ‘not an elaborate plot to capture him as a prisoner,’ even as another part of him notes the danger and opportunity in that kind of laxness.

Zuko doesn’t want to read too much into every little thing, but, well—it’s Caldera. A person doesn’t forget thirteen years of habits, even if none of them feel entirely instinctive anymore.

Zuko wanders familiar corridors, reacclimating to dark stone and deep shadow and torches and torches and torches. He reaches out with his fire sense to brush against them, not trying to hold or wrest control of any yet, just noting where the Fire Lords’ control begins to cede to Azula’s tight grip and then to the half-remembered rhythm of generals and ministers the further he gets from the Inner Palace. It’s a show of power, like everything is, and Zuko can’t afford to sit back too long. But he doesn’t want to disrupt that always-delicate balance before he’s sure of his own standing.
