It’s no surprise where his feet eventually take him, stone giving way to manicured grass and bright sunshine and the barely-there lapping of waves and the soft sounds of turtle ducks. It’s winter, which means this year’s hatchlings are almost ready to set out on their own, if they'll go at all. It used to be such a sad time for him, to see them leave, with such bright moments of joy when one sometimes decided to stay. Zuko wonders if he’ll be around to see the next generation hatch.

The whole garden is just as he remembered, from the landscaping to the benches, right down to the dip at the base of the tree that Zuko always preferred to sit against. Zuko takes it all in with stinging eyes, not sure if it all makes him want to cry from happiness or something else entirely. Settling down here, heedless of the potential for grass and dirt on his formal robes, the quiet lapping of water nothing like the ocean, feels the closest to coming home that Zuko has felt in…a long time.

Azula finds him there when Agni has started his descent toward the horizon, steps sure and confident as she comes up on his left side. She doesn’t say anything, crossing her arms and gazing at the bathing turtle ducks that begin to wander closer in hopes of bread. Does she find it as grounding to be here as he does? Or is it something else entirely for her, more a goad than a place of welcome?

The turtle ducks eventually give up on food to paddle back into the reeds, and like that’s its own signal, Zuko and Azula finally stir.

“Are you ready?”

A sideways look. “Best not to keep Father waiting.” Which isn’t an answer, and they both know it.

“No, we wouldn’t want to disappoint him, would we?”

A beat of silence, and then a snort of so-dry-it's-barely-there amusement before they both head back for the palace.

&#45;-

Zuko kneels before his Father again in a hall of flames and is miraculously able to fold himself smoothly into a full dogeza. Out of the corner of his eye he can see Azula’s fingers twitch on her lap, which might as well be a shout of surprise. He holds the bow for the requisite number of degrees, the stone fire-warm against his forehead, before settling back into seiza, all without letting out a single hint of how close he actually is to completely losing his shit.

The Fire Lord’s control is on full display here in what is meant to be the seat of his power, in the curtain of fire and the ceremonial braziers and the torches circling the room. His bending keeps the flames stoked oppressively hot, keeps the fire feeling hostile, ravenous. Zuko wants to pull his fire sense in tight to avoid touching it, and he grits his teeth and forces himself to reach out wider. Such a retreat would be an irrecoverable weakness, now, and impossible to hide.

“Azula tells me that you acquitted yourself well in battle.” Ozai’s voice hasn’t changed a bit, and Zuko forces his inner flame to spiral out instead of in. “That you were truly ferocious and unwavering in battle.” It sounds like he’s picking the words carefully, like the praise doesn’t sit naturally on his tongue, at least not in proximity to Zuko.

Zuko doesn’t react, doesn’t reply, because none of that is a question.

“She tells me that you killed the Avatar with your own hand, Prince Zuko. That when the time came you were the one to strike the fatal blow and that you did so without hesitation.”

The only reason Zuko doesn’t break and glance toward Azula is because he can’t bring himself to take his eyes off the Fire Lord. Azula said *what*? Fuck, it’s a good thing Zuko doesn’t hold any of the flames in this room because his heart is *pounding* and there’d be no way to hide it, so hard it must be visible in the hollow of his throat. Praise Agni that the fashions are still for high, formal collars.

“I am…proud of you,” Ozai says, smiling, magnanimous behind his wring of fire. “Well done, Prince Zuko.”

“Thank you, Father,” Zuko murmurs, bowing low again, attention split between the Fire Lord in front of him and Azula at his side, steady and unbothered and unbowed as ever.

Agni's balls, she could have fucking *warned* him. But then, Azula doesn’t exactly believe in advance notice before a test, and Zuko needs to get used to that sooner rather than later. He wouldn’t be worthy of the warning if he couldn’t’ get by without it, in her eyes. Anyone who needs to prepare in advance isn’t suited to walk the same halls as she is, to take a place at the Fire Lord’s side, to set themselves between the gears of war and the innocent once again and hope to come out marginally intact on the other side.

## Chapter 3: Now and Then

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular warnings for this one!

### Text

Sokka is absolutely working on his own hand-eye coordination and dexterity, and that is the story he will maintain regardless of how much it might look like he is just desperately trying to keep his morning snack of dried berries from being snatched from his hands on the way to his mouth. Momo is small, quick, and has a much longer reach than he seems like he should for something that can curl up all deceptive and cute like that.

Sokka might be succeeding a bit more often than not if he weren’t keeping at least one whole corner of his eye on Katara and Aang the entire time. They’re working together at the head of Appa’s saddle, flowing through bending forms to hold the clouds in a convenient covering pattern around Appa’s bulk. It’s early in the day and Sokka can already feel the rising heat, can see the extra strain the sun above them puts on the pair to hold onto the cloud cover, even with the humidity of the tropical climate below them.

They’re only a few days into this infiltration journey and honestly, Sokka is worried that being the lone cloud in the sky moving against the wind isn’t going to be worth exhausting two-thirds of their benders by the time they arrive at the rendezvous point.

Sokka feels little paws suddenly patter against his shoulders and sighs as Momo snatches his last bite. “What do you think, buddy,” he asks, grabbing up the lemur, who is perfectly content to be cuddled now that there’s no food on the line. “Say something to them for me?”

Momo pauses in his chewing, cocking his head before rocketing out of Sokka’s lap by way of his face to make for the far end of Appa’s saddle.

“Guess you’re going to have to do it all yourself, Snoozles,” Toph says, tossing one of her own dried berries into her mouth with a smirk.

Sokka eyes her non-Momo depleted stash and sighs, resigning himself to a hungry morning of plotting his post-lunch break intervention.

&#45;-

“It’s fine,” Katara exclaims. “I’m fine! We’re both fine! I don’t need to stop, I’m not even tired yet!”

Sokka eyes her sweat-covered brow and the damp collar of her dress.

“It’s from the heat! Water Tribe clothes aren’t made for this!”

“That’s another thing,” Sokka sighs, switching tactics. “Maybe we should just…try to blend in a bit?” He ignores Aang’s frown and waves vaguely toward his own sweat-soaked summer-weight Water Tribe tunic, which is still far too much for this travesty of a Fire Nation winter.

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” Toph drawls. “You all look great to me.”

“We only need to blend in if we’re going to be seen,” Katara points out.

“And we won’t be seen if we keep hiding on Appa in the clouds,” Aang finishes.

“Or—or—just consider—” Sokka wraps an arm around Aang’s shoulder, throwing out his other hand in front of them like he can paint a picture to match his words. “—traveling by night and looking like the locals. Don’t say no yet!” He hurries to add. “Just think about it. Just let it sit until it starts to feel good.”

“But moving on foot?” Katara frowns. “It’s a bunch of islands.”

“Which means we can’t just—” Sokka flails a little to try to describe their usual tactics. “— chaos off into the distance if something goes wrong.”

“Mobility is important,” Aang allows, but he says it while eyeing Appa the way someone eyes a nice pile of gold.

Sokka sighs. “Can we at least agree that some disguises would be good?” He’s willing to concede modes and times of travel, but only if they don’t blatantly look like they don’t belong.

“Fine,” Katara huffs. “But! I am *not* getting an elaborate backstory, Sokka. So help me Tui and La, if you try to spend the rest of this trip quizzing me about what fruits I prefer for breakfast and my fictional past—”

“It’s not fictional if you feel it in your heart! You can’t just *wear* your disguise you have to *become* your disguise!” Amateurs, the lot of them. Sokka will show them how it’s done.

&#45;-

They wait until dark for the raid—

“It’s just taking clothes from a line, Sokka.”

“It’s a *raid* in enemy territory, Katara.”

They wait in the dark for the *raid* to minimize the chance of being seen. Aang suggests early morning and Katara noon when the sun is at its hottest and Toph says she doesn’t see how it makes a difference either way. But Sokka points out firebender circadian rhythms and climate acclimatization and tries to articulate the advantages of the cover of darkness to someone who’s never known anything else and manages to make his case. Plus, there’s a pond they can paddle in like the old days, so really, it’s not all that hard to convince the others to wait for dusk.

“You’re good to make the fog on your own?” Sokka checks as they crouch at the tree line, slowly scanning for anyone still outside. It should only be a few more minutes now before it’s safe to go.

“After the clouds?” Katara snaps her wrist and mist begins to coalesce around her. “No problem.”

“And we all know how we’re going to get in and out?”

“Straight in, straight out the other side,” Aang rattles off. “And make sure Toph is actually concealed when we hide.”

“Good.”

“Do we really need to steal, though?” Katara sighs, and Sokka barely holds back a groan. He knew it was coming, but really, to wait until *now*? “I know we *can*, but—they’re probably just normal people, not like—”

“High-risk traders?”

“I doubt they’re *pirates*, Sokka,” she snaps, mist turning cold as Aang suddenly takes up a careful contemplation of the darkening sky.

“…Are we expecting pirates?” Toph asks. “Because I think I missed that part of the plan.”

“Depends on your definition of a pirate, I supp—”

“What if we left some money behind in exchange,” Aang jumps in. “Then it won’t be stealing, it will just be, uh…”

“Forced capitalism?” Sokka offers, voice dry.

Toph looks intrigued by that idea. “Even if we wanted it, though, it’s not like we have any money. What are we going to do, leave Sokka’s boomerang behind for them to melt down?”

“*No*,” Sokka says, hugging his boomerang to his side. “We would never abandon Boomerang like that! He isn’t just some tool to be used!” He ignores Katara’s snort. “Besides, wouldn’t it be easier to just exchange the taro root?”

“…Why, though?” Katara asks into the silence.

Sokka blinks. “Because it’s an all-purpose staple that’s rare in the Fire Nation and will last for months?” Blank stares all around. “And besides, it's poisonous if you don’t process it the right way before eating it and we don’t have time to rig up a camping oven and I’m not trying to kill ourselves for it.” More blank stares. He hunches his shoulders up, fiddling restlessly with the cuffs he put on instead of his usual wrist wraps. “The worst they can do is resell it if they don’t want it.”

“That…is actually a good idea,” Toph finally says, sounding vaguely surprised in a way that Sokka thinks he should maybe be insulted about. “The latest harvests in the northern Earth Kingdom weren’t good, and with the kind of tariffs they’d be slapping on it in the Colonies, the resell value would be excellent for its weight and portability.” She throws a considering look in his general direction. “It’s a good trade.”

“Alright then,” Katara says, satisfied. “So we aren’t stealing then, we’re bartering.”

“Forced bartering,” Sokka mutters.

“Sounds like a plan,” she says brightly.

Zuko rises with the sun. He would say that he wakes up, except he didn’t sleep, because some things never change. When he was twelve, a Sage had suggested that Zuko’s trouble sleeping was a sign of Agni’s strength in his blood, that even when the world was dark Zuko could feel the pull of the sun.

That had been poorly received.

Zuko realizes as his bare feet hit the warm wooden floor that he could stay in bed even though he’s awake. There’s no shift in a teashop to get to, no meditation he will be expected to make an appearance at. He might be a ‘Highness’ again but he has no responsibilities yet, no expectations except the ones he’s given himself. He could hide away for a bit longer from all the little things that *have* changed in the time he’s been gone.

But Zuko doesn’t exactly relish the opportunity to sit in silence with his own thoughts any more than he already has, and his expectations for himself are not small things, to be set aside even for a morning.

He’s halfway through getting dressed when a maid comes in and Zuko almost lights her on fire in his shock, dropping his over robe to the ground in order to trip out an apology with his dry hands raised. He stops when that only seems to make her stammer her own apologies even faster, trying instead to help her gather up the fallen linens, and fuck, that’s the wrong move too as she squeaks and ducks down even closer to the floor.

Zuko gives it up with an anxious twist of his inner flame, escaping across the room to pull on his shirt while assuring her its fine, it’s *fine*, alright, thank you, no harm no foul, he’s fine, *no* he doesn’t need any help getting dressed.

He flees the room to the sound of her high, tight, overly loud breathing, acutely aware that that could have gone better. Every inch of his skin prickles with discomfort and it takes until he reaches the kitchens to stop hearing the sounds of her panic. Which is maybe why it takes him a heartbeat too long to register the way the flurry of movement around him slows to a halt, rippling out from his presence.

Zuko stutters to a stop, scanning the mix of tightly neutral and wide-eyed faces turned back toward him. Something in him sinks when he realizes that Chef Azumi is missing, then sinks even further as he registers the rising tide of fear around him, like a den of sparrow mice sensing an approaching cat owl.

Maybe he can wait until after training to eat breakfast.

Zuko beats a hasty retreat, more flustered than he wants to be by the time he reaches the training ground. Azula, Mai, and Ty Lee are already there—Mai looking as happy to be awake this early as ever—and something in him latches onto that one piece of familiarity as his inner fire churns over the way things have changed.

Azula casts him a critical glance, taking in his training attire and the lack of swords in his hands. “Will you be joining us? Or just gawping like a mountain bumpkin at his first puppet show in the city?”

Zuko rolls his eyes as Ty Lee snorts at Azula’s particular brand of…evocative description, wordlessly joining in the warmup beside her. It’s the same progressions they learned as children, Caldera Standard forms at their finest, and Zuko does his best to turn off his brain and ignore the glances he can feel flicking his way as they flow through the katas together. Azula is hawk-eyed on his form, Mai and Ty Lee curious, and the servants peeking from the shadowed palace walkways as the day truly begins. He wonders what they’ll have to say about the Fire Prince and the Lightning Princess sharing the same space again. Azula would already know, if he cared to reveal his interest.

They advance more and more quickly through progressively more difficult forms until Mai and Ty Lee finally break off to spar as Azula calls flames to her hands, Zuko a half-beat behind. They snap their way through the foundational sets, using the basic forms to center their breath control and focus before launching into the complex katas.

It…doesn’t feel great.

Zuko feels just a little bit off on nearly every step, like his fire is coming just a little too slow, too cool, too used to only expressing itself as heat. Azula is scathing in her critique—“Really, Zuzu, I’ve seen toddlers with more breath control than that”—and the more he grits his teeth and doesn’t react, the more biting she becomes.

She snorts when he lets himself fall out of a spinning fire whip because his center of balance just isn’t where it should be, where it was the last time he did this. “You’ve been too long without a Master, Brother,” she says, raking him a disgusted look, her unspoken condemnation of Uncle’s capabilities clear.

“They were a little thin on the ground in the Earth Kingdom,” Zuko snaps, even though engaging with her when she’s in a mood like this is nearly always a mistake.

“Excuses,” she says, unimpressed. “Fix yourself, Zuko. If you let every growth spurt ruin your form, then you aren’t fit to call yourself a firebender.”

Zuko glares but bites his tongue until he tastes copper and throws himself back into the foundational sets. She’s right, is the worst part—she’s always right, is the truly worst part. Zuko’s gone too long with just himself to guide his form, too long since he honestly even tried to hold himself to Caldera Standard technique. He let himself get sloppy, let his discipline become shallow when he should have been digging in deepest. His inner fire is far too wild around the edges for this anymore, mere months of laxness eroding sixteen years of training until his flames come out just a hair too wide or short or overstretched or just… wrong. And blindingly noticeable next to Azula’s perfection.

Zuko wonders if he really could have expected any other omen than being back to the basics again, for his first sunrise back in Caldera.

In retrospect, Sokka didn’t actually need a trip into a larger town for supplies that couldn’t be stolen off a laundry line to realize that the others are terrible at blending in. Toph is fine for all that she can’t do anything but stand out—her brand of brash disregard for authority or opinion knows no national boundaries. But Katara and Aang are…distinctly not Fire Nation. Aang is running around using archaic slang and displaying an unreasonable level of curiosity for someone who nominally grew up at least occasionally in this environment, and Katara’s approach to haggling and Spirits, even her *hair*, are drawing its own kind of attention.

And Sokka himself is still too much in the mode of their early days in the Earth Kingdom, maybe, when they could waltz in and out of villages, always secure in their ability to just run away from any problems. But trying to infiltrate to the heart of the Fire Nation unseen as a pack of non-fire benders? They might need more subtlety than is their usual style—they can only attribute so much weirdness to being Colonists before the façade starts to wear thin.

Sokka jumps at the first largely inconspicuous opportunity to round them all up, shoving Toph and Katara into a private-enough alley and hauling Aang away from his attempt to ask “my good hotman” about his slippers.

“So,” Sokka says, looking around the little circle. “Let’s have a mid-plan redirect.”

“Why?” Katara frowns. “We’re working through the shopping list, right?”

“Yes,” Sokka allows. “But we’re being rather…obvious.”

“What do you mean?” Aang asks, as if he shouldn’t change his name right now to Primary Offender.

“You guys are standing out.”

“Well, so are you,” Katara challenges. “People are looking at all of us.”

“Yes,” Sokka agrees easily. “I stand out because it’s a small town and I’m a stranger. Not because I don’t know how to function in society.”

Toph lets out a cackle as Aang makes a noise of outrage. “*What*?”

“Fire Nation society,” Sokka clarifies. “Specifically.”

“I’m the expert here,” Aang protests. “Maybe the rest of you don’t know how to act, but I do!”

Sokka can’t stop his own surprised laughter. “Uh—excuse me?”

“I’m the only one who’s *been* to the Fire Nation before.”

“Yeah,” Toph snorts. “Like, a hundred years ago.”

“Which is more recent than you,” Aang shoots back. “None of you have ever been in it before.”

Sokka rubs the back of his neck in lieu of having a wolf tail to tug on. “I mean, I’ve been in —”

“Stop!” Katara exclaims, slapping her hands over her ears. “Right now! Stop!”

“Wha—*Spirits*, Katara, *gross*, why do you make *everything* weird?” Sokka scrubs his hands over his face, barely suppressing the urge to dramatically retch. “I was *going* to say that I’ve been in *a Fire Nation ship*. As a *prisoner*.”

Toph is laughing so hard she can barely breathe, but she somehow manages to get the words out clearly enough between wheezing. “Sokka *does* have some more recent experience than you do, Twinkletoes. On a number of fronts.”

“Fine,” Aang agrees quickly, looking desperate to change the subject. Sokka is fine with that. His face is on fire, and any more of this and Zuko would be able to bend *him* and—fuck, now Katara’s in his head, too. “What are we supposed to do different, then?”

&#45;-

Sokka is trying to explain the concept of public reserve and private passion to Katara in a way that won’t send her straight back to the gutter when he realizes that they’ve lost Aang.

“Where the—when—”

“About ten minutes ago,” Toph says casually. “When you were trying to find another word for ‘release.’”

“Spir—Agni’s balls.”

Katara and Toph both turn to him, Toph looking absolutely delighted, Katara horrified.

“What,” he shrugs, defensive. “It’s what Zuko always says. We need to sell the role.”

“With some kind of aristocratic curse?” Katara says skeptically.

“I…don’t actually think that’s where they come from,” Sokka says slowly, recalling the vaguely scandalized expression that crossed Iroh’s face every time Zuko said it in his hearing.

“’*They,’”* Toph echoes, sounding awed. “There are *more?”*

&#45;-

Zuko walks into the washroom and startles so hard to find servants already there that he nearly drops his towel.

“Agni’s bal—lessed form, what—” He stuffs the rest of his words back into his mouth. Fuck. At least there was no fire this time. At least he hadn’t undressed in his bedroom. The habits of communal bathing are still built too deep for that.

The three servants are frozen at his entrance, even though it’s *his* washroom, why *wouldn’t* he be here. They take quick, darting glances between the floor at his feet and the towel in his hand, something close to dread settling over their faces.

Oh, Zuko finally realizes. They think they failed to anticipate his needs. Which they did, but…Zuko doesn’t expect them to.

“You, ah—carry on?”

All three relax at that, thank Agni and anything else listening, the trio dipping into quick bows and a murmured rush of belated greetings. One of them—the oldest one, he thinks, though it’s hard to tell—takes a deep breath and risks a peek at his face. “Would His Highness like assistance bathing?”

“*No*,” Zuko bursts out, shocked and probably more vehement than he should be. Agni’s flaming cock, do they—shit, they’re all *young*, and objectively beautiful, and he hadn’t thought much of it but what the actual fuck, is this how things *are* when you’re no longer a child? Is this—what—is he even reading this right? It’s not like there’s been another royal even remotely near his age that he could ask, not since Lu Ten left.

“Of course, Your Highness,” the woman murmurs, bowing again like nothing is out of the ordinary in his refusal. “Would you care for us to tend to your hair, after?”

Zuko flicks a look toward the tub. “Uh.”

“In the refreshment chambers, of course,” she smoothly finishes. She hazards another glance up when Zuko still hesitates, voice suddenly edged with tentativeness. “Her Highness often enjoys it after training. Many people find it relaxing.”

“Ah…sure,” Zuko slowly agrees. If it’s a thing that people do…and if Azula is doing it, then it can’t be too suspicious. Relaxing *would* be nice.

&#45;-

It’s relaxing for no one.

The ‘refreshment chambers’ are exactly as Zuko remembers them, an extravagant room for washing hair and buffing nails. Looking at it now, though, Zuko feels vaguely embarrassed by the whole thing, especially as the attendants begin quietly mourning the state of his cuticles. Sokka would lose his mind over how much space is being devoted to this. It’s at least blessedly empty of anyone else, which is about the only good thing Zuko can say about it.

The women are all jumpy because Zuko is visibly tense, and everyone knows that if his tension breaks the fire will come first to the hands they’re trying to buff and smooth. He tries to loosen, but how is he supposed to relax with his hands in someone else’s hold and his head tipped back and his throat bared and so little line of sight on what, exactly, the three of them are doing. It should theoretically be comforting and familiar, the scalp massage and tutting over the state of his split ends, the gentle fingers carding through the strands.

Zuko can’t make his body believe that, though. No one has touched his hair except for himself and Sokka in four years, or Azula in those few instances she felt like driving home a point. Zuko doesn’t know how to accept this intimacy that he used to take so much for granted, the invasion of his personal space that he’s expected to not even notice—to welcome, really—because of his station.

He is aware, acutely, of the dramatic irony in finally clawing his way home only to find this waiting for him. It’s like he’s in a fucking Ember Island Players production.

&#45;-

“So just making sure I have this straight—you ditched us all and played hooky in order to *go* to school.” Toph sounds absolutely tickled.

“They thought I was skipping class!” Aang protests. “I couldn’t let them think that I don’t value a good education!”

“You aren’t enrolled, though,” Sokka says, pressing his fingers to his temples. Let’s just inconspicuously have their false names put down on some kind of official record. The Fire Nation doesn’t seem as hopped up on paperwork as the Earth Kingdom, but they certainly like it more than enough for Sokka’s comfort.

“Well, I couldn’t tell them that,” Aang says reasonably. “Then they’d want to know why.”

“Because we’re trying to be in *hiding*. *Disguised*. *Undercover.*”

“Well, my disguise is apparently a student. Running away would stand out more, right?”

Sokka scowls. He can’t argue with that. “What’s your name?”

“Kuzon,” Aang says immediately which…Sokka could have guessed.

“Where are you from?”

“The Colonies,” Aang says easily. “I recently immigrated with my family back to the homeland and I’m eager to learn.”

“Why is there a belt on your head?”

Toph lets out a burst of laughter and Katara blinks. “What?”

“Because I have an unsightly scar and I’m very self-conscious about it,” Aang says, sounding prim even as he throws on a pitiful look, eyes going wide and wounded, lip trembling just a little. Oh, that’s a nice touch.

Sokka narrows his eyes. “What’s your favorite schoolyard game?”

“Hide and explode,” Aang says. “We played it this afternoon. It was a big hit.”

“…Fine,” Sokka sighs, relenting. “It’s a waste of time, but your cover is decent if you keep your head down. Fine.”

“We can spend a day or two here,” Katara says, giving Sokka what he’s pretty sure is meant to be a soothing pat. “We have a lot of buffer in the timeline.”

“That we can’t just burn all at the beginning,” Sokka says, already feeling like he’s going to be repeating himself frequently. Shit.

“Not all of it,” Aang reassures him with a grin. “Just a bit!”

Sokka eyes that cheerful smile. “This isn’t going to be like when you tried to find an earthbending school, is it?”

Toph makes a disgusted noise in the back of her throat, not even bothering to voice an opinion of *that*.

“This will be different,” Aang says confidently. “And besides, you were just talking about blending in and understanding the culture and all that. Isn’t it valuable for someone else to know about the Fire Nation?”

Katara purses her lips, giving Sokka a half-apologetic look. “It *would* be good to have some perspective that doesn’t come from…”

“Sokka’s fun buddy?”

“*No,* Toph, I was going to say—”

“Probably the least generalizable experience in the entire Fire Nation?”

“Well, actually, I was thinking more—"

“An isolated rich kid?”

Aang opens his mouth, then closes it, scratching under his headband.

“What,” Toph shrugs. “I know it when I hear it.”

“Just…try not to stand out?” Sokka finally says, turning back to Aang and hearing his own words edge dangerously close to pleading.

“Flameo, hotman!”

&#45;-

“A *parent-teacher conference*,” Katara repeats, incredulous.

“There’s a note,” Aang mutters, digging it out of his pockets and kicking at the ground. “It’s in the afternoon.”

“Aang,” Katara says slowly. “We don’t *have* any parents.”

Too true. “Sounds like it’s time to leave,” Sokka says, already glancing around the cave and mentally inventorying their supplies. They can pack quickly. “They don’t expect us until tomorrow? If they think Aang’s already a troublemaker maybe they won’t care all that much that he’s gone.” That feels…very Fire Nation, to Sokka.

“But I don’t want to go yet!”

“Where are you going to get some adults from, Twinkletoes?” Toph asks.

“Well…” Aang puts on a winning smile. “*You* guys could be my parents.”

Sokka stares. “You want Katara and me to pretend to be your parents?” Aang shrugs, so Sokka tries again. “You want *Katara* to be your *mom*?”

Toph lets out a single shout of laughter, Aang flushing bright red as Katara frowns in confusion, glancing between them all. “What? What are you guys talking about? Why’s funny?”

“Don’t worry about it,” Sokka says.

“What did Aang do, anyway?” Toph cuts in, graciously saving the airbender from his uncertain fate instead of digging him in deeper.

Or maybe just digging him in deeper in a different way, as Katara immediately redirects to the note with a scowl, her expression twisting in pure maternal disapproval as she reads. “He *roughed up another student?* Aang!”

Sokka snatches the note from her hands. “He did what?” He glances over the characters, gaping up to meet Katara’s shocked eyes. A schoolyard fight? *Their* Air Nomad?

“I didn’t even touch him!” Aang protests, sounding indignant and persecuted and…a perfect model of filial outrage.

“…Okay,” Sokka says slowly, glancing down at the note and then between Aang and Katara. “Okay. This…might actually work.”

Toph laughs and laughs as Aang rocks back onto his heels. “Wait, really?”

“Toph, shut it for a second,” Sokka says, absent, already working on how to slot the pieces into place. “Alright, here’s how we’re going to play this. Kuzon, our recent Colonial immigrant, is acting out due to the loss of his friends. His loving parents are at their wits ends, but nevertheless…”

Zuko drifts through the empty hallways, into and out of pockets of sun and shadow. He can’t spend all his time trailing after Azula, can’t train when he’s so visibly imperfect, can’t hole himself up like he used, not if he’s going to stay true to his purpose.

The temptation is strong, though, because the opposite of hiding away means being *seen*.

There are ministers who don’t quite know what to do with him yet in the political web of Caldera, guards who see everything even as they pretend to notice nothing, and servants, always servants, who never look higher than his ankles. Zuko doesn’t like being watched, stared at, gawked at, especially with his scar on display the way his hair is pulled up. But this isn’t exactly comfortable. How can he glare someone down if they never actually *look* at him?

It might not bother him this much—though really, who is he kidding with *that* thought—if he had something to actually *do*. But it’s too early yet for what he wants to do without being obvious about it, which he can’t afford, and an un-exiled Crown Prince only gets welcomed back into the halls of power so quickly.

So Zuko drifts. His feet find their way to the turtle duck pond, the library, through the mews to visit Gao, avoiding being alone with the servants as much as he can because it makes everyone involved too nervous. And eventually, his feet always seem to take him to the prison that he really isn’t supposed to visit at all.

But then, one of the advantages of no one looking above his ankles or reacting to his presence is that no one can tell him what to do. Besides, Zuko knows how to hug the shadows as well as any palace-trained servant, even in the daytime.

Uncle’s back is turned like always, and the door to the room already open when Zuko slips in on silent feet. Maybe that’s why Uncle doesn’t turn around, doesn’t acknowledge him. Maybe.

Zuko stares at the familiar, broad expanse of Uncle’s back, aware of his own perfect posture and neat hair and fine robes, even his inner flame behaving itself, locked down to stillness. Zuko doesn’t try to speak, not this time, and Uncle doesn’t say anything either. Zuko could press, could rage, could demand a reaction, and he probably will later. But for now, he just reaches out with his fire sense and paces his breathing to the steady, strong beat of Uncle’s inner flame and reminds himself of why he is here.

&#45;-

Sokka can tell that this parent-teacher conference isn’t going well. Outside of Aang’s apparently deplorable and spotty education, Sokka can tell they aren’t exactly selling their role as distressingly young parents well enough, even with Sokka’s glorious beard. But is it his fault that he didn’t realize he needed a last name? Who’d think that something as small as a single word would matter so much? Last names aren’t a thing in the Water Tribe, and it’s not like Zuko has one, and Toph does, and, well—“Fire” seemed like a perfectly good one to him on the spot…

Katara doesn’t even blink as she adjusts to being named “Sapphire Fire,” quick on her feet and working it like a professional actress as she glances at Sokka with fond exasperation and then offers the headmaster a half-rueful grin, sliding right into the guise of someone taking on a terrible last name for love. Fuck, maybe she should get into theater when all this is done. Sokka can’t just ride her coattails, though, they’re in this as a team. He tries to layer in some authenticity with some of Zuko’s favorite curses when the headmaster describes Aang’s crimes. The way the man’s eyes pop suggests that maybe Zuko shouldn’t have been Sokka’s template, which…Sokka is really off his game if it took him until now to realize that growing up on a naval vessel with no other kids maybe isn’t a model Fire Nation upbringing.

Fuck, maybe Sokka’s the one who needs to go to school…

“Where did you say you were from again?”

“The Colonies, my good sir,” Sokka harrumphs cheerfully while frantically searching his head for the name of a single Colony town. Katara smiles beatifically and rests her hands on her laundry-stuffed belly.

“Hmm…” The headmaster’s eyes are steely as he taps his brush against his desk. “And remind me what curriculum they’re on these days? Is it still the Akuran progressions? Or is Izaron?”

“Oh, you know how the Colonies are,” Sokka blusters, scrambling.

“Behind,” Katara supplies knowingly.

“Yup, behind!”

“It’s why we came to the homeland,” she adds on, giving her belly another meaningful pat.

The man’s brush is hitting the desk even harder now and Sokka casts desperately around for some inspiration and maybe a weapon and an escape route. This is a learned man’s office though, not even a nice sharp letter opener within reach, and no windows to dive out of, just scrolls and art and—

“They’re all into literature and symbolism,” he bursts out, barely managing to keep his voice at the lower end of his range. Spirits, if it cracks now... “Not enough time on engineering, if you ask me! Why, my Kuzon couldn’t tell a desalination tank from a furnace, isn’t that right, Sapphire, dear?”

“Right!” Katara manages to sound just the right amount of disgruntled.

“But let me tell you,” Sokka says, digging into the tones of an adult really hitting their stride in a lecture. How did Pakku sound again? “He can rattle on about the meter and rhythm in the Second Naturalism Revivalist period for days.” Bless Iroh, and fuck everything for making Sokka think that.

“He talks your ear right off,” Katara confirms.

“But the important stuff, like history, or practical skills?” Sokka continues. Katara rolls her eyes, shaking her head. “Hopeless, over in the Colonies.”

“Utterly hopeless.”

“Hm, I suppose so,” the headmaster said, the pace of his brush-tapping slowing. He leans back, looking half-mollified, and begins searching around his desk for papers.

“At least it’s not the Third Revivalist period, small favors,” Sokka offers into the silence, holding back his wince when the headmaster gives him a startled, scandalized look. It’s probably time for Sokka to shut up.

The headmaster gives him one last disapproving stare before going back to his desk. “We will of course need you to sign the usual paperwork related to our discussion.”

“Of course, of course,” Sokka agrees.

Katara leans forward to take the offered paperwork, settling back into her chair with one hand on her stomach and freezing a little bit as she stares down at the page. It's barely a hitch, but it’s enough to grab Sokka’s attention as she takes a slow, careful *oh shit* kind of breath.

Sokka makes a curious harrumph, leaning over and quickly scanning the text. Nothing seems out of order, but the severity of the punishment could be a trap to try to test their parental instincts? “Really, expulsion? That seems harsh. I know the Colonies aren’t up to the rigor of the fine schools here, but how will our Kuzon ever learn!”

“Hm,” the headmaster seems to relax so Sokka must have hit it right, his tapping brush falling silent. “I suppose that could be extreme, for a first-time offense.”

“This bit about a temporary suspension—” Sokka taps the relevant paragraph. “How about we check that box instead?”

“And how long do you think is appropriate, knowing your son and his temperament?”

Forever? Sokka does some quick math on their schedule and tries to remember what day of the week if is. Fuck, did Zuko ever say anything about how the Fire Nation does weekends? Zuko had shifts every day, but he was in the Earth Kingdom and then on what was definitely an active military vessel no matter how Zuko insisted it was decommissioned. “Five days?”

&#45;-

Sokka waits until they are out of sight from the school before letting all his relief hit him in the form of an explosive sigh, and then furiously scratching at the fake beard glued to his face. The thing looks majestic, but Spirits is it itchy. How does Dad do it?

“So what’s the deal with the third period movement or whatever?” Katara asks as they trek past the edge of town, her hands clasped beneath her belly to keep any laundry from falling out. “I thought he was going to choke on his tongue.”

…Sokka had been hoping she wouldn’t ask about that. “It seems like it’s all about flowers and really it’s all about sex.”

Katara snaps her mouth shut.

“*Lots* of fire lily imagery,” Sokka adds.

She clears her throat. “And you could read that paperwork?”

“Fire Nation Imperial Calligraphy. It’s got a lot of fancy curlicues and shit.”

Katara takes a breath, pauses, and puts it together on her own with a grunt. “How’d you ever end up writing to him if it took that much work just to read in the first place? Tui and La, you’re so weird.”

Sokka shoots her a dry glance. “I was highly motivated and had a lot of time on my hands while you and Aang were off playing in puddles.” He skips away from her half-outraged shove. “Not let’s head home, Mrs. Fire. We have a wayward child to punish.”

&#45;-

“I don’t think,” Katara says slowly. “That a dance party is quite the punishment we had in mind to get our son back on track in life.” She shakes the laundry out of her tunic, wrinkling her nose as it falls into the dust of the cave floor.

“I was thinking something more along the lines of ‘no more school for you, young man,’” Sokka agrees.

“Good riddance to it,” Toph mutters.

“But guys,” Aang says earnestly. “I need to *help* them!”

“We’re going to help them by overthrowing their imperial, authoritarian government that feeds them propaganda in place of an education,” Sokka says, releasing his hair from its topknot with a huff of relief. He’s fine to grow out his wolf tail to fit in more, but his scalp just doesn’t love that kind of tension.

“Or, or—” Aang pauses until they look at him, then throws his arms wide, wiggling his fingers. “Dance party!”

Toph hums with exaggerated thoughtfulness. “Sounds about the same to me.”

Don’t laugh, don’t laugh, Sokka will completely destroy the dignity of wearing this bear if he laughs. “Why, specifically a dance party?”

“This is the next generation of the Fire Nation! This is who we’re trying to help! Nothing is going to change if we overthrow the Fire Lord but all the people who live here still don’t know how to be free.”

“And a dance party,” Katara clarifies, “Will teach them freedom?”

“Freedom of expression! Reclaiming their cultural heritage! Teaching them something in return after they’ve taught me so much!”

Everyone looks at Sokka—well, except Toph, but she has a way of tilting that conveys the same idea—and he briefly considers trying to explain again the schedule and how buffer time is not supposed to be used all at once, and also what going unnoticed generally means.

Fuck it. His face is too itchy for that today.

“Whatever, it’s your risk to take,” he says, throwing up his hands. “Let’s dance as punishment, why not. Zuko loves dancing, maybe they will too and then they won’t snitch on us for being a bunch of children living in a cave.”

“…Sparrowkeet loves dancing?”

“Yup,” Sokka enunciates, popping the sound.

“…Are you going to take that beard off for the dance?” Katara asks into the silence.

“Nope,” Sokka says with the same pop.

“…Why not?” Aang asks.

“It looks stately and distinguished.”

Toph raises her eyebrows and shifts her foot threateningly over the floor.

“And also it's permanently glued to my face.”

&#45;-

Zuko gets the impression that the Fire Sages are somewhat less than pleased to be dealing with another member of Agni’s line. Which is…not quite how it’s supposed to work. Sure, the Sages are Agni-touched too, in their own way. But Agni’s wisdom on earth is not supposed to be quite so visibly disgruntled when it looks at Agni’s body made manifest. Though maybe they have some right to be upset when this particular piece of Agni’s body took part, even tangentially, in destroying one of their sacred spiritual sites and melting it into the ocean.

Or maybe Zuko is just reading too much into it all, and their not-fully-concealed displeasure is because he can’t quite remember the proper forms and verses and chants, and it’s a bad look for Agni’s wisdom and Agni’s body to be visibly out of step.

Azula jabs him in the side with a pointed elbow, scowling when it hits the unyielding ridge of his ribs instead of his kidneys. “Get it together, Brother.”

“Shut up,” Zuko hisses. They shouldn’t even be talking when they’re at the front of the altar and visible like this, guiding the sacred flame along with a pair of Sages.

“You shut up if you can’t remember the words,” Azula snaps, lips barely moving.

Zuko glares as they sweep into the final movement, coming to rest along with the others and making a point of enunciating the next invocation with unnecessary precision as he stares her down. Which isn’t, traditionally, what one of Agni’s line is supposed to be looking at when one is meant to be contemplating the nature of the ever-burning flame.

“Burn bright, Child of Agni.

May the light and flame be one inside you

May you be as Agni’s hand upon the earth.

Burn strong, Child of Agni.

Shine bright and clear,

And light the way ahead.

Burn pure, Child of Agni.

See no way but forward,

Walk no path but the path of flame.

Burn bright, Child of Agni, and be everlasting.”

Zuko calls fire to his cupped hands in time with the words, shaping and twisting the flame through the precise, finger-aching forms as his body moves through half-remember devotions. He ignores the way it feels almost as awkward as training. It isn’t supposed to feel that way for a true Child of Agni, for one who’s supposed to know the nature of fire better than anyone.

But then, Zuko supposes he doesn’t know fire as a true Crown Prince would. Not anymore. He relearnt his flames in laundry duty and the rhythm of waves and lightning storms. In the beat of Sokka’s heart and the surge of his body and whisper edge of control they danced along together. In cups of calming tea and the blades of his dao and earth baked so dry by the sun that nothing seemed to exist in the world but heat.

No, Zuko doesn’t know the nature of flame as a Fire Prince should, anymore. But he does know that it’s not easy to tame something back once it’s learned what it feels like to be unchained.

&#45;-

“I’m glad we could do that,” Aang grins, falling back against Appa’s saddle and looking up at the night sky.

Sokka nudges Katara. “You seemed like you enjoyed the dancing back there.”

“Yeah?” She eyes him, still breathless from making their escape from the authorities. “So?”

“Dancing with Aang.”

“Shut up, Sokka,” Katara mutters, pink dusting her cheeks. Sokka bares his teeth in something like a smile. Turnabout is going to be *great*.

Aang misses all the byplay. “They’re being taught so many things that aren’t true,” he sighs. “About Air Nomad armies and how the world was back then…I don’t get why they would want to teach their own children lies.”

Toph shrugs, lounging back against the side of Appa’s saddle in a way that lets her grab onto a fistful of fur for anchor. “You control people with what you let them know.”

“I’m not trying to control anyone,” Aang frowns thoughtfully, tugging the headband free from his hair. “I just…”

“Want to upend the system?” Toph fills in. “Stick it to the man?”

“It’s not about upending the system,” Katara insists, still looking a little flushed. “It’s about giving something back.”

“It seemed like it was about dancing to me,” Sokka puts in, swaying out of the way of her annoyed swipe.

“That’s still *something*, Sokka. It’s…cultural heritage.”

“Is that what they’re calling it these days?”

“You said yourself that he—that Zuko dances,” she huffs.

“Yeah,” Sokka says with a little smile, knowing Katara will take it completely out of context and unable to resist. “He does.”

“And that shows that things don’t have to be the way they’re being taught,” Aang says, Sokka’s teasing still going completely over his head. Poor sucker. “People can change if you just show them another way!” Though maybe Sokka should stop teasing, if Aang is going to keep doling out that kind of positivity around the likelihood of Zuko’s changed-ness.

“What you do doesn’t always show what you actually think,” Toph warns. “Sometimes it’s just so people *don’t* know what you’re thinking.”

Aang makes a thoughtful noise. “Sokka, maybe that explains Zuko!”

Sokka glances up, wary of the conversational shift as he puts aside thoughts of Zuko and dancing and grace, and what it would take to break down all that tight self-consciousness to a place of easy physicality. “How so?”

“Just…doing stuff and, you know.” Aang shrugs, half-apologetic. “Hiding what you think?”

Sokka winces, glancing down to check that they’re not flying over any populated areas and mostly to avoid Katara’s telling silence, finally allowing, “Zuko knows more than he lets on, usually.”

“He seems like he does lots of things more than he lets on,” Katara mutters, tart.

Sokka pulls a face at her, because *he* wasn’t the one out there dancing and now pretending it’s nothing, and maybe more because he can’t stop feeling instinctive defensiveness over jabs in Zuko’s direction. “He isn’t exactly unique in that.”

Katara sputters and grumbles and makes a big show of digging out snacks, but she settles next to him again when she finishes doling out food, so she can’t be that mad about any of it. She’s watching as Toph and Aang keep talking about the difference between burning the system down and teaching people new ways to see, but her words are quiet, just for him. “You did good, with all this, you know.”

He hastily swallows his mouthful of bread, half-surprised and absently batting Momo’s reaching fingers away from the rest of his food. “Thanks?”

She shrugs. “You seem less…broody than back on the ship.”

Sokka slowly chews another bite. “I guess Fire Nation ships have a lot of memories for me,” he says. Which isn’t *all* of it, but—being away definitely helps.

Katara flicks a glance his way, probing. Sokka is aware that he has always been more than a little bit cagey about talking about what happened on Zuko’s ship, and that she isn’t an idiot about it. “I guess so,” she finally says, clearly letting it drop. “It’s good you’re feeling back to normal.”

Sokka almost doesn’t say the words, but avoiding asking painful questions is a big part of what got him here in the first place. “So does that mean you trust me again?”

“I trust you to make the right decisions,” Katara says. “And to be willing to adjust once you get all the facts.” She shoots him a quick glance, then sighs, resting her head on his shoulder. “You don’t need to prove yourself to me, Sokka. That isn’t what this is about.”

Sokka nods in acknowledgment, appreciating the sentiment and the fact that she verbalized it even if it just stirs up a fresh kick of anxiety in his gut. He wants to be worthy of that confidence, but Sokka can’t help but think it’s a scary amount of faith to put in his ability to determine right from wrong, given his short but spectacular track record of blurring all the crisp, clear lines to justify the things he wants badly enough.

## Chapter 4: Masquerades

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Some brief sexual references in this one!

### Text

Sokka is learning that supply runs in the Fire Nation are nothing like supply runs in the Earth Kingdom, which…he really hasn’t planned for. Maybe he shouldn’t have needed that particular lesson, because what in the Fire Nation *is* like anywhere else, when you get down to it. But he’d assumed that the basic plan of attack—make a list, divide and conquer, stay focused, regroup at the rendezvous point—would work just about anywhere.

So the fact that it keeps *not* working…

“I don’t know *what* is going on,” Toph announces for anyone in the market who cares to listen. “But tell me we are *not* planning to eat whatever smells like *this*.” She waves her hand in a way that could encompass the stall in front of them, or the market itself, or maybe just the general miasma that seems to hang over the town.

“I’m not sure if we have any other options than not eating,” Sokka mutters, heart sinking as he takes in the display of two-headed fish laid out for their perusal. Who knew clams even *had* discernible heads, to be able to tell if there were two of them?

One genetic deformity, sure, it happens, nature is weird. But half the catch? More than half, judging by what he’s seen on offer? Sokka doesn’t want to find out what eating something like that would do to them.

“We could go without any meat until the next town,” Katara suggests, wrinkling her face and glancing toward Sokka to what he thinks of it. It’s an idea Sokka would normally resist, but he’s *definitely* willing to give it a try right now.

“Does this look any better?” Aang asks, carefully holding pinched between his fingers some…completely unidentifiable thing that, judging by the faded stand sign, is supposed to be a vegetable. Sokka’s stomach lurches as he realizes he prefers the fish.

Toph shifts her weight. “Your collective silence is leading me to think that the answer is no, it doesn’t.”

“What is *wrong* with this place,” Katara says with a sort of horrified wonder as she looks around again.

“The smell of the river isn’t enough?” Sokka sighs. Something about bad water just makes his skin crawl, and this is brackish, acrid, grey-brown in a way that water is never supposed to be even in the soggiest swamp. Sokka is keeping a firm grip on Momo just in case, not that Momo is dumb enough to try drinking it.

Aang rubs uncertainly at his hairline. “Do we still try to do the list?”

Sokka takes a deep breath that he instantly regrets, trying to rally the troops. “Let’s do our best. Dried grains, maybe something imported…” He looks at Katara, who shrugs and nods. She can work with that. “Let’s just see what we can do.”

&#45;-

What they can do, apparently, is make a scene.

Sokka quickly realizes that there’s nothing that they can afford to buy even if the townspeople could afford to sell it. That two-headed fish isn’t exactly looking better, but… maybe if they boiled it? Twice? And if Katara purified the water first…

But the time searching for the items on their list is just enough time for the true state of the town to become apparent. They see openly sick children, more kids begging, which Sokka doesn’t know if they’ve ever seen before in a village this small. Everyone would *know* each other, to beg like the people around you don’t know that you’re suffering, that you need…

There are gaunt faces, dry coughs, so much Fire Nation-pale skin looking yellowish and grey. At one point the factory up the river must have done something, and all the townspeople barely reacted as the air itself became so thick and *dry*, but in an almost burning way, so much that it was dizzying to try to breathe for a few steps.

Sokka finally manages to suck in a deep enough breath to straighten upright, eyeing the dark, sooty, low-hanging smog drifting downriver. This isn’t good, on a number of fronts, and the need to get in and get out fast stats buzzing like adrenaline through his veins.

Sokka has no idea what it’s making and can’t care no matter how curious he is. A factory like that would be too much of a military asset for this to be a safe place to linger. Especially when there’s no real reason for them to be here without supplies to buy, or to be traveling in the first place. They stand out too much even with their Fire Nation disguises, Sokka painfully conscious that there are too many eyes following them across the market, the gazes not entirely suspicious yet, but…seeing that they *have*, when the town has so little, and envying.

Aang’s voice is small with sadness. “This isn’t a good place, Sokka.”

Sokka grunts in agreement, scanning for Katara and Toph as they approach the meetup point, hugging Momo to his chest and itching to get out of here.

“This town should be in harmony with the river. It sits between elements…there should be abundance here.”

“Just because there should—”

“The spirits of this place must be angry,” Aang continues, brow twisting even more with concern. “If they keep desecrating the land like this…”

“It’s not the villagers doing it.” Not that Sokka actually thinks that would matter to spirits. Every encounter he’s had has shown that they’re a real pack of assholes.

A sudden commotion cuts off whatever Aang’s reply might be, drawing their attention toward a cluster of what Sokka would otherwise classify as street urchins but here are probably just the local children. And Toph. With Katara crouched down, level with a little boy who is looking at her with wide, shocked eyes.

Fuck.

“Come on,” Sokka urges, hurrying Aang over just in time to hear Katara say that she knows something of healing, and maybe she could just take a—

“We don’t have time for that,” Sokka bursts in, half-breathless and more than a little frantic to cut off whatever she might have finished with.

“It will just take a minute,” Katara frowns. “Don’t be heartless.”

“I’m not being heartless,” Sokka snaps, stung. “I’m being realistic. We don’t have a lot of time, and maybe it’s a minute the kid can better spend somewhere else, considering you don’t have any of your *healing supplies* with you.”

Katara is clearly fighting a glare. “I could at least *diagnose* it.”

“Fine,” Sokka sighs. “Diagnose it.” For all the good that knowing the problem will do anyone, with no way to fix it. “But then we need to leave. We need to stick to the schedule.”

“But all these kids…”

“I think we can help them most by not making any more of a scene than we already have.” Spirits, Sokka hates things like this. Absolutely loathes them. These moments that make him feel like he has to be the bad guy, when Aang’s idealism or Katara’s urge to help or Toph’s confidence run up against the reality that only Sokka ever seems willing to speak to, and then they look at Sokka like *this*, like they don’t even know who he is.

“Ah,” Toph grunts, a little understanding noise as she flexes her bare toes against the ground. “Give Sweetness here five minutes, Sokka. Then we can wrap it.”

Katara makes a sad noise, glancing to Aang with pleading eyes which is *not* fair.

“These people need help,” Aang says slowly, glancing around.

“And we are on our way to *help them*. Permanently. As long as we stay on schedule.”

“Fine,” Katara bites out, selling the word even worse than Zuko—which Sokka didn’t think was possible—and hitting him with one last glare before turning sharply away. Sokka takes a deep breath and forces his fists to uncurl. The knowledge that Katara wears her anger like armor doesn’t do much to actually make being on the receiving end of it any easier.

Sokka hovers throughout the whole process, closer than maybe he should when he’s not trying to piss off Katara even more. He can’t bring himself to back off, though, not when he can practically see her thinking about how easy it would be to pull water from the river and start setting things right.

Sokka admires the way Katara wants to help everyone she comes across. He’s proud of her for it, finds it impressive, even, the way that she’s managed to hold onto her convictions and that core of goodness after everything that’s happened to them. Spirits, after everything that’s happened to the South. But they can’t be running through the Fire Nation like this, doling out help in every village and town and leaving a breadcrumb trail behind them for anyone to follow. Not with the time they have to work with. Not without endangering the mission.

Katara is openly giving away what she has to those in need and asking nothing in return. It’s a perfectly normal thing to do within the Water Tribe, expected even. But Toph already showed him how the same thing earns at best outraged indignation in the Earth Kingdom. And here?

Sokka doesn’t know for sure—he’d need to ask Zuko, and Sokka needs to ask Zuko so many things that this is absolutely never going to make the list—but he has letters and comments and Zuko’s own disgruntled reactions to guess off of. Enough to have a sense that having when others don’t, and making a point to show it off, could be a sign of status in a place where status matters very much. Enough to have an inkling that the Fire Nation is very aware of power, and who holds it, and who doesn’t.

What Katara is doing is *dangerous*. Outside of the risk of revealing her bending, or leaving too much of an impression, they just don’t know the kind of missteps they might be making once they step outside the space of making purchases in a market. For all they know, Katara could be running around flaunting her power to change lives in this town, making some kind of threat, or power play, or bid for loyalty, or some other Fire Nation thing Sokka doesn’t understand but is pretty sure either way the Fire Nation soldiers aren’t going to like.

Even if it seems like the right thing to do. Even if Sokka is acutely aware that he is the only one protesting it. Even if that fact doesn’t make him wonder if he’s wrong about this, too.

“It’s despicable,” Katara grumbles as they finally leave the market with one of those deformed fish and a bag of fruit that they can probably cut some good flesh out of. “That things could be allowed to get like this…”

“But with the soldiers garrisoned up the river, what can the village even do,” Aang sighs.

“Where are the elders?” Katara is working up a head of steam. “Where are the town leaders?”

Toph scoffs in the back of her throat. “Probably hosting Fire Nation soldiers for dinner every night. Whether they want to or not.”

Katara makes a disgusted noise. “There’s no care for the people here! How does the Fire Lord think he deserves to rule the world when he can’t even take care of what he already has?”

“Katara,” Sokka cautions, but eyes sharp as he glances around. Thankfully they’re close enough to the sparse docks that there’s no one around to overhear.

“Don’t ask me to be careful of your feelings right now, Sokka,” Katara growls. “Not after I just had to walk away from that. I don’t care what Zuko—”

“Stop,” Sokka orders, tone mild as he takes another wary look around for listeners. “I’m not talking about my feelings. You need to be careful not to be *heard*.”

“Why?” Aang checks for anyone lingering in earshot anyway. “It can’t be anything the villagers aren’t already thinking.”

“The Fire Nation doesn’t talk about their leaders like that,” Sokka says, trying to pitch the words low. He would love to be out of a Fire Nation town for this. “I know we say what we want in the Water Tribe. And the Earth Kingdom—” He glances at Toph.

“Eh,” she shrugs. “Enough. Opinions are valuable to the right people.”

“But the Fire Lord can never be wrong. Not that he isn’t wrong,” he adds quickly, seeing the incredulous twist of Katara’s expression. “But you can’t stay it, you can’t write it, you can’t act like you think it. Not here.”

“…More propaganda?” Aang finally asks into the silence.

“More something,” Sokka sighs. “Just…be careful. We’re already noticeable enough without someone thinking we’re trying to incite a rebellion.” He pauses for a moment, replaying his own words. “Not before we’re ready, at least.”

&#45;-

Sokka is dreaming. He knows he is, knows it’s not real, but oh, does he want it to be. Featherlight, callused fingers skating over the curve of his waist, reverent lips trailing down his stomach. A hoarse voice whispering ‘*Sokka’* with that extra gravel it always got, gold eyes dark and wicked and molten. The breath against his hip pauses, the kind of deliberate concentration-pause that always presaged sparks or heat or a lick of flame just above his skin. Sokka’s response to it is instinctive, so well-trained his body is tensing in anticipation before he even—

A clatter of iron on stone and a muffled curse has Sokka snapping into wakefulness, strung tight and cock hard and hips rocking into the ground and Spirits, it’s a fucking miracle that he still has the cover of a dim, overcast early morning to conceal himself in. And that he didn’t come in his pants, because Spirits, Sokka is shuddering along the edge of it, but fuck dealing with that right now on top of everything else.

Sokka thunks his face back into his bedroll, muffling the quiet sound of pain over the state of his life that manages to slip free. He needs to think of other things, because Katara is clearly stirring for the day and even if she wasn’t, this wouldn’t be the time or the place, but…fuck. Sokka misses a lot of things right now. Privacy being somewhere near the top of the list.

Sokka wonders if he can blame his unruly subconscious on that fish last night. But no, it’s not like this is the first time he’s had a dream like that, or woken up with a…*situation* to deal with. It’s just the most…actively involved he’s been on waking, which…probably has more to do with that lack of privacy than with dinner.

Fuck.

But thinking about what terrible things that deformed fish could do to him is doing wonders for deflating his particular issue, as is the progressively louder sounds of Katara getting breakfast ready. He wonders what she’s putting together—water flavored with grass, probably, if they even trust that much around here.

“Uh…Sokka?” Katara’s hesitant voice has him breaking free of the last of his dream, alarm tightening his shoulders. Katara doesn’t do hesitance.

“What,” he demands, scrambling out of his sleeping roll, shoving loose hair out of his face and trying to tug his clothes into some semblance of order.

“We might need to go back into town for more…supplies…”

Sokka pauses with half his hair pulled up into a knot, because he still can’t remember to grab all the long edges. “Why would we do that?”

Katara wordlessly points, and he follows the line of her finger to…

“Fuck,” Sokka breathes. Air bison are *not* supposed to be that color around the mouth. “Did he eat something?”

Katara makes a drawn-out sound in the back of her throat. “I don’t think his tongue is supposed to look like that…”

“Shit,” Sokka mutters, readjusting their calendar again and frantically trying to see where they might be able to scrape up more wiggle room. If this illness takes more than a few days…Fuck, his stomach turns over at the idea of needing to talk about leaving Appa behind and stealing a boat instead. Another right thing that feels wrong. Or wrong thing that feels right. “You get to tell Aang.”

Katara opens her mouth like she wants to argue before pausing and finally making a grumbly sound in the back in lieu of protest as she goes back to prodding at breakfast. They both know that Aang will take almost anything better coming from her than from Sokka, not that Sokka is in the mood to tease her about it right now.

“Can you heal him?” Sokka asks, joining her by the little fire and peeking warily into the pot. The water looks clear, at least.

“I can *try*. But animals are different than people, and I focused more on wounds and injuries than illness,” she sighs, worrying at her lower lip.

“Fine,” Sokka sighs. “Just…fine.” And now he sounds about as convincing as Zuko, too.

&#45;-

Azula finds him in his rooms. Not that he was trying to hide, exactly, just that…maybe he would have normally left them by now. She lets out a sharp ‘*tch’* when she sweeps into his bedroom to find him standing motionless, staring at the half-rolled scroll on his desk where he’d dropped it in his numb shock. Which was…who knows how long ago. Long enough for Azula to come looking.

“It’s not a buzzard wasp,” Azula says, arms folded, fingers tapping impatiently. “It’s not going to bite you.”

Zuko makes a skeptical noise, keeping his right eye on the scroll. He isn’t so sure about that.

Azula snorts and shifts to her second-most favorite topic: Zuko’s substandard appearance. “Were you going to show up looking like that?”

Her tone makes it clear the answer should be ‘no,’ and Zuko reflexively glances down at himself. Sure, it’s not High Court finery, but this isn’t High Court.

“Really, Zuzu, you look like a vagrant,” she says, scraping him with critical eyes and ignoring his glare. Zuko’s *been* a vagrant, and he would have been fucking lucky to have clothes this nice to sell. “At least your hair has grown out enough for that—thing,” she adds with a grimace for his topknot, which is more blunt club than majestic waterfall.

“Yes, thank Agni for that,” Zuko mutters.

Azula gives him a flat stare before snapping her fingers, then glancing around in annoyance after a few heartbeats when no one appears. “Of course,” she mutters to herself, giving him another scowl. “Fine. Change your robes and pay attention, if that’s how you want it. We don’t have time for this. Councilor Chen has been trying to use the recent production numbers from the smelting factories as a way to undermine Councilor Xi’s control of the research grants, and…”

&#45;-

It takes Sokka about two steps onto the dock to realize that something about the town is different. His shoulders tense, eyes scanning to try to pin down what, exactly, has changed overnight. Even Aang, wrapped up in worries for Appa, slows and looks around in confusion. Were they recognized? Are there soldiers hidden in the crowd? His hand drifts toward his knife and man, is he ever regretting leaving his boomerang behind, even if it’s far too distinctive for anyone in the Fire Nation to walk around with.

“Huh,” Toph says once they move from the dock to the earth of the island, her head tilting with interest. She wiggles her toes deeper into the dirt. “People seem…happier?”

“…You can sense emotions?” Kill him now.

“No,” Toph says absently, frowning with concentration. “It all just feels…more active? And like more people are congregating? Yesterday was much…less.”

“I wonder why,” Katara says, turning toward the town square with bright, curious eyes, practically vibrating to be cut loose.

“Let’s ask!” Aang suggests, shooting off with Katara a step behind.

Sokka sighs. It’s a one-item list, so he supposes he can handle it without them, even though a healer would have been nice for it. “Think the market will have turned around too and have some medicine?”

Toph wrinkles her nose as the wind changes, bringing the acrid stench of the factory toward them. “Don’t get your hopes up, Loverboy.”

&#45;-

Zuko wonders at his own arrogance, to think that he could throw himself at this again and expect to survive a second time. He already had his shot at living when he should have died —maybe twice, or three times depending on who you ask. To try to retread that same ground is the kind of thing that Agni struck people down for in all the stories of the world before Agni gave his wisdom and his body to the earth.

Zuko already tried putting himself between the gears of war and the innocent, and he doesn’t need Azula’s regular reminders of the consequences to remember how it went. What does he really think that he can do differently, this time? Does he really think he can make it come out any differently than before?

Zuko may have clawed his way back to Caldera, to the palace, to this room, but he knows that none of them will pretend they don’t see the stains left by what it took to get here. To get right back where it all started, except now Zuko doesn’t know the players, the undercurrents in the room, the agendas or the power plays or the jockeying for dominance happening on top of and beneath the surface and buried three layers deep.

All he has is an invitation, this time. And the fact that he survived, before, and—

Azula’s inner flame flares in a way that has Zuko snapping his attention toward her, no sign of that brief flare in her demeanor. Right. He might as well try, before spiraling down toward failure.

“Burn bright.” The words are barely audible, a dangerous reminder as Zuko and Azula begin the long walk toward the war room.

A pause, before the quiet agreement that some things can’t be stopped once started. “No way out but forward.”

&#45;-

“This is great,” Aang enthuses as they step back onto the riverbank, sounding remarkably upbeat given the lack of medicine for Appa. “The Painted Lady intervening is a really good sign!”

“Really?” Toph asks, finally uncurling her fingers from Sokka’s forearm as her feet settle back on the ground.

“It means that despite all the damage to her land, the spirit doesn’t hold the townspeople responsible! She must know that they still honor her, and that’s why she’s still acting on their behalf.”

“It seems like she could have done her acting a little earlier,” Sokka points out, ignoring Katara’s glare. It seems mighty fucking convenient for the Painted Lady to wait until the Avatar comes to town to make anything better for her people. He doesn’t like the way it feels like a bid for attention, and Sokka doesn’t trust one bit.

“The spirits can be hard to understand if you don’t know how to speak to them,” Aang says. “Who knows what made her decide to act?” Sokka snorts. He has some guesses. “We can’t just demand gifts from them.”

“Then what’s the point,” Sokka mutters under his breath.

“It’s too bad she didn’t come heal Appa last night,” Toph says as they begin the climb back up to their campsite.

Aang hums thoughtfully. “Maybe we need to do something to get her attention.”

Sokka nearly trips. “*No.”*

Aang and Katara actually come to a surprised stop at his vehemence, Toph twisting around toward him with a confused frown.

“Why not?” Aang asks. “She’s helping the people in the town, and we want to help them too. I think—”

“No,” Sokka cuts in, scowling down at the betraying ground for any more hazards. “No rituals or spirit quests or whatever. No trying to get some random spirit’s attention. We don’t know anything about her, we don’t know why she let it get this bad before doing anything to help. We have no idea what she wants, or what she’ll do if she doesn’t get it.”

“Help can just be for the sake of helping,” Katara protests. “It doesn’t have to be part of some —scheme or whatever.”

“I don’t think she would be upset if we also honored her,” Aang tacks on.

*“No,”* Sokka repeats, hands curling into fists. “Do you remember what happened the last time we messed around with spirits when their land was being disrespected? Because *I do*.”

“…Oh,” Katara says, suddenly searching his face in a way that makes Sokka itch.

“Yeah, *oh*.”

“…And what happened, again?” Toph asks, and Sokka doesn’t stick around to hear what the half-apologetic glance Aang sends his way is going to mean for Aang’s explanation. He stalks ahead of the group, trying to breathe out his frustration as he goes. He doesn’t want to rehash it and doesn’t want to listen to anyone else doing it, either. He remembers the Spirit World perfectly well without needing to hear their versions, the sick sense of shifting unreality and all his closest people made *wrong*, the malicious not-him peeking out from behind familiar eyes, pushing at Sokka to—

Enough.

Sokka remembers Hai Bei far too well to want to mess around with the Painted Lady, no matter how benevolent she might seem right now. He remembers the scar in the land and what they found beneath the ash and the agony that haunted each captured villager’s eyes afterward they returned home. It was another thing to add to the list he had back then of all the things the Fire Nation had to atone for. And now…

Sokka finally reaches the top of their little summit, glancing back to make sure he hasn’t lost the others, then past them down to the brown-grey river and dingey, soot-covered town.

…Now, Sokka is pretty sure that polluting the entire local ecosystem is worlds worse in the eyes of the local spirits than burning down a swathe of trees and what may or may not have still been alive there. Now, Sokka doesn’t know who owes what anymore, or what atonement even begins to look like in a world that feels like it’s nothing but shades of gray.

&#45;-

Zuko is the very picture of Fire Nation royalty as he steps into the council room—the war room, really, because when can anyone remember it being used for anything else. His face is held still, his inner flame locked tight, his dark armor sucking in the dim light. The only thing out of place is his hair, really. And his scar. But there isn’t a single face at this table who wasn’t there for that, so that makes the stiff, warped flesh almost part of the expected image, in its own way.

The room is just as Zuko always dreams it, the same inset map of the world spanning the table, the same cushions, the same lighting. With a lurch, he wonders if it’s the same boundaries being fought over, too, the same few hundred yards of land. It’s certainly most of the same people dictating the fighting.

A distant, quiet corner of his brain wonders how they all feel looking at him—at his face— having been here at the start of it, for that very first comment Zuko didn’t know better than to hold back. Did they know then what path Zuko was setting himself on? Or was that as much a surprise for them as for him, the next morning?

“Prince Zuko.” The Fire Lord’s voice is as deep as ever, pitched to cut through the dull roar of the massive fire circling his dais. “Join me.” He gestures, the flames parting with the motion to make it visible as he indicates one of the two empty cushions before him. It’s a sign of favor, theoretically, to be seated so close to the Fire Lord, and maybe enough of one to make up for the lack of ‘Crown’ in front of that ‘Prince.’ An honor that puts Zuko on the Fire Lord’s left, scar visible to the room and the Fire Lord behind him if Zuko looks toward anyone else at the table.

Right. Well then.

Azula strolls toward the other cushion without waiting for an invitation, like it's nothing to do so—because it shouldn’t be, for one of Agni’s line. Her steps are just this side of insolent, elegant and controlled like she owns the room at fourteen, the generals and councilors nodding in respect like they all agree.

That fact barely keeps Zuko steady as he does his own walk down the other side of the table, longer legs letting him easily match Azula’s pace. His inner flame twists in his chest as he claws to hold onto his façade of calm, of being untouchable, even though every single thing about this feels like it’s designed to make him crack.

He wonders which one of them organized it. It could have been anyone in the room, really. Or maybe all of them, together.

Zuko stills his thoughts as he finally reaches the ornately embroidered silk cushion. He drops smoothly into seiza at their Father’s side, moving in time with Azula and shoving his fire sense out because he can’t afford not to, can’t be felt pulling himself in tight, not here of all places. He doesn’t try to fight for control of any of the flames, though. Not yet, at least. No one but Azula would, with the Fire Lord on his dais, and even then, only at her boldest.

Instead, Zuko forces his fire sense to be present and his inner flame to be level, using Azula’s tightly controlled inner flame to keep his own breathing even as he turns his head toward the others, forcing himself to listen and hear what’s being said instead of the litany of names that st

used to be the 41 .

&#45;-

Sokka cannot wait to get out of this town. Everything about this place hits him all the wrong ways, from the borderline military occupation that no one living here seems to think is abnormal to how badly he itches to explore that factory and how much he flinches from seeing all that innovation with no regard for impact. From the dangerously active spirit shit to the fact that no one else thinks it’s dangerous, to the persistent nagging worry that the longer they stay here with all this bad air and bad water and suspect food, the more likely someone else is going to get sick, too.

Most of all, though, it’s the fact that he keeps having to stand here and advocate over and over for leaving all those villagers behind. It makes *him* feel like the bad guy, instead of the situation and the circumstance and the government, especially when Katara looks at him like that, somewhere between wounded and betrayed and angry. It makes Sokka wonder if there’s something wrong with him that isn’t wrong with the others, that he’s the only one who keeps saying it.

Sokka just doesn’t want to be the one who has to tell them that they can’t make the impact they want, at least not without giving up something else. He doesn’t want to have to keep telling them ‘no,’ like he’s their parent and not their friend. Like maybe he doesn’t share their goals, even though he’s the one reminding them all of the biggest goal of all.

Maybe it's unfair to blame all that on a physical place, on this village that probably didn’t do anything to deserve its plight other than to be particularly well located in a convenient river.
