But Sokka can’t stop feeling that, either, so he just grits his teeth and lets the uncomfortable feelings fester and grooms Appa, murmuring get-well lullabies under his breath like Gran Gran used to do and wishing that he knew some kind of science that could make any of this better.

&#45;-

Zuko collapses into the first seat he reaches at the table, grateful that this veranda Azula’s apparently taken a liking to is in the sun and soaking in Agni’s touch like a starving thing. If this is what he’s going to be like after every council meeting, after every time he has to exist in that windowless, fire-filled room…Fuck.

Azula sits across from him with stiff-backed precision, for once not commenting on his decorum or the fact that he’s definitely slouching. She looks vaguely bored by the whole thing, while Zuko feels wrung out, cracked open and scraped clean until he’s hollow, so brittle that an errant touch is all it would take to break him to pieces.

He can’t even muster up the energy to do more than stare at the food in front of them. It’s Azula’s usual elaborate spread, and objectively Zuko knows that it all looks delicious and must be delicious or else Azula wouldn’t allow it to be served to her. But the smell of it alone is nearly too much for his churning, tight stomach right now. He doesn’t want to bring anything any closer and risk a rather spectacular revelation that he is not, in fact, as unaffected by the morning as he needs everyone to believe.

“Oh, spiced buns!” Tai Lee chirps as she drops into the chair across from Azula, giving Mai the seat across from Zuko. “My favorite!” She grabs a bun and turns her grin onto him. “Zuko, are they still your favorite too?”

Zuko stares at her, unable to come up with a single food that he’s ever eaten that could qualify as a favorite.

“What are you waiting for, have some!”

Zuko transfers his stare to the proffered tray, eyeing it like the spiced buns might come to life and try to throw themselves down his throat.

“Really, Brother,” Azula sighs, opening her napkin with a snap before smoothing it onto her lap, the gesture somehow managing to be fluid and disinterred and full of potential violence. “Stop being so melodramatic. Eat something.” She rakes him with an annoyed glance. “You look like a refugee.”

“I wonder why,” Zuko snaps, stung into a response and immediately biting back anything else when Mai rolls her eyes and grabs the tray of buns, pointedly serving them onto everyone’s plate and following up with the pancake-wrapped greens that are apparently still Azula’s favorite. Zuko briefly considers ignoring the food still, then picks up his chopsticks with a sigh. Mai never was one to have much tolerance for picky eating.

Azula isn’t letting it go, though, even as she folds up her pancake with neat, quick movements. “You need to look the part since you can’t manage to act the part.”

Zuko briefly closes his eyes. “Azula…”

“Really, Zuzu, don’t go if you can’t handle it.”

“Don’t call me that,” Zuko mutters, somewhere between annoyed and rote.

“I’ll call you whatever I want, *Zuzu,”* Azula says, words edged in steel. “If you want me to call you something different then act like you deserve it.”

Zuko looks up in surprise to see her staring him down, her eyes as tawny and direct as Gao’s, and he belatedly sets his face and glowers back.

“Azula…” Ty Lee tries, but Azula ignores her.

“And if you can’t handle it,” she says, tone hovering between a snarl and a challenge, “Then you can run back to your little friends.”

“They’re not my friends,” Zuko says, and Azula’s eyes narrow because she’s as good at reading his lies as anyone, and that was nearly too plain a statement to conceal anything beneath.

“No,” Azula says slowly, finding the one gap he allowed himself. “Just your…associates.” She manages to make the word sound salacious. Dirty. Shameful.

Zuko stiffens, biting back any protest. He knows it would only ring false, even though silence is as good as an admittance, Azula’s eyes flaring with victory when he doesn’t pick up her challenge.

“The Avatar’s friends?” Ty Lee asks brightly around a mouthful of bun. “They were so much fun to play with!”

“Really, Ty Lee?” Mai asks, giving her a flat look before spearing a wedge of fruit.

“Didn’t you have fun? They were so interesting!”

“…No.”

“You just thought they were interesting to look at,” Azula says, leaning back and seeming to relent to Ty Lee’s insistence on a pleasant meal even as her smile drips poison. “One in particular. What was his name, again?”

Zuko glares, aware that he’s taking the bait even as he opens his mouth, and—

The surprisingly sharp tip of Mai’s palace slipper makes contact with his shin beneath the table. “Shut up and eat,” she grumbles without lifting her eyes from her plate. “No one cares about who thought what about who.”

Zuko transfers his glare to her, unable to let it go quite yet but at least having the self-control to stuff a bun into his mouth to give himself something to focus on other than the idea of reaching across the table and doing something that he would deeply regret. He chews grimly, ignoring the knowledge that the richness is going to upset his stomach and trying to focus on the flavors. If he’s going to do this to himself, he might as well enjoy it, because Ty Lee was right—they’re still his favorites.

&#45;-

Zuko is feeling…cautious about the invitation he received to join Mai for dinner. It was passed along through a servant, a smooth scroll with formal tassels and ornate characters, the usual channels one would expect them to use as nobility. But not the usual channels for them, when they see each other every day one way or another.

Zuko had stared at the note for far too long, considering the servant waiting for his reply, looking for some kind of clue or sign or code or anything. But that kind of subterfuge has never been his forte, not without anything to guide him, so he’d eventually given it up and sent back his reply. It’s not like Mai doesn’t know that he’s more inclined toward the type that’s as blunt and straightforward as you can get and still call it subterfuge.

Zuko dresses in more formal attire than he’s been wearing since he arrived, as if he were going to a dinner that the Fire Lord would be attending, but not so formal as he would dress for a banquet. That just feels excessive, even if Zuko doesn’t know who else might be there or what Mai is up to. Still, he takes extra care to sweep the barely-long-enough strands of his hair neatly into his topknot, to make sure that the headpiece is firmly fixed and upright.

The walk to her rooms takes more time than he expects, because Zuko’s never spent all that much time there, at least not without Azula leading them all there first. But when he arrives it’s just Mai, and a table set for two. And the servants, of course, which Zuko can’t seem to remember the trick of ignoring like the rest of them can.

This…doesn’t necessarily make him feel any less cautious. Zuko hasn’t had unmediated interaction with anyone except Azula, really, since he got back to Caldera. Silently staring— or raging—at Uncle’s back doesn’t exactly count.

“Zuko,” she greets, rising smoothly to her feet.

“Mai.” He doesn’t quite know what to do with his hands. Or his body. Or himself.

Mai is dressed slightly more formally than Zuko, but not so much that it’s particularly remarkable, especially given what everyone probably thinks of the habits he picked up from years or traveling. Her hair is in its usual buns, her underrobe it's usual crimson even if it’s of a finer fabric than her daily wear. The sleeves are wide enough for at least two knives, and he’s sure she has more hidden about her person. He would distract himself by trying to find them all, if he didn’t think that amount of staring at her body is a recipe for trouble.

“I thought you would enjoy a quiet dinner after all the…celebration,” Mai says, tone a shade wry at the end.

Zuko flicks her a quick glance, searching, but he doesn’t see anything beneath the usual impassiveness, so he takes the offered seat, belatedly tipping his head into some gesture that could be thanks. He spent more than a few afternoons this week remembering the motions of how to do tilt and move his head without disrupting his topknot and headpiece. He’s pleased that he didn’t have to actively think about it this time to pull it off.

The servants glide over in silence at Mai’s wordless gesture to serve them with no sound except for the barely-there noise of fine porcelain hitting the tabletop. He’s vaguely surprised to see that it’s one of those so-simple-it’s-fancy meals, which he doesn’t remember Mai enjoying but is…actually exactly what Zuko’s been craving, now that he sees it.

Mai waves the servants away, and as they file out on soundless feet, she flicks him a bland look and delicately picks up her chopsticks and begins to eat. Zuko takes his cue from her and does the same. In silence.

It’s…quiet. Obviously. Nothing but the quick tap of chopsticks and the sounds of their own breathing. But it’s quiet in a good way, especially with the servants gone and the eyes off his back and Mai seeming more interested in her plate than in anything else. Zuko feels his inner fire unfurl into the peace, different from the sharp, heavy absence of sound that comes with being totally alone. This feels like his fire sense is stretching to fit itself back into the spaces inside of himself that it usually occupies, like he can finally let his inner flame shift and move to its own rhythm for the first time in weeks.

It’s all surprisingly…nice. Zuko doesn’t mind the lack of conversation, or Mai’s bored expression, or the simple nature of the food and the need to serve themselves. The only discordant note in the entire meal comes at the end, when it closes with tea rather than dessert. Zuko doesn’t normally care for dessert—or tea—enough to mind its absence, but something in him was expecting it, or wanting it maybe, and all that he associates with it, and his inner fire can’t quite rush to fill that hollow, aching part of himself fast enough.

Mai finally speaks as they set their cups down, eyes contemplative on her tea in a way that reminds him of Uncle even though it’s really nothing like that. “It’s good that you’re back.”

Zuko studies her face, rising a beat behind her as she finds her feet. Dinner is over, apparently. “Thank you.”

Mai hesitates, a flicker of something crossing her face too fast for Zuko to tell what emotion it might be. “I had stopped hoping…” She shrugs, impassiveness falling back into place.

Zuko waits, but she doesn’t finish that thought, and he doesn’t know well enough where she may have wanted to take it to guess. She could have been hoping for so many things when it comes to him. But regardless… “I’m surprised you ever started.”

&#45;-

Sokka wakes up from a nightmare of the hands holding him going from warm to hot to burning, from holding him to trapping him, the voice in his ear warping and twisting like a thousand voices whispering all at once, the eyes watching him suddenly becoming something *else*—

His eyes snap open, a scream strangled in his throat as he frantically searches the darkness, heart pounding, pounding, pounding so hard that he can’t catch his breath, until it feels like he’s back in that dream, that *thing* wrapping its hand around his throat again in a sick parody of tenderness.

Sokka knows he’s awake even if his body is still clinging to fear. He knows it. He can feel it in the way his hands are trembling against his chest as his adrenaline beats in his throat, in the hard reality of the lumpy ground beneath his bedroll, in the soft heat of Momo curled against his side. He should settle soon, he usually settles by now, but he still feels on edge, taut, like the nightmare is lingering, why won’t his breathing—

Breathing. Sokka should hear Katara on his left and Aang to his right and Toph somewhere between them and all he can hear is one of those, not where it’s supposed to be.

Sokka lunges upright, tripping to get himself free from his sleeping roll without stepping on Momo, scrambling to grab up his knife and put his back to the rocky cliff face they’re sheltering against and—

“Relax, Snoozles,” Toph says quietly, shifting near the low embers of their fire.

“Toph—what—where—”

“They’re fine.”

“…What?” Sokka looks around only slightly less frantically than before, seeing no signs of a struggle, seeing a shape beneath Katara’s covers that would stop his breath with its stillness if Toph weren’t so calm, sitting with atypical quiet except for the regular movement of her hands as she does…some kind of bending thing, probably.

“Katara and Aang are out pretending to be heroes,” Toph says, his eyes not adjusted enough yet for him to be able to pick out the expression to go along with that tone.

“…What?” He must—he must still be sleeping.

“The Painted Lady has been among us all along,” Toph says sarcastically, tilting her head toward Katara’s empty sleeping roll.

“She—*what?”* Sokka spins toward the empty blankets like they’re going to have any answers for him, staring at the mockingly still pile shaped into a semblance of his sister’s body, the sticky remnants of fear sliding into anger. He *told her* what the risk was. She should know the danger for anyone to be doing what she’s doing, let alone a Water Tribe healer in the middle of the Fire Nation, she should know it better than anyone. And to drag an *airbender* with her*?*

Oh, none of them are going to have to worry about the Fire Lord. Sokka is going to kill them himself.

&#45;-

Sokka watches the sun rise and wonders if Zuko is looking at this one, too, from Caldera or wherever the fuck he is. He idly and uselessly hopes that Zuko is waking up to it, rather than being like Sokka—already awake and waiting with a grim kind of focus for the day to break. Whatever Katara and Aang are up to, they better have the foresight to at least limit themselves to the cover of darkness. Though Sokka isn’t sure if he can even grant them that much common sense, because who the *fuck* masquerades as a spirit on the spirit’s own land to intervene in local affairs when you’re *supposed to be in hiding*.

And feeding Appa some strange fruit to make him seem ill? What if they *actually* made the air bison sick? Sokka doubts Katara’s Water Tribe healing education included an extensive course in Fire Nation botany.

Sokka thinks of Zuko and contemplates that it might be a bad thing to be feeling this calm when he’s aware that he’s also this angry.

“Shh.” It’s a near-giddy giggle. “We don’t want to wake Sokka.”

Sokka closes his eyes at Katara’s muffled voice and takes a deep, bracing breath, reaching as deep as he can for patience as his calm shudders around him.

“It’s a little late for that, Sugar Queen.”

“Oh!” Sokka opens his eyes at her audible surprise. “Toph! And, uh—Sokka.” Unmistakable guilt crawls over her face. “What, uh—what are you doing up so early?”

Sokka slowly raises his eyebrows, fingers stilled where they’ve been running over the rough leather of his wrist cuffs and the edge of scar peeking out from beneath. “That’s what you’re going to lead with?”

Katara flushes. “We were just on a morning walk…”

Sokka flicks his gaze over to Aang. “A nice romantic stroll through the night?” Aang muffles a sound dangerously close to a squeak.

“No! Just—”

“Or maybe a walk through a local center of industry. Taking in the sights?”

“We just—”

Something boils in his chest that might be anger or fear or hurt that she’s still acting like she can dodge this, like she can pretend she didn’t do anything wrong, and with a sharp noise of frustration he lashes out, kicking over Katara’s sleeping roll and scattering the blankets and hay stuffed inside. “Or maybe,” he says, the cold ice over his words belying the anger thrumming through him, “You wanted to find some more feed, since you found other uses for Appa’s. More local plant life for him to sample?”

Even Toph doesn’t touch the silence.

“I know you’ve been sneaking out at night,” Sokka says, feeling the ice begin to crack under the mix of hot fury and jagged fear churning in his gut. “I know you lied about Appa. I know you’ve been pretending to be the Painted Lady. Anything else I missed?”

Katara folds her arms and kicks at the ground.

“Aang? Anything to add?” Sokka feels fucking…ancient. Disappointed and despairing and like their fucking *dad*.

Aang looks petrified for the eyes to suddenly be on him. “Uh…”

“I hope it was worth it to go play dress up and call yourselves heroes,” Sokka says, barely restraining the urge to kick something else across the campsite, “Because you both put the *entire* mission in jeopardy.”

“Hey!” Katara exclaims, indignant.

“*What*, Katara?”

“I wasn’t—we weren’t—*you’ve* put the mission in jeopardy before, too! Don’t get on some high ostrich horse and act all—all—like you haven’t—”

“What, with Zuko?” Sokka snaps, too angry to feel bad about the way she flinches at his tone. “Yeah, I did. And I admitted it and I learned from it.” Though not well enough. Or maybe too well. “But you’re still doing the exact same vigilante *shit* like I haven’t asked you to stop. Like none of us are here with you! Because it makes *you* feel better. And you know what? We *still* don’t have time for any of it.” He glares. “So start packing.”

Toph is mostly packed, but she goes to her roll anyway, and Aang silently moves to gather up the cooking supplies. But Katara still has her feet dug in, eyes narrowed as she crosses her arms, jaw going set in a way that immediately makes Sokka’s temper spark in recognition. “It’s not about me,” she insists. “It’s about the people who needed our help!”

“Don’t lie to yourself,” Sokka says, furiously grabbing things for his own bag. “None of this wasn’t about what the village needed, it was about what *you* needed. You didn’t give a single thought to what happens to them.”

“That’s not true!”

“Oh yeah?” Sokka shoves his blanket into his bag so hard he hears a seam tear. “Everything you did is a short-term fix, Katara. Making them think some spirit is going to save them? When really they only have themselves to rely on? They’re going to think they did something to offend the Painted Lady when you’re gone, and they’re going to worry about appeasing her instead of fixing their own problems. And they’re going to waste what little they do have on some spirit that never cared in the first place, all because you couldn’t deal with the guilt.”

“But she did do a long-term thing,” Aang protests from where he’s bundling up his sleeping roll.

“What?” Sokka spits. “Single-handedly damaging the self-reliance of an entire village for the rest of a generation?”

“We got rid of the factory!”

“…You what?” He slowly sets his pack down, that numb disbelief creeping back over him. Sokka must have heard wrong. Sokka better have heard wrong.

“The factory,” Aang repeats, looking earnest and proud and unsure all at the same time. “It was the source of all the pollution that was harming the town. So we took care of it!”

Sokka can barely speak through the dread suddenly settling over his shoulders. “…What did you do to it?”

Aang snaps his mouth shut, uncertainty winning out as he registers Sokka’s tone, but Katara steps into the gap. “We thought long-term about more than just ourselves,” she says, tossing back her hair, defiant.

Sokka presses the heels of his hands to his eyes, like maybe that will help keep the scream in his chest. “Not. Enough,” he grits out. “Is it still standing?” He takes their silence as answer enough, mind cycling into damage control. “How many soldiers were there?”

“We didn’t get seen,” Aang assures him.

Fuck. *Fuck.* “That’s even worse.”

“What?” Katara frowns. “How?”

Toph’s words are crisp and sarcastic. “People who get their property destroyed tend to look for who did it.”

“And they aren’t going to think it was the fucking Painted Lady,” Sokka bites out. He doesn’t feel even a lick of satisfaction at the dawning horror on both their faces.

“We—we have to—”

“Do something?” Sokka cuts in. “You better. You’re the one who did this to them.” He finishes tying his bag closed and gives a quick glance over the bundle Aang’s made of their supplies, pausing when he suddenly thinks of all the food that had appeared in town the day before. “Where did you get the food and blankets and stuff you were giving them?”

“…The Fire Nation garrison,” Aang admits.

“…Shit balls,” Toph says, for once getting it perfectly right on the first try.

&#45;-

After a hard day of revealing all their secrets to an entire Fire Nation town that sits a casual walk from an entire garrison, all Sokka wants to do is finish cooking this non-deformed fish and eat dinner. That’s all. That’s it.

“I can hear you brooding, Snoozles.”

That’s truly, really, all he wants. Is to just…eat and go to bed and not have any disasters happen while he’s sleeping.

“If you don’t get it out, you’re not going to be able to sleep cause you’re still going to be brooding.”

…Fuck.

“And then you’ll keep me up with your tossing and turning and then I’ll be cranky tomorrow.”

Oh, Spirits.

“And we don’t want that, do we?”

“I hate you,” Sokka mutters, giving the fish he’s roasting a careful turn.

“You wouldn’t know what to do with yourself without me,” Toph says confidently, giving his ankle a kick with unerring accuracy. “I know Katara and Aang messed up, but at least the town ended up in a better spot than we found it, right?”

“I know,” Sokka sighs, shoving a hand through his hair. “And that’s great. Helping people is always great.”

“Your conviction is overwhelming.”

“Shut up,” Sokka grumbles, throwing a twig at her, and fuck, his heartbeat must be all over the place because she doesn’t fire a rock immediately back at him. “I just—Spirits, couldn’t I have all waited a few more weeks? We’re going to defeat the Fire Lord! Once we do that we can come back with a whole herd of waterbenders to clean the river if we want to.”

Toph cocks her head, looking thoughtful. “You think a group of waterbenders is called a ‘herd’?”

Sokka opens his mouth to continue venting about revealing themselves to an entire village, and announcing their location in the middle of Fire Nation territory, and then pauses. “Maybe if it’s a group of earthbenders.”

“A group of earthbenders if *definitely* a rumble.”

That works. “Waterbenders would be more…a swarm? A school?”

“What are they, fish?”

“What are you, the personification of sounds?”

“Point,” Toph allows with a shrug. “Okay. What are firebenders? A horde?”

“Eh.” Sokka doesn’t know a lot of firebenders, but Zuko and Iroh don’t exactly scream ‘horde’ to him. “A pack? An inferno?”

“Or,” Toph says, face lighting with a wicked smile, “What about a—”

Sokka never finds out what exactly put that look on Toph’s face—he’s not sure if he’s relieved or disappointed—because Katara chooses that moment to burst back into camp, with far more energy than she left it.

“Guys! You’ll never believe what just happened!”

“You blew up another piece of major local infrastructure?”

Katara ignores him, which is probably what the comment deserves. “The Painted Lady was just here!”

“Really?” Aang exclaims, whirling around where he’s been grooming Sokka. “What happened?”

Sokka chokes for air. “The—the spirit? Not your alter ego?”

“Yes, the spirit,” Katara rolls her eyes, grinning. “The real thing! I was just looking out at the river and she just—came up right out of the mist!”

Sokka scans her quickly for injury, for harm, for signs that she’s still herself, shifting to catch her eyes so he can look for anything lurking behind them. “Are you okay?”

“What’d she want?” Toph asks, shooting a sidelong look in his direction. Fuck, what is his heart doing right now? Because *he* can feel it stuttering and tripping in his throat.

Katara grins. “Just to say thank you, I think!”

“Huh, really?”

“Did she say anything?”

“*Are you okay?”* Sokka is distantly aware of the others flinching back from the sudden urgency of his words, but Sokka has eyes only for his sister, his chest tightening when she falls back a step in surprise. Is that normal? Katara is always so solid on her feet, would she give ground like that?

“I—yeah,” Katara says uncertainly, with the tone you would use on a spooked, half-wild polar bear dog as she searches his face. “She didn’t stick around long, or ask for anything…” Sokka checks the sky even though he already knows it’s too dark. Shit. “It’s too late to move.”

Aang’s words are careful, gentle, like Sokka’s the one acting unreasonably. “Why would we want to move?”

Sokka shoots him an incredulous stare. “Because there’s actually a spirit out here!”

“There has been the whole time,” Aang points out.

“Which means we’ve been in danger the whole time!” And Sokka doesn’t understand why he’s the only one who seems concerned about that fact.

“The spirits aren’t our enemies,” Aang frowns, the expression somehow looking even more serious when it’s under a bristly head of hair. “The human world and the spirit world operate in balance.”

Sokka shudders. “There is *nothing* balanced about the spirit world. We need to leave as soon as we can. At first light. We’ll wake up sooner so we can be packed and ready to—”

“Sokka, she clearly cares about her people,” Katara protests, confused. “She’s happy that we did something.”

“You don’t know that! You don’t know anything about her!”

“Spirits are easy to understand if you know what they want,” Aang soothes, as if ‘knowing what they want’ weren’t the whole problem in the first place.

“Snoozles, you’re pretty worked up,” Toph says, a surprisingly cautious observation for her, and one that Sokka should maybe take as his clue to calm down. Except he still feels like everyone else should be *much more upset*.

“Because I’ve dealt with more spirits than you!” He shouts, turning to Katara, hearing his own voice crack around his fear. “And I *never* want you to have to do that again. *Never.*”

“Sokka, it’s—it’s fine,” Katara assures him, exchanging a wide-eyed glance with Aang before taking a careful step forward, holding her hands out. “I’m fine.”

“Yeah, *this time*.” Sokka fists his hands into his hair. “What about next time? Don’t—don’t mess around with this, Katara. Don’t. Being a spirit doesn’t mean it’s *good*.”

“The spirit world—” Aang starts.

“Is filled with *terrible things*,” Sokka finishes, nearly pleading now. “Don’t draw its attention. You don’t want—Don’t do that again. Spirits, don’t do…any of this again.”

Sokka runs out of words, dropping his face into his hands and suddenly feeling all his exhaustion, suddenly feeling like he’s going to snap from the tension building inside him. Fuck, he can already tell, hours from sleep, that it’s going to be a bad night. Is this what Zuko feels like all the time?

“No more secrets,” he finally says. “*Please*. No more tricks and lies and going off on your own and assuming no one else will help without even asking first.” He forces his head up, catching Katara’s eyes. “No more planning without input. We’re a *team*. That’s what we said back on the ship, right?” He doesn’t know he can handle it if Katara was just saying it, if she didn’t mean it.

A snap from behind him has Sokka flinching around, hands flying to his weapons. He stares, nearly shaking with adrenaline as he takes in the fact that the flames must have weakened the skewer he made for the fish he caught for dinner, and in his distraction it's pitched into the fire, burning now directly on the logs. Sokka strangles a noise of endless frustration in the back of his throat and seriously considers that this fucking *fish* is going to be the thing that breaks him.

A sudden gust of air beats back the flames, and Sokka watches, frozen, as Toph stomps and sends the fish flying up on a nice clean little rock pillar, Katara dousing the fire that’s sparked in the grass from Aang’s bending. Sokka gapes at the perfectly roasted fish, speechless, then drops his face back into his hands, feeling heat prickling behind his eyes.

“Together,” Aang repeats, a vow and an apology and maybe a bit of a request, too, and Sokka makes a wordless sound of agreement as Katara’s hand drops onto his shoulder and squeezes her own quiet promise. Together, even when it seems like they’re all alone.

&#45;-

Zuko’s exhausted body finally drags him down into a doze some point after he curls up in his windowsill, though not for more than few degrees. In short order he slams his nodding head against the glass, jerking back out of his nightmares into a fuzzy wakefulness.

It was one of the new ones, where his mind shows him all the many ways everything could go wrong, as if Zuko weren’t already well aware of how thin the line is that he’s trying to walk.

Movement outside catches his attention. He can’t feel Agni the same at night, but it must be late judging by the sounds of the palace. He watches Azula slipping across the grounds. She’s dressed more plainly than her usual garb, moving with purpose, close to the shadows but not furtive. He flicks his eyes back in the direction she came from, toward Caldera, and firmly decides that he doesn’t want to know what she snuck out to do. It won’t be anything he would be safe knowing.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

Remember that time Sokka was traumatized like 50 chapters ago? Because his subconscious sure does!

## Chapter 5: Among Dragons

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

No particular warnings for this one!

### Text

“Hey, that looks like Zuko!”

Sokka nearly trips he spins toward Aang so fast, ignoring Toph’s muffled giggle as he scans for the familiar width of Zuko’s shoulders, then again lower just in case Zuko’s sitting, then a third time along the tree line because Zuko does like high places. He hesitates, then glances back over his own shoulder in the direction he’d been walking in ahead of the others. Nothing there, either.

They’d all been enjoying the opportunity to stretch their legs while giving Appa and their benders a rest on this cloudless day, but now Sokka’s chest feels like it’s full of bumble flies, excitement and shock and something that might be nerves beating a rapid pulse in his throat.

“I think he means that,” Katara says dryly, tilting her head toward a signpost Aang is examining at the side of the road.

Sokka stares a moment, considering whether he truly wants to let himself feel devastated over something like this, then pulls an exaggerated I-knew-that-shut-up face at her and hurries to Aang’s side. He takes in the flyers and notices plastered all over the post, not even thinking about feigning disinterest. Any hint of cool distance he could have claimed on the topic of Zuko went up in smoke a long time ago and they all know it.

His eyes flick rapidly over the layered notices, then again slower, seeing…nothing. “No, it doesn’t,” Sokka finally says, trying to push aside the tight kernel of disappointment lodged in his chest.

“Yes,” Aang insists, bumping his shoulder against Sokka’s to grab his attention. “That.” He points to one of the wanted posters in the only clear square of the message board. “That’s Zuko.”

Sokka blinks. “It says that’s the Blue Spirit. And to disregard the rumors that he’s a ghost.”

“That’s Zuko,” Aang says with total confidence. “He wore that mask to break me out of prison.”

Katara clears her throat. “It’s, ah…distinctive.”

“He wore a *mask* to break you out of prison?” Toph asks, before pausing as if just hearing her own words. “No, back up—the Fire Prince *broke* you out of *prison*? Was it a Fire Nation prison?”

“Yeah,” Aang shrugs, scratching at his hairline. “And I mean, he had to do something. He’s pretty recognizable.” That’s…one way to put it. “And I don’t think he was supposed to be there.”

“…No,” Sokka says, feeling a little numb around the edges. “He definitely wasn’t.”

Sokka ignores the others as Toph presses for more on Aang’s prison break, staring at the inked figure with its bristling tusks and exaggerated, ridged features. His mind drifts toward the way candlelight always played along the landscape of Zuko’s scar, to the way Zuko had looked slipping a blue mask over his face at that dance. To the fact that Sokka knows that Zuko is good at sneaking, but in a way where he almost absorbed the knowledge through proximity rather than any direct conversation. To the similarly slowly pieced together awareness that Zuko’s decision to stop stealing in the Earth Kingdom was a matter of ethics, not ability.

Sokka knows all those things, but somehow this particular part of it never came up. The part where Zuko ran—runs?—around the Earth Kingdom in an *opera mask* which…Spirits, Zuko would. He probably picked this particular opera mask for its symbolism, too, and stays in characters the whole time.

Sokka wonders if Zuko sees it as a character, and that’s why, in all their time together, Zuko never even referenced this very core, very visible, very *wanted by his own government* part of himself. Even though the kind of confidence and comfort in the guide that it would take to break Aang out of Pohuai Stronghold in a getup like that means that being the Blue Spirit couldn’t have been just a one-time thing. This was something Zuko *did.*

Sokka…doesn’t know how to feel about it. Part of him is hungry for the backstory, the part that’s eager to know every single thing he can about every single piece of Zuko and is nearly vibrating with excitement over the potential of getting to learn a whole new side of Zuko that Sokka didn’t even know existed.

The other part of him keeps tripping over the fact that this is a whole new side of Zuko that Sokka didn’t even know existed. A side that feels like a big part of Zuko, one of those things that might seem small on the surface but is huge underneath the water. Big enough that withholding it feels…significant, but in a way that Sokka isn’t entirely sure of yet. And can Sokka even rightfully call it withholding if Sokka never asked for any details? When he knows that Zuko isn’t exactly one to volunteer?

Sokka chews on the inside of his cheek, meeting the dark eyes of the drawing and trying not to flinch from the realization of just how many things there could be that he doesn’t know, things he would never even realize that he needed to ask about. Trying not to let his head spin too far with the idea of Zuko wearing Water Tribe colors like that, for who knows how long. Sokka had felt the significance of Zuko donning that blue mask at Jin’s dance, when Sokka put on red. But maybe for Zuko, it had been significant in a whole different way.

“Did you not know?”

Sokka startles, smoothing out whatever expression is on his face even though not turning in response to Aang’s question is telling enough on its own. “No,” he finally says, hearing the word come out flat and deciding that he doesn’t care to elaborate, or to look away from the poster just yet.

“…Do you want to keep the poster?”

“No,” Sokka sighs, finally stepping back enough to nominally be back in the conversation. It’s just a random ink drawing, really. You can’t even tell it's Zuko just looking at it, not unless you know. Which Sokka didn’t, even if now he does, and…Fuck. Part of him kind of does want it. The paper looks official though. Would taking it down be illegal? Does Sokka even need to care about that when he’s trying to topple the government?

Katara gamely jumps into the awkward, borderline brooding silence. “Should we go into town?” She nudges Sokka, giving him an overly bright smile. “It wouldn’t hurt to get some more rice and dried fruit.”

Sokka does a quick mental inventory of their stores, even though he knows she’s throwing out a blatant distraction. But Momo *has* been doing a number on their snacks, lately…

“And the town seems like it’s big enough that there might be some good shopping, too,” she adds on with an air of such forced casualness that it’s almost comical. It’s a transparent attempt to cheer Sokka up, and…Fuck it. Why not. Why not ignore the sound of Aang tearing a piece of paper off the signpost behind him and take what Katara is offering.

An unplanned, unscheduled supply run in enemy territory might not be the best idea they’ve ever had, but right now Sokka suddenly feels like he could really go for the distraction that comes with shopping. And if the trip goes entirely to shit like all the ones if the Fire Nation have so far? Well, that will be a distraction, too.

&#45;-

Sokka wonders if some malignant spirit has a direct window into his thoughts, because it’s starting to feel like the universe is taking his inner monologue as a challenge. A meteor landing right along the road? Right as they walked past? Needing their—well, the benders’— collective intervention? Sokka had thought that surprise parent-teacher conferences and run-ins with actual spirits were bad enough, but now he’s just vaguely astonished that there’s anyone left alive in the Fire Nation in the first place if this is the kind of thing that happens regularly.

Zuko didn’t exactly mention this kind of thing, so maybe it's not normal. Or maybe it's so normal that he never would have thought to tell Sokka about it. Maybe Sokka needs to explicitly ask about the incidence of meteor strikes and natural disasters, just like he needs to explicitly ask how many alter egos and aliases Zuko might go have out there.

Maybe Sokka is feeling hurt, that Aang was in on the secret when he wasn’t. Maybe Sokka doesn’t want to be around everyone else as he tries to figure out why Zuko wouldn’t have told him.

Sokka sighs, trying to blow out his frustration and concerns and the heavy discomfort of being particularly useless in the face of certain kinds of trouble and the low ache of missing someone he can’t rightfully expect to be here. He has rows of storefronts in front of him leading to the center of town, all calling for his attention, and Katara for once is encouraging him to dive in.

Sokka’s always loved shopping, even when he was little and it was just the excitement of figuring out what Gran Gran’s best skillet cakes might trade for this year on his birthday. It’s always felt so full of possibilities, bursting with what-ifs and anticipation and the thrill of victory at the end. It’s a feeling that somehow always manages to cut through the other noise in his head, even if it's just for a bit, the clean distraction of new things to discover.

And that sense of discovery feels even bigger and brighter than usual, being in the Fire Nation. There’s so much to take in that Sokka is desperately pretending he isn’t seeing with fresh eyes, so many things to note and carefully compare to Zuko’s behavior and letters and unvoiced expectations, even now his mind trying to parse the things that are uniquely Zuko from the things that are distinctly Fire Nation.

Like discovering that there don’t seem to be many awnings or stretches of shade in any of the towns they’ve gone through so far—is that because everyone is like Zuko here, constantly soaking up the sun? Or because people don’t generally congregate outdoors in this heat, which is brutal even in what’s supposed to be winter? Or something else entirely—to do with Agni, maybe?

Or discovering that this satchel looks amazing, even if everyone else keeps mocking it. Did Zuko ever say anything about Fire Nation craftsmen? There’s so much leather in Fire Nation armor---maybe it’s a particular skill? Or maybe this is just a really great satchel.

Sokka does crack a smile when they all discover how absolutely ridiculous Aang looks clanging around in a full suit of armor. Sokka can see at least three ways he’s wearing it wrong, on top of the fact that the concepts of ‘airbender’ and ‘armor’ don’t exactly live in the same place in his mind.

Sokka doesn’t bother commenting on it though, because the reason the satchel is the best find in just this half of the store rather than the whole shop is because the other half has *weapons*.

Sokka barely has names for all that’s on display, and he promptly loses himself in daydreams of actually knowing what to do with all of them, other than waving one in the general direction of his enemies. There are maces and flails, hooked swords that he refuses to touch, and dual dao that he can’t keep his hands off of. There’s even a boomerang, mostly ornamental judging by the filigree, and frames of ornate iron-tipped staves and a row of whips and crops and polishing oils and…huh.

Sokka looks toward the leather-goods half of the store and gives his satchel a second glance, wondering if this weapons and leather goods store might have another secondary business entirely.

Well. If there *is* something else being sold here then the Fire Nation is certainly much subtler about it than the Earth Kingdom—which feels…expected, actually—so Sokka shrugs and continues to peruse the offerings. He’s fascinated by the variety on display, the range and the quality that seems to go far beyond what he’s seen from Fire Nation soldiers. He thoughts the Fire Nation was all about firebenders, from the way Zuko had talked about it, but…maybe that’s just if you’re an Imperial firebender. Regardless of how good you are with a set of blades.

Sokka rubs absently at the ache in his chest, finding himself drawn over and over to a truly gorgeous sword. It shines almost blue in the early afternoon light, with great balance when he works up the nerve to actually take it off the wall and a grip that feels sized just right. It handles beautifully when he tentatively moves through one of the warmup sets Zuko had shown him, though it’s heavier than Zuko’s swords, clearly intended for two-handed use which Sokka doesn’t wholly have a feel for yet.

Sokka feels like he’s maybe halfway good enough to have earned the right to walk around with a sword by this point, and he would love to have this one. Which is…an intense understatement, actually. Sokka lusts for this sword with a near-sexual intensity that would… actually maybe not freak Zuko out, all things considered. But Sokka can tell without even asking that they could never afford something like it. Every line of this stunning, amazing thing screams ‘multiple years of annual income,’ when every single of Sokka’s coin purse shouts ‘what can I get for a winning smile.’

“Maybe we could trade some of that space rock for it,” Aang suggests, voice muffled as he tries to fight his way out of his helmet.

“I don’t know if there’s much of a market for space rocks,” Sokka sighs, glum even as part of him delights in the way the sword cuts through the air. He has more than enough practice in taking pleasure in the immediate moment while fully aware that the moment will end all too soon.

“Well, we won’t know until we try!”

The shopkeeper drifts over, maybe sensing the ‘ready to buy’ in the air, or else attracted by Aang’s eagerness and clanking. “Admiring our longsword? You have excellent taste, the best sword maker in the whole Fire Nation made that blade.”

“Oh. Wow.” This is *definitely* out of his price range, unless that space rock is full of gold.

The merchant nods agreeably, his enthusiasm warm and genuine. “We get them every once in a while at a special discount since he lives nearby. His training facility is just over the ridge, and he does his smithing there too. That one there is only one hundred gold pieces.”

Sokka hastily sets the sword back on its stand, anxiously looking for smudges or fingerprints on the blade. That’s the *discount*? That’s an astronomical—*ha—*sum. The shopkeeper smiles kindly as Sokka and Aang both take a wary step toward open space, hyperalert for any fragile displays they might bump into. Sokka appreciates not being sniffed at and hustled out for not having money, and he consoles himself that the contents of his coin purse and a winning smile—and maybe his clear disappointment—end up being enough to purchase his perfectly lovely satchel. Which Sokka is still excited for it, even if—Spirits. Even if he’s pining over a sword. Over a fucking *sword.*

Sokka might have more things crossed and tangled in his head than he realized. Though maybe it’s just a general attraction for bright, dangerous things.

“The sword maker lives nearby?” Katara asks, putting some extra emphasis on the words. “Right nearby? Just over the ridge? Where he trains people? And makes swords?”

“Yeah,” Sokka sighs, casting a wistful glance back over his shoulder toward the shop.

“Maybe we could visit. Or something.”

He twists back around to look at her, half-startled, half-confused. “…Why?” He strokes an absent hand over his satchel. The leather is buttery and smooth and soothes the pang of longing away a little bit at a time.

She makes a little noise of exasperation. “You could go—learn? Or something?”

“…Learn sword making?”

“I mean, okay, well. What about training? You could train?”

“I can’t just—you don’t just *walk* in on a Master,” Sokka says, unsure why exactly Katara seems to want him to go there so much. Is she—shit, is she still worried about him? Spirits, how devastated did he look at that fucking signpost…And regardless, it’s not like Sokka has an invitation, or even knows the man’s name.

“Yeah?” Toph as all over the hint of hesitancy in his answer. “Why not?”

“What’s the worst that could happen?” Katara adds, giving him a bright, encouraging smile.

Sokka opens his mouth to list all the terrible possible outcomes, starting with dismemberment and ending with crippling embarrassment, then pauses. He glances between the greatest earthbender in the world who taught herself by imitating badgermoles, and the last waterbender of the South who literally punched her way into an education, and the last airbender who has never *not* just walked up to a Master and asked to learn in his entire life. “…Fair enough.”

&#45;-

Sokka is astonished that he even makes it past the skeptical wall of a man that answers the door of the castle—a real-life fucking *castle on a mountain—*let alone that he makes it to an actual interview with the sword Master. Piandao, he reminds himself, desperately repeating the name over and over. Spirits, what if he calls him the wrong name and gets thrown out? He had mostly been expecting some kind of touristy thing, a brisk walk through a model forge that ends with getting dumped into a gift shop, not to actually be *talking* to the guy!

“What’s your name, son?” Piandao asks without looking up from his calligraphy, something that’s maybe meant to be an insult, if he can judge anything by Iroh, except Sokka can’t stop being impressed by how straight the man’s back is.

“Uh, Sokka.”

Piandao somehow manages to convey a single raised eyebrow without ever looking up from his brushwork.

“It’s a family name,” Sokka blurts out in explanation, immediately regretting it. Spirits, that’s…worse? He does so much better with a backstory prepared ahead of time, but he hadn’t bothered because he hadn’t actually expected anything. And Wang Fire, Colonial transplant and disapproving father, doesn’t have a military background that would explain his familiarity with weapons.

“Master Sokka,” Piandao says slowly, and Sokka hides a wince. That reminds him of Iroh at his most neutral-but-letting-you-consider-the-full-weight-of-your-pai-sho-error. “What have you brought me to prove your worthiness?”

“I, uh, didn’t realize…that I was supposed to do that…” And he doubts he could afford it, anyway, not unless the Fire Nation puts a lot more value on a winning smile than Sokka thinks they do.

“Hm.” The Master dips his brush into his inkwell with a sharp, tight flick of his wrist. “Let me guess: You are the best swordsman in your little hamlet on the mountain, and you decided that you deserve to learn from a Master because more often than not you can knock down the other four kids your age.”

“There wasn’t really anyone else my age,” Sokka mutters, tugging on his top knot. He had a few months with Zuko but Spirits, does that ever feel brief right about now. “But yeah, I’d like to learn from a Master. All of my friends…Well. I’d like to learn what I can.”

“And what makes you think you deserve it?”

“Uh…”

Piandao sighs. “Do you even have any training?”

This is not going well, Sokka can already feel the rambling trying to burst out of him. “Well, I learned the club and boomerang and spear growing up, mostly. And then I did some staff work for a couple of months, and some hand to hand. And I got…informal tutoring, I guess, in some sword basics.” Spirits, that sounds even worse outside his head. Maybe he should have spent less time letting himself get distracted by how beautiful Zuko looked with a sword in his hand. “I don’t need you to tell me it’s a hodgepodge. I know I’m probably not the caliber of student you usually take on. I mean, I only know, like, half of a dao, but I’d—I want to learn. I would try really hard.”

Piandao sets down his brush, finally turning to take Sokka in for the first time, sweeping him with an expressionless glance that gives nothing away. “Half a dao, hm?”

Sokka fidgets with the cuffs on his wrist, wishing he had his wraps to retie for something more to do with his hands. “Yeah, I—yeah.” He wouldn’t exactly call what he did with Zuko formal training, but he also doesn’t want to admit to the best sword maker in the entire Fire Nation, who trains people in a castle on a mountain, like something straight out of a story, that they were just fucking around.

The Master gives him an excruciatingly long stare before suddenly rising smoothly to his feet. “It would be a shame to leave one half of a pair unmatched.”

Sokka…feels like that was a bit on the nose. Between this and Katara…does he really give himself away that obviously?

“Come,” Paindao says, striding away without apparently needing any reply. “Show me what you know.”

Sokka gapes before scrambling to catch up, Piandao moving surprisingly fast for all he seems to just be gliding beneath his robes. It makes Sokka feel like he’s bumbling after him, but he shoves that thought aside to be embarrassed about later and accepts the practice sword the doorkeeper offers him, only bobbling it a little. He ignores the man’s little eyeroll—wow, rude, he’s allowed to be *surprised* by all this—and turns to see Piandao twirling his own wooden weapon with the kind of casual ease that makes it clear how deeply out of his depth Sokka is.

Piandao’s face is calm, voice soft but somehow filling the space. “Begin.”

Sokka throws himself into the bout. He can tell before he even launches his first strike, purely from the way Piandao holds himself, that he’s going to be so much more than inadequate. But Sokka isn’t supposed to be perfect, he’s supposed to be here to learn, so he sets aside his uncertainty and wracks his brain for every little twist and block and stab that Zuko ever half-showed him, even daring a few of Zuko’s flashier moves and nearly stumbling when he braces himself for a blow that never lands, Piandao stepping back with a frown instead of pressing his advantage.

“I thought you had a ‘hodgepodge’ of training,” the Master says, a kind of neutrality on his face that Sokka can tell is just this side of disappointment.

“Yeah…”

The single raised eyebrow is visible now, and scathing. “Then why are you acting like you only know half a dao?”

“…Oh.”

Sokka takes the moment to catch his breath and reset his brain, then throws himself back into the bout without waiting for Piandao to signal to start because the value of surprise is one of the first lessons Sokka truly learned. Instead of thinking about fighting with a sword in his hand, Sokka channels that afternoon of blowing off steam with Zuko back in Ba Sing Se and thinks about fighting with a length of wood, and his two hands and two feet and anything else he can think of.

Sokka isn’t expecting to win, but he’ll make it as hard for Piandao as possible, no matter how unconventional he has to get. He darts around the room, forcing Piandao to chase him, using his body to block blows he would need to dodge if their blades were real, leveraging the advantage of surprise and unpredictability until he can barely lift his arms. Finally, his sword clatters to the floor as Piandao lazily swipes it from nearly numb fingers, only the Master’s deliberate step backward stopping Sokka’s uncoordinated lurch toward the practice sword from turning into a full-on dive.

“Enough,” Piandao says, giving Sokka a long, critical look. “It’s…a start.” That…well, Piandao’s tone is more promising than the words on their own. “You have the one thing that can’t be trained, it seems.”

Sokka perks up even as he heaves for air. “A sword master’s instinct?”

Piandao gives him a dry look. “Creativity.”

&#45;-

Zuko nearly smashes his teacup in the middle of a meeting with the Junior Minister of Education—who *cannot* get to the point—when he realizes that he fucking *misses* being surrounded by tea. Not serving it, or making it, or needing to sample it. But he’s suddenly deeply aware of how having all that heat rising and dissipating and moving around him allowed him to play idly with his bending, to work off energy and nerves and anything else, in a way that’s a lot harder when suddenly all he has is stone and torches. Sure, he could lose himself in testing out the heat retention properties of different veins of marble throughout the palace, but even Zuko can tell that isn’t exactly subtle.

Zuko looks up when he suddenly registers the silence, catching the edge of a half-disapproving, half-uncertain expression on Minister Izo’s face. Right. Zuko’s supposed to be acting like he’s a competent and balanced individual.

Zuko takes a deep breath and waves the meeting onward, letting the fire in the room flare a bit with the gesture because why not, competent and balanced doesn’t have to mean ‘mild’ too. Izo clears his throat, smoothing his face back to neutrality and continuing on with his meandering explanation of why maintaining the quality of the Fire Nation education system requires replacing the literary arts for older students with more history and math.

It’s drudgery, blatantly so, something that a secretary should probably deal with and likely meant as an insult in a not all that backhanded way. But Zuko does his best to pay attention anyway. The Fire Lord had said that Zuko needed to relearn from the ground up, and Zuko isn’t trying to make waves yet to protest something that’s blatantly true.

Besides, for all that the conversation is ridiculous—Izo doesn’t actually want or need Zuko’s support, and they both know Azula won’t give Zuko the time of day if she hasn’t already decided to what she thinks—Izo will support General Shun’s position in the conversation over infrastructure repairs. It isn’t worth offending the man, and risking pissing off Azula, not when sentiments are split enough that a Junior Minister’s opinion matters in the first place.

And maybe Zuko doesn’t need tea and heat, to burn his distraction and constant anxiousness away. It’s an inner fire, after all. And the Fire Nation is always so pleasant full of flammable things.

Zuko tears the ink-splattered bottom off his notes, tucking the scrap of paper into his free hand and letting his inner flame slide outward. It pools in his palms, a familiar sensation by now, and its easy habit to split his attention between an idle bit of bending and the task in front of him. His brush moves smoothly over the page as he calls his flame to life and holds the shred of paper on the edge of burning but never letting it truly ignite, until his inner fire finally settles into rhythm with his even breaths.

&#45;-

It turns out that training with Piandao is nothing like training with Zuko, which…good, actually. Sokka doesn’t know if he could function if it was similar, for a number of reasons.

After an art lesson and a digression into calligraphy—Piandao had been vaguely satisfied with Sokka’s abilities in both, which did wonders for quieting Sokka’s questions about how, exactly, they related to swords or combat—they’re finally doing something more like Sokka expected.

Fat is calling out steps and forms while Piandao presumably assesses Sokka’s performance, or maybe his ability to actually know what anything Zuko showed him is called. Sokka isn’t entirely sure, because he’s blindfolded, supposed to just react and keep his balance and *feel* whether his execution is right or not. Which…fine, the room has mirrors on three walls, but whatever, Sokka can see the point. There won’t be mirrors around in a fight, or a distracting firebender at his back nudging him into the correct position.

Fat calls for a bending crane fish which Sokka, in retrospect, recognizes as one of Zuko’s more complicated moves from a more advanced kata. The only reason he knows the name to go with it is because Sokka spent so much time trying to drag an explanation out of Zuko of what, exactly, he was supposed to do. But in the moment Sokka just reacts, throwing himself into a low lunge and up into the spin and landing with the twisting slash and managing to correct his balance with only a moderately large wobble.

“…Huh,” Fat says, instead of another move.

“Interesting,” Piandao comments from somewhere to Sokka’s left, thoughtful. “Watch your under-rotation next time.”

&#45;-

Ty Lee pauses in the middle of tossing the snare for Gao to dive down on, ignoring the messenger hawk’s annoyed screech as he glides back up out of his preemptive dive. “Did you *want* to join Azula for firebending training?”

Zuko snorts. “Don’t be an idiot,” he says, not looking up from the flame he’s bouncing from a patch of grass to a weed to an errant flower and back to grass in front of them. “It doesn’t suit you.”

&#45;-

Sokka is *starving* after a full day of hard training, collapsing into something that could generously be called a pile as his legs give out halfway toward the cushion instead of settling him neatly onto the seat. Whatever. Fat and Piandao have both seen him doing significantly less graceful things, today.

Sokka arranges himself comfortably cross-legged and eagerly takes the bowl Fat passes over. Sokka would eat just about anything right now, but he grins to see cold noodles, with an array of toppings and add-ins already on the table. It’s the kind of meal Zuko always tried to push on him after training, one that apparently transcends borders, and Sokka sets about making it the way Zuko always did for him, focusing on the food and ignoring the wallop of nostalgia and longing and fondness so strong that it makes his eyes prickle.

He hums happily around the first bite, the explosion of flavors and starch and umami and spice exactly what he’s craving after a workout. He’s so hungry that it takes him multiple bites to register the stillness at the table. He looks up around a mouthful of noodles to see Fat and Piandao staring, freezing a moment before hastily setting his bowl down onto the table and guiltily swallowing. Shit, is it rude in the Fire Nation to eat before your Master? Sokka’s never had a Master before, he has no idea. Fuck, is it rude everywhere?

The other two don’t exactly seem put out though…Piandao in particular looks more thoughtful than anything else as he twirls his chopsticks slowly through his bowl, which looks…way different from Sokka’s. Shit. Is he doing some blatantly not Fire Nation thing with his toppings? Except it’s how Zuko does it, Sokka’s watched him do it enough times to know.

“Interesting,” Piandao finally says with a little shake of his head. “Eat, eat. You will need your strength.”

&#45;-

Zuko sits with Mai on the little balcony attached to her rooms, finally managing to do something reasonably close to relaxing away from the watchful eyes of the court and letting the lingering heat of the day seep into him from the stones below, blanking his mind until everything in him seems to just unwind. He plays idly with the dessert spoon he somehow managed to never put down after dinner—Mai had given him a confused look, when he asked for dessert—and the metal is warm from the air, from the food, from his touch in a way that Zuko’s fire sense can’t stop sliding over, lingering around, testing the edges of.

“Tell me something,” Mai suddenly orders, the demand softened slightly by her idle tone.

Zuko drops his eyes from the slowly darkening sky and the way the lights of Caldera are already bright in the shadow cast by the crater’s walls. “Tell you what?”

“Whatever,” Mai shrugs. “Something about the past four years.”

That’s…broad. “What do you want to know?”

“What do you want to tell me?”

Zuko sighs. They could do this forever, waiting for the other to be the first to break, to admit something, and Zuko doesn’t have the stamina for this like he used to. He sorts through all the things that come immediately to mind—hunger and hiding and boredom and desperation and Sokka and Jet and Lieutenant Jee—before finally settling on, “In the Earth Kingdom, they’re putting on dramatic plays with ballads between the acts.”

“...What,” Mai says, with the kind of flatness that means she’s horrified.

“They say it’s a new experimental style.’”

“Did you *pay* to see that?” Mai sounds like she’s about to throw him out if the answer is yes.

“Of course not,” Zuko snorts. He snuck in and sat in the rafters. But he still tells her all about it as he plays heat idly through the metal in his hands until it folds gentle and soft to his touch.

&#45;-

Even knowing that Piandao is a Master sword maker on top of being a sword Master, Sokka is still shocked and delighted to find out that he’ll get his very own custom weapon at the end of his training. Especially when he clarifies that he does, in fact, need to leave soon, and Fat just stares and replies that all students leave with a blade.

“All my worthy students do,” Piandao clarifies, which is even more thrilling. “Suited to their needs and abilities.”

Sokka is flattered by the idea that he has *abilities*. “And I get to pick the materials?”

“Yes,” Piandao cracks a smile at Sokka’s unconcealed excitement. “A true sword Master should know his weapon, not just carry it.”

Sokka can get behind that. Sokka can *so* get behind that. It makes the part of him that always insists on knowing how things work feel stupidly happy as he wanders through the neat storeroom of materials, appreciating the straightforward, basic nature of the workspace in the otherwise rather ornate training grounds. There really must be good money and prestige in skill with the blade in the Fire Nation than Sokka expected. It makes Sokka’s chest hurt a little, thinking of the good it would probably do Zuko to find himself to a place like this.

Sokka runs his hands over the bars of iron and lumps of ore, weighing the sample blades, testing out the leather strips that would wrap the grip. “Is it all about the metals?”

Piandao hums in a way that Sokka has learned to recognize as approving. “The metals, but also how you work with them. There is the heat you use to melt them down, how you work the blade to build strength and edge, even how you quench the blade when you are done.”

Sokka makes an absent sound of acknowledgment, his mind suddenly spinning through everything Toph has ever said about metals and everything Zuko has ever said about heat retention and melting points. He remembers with a kick of misplaced desire—save that for *much* later*—*Zuko’s swords dripping with fire. An idea is forming in his mind, but none of the options here seem *right*.

“Can I bring my own metal? Or do I have to use these?”

“…You have raw material on hand?”

“My friends have…something.” Sokka waves vaguely in the direction that he thinks the base of the mountain is.

“Interesting,” Piandao murmurs, shaking his head. “Very well. Don’t take too long to get it. You are on a schedule, after all.”

&#45;-

Azula’s hiss is low and biting as she comes up on his left side, pacing him perfectly despite his longer strides away from the council room. “If you don’t want to be there—”

“I do,” Zuko cuts her off, equally low and refusing to turn around as the proximity of her contained-explosion inner flame presses against his heat sense, spread wide and strung tight with his agitation.

“Don’t try to lie to me, *Brother*.”

Zuko sighs, correcting himself. “I need to be there.”

Azula tsks, but doesn’t press, accepting the words. “For the Fire Nation?”

“Of course,” Zuko says, throwing her a glare for the implication.

Azula knows him too well for that, though. “For the Water Tribe?”

Zuko grits his teeth, snapping his gaze forward again and letting his silence turn icy.

“Water is next in the cycle.”

Zuko is more than aware of what comes after air.

“It would be a shame,” she says thoughtfully, testing, “For the Avatar to fall by your own hand, and have that be what erases what’s left of your little peasant’s homeland.”

“It would be,” Zuko agrees softly, inner fire skating just under his skin.

Azula hums, looking…pleased, almost, finally falling back and peeling away at the next intersection and ignoring Zuko’s warning like she always does.

&#45;-

Sokka comes back with the space rock, grinning through his panting—Toph might have done most of the work, but he still *helped*—as Piandao raises an eyebrow and takes in the hunk of stone and metal.

“How’s this,” Sokka asks, shoving loose strands of hair out of his face. He still isn’t used to needing to gather up the edges, along with the top.

“…Interesting.” Piandao glances at the size of the rock, then down the winding mountain path. “That…should do.”

&#45;-

“Where are you going?”

Zuko glances in the mirror to see Azula lounging in the doorway of his room like she usually does, breezing in without warning or asking as if there’s no boundary between things that his and things that are hers. Which Zuko has learned in fourteen years of knowing her that there aren’t. In her eyes, there are only things that are hers and things she doesn’t care enough about to claim.

“Mai and I are going into Caldera,” Zuko says, keeping half an eye on her as he goes back to fastening his boots.

“…Oh?”

Zuko gives her more of his attention, wary of that pause, as he tucks a coin pouch in his belt. “Yes.”

Azula's face is still in a way that is very un-still. “I guess you know how to take someone out, now.”

Agni’s balls, but Zuko is tired of dancing around this with her. “Azula…”

“Focus on what you want to, Zuzu,” Azula interrupts, straightening her cuffs with a sharp jerk. “Just remember that this is a Fire Nation noble, not a Water Tribe—”

“Watch it,” Zuko snaps, reacting to the venom in her voice without thinking—*stupid, stupid*. He braces himself for her retaliation but she just snorts, rolling her eyes and turning to leave with as little regard as she’d shown in arriving in the first place.

“If someone is going to lead you by the dick,” she tosses over her shoulder, ignoring his shocked “*Azula,” “*Then it might as well be Mai. Don’t fuck it up, Brother.”

&#45;-

Sokka is delighted that his space sword came out with such great balance and that the metal seems to have the right mix of rigidity and barely-there flex to keep it from being too brittle. Though he does find himself wishing it was maybe a tad less awesome, because Piandao is wielding it against him right now and Sokka is fighting for his fucking life.

Honesty, as it turns out, is not always the best policy when it comes to revealing your true origins and trail of deception to a Fire Nation weapons master. Sokka makes a note to be concerned, later, about Zuko’s chronic inability to lie.

Sokka scrambles along the perimeter of the room, hurling practice blades and throwing down weapons racks haphazardly behind him to try to keep Piandao at a distance. He finally reaches the stately floor-to-ceiling openings that he would call windows if there were any glass. Thankfully there isn’t, and Sokka can throw himself outside without needing to worry rolling through shattered glass, coming to his feet with a gasp and letting his momentum carry him forward across the paved courtyard, making for the manicured gardens.

Piandao is taller so Sokka does what he can to limit the Master’s reach in the shrubbery, yelping as the blade slices through leaf and branch and flowers with barely any resistance. A good edge, on that blade. Fuck. Piandao is agile and quick, so Sokka tries to choose ground that’s as uneven as possible, knocking down his own branches to add some additional chaos —which earns him a crushingly calm “interesting.” Piandao’s a Master of the sword, so Sokka throws a handful of rocks into his face and breaks for cover—which earns him a *laugh* and an “interesting.”

Sokka is going to lose, he knows it, and all he can hope is that Fat cleans up the blood and his body before Katara comes looking for him. She doesn’t need to see another family member cut down by a Fire Nation blade.

*Please*, he thinks as he jumps on top of a planter and then onto a retaining wall. *Don’t let this* *be the thing that lets the Fire Nation win*.

Please let the others be able to get on with him. They know the plan, they know what to do. Sokka did the work to come up with it, he doesn’t *have* to be there to see it executed. Please let them keep that in mind, that there are things more important than just one life. Will Toph have the foresight to keep them on track? Or the influence to at least make Katara and Aang’s vengeance quick?

Would any of them think to find a way to tell Zuko?

He stumbles to level ground, aware that he’s at a disadvantage here more than ever, that he’s running out of space. Spirits, Sokka has mostly made his peace with the fact that he might end up, through no intent of his own, being the weak link that takes the team down. But he never thought it would be quite like this. Fuck, there’s no way the Fire Nation won’t know exactly where the Avatar is after this, and Sokka’s heart gives a stutter he can ill-afford as a wild corner of his mind wonders if that’s all Zuko will ever know—that the Avatar went into a rage, and that Sokka never tried to find him again.

Sokka sets his feet as Piandao slows now that Sokka’s thoroughly hemmed in, casually stalking forward. He almost wishes that the Master would just get it over with and make it quick, because Sokka certainly doesn’t have the ability to just stop fighting. Instead, he keeps *pausing* all the fucking time, and letting Sokka get away, and saying ‘interesting’ instead of ending things, his favorite fucking word and what the *fuck* is so interesting about it.

The moment finally comes that Sokka’s known has been hurtling closer, the moment when he has no tricks left but the ones he’s already used, when his own tired legs betray him over the deceptively uneven ground. Sokka trips backward and Piandao glides in as smooth as death, the dark-bladed sword sucking in the light as it whistles through the air to stop a bare inch from Sokka’s throat.

Sokka stares at the metal, frozen, waiting. He slowly, agonizingly, manages to drag his eyes up the length of the blade, over the guard and Piandao’s relaxed grip—fucking textbook, so *that’s* what Zuko was always trying to show him—up the smooth line of Piandao’s arm to his face which is…thoughtful? And vaguely…approving?

Piandao steps back—is this man a *sociopath?—*and Sokka scrambles to his feet, bracing himself to go hand-to-sword which…has to have only rarely ever gone well for the ‘hand’ half of that matchup. But Piandao just flips the sword into the air instead of swinging it, catching it by the blade and presenting it, hilt-first, to Sokka along with a small bow. “You have made a fine weapon, Master Sokka.”

“…What.” What the *fuck*.

“It is a unique blade for a most unique student,” Piandao continues in the tones of someone commenting on the nice weather for walking, today. “Well earned.”

“…What.” Is he…is Sokka *not* about to die?

Piandao looks amused. “It is yours, Sokka, no last name, of the Colonies.”

The last is with no small amount of sarcasm, and Sokka belatedly remembers that the Fire Nation does last names unless you are nobility, which Sokka so thoroughly is not. Maybe he didn’t need to come clean about anything after all. “Uh…”

There’s the ghost of a smile on the Master’s face as he inclines his head. “The art of the sword belongs to all nations who would have it. Including the Water Tribes.”

“…Oh.”

Piandao’s face is neutral, but his tone is distinctly sardonic as he says, “One might suggest not using one’s real name, or letting one’s companions openly use other kinds of bending, if one is traveling with the Avatar and doesn’t want to be recognized.”

“…Right.” What…is happening. How does—did Sokka mention Aang? Did Piandao see him helping with the space rock?

Piandao presents the sword again, looking increasingly amused, and Sokka finally unfreezes enough to take it, part of him expecting some elaborate trap because, well…Piandao seems to like dramatic, elaborate things. The Master easily hands over the sword, though, and part of Sokka marvels at the weapon even as he continues to be freaked out and not entirely certain that he isn’t going to die. Is Fat waiting to jump out of a shrubbery at him?

Sokka would be better prepared to defend himself with this in his hand, though. The sword feels like it was made for him, which he supposes it was. He runs his finger along the blade, unscratched and undulled despite the bout, turning it in the afternoon sun and wondering how it would take to fire.

“It is a good blade,” Piandao says, tone serious. “I look forward to seeing what you do with it, *Master* Sokka.”

Sokka blinks, thrown, wondering if he imagined that extra emphasis that seems to suggest…“Thank you, Master,” he finally croaks out, clearing his throat and sketching his own half-bow without fully taking his eyes off the other man.

Piandao accepts the words with a rather stately nod, beckoning Sokka to join him as they start moving back toward the castle. Aiming for the window Sokka jumped out of, it looks like, and he isn’t quite sure how he’s supposed to take that.

“You will need to be continuing on your journey,” Piandao observes, pulling Sokka back into the moment.

“Oh, yes—yes.” Spirits, how much does Piandao know about *that*? Is the man some kind of mind reader?

“Fat will have your things ready to go.”

“Right. Okay. Yes.” It all feels rather abrupt, Sokka’s hands still trembling with adrenaline, his heart still aching with thoughts of Katara, and Aang, and Toph, and Zuko. But they *do* need to get moving to get back on schedule. They’ve made up some of the time they’ve lost, but they still have less wiggle room than Sokka would like. And Sokka supposes this was a rather…*final* way to conclude his training. Spirits, is it this dramatic for everyone? Or did Piandao do it just for him, for some reason?

“I would ask one last thing of you, as you go on your way,” Piandao says as they step inside, straight-backed and gliding as ever when Sokka feels like he still isn’t sure if his legs work.

“Yeah?”

“I would ask, if you see a mutual friend,” Piandao says, voice level as Sokka trips at the words, nearly impaling his own foot. “That you remind him that the dual dao are not meant to be separate.”

Sokka gapes, fumbling utterly without finesse to keep his grip on Space Sword in his shock. “Um—I—Okay? Sure.”

Is…is Piandao talking about who Sokka thinks he is? Did—did Sokka just get relationship advice from a random old man? Or rather, did *Zuko?* Which…fuck, which would mean that Piandao *knows* Zuko. Knows him well enough to tell that Sokka knows him, too. To recognize some element of Zuko in his training? Or shit, in his fancy calligraphy, or his food prep, or his half dao, or his knowledge of the heat retaining properties of metal…Fuck, Zuko is everywhere. But for Piandao to see that would mean that Zuko must have trained here, before leaving the Fire Nation, which means…

Sokka clutches Space Sword a little together to his chest, suddenly feeling overwhelmed. Spirits, there’s so much more to Zuko’s past than they ever touched. Sokka knows so *much*, but it feels like he keeps running up against how little that still is, in the grand scheme of things, like every new thing he finds out just highlights how little Zuko gave him. How little Sokka thought to ask after, because he thought he knew. Because he didn’t realize there was anything to even ask a question about.

Spirits, does everyone feel this way when they’re trying to learn another person? Or is Sokka just experiencing every new revelation of his ignorance like a sharp stab somewhere in the center of his chest because he can’t stop himself from thinking that if he can just figure out how Zuko works, what made him how he is, what compels him to act, if he can just *understand*, then somehow Sokka will be able to figure out a way for Zuko to stay, next time, and be happy about it. Or a way Sokka could stay, and not have to leave.

Sokka casts his eyes around the training hall, seeing the space with fresh eyes and trying to picture Zuko here. And it's more than easy to conjure an image Zuko, like it rarely is, to see him here, scowling and training and giving everything he has to each task Piandao would have set him with completely, earnest determination. Maybe because part of Sokka has felt the echoes of Zuko in this space the whole time he’s been here, in mindset and theory and training until you drop. Did Piandao train Zuko the same way, with art lessons and surprise bouts and—

“Has your training style changed?”

Piandao glances back at Sokka’s abrupt question, pausing to allow Sokka to catch up to him again as they reach the entry foyer. “My training style is unique to each of my student’s needs.”

Sokka nods, trying to keep the unease off his face as he reshuffles his grip on Space Sword. All of this worked for Sokka—the blindfolds and the surprises and the weird seeming-tangents. And Sokka might not know everything about how Zuko was trained, but he knows enough. Maybe it was just the firebending, that drilled into Zuko the need to get everything right on the first try. But Sokka doesn’t like the lingering implication that Zuko might have *needed* the succeed-or-suffer approach that seems to have been such a core part of his education.

&#45;-

Zuko stands in the hall of portraits, one of the few corridors in this part of the palace where the sun still streaks in, that wasn’t closed decades ago for security. His hands are clasped in a loose parade rest behind his back despite his lack of armor, hair perfectly in his topknot—he can tell from the way it tugs on his scalp—holding his face carefully impassive as he looks at the painting of his family from ten years ago. Father, mother, sister, and him on left-hand side of the throne, grandfather in the center, Uncle and cousin on the other.

Only seven of them, even then. Such a small number, but so large compared to what they are now.

It would normally be time for a new portrait, with the children grown and fashions changed and inheritances usurped. Zuko is vaguely surprised that the Fire Lord has allowed this one to hang, with its suggestion that Iroh was Azulon’s favored son.

He desperately hopes no one suggests an update, with Zuko returned to the palace. None of the advisors would, at least not until they’re more sure of how Zuko’s presence reshapes things. Agni’s tits, until they all see whether Zuko lasts long enough for his presence to matter in the first place. But Azula might toss out the idea, just to be a bother. To force Zuko to publicly accept a place on their Father’s left, or to fight the issue.
