But even she would only do it if she thought their Father would appreciate the opportunity to play power games in front of an audience that has to pretend not to see them.

A flicker at the edge of his heat sense has Zuko suppressing a grim little smile. Think her name and she will come. Azula’s contained blast of an inner flame is heading toward him, likely cutting across the hall of portraits on her way to the training grounds on the far side of the palace.

It’s a long hallway, so there’s plenty of time for her to see him, for Zuko to stand unmoving as she walks in silence toward him. Plenty of time to brace himself for her to pass. She pauses a beat, hovering behind his left shoulder because she does that at every opportunity, to the point that Zuko almost expects her to be there now.

“The picture of a perfect family.” The words are low, barely crossing the space between them.

A scoff. “You can’t burn it.”

A considering silence. “Not yet.”

&#45;-

Sokka feels practically giddy as he finally reunites with the others, grinning so wide his face hurts as Toph makes a show of admiring Space Sword and playfully threatens to bend it into a more useful shape. At least, he hopes it’s playful. He has one arm around Aang’s shoulders as the airbender eagerly asks about his lessons, and he can’t stop laughing at the way Katara is trying to plan twice as many stops into their journey for training so they can all see what he learned.

Sokka is trying to insist that they need to get back on schedule and get going, his authority thoroughly eroded by Momo pulling apart his hair, when a shout has them all spinning toward the mountain path. Sokka reaches for Space Sword as Toph slides into a bending stance, his gaze finally finding Fat running toward them, a bag in hand, waving as if they’re about to take off when Appa isn’t even saddled yet.

“Wait,” the man calls, seeing that he has their attention. “Wait!”

“It’s fine,” Sokka says, gesturing at them all to relax and lowering his sword. “He’s Piandao’s assistant.”

“He doesn’t look like a swordsman,” Katara frowns, hand still hovering near her waterskin.

Toph cocks her head to the side. “He sounds like one.”

Sokka…will follow up on that later.

“You left before I could pass everything along,” Fat says as he gets close enough to not have to shout about it, sounding significantly less out-of-breath than Sokka expected.

“I have the sword and my bag,” Sokka says, glancing down to confirm. He hadn’t brought much, and it had all been waiting for him by the door by the time he and Piandao got there.

Fat’s mutton chops lift with his amusement. “Traditionally students are also sent on their way with supplies for the journey, rather than just what they brought on their backs.”

“Oh,” Sokka says, trying to shrug Momo off his shoulder so he can shoulder the offered sack instead. It doesn’t work, so he passes the bag to Katara. “Right.” One more thing he had no idea about. Is this just a Piandao thing? Or a Fire Nation thing, an offering of resources in exchange for…what?

“The Master also had a gift,” Fat says, smiling as Sokka touches Space Sword. “Other than that.” He presses a much smaller bag into Sokka’s hand, turning with a wave to head back up the mountain.

“Thank you!” Sokka shouts after him, a little bemused by…honestly his entire time with Piandao. He hopes they can get some time on Appa-back soon, because he really could use some space to just think.

“It was nice to meet you!” Aang adds.

“What is it?” Toph says, getting to the point as always. “What’d you get?”

Everyone crowds around curiously, Katara making happy noises over whatever she’s finding in the supplies, as Sokka opens the little bag and pulls out a length of fine silk.

“A scarf?” Aang asks.

“Uh…” Sokka lets it unravel, trying to understand what about this, specifically, is for him. The fabric unwinds like liquid in the light breeze to reveal, nestled at its heart, a pai sho tile. Just one. A white lotus tile, specifically. The kind of that Iroh always made such a point of commenting was rare and not found in many sets whenever he happened to play it.

…Oh. Fuck.

“What’s that,” Aang asks, as if he doesn’t even notice that the world is suddenly rearranging itself around him.

“What’s going on,” Toph asks with significantly more urgency, because if Sokka can suddenly hear his own heartbeat tripping and pounding then he’s sure she can, too.

Sokka can’t even begin to find the words to explain, though, even as she begins casting around for threats. It feels like seemingly disconnected pieces and bits of knowledge are suddenly lighting up in his mind, like he’s only just now seeing the strands connecting them all. It’s the kind of leaping series of assumptions and associations that usually goes along with too much caffeine and too little sleep, a string of conclusions that Sokka would never be able to reason and logic his way into. But once he’s there, no matter how he turns it, he can’t find a way to break the web apart.

His mind flicks through Piandao’s home, where the lotus symbol was in the floor tiles and wall hangings and teacups. He jumps to after-dinner games with Iroh where the conversation touched on the war and the paths of nations with what now feels like surprising frequency, considering the audience and the occasion. He lingers over Zuko’s offhand comments about international pai sho partners and grumbling stories of plans gone awry in pursuit of a missing tile. He spirals to the center of it, to a Crown Prince banished and a former Crown Prince, cut from the line of succession and joining him in exile. And the best swordmaker in the Fire Nation, the best sword Master, the kind of person that might be tapped to train a Prince.

…Shit.

Sokka suddenly—weeks and weeks and weeks too late—thinks he understands why Zuko was always so fucking twitchy around pai sho. Spirits, what is Iroh *doing?*

Sokka thought it was bad enough that Zuko went through so much nominally on Iroh’s watch, but this…for the first time Sokka truly thinks he might understand why Aunt Wu referred to the Imperial family as a nest of dragons. What kind of environment would cause someone to use a child that way? Would turn a family against itself like that? What upbringing would plant in Zuko that deeply rooted, only once-voiced fear that Azula won’t make it to adulthood? Spirits, what kind of upbringing would produce *Azula*? And also Zuko, who seems so straightforward and incapable of guile, and who Sokka is slowly coming to realize might habitually withhold as much of himself as he can get away with, without ever seeming to do so.

Sokka can feel the pai sho tile biting into his hand as he clenches his fingers around it, unable to stop the surge of adrenaline and fear tightening his grip. What would it be like to be a kid in the kind of web shining in his mind’s eye, the kind of web Sokka desperately hopes he’s wrong about? Fuck, to be at the *center* of that web? He feels a dawning kind of horror when he realizes he can’t even begin to grasp it, that the extent of what he doesn’t understand about Zuko might be truly unfathomable, so much more than Sokka ever suspected and so much more fundamental to who Zuko is than Sokka would ever want for him.

What would it take to survive if you grew up with dragons instead of family? Is there any way to survive it, except to become a dragon yourself?

Sokka feels cold down to his bones, a surge of heart-wrenching sympathy for Zuko’s childhood chilled against the suddenly real-seeming possibility of Zuko’s ability to lie and manipulate just as well as with the rest of his family, and what that might mean for all the things Sokka thinks he knows.

## Chapter 6: In the Blood

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Some warnings for what could maybe qualify as body horror in this one (It's the Hama episode...)

### Text

Katara is far too good at Scary Story Night for her own good. Or maybe for everyone else’s good, considering the escalating squeaking and cringing happening around the campfire. She somehow knows just where to put her face relative to the flickering light to make her expression that much more ominous, just how to pitch her voice to make foreboding crawl over your skin. Even when Sokka knows how the story goes—he always knows how the story goes when it’s her turn to share, it never *helps*—he can’t stop the way his heart rate picks up, the way his fight-or-flight always takes a hard swing toward fleeing.

“And when Eska got back out of the storm, her village rejoiced, for she was alive and well when they had thought her lost,” Katara says, drawing out the pauses to make the usual cadence of the tale stretch and fill with nervous anticipation. “'How did you survive in such a terrible storm,’ they asked her. ‘Why did you go out alone?’

“And when Eska said ‘I wasn’t alone, I was with Desna,’ everyone looked confused and asked who Desna was. Was it her polar bear dog? A new Spirit of the frozen plains? And when Esksa said ‘No, Desna is my friend, Desna is my twin born of a different mother under the same moon, Desna sleeps next to me by the fire every night,’ the village whispered about ice madness and showed her the space where her empty bedroll was laid out, alone.” Fuck, Sokka hates this part.

“And Eska mourned and wept in her heart, because her hair still bore the braids Desna had woven for her, because her hands still knew the feel of chafing Desna’s by the fire after a long day’s work, because her ears still remembered the sound of shared laughter. But Eska stayed silent.” Katara lets the words hang for a moment, heavy. “For she also remembered a sudden storm, and her own carelessness in leaving her home in anger without her best parka, and Desna’s kindness to share. And the temptation to stay warm just a few minutes longer.

“Maybe,” she says, sweeping her gaze around the circle, her hair swinging forward to curtain her face in shadow, “It was better that no one remembered Desna but her. Maybe it would be better if Desna had never been there at all, just a dream of Eska’s mind, because dreams can be left behind on the ice when moon twins cannot.

“But—if you walk out on the ice and listen in quiet for the wind to howl, they say you can still hear Desna’s voice calling out, waiting to this day for Eska to come back, waiting for his moon twin to fulfill her promise and bring him home from the ice.”

Sokka throws another log into the fire in the ringing silence, and he does *not* let out a relieved breath when the sudden flare of light turns Katara’s face from some spirit-touched creature back into his little sister.

“That part’s not true, right?” Aang asks, tugging on his headband. “That’s just part of the story. You’ve never heard that, right?”

Katara’s grin is wicked, and Aang should know better by now than to give her an opening like that. “I don’t know, Aang. Sometimes when you’re out there on a clear night, and the wind is—”

“Alright, alright,” Toph breaks in, crossing her arms as if she wasn’t just shivering along with the rest of them. “It’s Snoozles’ turn, before you give the Avatar a heart attack.”

“Sure,” Sokka snorts, like his own pulse isn’t still pounding. “Once, there was a band of friends trying to travel through an enemy land. They were on a special quest, but at every turn, they were chased by an assassin who could shoot fire out of his head, so that none of them were safe wherever he could see them. But the oldest of them was a strong, brave, warrior and he took it upon himself to—”

“Okay, okay,” Toph says over his tale. “Enough of that.”

“That’s not a real scary story, Sokka,” Katara says, rolling her eyes.

“It was scary enough for me at the time,” Sokka says dryly.

“Yeah, because he kept chasing you.”

“Which is still weird, by the way,” Toph mutters.

Aang grins. “I didn’t mind!”

“What can I say,” Sokka says, making a show of straightening the cuffs on his wrists and doing a little gratuitous flexing in the process. “You can only hide my true genius for so long, before they realize that you guys wouldn’t make it off the ground without me.”

“Sounds like a nice story to tell yourself at night,” Toph says, flicking a stone across the fire that Sokka doesn’t pretend misses him because of his own skill. “Maybe practice it in your head before you share it.”

“I’m sorry, did we not just listen to your rendition of the third Earth Rumble championship —”

“*Fourth.”*

“—Oh, well in that case—”

“And I think it’s Aang’s turn now!”

Sokka huffs but sits back, ignoring the fact that Toph is huffing and sitting back in exactly the same way—Spirits, they spend too much time together—and making a show of giving Aang all his very attentive attention.

“Alright, this one’s a classic,” Aang says, face alight with anticipation as he wiggles forward into the light. “Once, in the not so distant past, there were two girls. They both wanted the most beautiful pair of dresses in the shop, but they had no money and nothing to trade. ‘We could get a job’ said one girl, but the other said ‘No, that will take too long.’ So instead, they set up a rigged gambling ring and committed insurance fraud, and—”

“Hey!”

“Over a *dress?”*

“—ended up in prison where there were no beautiful clothes at all.” Aang easily ducks the handful of leaves Katara hurls at him. “And they screamed for their friends to come save them, but—”

“But their friends were being chased by a Fire Nation assassin shooting firebolts out of his head,” Sokka says, voice dry.

“*But*—they had sought gains through underhanded means,” Aang finishes, airbending his own pile of leaves toward Sokka, which is just *rude*. “And though it pained their hearts, they —”

Toph straightens on her log. “Does anyone hear that?”

“What, the sound of Aang laying down some Air Nomad judgment?”

“No,” Toph says slowly, face serious enough that Sokka immediately tries to swallow his amusement and focus. “The screaming.”

Sokka blinks. “The…screaming?”

“…Like the girls in prison in the story?” Aang tries.

“Like a bunch of people are screaming somewhere over there,” Toph says, gesturing toward the trees behind Aang. Aang gulps and scoots closer to Sokka’s side of the fire.

“Come on, Toph, knock it off,” Katara says. “Mysterious screaming in the woods during scary story night? You did that two weeks ago.”

“Maybe do ominous footsteps next step,” Sokka suggests, relaxing back.

“Fine,” Toph says, audibly annoyed. “Because I hear that, too.”

Sokka twists to follow her pointing finger, halfway through an eye roll when he makes out a human-like shape in the darkness. He jerks back, sliding off his log in surprise and alerting the others with a very manly shriek.

“What the—”

“Ahhh!” Aang dives toward Katara.

“Told you,” Toph says, arms crossed and face annoyed even as she rises into a bending stance.

“My apologies, children,” calls an unexpectedly warm, unexpectedly human voice, and with a rustle of underbrush, a…really old woman steps into the light of their fire. “I saw your fire from the road. I didn’t mean to frighten you.”

She smiles to match her voice, and in the light, Sokka can see that the oddness of her silhouette comes from the yards of fabric draped around her. He wants to relax, but first… “You’re not a ghost, right?”

“I’m not,” the woman assures him, amused and holding out her hands as if to demonstrate her humanity.

“Aang,” Sokka checks. “She’s not a ghost, right? Or a spirit?” Aang shakes his head, still huddled against Katara’s side. “Oh, thank the Spirits,” Sokka says, collapsing back in relief. The last thing any of them needs is more Fire Nation weirdness, especially this late at night.

“My name is Hama,” she says. “I couldn’t help come over when I noticed your camp. We don’t have many travelers around here these days. Can I offer you a warm place to stay? The nights can get cold at this elevation, it’s no place for children.”

Katara speaks up before Sokka can protest that descriptor. “That’s kind of you, but we wouldn’t want to impose.”

“Nonsense! I have an inn, there’s plenty of room. Besides, I couldn’t live with myself if something happened to you out here by yourselves.”

“We can handle ourselves,” Sokka says. Sure, they’re all a bit jumpy from scary story night, but they haven’t exactly had adult supervision in…a long time. And they’re doing fine. Right?

“I’m sure,” Hama agrees with a twitch of her lips as she takes in how he’s still sprawled on the ground. Unfair. “But people have been disappearing in these woods recently during the full moon. I would feel better if you were safely within my walls.”

Sokka shoves himself up onto his forearms. “Disappearing?”

“Yes,” Hama says gravely. “The entire village is quite distraught.”

Well shit. Sokka glances across the fire to the others, wondering why he even bothers checking in. The dual offers of a warm bed and a localized mystery are just the right mix to entice the whole team. This really is right up their particular distraction alley.

“Okay, then,” Aang says, straightening and giving a little bow. “We would be honored.”

Sokka wouldn’t go quite that far, but he’s certainly curious. And he’d already budgeted a whole day for their supply run, given how those seem to be going in the Fire Nation, so it’s not like they don’t have the time to poke around for a bit.

&#45;-

Zuko startles a little less hard when the servant slips into his room this morning. It’s probably because he’s already dressed this time, instead of scrambling for his shirt or still tight with anxiety from rushing through shucking his sleep pants so as not to get walked in on. But part of him would like to believe that it’s because he’s finally…adjusting? Becoming more comfortable? Agni, is it even a good thing if he is?

Maybe not, but at least Zuko won’t risk lighting this woman on fire every time she walks in. This time he only flinches hard enough to drop his boots, and now they’re doing that awkward staring thing that makes up most of their mornings, where both of them clearly want to apologize and neither feels they can.

Today she’s the one to finally break first, tentatively clearing her throat and dropping into a deep bow. “My apologies, Your Highness, for being late again. It is not my intent to neglect my duties.”

“No, it’s…fine. It’s fine.” Zuko says hat to her…often. “You’re—I don’t actually *need*—”

“Your Highness!” She’s so aghast that she actually interrupts. Zuko…thinks that’s a good sign? As long as she doesn’t do it in front of anyone else. “It’s my *duty*.”

“Uh. I guess…”

Her face goes firm, face losing the shadow of uncertainty it so often has around him. “It is my honor to serve the blessed of Agni’s line.”

Zuko clears his throat, shifting awkwardly. “Okay, well…”

She nods, sharp. “I will be here earlier tomorrow, Your Highness,” she resolves.

Zuko sighs and resigns himself to getting out of bed even earlier so he can be dressed when she shows up. “That’s…fine.”

He puts his head down and finishes putting on his boots, trying to shrug off the way her bustling around and straightening his space sets him ever so slightly very much on edge. He knows that there’s nothing here that’s truly secret—at least not that she or anyone except maybe Azula would recognize—and he knows that it *is* normal for one of Agni’s line to not be expected to handle the mundanities of making beds and tidying dressers and gathering laundry. But Zuko hasn’t tolerated anyone who doesn’t already hold a measure of his trust in his space since the day he barred the door on the *Wani* when the pain finally lessened enough for him to shave his own head. It’s not an easy habit to break.

There’s no space in the palace for thinking about times when he was weak, though, so Zuko shoves away the memory and offers the woman a brisk nod on his way to the door, his shoulders itching as he keeps going instead of turning back when she drops her armful of laundry in surprise. Trying to help won’t actually make it go faster for her, with the way she will get agitated by a Child of Agni doing something so base as picking something up off the floor, and Zuko can’t afford to be late *and* flustered by the whole thing.

He slips onto the training ground only a step or two behind the others despite the delay, which is enough to earn him a pointed glance but not a comment. It’s a sparring day in Azula’s training schedule, so it’s a sparring day for everyone, and the warmup is quieter than usual as everyone falls into their own ways of focusing.

Zuko is trying to appreciate having another firebender to train against again. Azula, unsurprisingly, doesn’t make it easy. She doesn’t know what it means to hold back except as a taunt, and Zuko still needs to consciously think about adhering to the standard forms. Needing to actively remember what he can and can’t do before actually doing them is just the kind of hindrance Azula pounces on, and is just the kind of thing that leads to sideways glances from anyone who just get yet more confirmation that Zuko is still far outmatched by his little sister.

Zuko is resigned to the way it works against him by now—he can grit his teeth and tell himself it’s just practice, and he knows how to ignore sideways glances like he knows how to breathe—because he can’t *not* think about it. Because even with active though, sometimes Zuko still forgets.

It happens past the usual hallway point in their training, when even Azula is starting to show signs of exertion. She slashes out twin arcs of flame, precise as a textbook, and Zuko throws up his own Caldera Standard perfect shield. Except instead of shoving out to reflect it back, he lets his heat sense suck *in*, Azula’s blue fire somehow getting *wrapped* in Zuko’s shield, not entirely his but not entirely hers anymore either in a way that feels like stepping on a nest of beetle ants with bare feet, except over his entire body.

Zuko instinctively shoves the whole mess of it outward and away from himself, but he can’t dissipate the flames in the middle of a bout, and he only has a bare heartbeat of relief before the shield collides with Azula’s next punch of fire in a way that shudders across his fire sense like slamming his elbow against the edge of a table, all tingly numb not-quite-pain.

It must do something to Azula too, not that she would show it, because the only explanation is that neither of them quite have a handle on their fire—that neither of them can kill the instinct to never let their flames die when they might still be needed—as the sheets of flame slide and shudder and *tangle,* superheating as both Zuko and Azula wrench the wrong way for control of the fire, and then combusting *outward*.

Zuko barely has enough time to suck and redirect the heat of it before it hits Mai and Ty Lee, and not nearly enough time to keep him and Azula from getting blasted off their feet. Azula isn’t even down for a breath, though, before she’s shoving herself upright, pristine armor streaked with dirt. “What the *fuck* was that you incompetent—” A chunk of hair falls into her face and she claws it back with a snarl. “A Colony *hack* could do better than that sorry excuse for a—”

“Maybe if you could *control* yourself,” Zuko snaps back, staggering to his own feet. “Agni’s flaming dick, I’ve met *toddlers* with better heat control than you!”

She lets out an animal noise as they square off, both of them singed and glaring through their straggling hair from opposite sides of the training ground, fire crawling back over the packed earth from where it was flung to gather at their feet, pooling and building, heat rising, the flames climbing higher and higher, not even Mai or Ty Lee daring to intervene, then—

“Was that really necessary?" The words are maybe mocking, maybe truthful. "That hurt.”

“Hurting is what makes you strong.”

Another tense heartbeat of staring, then they both let out what can only be called a cackle, Zuko finally dispersing the flame and thoroughly ignoring the way Mai and Ty Lee suddenly edge away from *that* rather than the fire.

&#45;-

Hama joins them for their shopping trip the next day, nominally to show them all the right shops to go to but really because she seems to inexplicably delight in Katara’s company. Sokka does agree that they seem to be getting along swimmingly, to use Hama’s words— Toph rolls her eyes so hard that Sokka wonders if they can fall out, but *he* thinks it's clever— so he leaves the shopping list to them and tags along with Aang and Toph to explore the local rumors.

The villagers talk about disappearances during the full moon, about people going into the wood and never coming out again, and then never coming back from the edge of the forest, and then walking the pathways through the trees that used to be safe but apparently aren’t anymore, the danger creeping closer and closer with each full moon until it reaches the very edge of town.

“My family has lived here for generations,” one woman confides, shaking her head as she deftly arranges bundles of flowers into paper-wrapped bouquets. “I don’t know where I’d go, I don’t have family elsewhere. But how can I stay if I can’t know that even staying inside will keep my daughter safe anymore?”

“Do you think they did something to make Yue mad?” Sokka wonders as they reconvene over warm buns. This kind of vengeance doesn’t seem entirely her style, but she wasn’t exactly a fan of the Fire Nation even before they attacked the North…And he must be spending too much time with Aang if he went to Spirit-stuff, first.

“Maybe one of the local spirits,” Aang says, eyes watering from the spice. Sokka still gets a kick out of that, even distracted by a mystery. “The full moon could just be a timing thing, not the reason.”

“Or bandits,” Toph suggests around a mouthful of bun.

Sokka eyes her sidelong. “You sound way too cheerful about that.”

She shrugs. “You get to knock heads around if it’s bandits.”

Fair point. And it *would* be nice if it was a nice human threat like bandits for once, one that you knew you could smash with a boomerang or threaten with a sword.

“Interrogation time?” She asks, polishing off the rest of her snack, and Aang coughs his way through his last mouthful and nods his agreement. Sokka bites back a laugh, wondering if Fire Nation food really changed *that* much in the past hundred years or if Aang never had a tolerance for spicy food to begin with. Another question to add to his list for if—*when—*he sees Zuko again.

They spend the rest of the morning gently interrogating the villagers, hopefully without being too obvious about it, because even though it might be a lost cause Sokka isn’t ready to give up the commitment to at least *trying* to be inconspicuous. And after Ba Sing Se they’re all far better than they should be at getting information out of people without making it clear what they’re after—even Toph knows that ‘*What did you do to piss off the local supernatural* *wildlife and/or band of miscreants’* probably won’t go over well.

Good as they are, though, no matter who takes the lead in the conversation or what angle they take, nothing the villagers have to say seems the least bit out of the ordinary, or even particularly supernatural.

“This is weird,” Toph mutters.

“I don’t like it,” Aang says, and Sokka grunts his agreement. At this point, he’d even take secret pollution the village doesn’t know about upsetting local spirits. He doesn’t *want* it to be some spirit mumbo jumbo situation, but the more and more they come up with absolutely nothing beyond the fact that there are, indeed, disappearances happening, the sketcher and sketchier Sokka is starting to find the whole thing.

&#45;-

Azula leans over during a break in this ‘working lunch’ that features more work than lunch, taking the opportunity the Fire Lord’s brief absence provides to hiss into his ear, “Whatever you’re fucking around with, leave it alone.”

“What?” Zuko only jerks a little in surprise, tossing her a half-hearted glower of confusion.

“Get your hands out of your fucking pockets, Zuzu. You’re an embarrassment.”

“I’m not—”

She cuts him off with nothing more than a disdainful look, words scathing. “Do *not* make people start wondering what you’re doing beneath the table, Brother.”

Zuko flushes and glares for real at that, but he forces his fingers to uncurl from the little ball of metal in his pocket that used to be a spoon, drawing his heat sense back in as he shoves his fire sense out where it’s supposed to be.

Azula grunts in satisfaction, straightening back in her seat as murmuring from the hallway heralds the Fire Lord’s return. Zuko keeps his gaze on the table even as Councilors and Ministers and Generals begin to file back into the room, gritting his teeth and refusing to meet anyone’s eyes until he knows that the redness is gone from his face. Azula has a way with words, as always. And a way to prodding right to the itchy, restless feel of his inner flame. Fuck, at least they’re going to finish this endless meal with tea.

&#45;-

Zuko should have known that looking forward to tea would betray him. It’s an opportunity to sink into his heat sense and breathe and level out of heartbeat, to burn away the way his entire body wants to shudder at being in this room, to get his back to a wall and everyone away from his left side.

It’s also, apparently, an opportunity for Azula to idly—he could scream at the pretense of that —pour tea from one cup to another instead of drinking it. Over and over, back and forth, the sound of water splashing, sloshing, breaking against the sides of the stupid, useless, fancy metal cups a constant melody over the low roar of fire.

Zuko wants to scream, wants to bolt from the room, wants to ignite his hands to remind himself that they aren’t numb with cold, wants to boil the tea right out of her cup even though it would only make her pour out more, probably staring him down again with that smirk on her lips.

He transfers his glare from her cup to her face—she isn’t even fucking *looking* as she pours which means she fucking *practiced*—in time to catch the end of an assessing look, her tawny eyes as sharp and piercing. Agni, Zuko *hates* feeling seen.

&#45;-

“So…” Aang’s voice is fully awake despite the late hour, the three of them sprawled on Sokka’s bed with the lights still blazing. “Did anyone see that one coming?”

“Definitely not me,” Toph says.

“Can’t say I did,” Sokka mutters. Hama being a lost Southern Water Tribe bender is…a total curve ball. He didn’t see that coming in any of his contingency or backup or just-in-case-things-go-to-shit plans.

“I can’t believe we found an actual Southern waterbender in the middle of the Fire Nation,” Aang says, sounding some mix of awed and dumbstruck still. Sokka sympathizes. “It’s amazing how these things work out.”

Toph makes a thoughtful noise in the back of her throat. “She’s got to be pretty good to escape the Fire Nation in their own land, right?”

‘Pretty good’ is probably selling her far, far short. “It’s a pity she never came back home.”

Sokka can feel Toph’s shrug through the mattress. “Sometimes you change too much for home.”

Aang sighs. “Sometimes home changes too much for you.”

Toph kicks Sokka in the shin with way too much accuracy this far off the ground. “Would you go back home? If you were in her shoes?”

“Yes,” Aang says immediately, but Sokka takes a moment to really try to consider it, to try to imagine what it would be like to be imprisoned so long, gone for so long, and suddenly have freedom again. Trying to take that feeling of leaving Zuko’s ship and magnify it by years and years and years.

“I think so,” he finally says. “Maybe I’d feel like I had things to settle here first, figure myself out or whatever, but…I’d miss it. The Fire Nation isn’t so bad once you get past the whole, you know—”

“Crazy imperialist thing?”

“Yeah, that. But I can’t imagine never seeing snow again.” Or eating foods that feel like sixteen years of memories, or seeing the stars with the piercing clarity that even the most cloudless nights in the Earth Kingdom and Fire Nation can’t seem to match.

“Lots of water, though,” Toph observes. “All the islands must be nice for a waterbender.”

“True. I wonder how she managed to hide for so long.” Sokka can’t imagine Katara concealing her bending for more than a day or two. It’s just such a part of who she *is*, and it boggles Sokka’s mind again that Zuko lasted as long as he did in Ba Sing Se. Sokka doesn’t know if he could do it even without bending, hiding who he is like that with no end in sight.

But then, Sokka knows that captivity takes people in different ways. He certainly isn’t going to judge how anyone reacts in the aftermath, even if part of him can’t stop imagining what could have been different if they had a Master waterbender for the raids.

“So,” Toph finally says into the contemplative quiet. “Think Katara is ever going to join us?”

“Tonight?” Didn’t she see—or hear, whatever, it’s an expression—how excited Katara was to talk to Hama? “Probably not until we’re already asleep.” Aang lets out a huge sigh and Sokka refrains from teasing, because it really isn’t the same without Katara there to get worked up. “Would *you* pass up the chance to talk to some lost Beifong bending master?”

Toph scoffs at the idea. “Like they’d deserve the title.”

“But you’d still talk to them before knocking them down a peg.”

Toph considers it for a moment. “Words would be exchanged first,” she allows. “But I can’t say that there’d be a lot of them.”

“Hey,” Aang says, blatantly changing the subject from Katara’s absence, “If we’re staying an extra day…”

“We are,” Sokka confirms. He already checked the schedule to make sure it would work. He isn’t so heartless as to pull Katara away from not only her first glimpse of Southern Water Tribe traditions but the first teacher who hasn’t treated her with open contempt. And he isn’t going to make Katara feel like she has to ask for it, either.

“Then we can figure out what’s going on with the disappearances, too,” Aang decides, cheer filling his voice again.

“Sounds like a plan,” Sokka agrees, wondering if they can really manage to solve the whole thing in one day when the villagers must have been trying for months now. But then, they’ll need something to keep them busy tomorrow, and maybe all this puzzle needs is a bit of new perspective.

&#45;-

“I don’t get it,” Aang mutters to his lunch, openly frustrated as they settle in a nice little clearing partway between the inn and the village.

Sokka glances up from his own food and hastily swallows his first very delicious bite. “So you see, you take the noodles and minced vegetables and whatnot, and you put them into the pancake thing, and then—”

“No, the—I’ve *been* to the Fire Nation before, Sokka,” Aang says, taking a pointed bite of a very neatly rolled pancake while Toph snorts out a laugh. “I *meant*, I don’t get what’s going on with the missing villagers. They all seem great, all the nature around here is great, there’s no disharmony…”

“Maybe—and just consider for a moment—maybe the local spirits are just jerks.”

“I’m still holding out for bandits,” Toph says, seeming to delight in wiping her messy hands on her tunic.

“There were no tracks or anything, though,” Sokka reminds her.

Toph shrugs, unconcerned. “We still have to talk to that one guy who escaped.”

Sokka hums, considering. “You’re thinking accomplice?”

“Let’s not decide anything before we talk to him,” Aang cautions.

“Fine. But I’m still thinking it,” Toph says as she polishes off her lunch in a bite so massive that reasonably she should be choking. “Hurry up and eat, we’re burning daylight here and you sighted people seem to care about shit like that.” Sokka rolls his eyes at the enthusiasm with which she finishes her sentence but obligingly turns back to eating. He doesn’t need to be told twice.

&#45;-

Sokka keeps his voice low as they hover behind Aang, listening in to the very polite, very earnest questioning. “We still thinking accomplice?”

“I don’t judge based on appearances,” Toph says, but even the joke lacks conviction. Even without sight, Old Man Ding’s trembling voice and creaking steps must paint a clear enough picture.

“And you never saw the spirit,” Aang presses.

“No, no, never saw it,” Ding confirms. “But I felt it! A terrible feeling,” he adds with a shudder, which proves that he’s a smart man, even if he’s not the local contact for a ring of bandits that Sokka was expecting.

“Wow,” Aang breathes, all wide-eyed fascination. “What happened?”

“I felt compelled! I couldn’t control my body, not one bit.”

“Like you were scared?”

“Scared,” Ding snorts. “I’ve fought in the war, son! I’ve seen too much in my life to be scared by that. No, it was like I was possessed. Something was making me walk to the mountain.” Toph jerks a little, and Sokka shuts up, paying attention now that they’re getting into details. “I couldn’t stop no matter how much I fought it. I almost went right into a cave! But just as I would have been dragged into darkness forever—” Old Man Ding has a knack for storytelling. “—Agni rose into the sky, and I was saved from the evil by his purifying light.”

“A cave?” Toph says before Aang can formulate his next question. “Under the mountain? In that direction?”

“Yes,” Ding says, glancing in the direction she points, which must seem normal to him except Sokka is wondering how she even knows what she’s pointing at. “Away from the path through the pass, and toward the old abandoned mines.”

…Spirits. “Old abandoned mines,” Sokka repeats, just to make sure he heard that correctly.

“Yes, those,” Ding nods. “They haven’t been used in generations.” He pauses to consider a moment. “There are lots of stories about them.”

“I’m sure,” Sokka mutters. Fuck, why does everything in the Fire Nation have to be so *creepy*.

“Thank you for your time, sir,” Aang chirps, quickly ending the conversation, half his attention clearly on Toph’s sudden vibrating urgency.

Toph barely waits for them to get out of the old man’s earshot. “That’s where the screams were coming from, two nights ago. That direction.”

Aang blinks in surprise. “Those were real?”

“Yes,” Toph says, crossing her arms. “I told you guys what I heard.”

Aang chews on his lip, glancing toward the mountain peak. “The villagers?”

Sokka takes a deep breath, looking toward the darkening sky and reflexively checking his weapons. “There’s only one way to find out.” They’ll need to be fast about it, though. It’s a full moon tonight. Spirits, he hopes Katara and Hama will be safe.

&#45;-

Zuko is grateful for a number of reasons when a storm rolls through Caldera that night, covering the full moon and turning the sky to black except for the flow of firebender-held torches and flashes of coming lightning. He wasn’t sure if it would actually break, had been feeling it for hours and hours at the edge of his awareness, hanging out over the sea, boiling and roiling and building and making all the stronger firebenders in the palace more restless and short-tempered than usual. Which none of them exactly need.

The wind had finally shifted after dinner, though, and the storm had shifted into motion with it, crawling over the island with an approaching wildness that Zuko can already feel trying to slide into his veins. He’s kneeling on his window seat, sword and polishing cloth in hand as if he needs to pretend to himself that he’s doing anything other than pressing up against the glass and watching the rain come. It hasn’t reached the palace yet, but Zuko can see it faintly hazing the lights along the ridge of the caldera. Soon.

Zuko doesn’t turn when he hears his door open just as the first drops of rain hit the glass. Azula pads over with familiar steps, moving in near-silence outside her armor but still loud against his heat sense. He shifts to make room without taking his eyes off the coming storm, and she takes her spot at his side without speaking, as if there’s still as much space for two bodies here as there used to be, as if there hasn’t been a storm since Azula was old enough to wiggle away from her nurses that she hasn’t spent at his side.

It feels just like when they were kids, except not at all. Because Zuko’s heat sense is different now, and so is his fire sense. Because where storms used to just be fascinating, captivating in a way he couldn’t explain, now Zuko feels them in his blood and in his inner flame. Because lightning used to be far above them, and now it’s Azula’s to master, and Zuko’s to play with.

He only has a half-second to give toward trying to hold himself back from greeting the storm before the first peal of thunder rumbles over the palace and Zuko’s inner fire is leaping in response. He manages to keep it underneath his skin, just, not fully cutting loose. But he can still feel the electricity coalescing around him, can see the way lightning breaks toward the family wing of the palace more than anywhere else, can feel his breaths matching the pulse of that wild power wanting to twine with his inner flame.

Zuko is used to bright, skipping Earth Kingdom storms that race over open plains, wholly unconstrained. He’s used to the half-crazed feeling that there’s no difference between sea and sky out on the ocean when the waves get big enough and the rain falls hard enough.

This storm is a different thing, slow and serious and deliberate, weighty, and Zuko might be able to hold his inner fire inside against it, but he can’t resist the energy sliding over and beneath his skin. Zuko wishes he were on the roof, or at the top of Iroh’s prison tower, truly inside the roiling intensity that presses against his chest so hard he feels like he’s being shoved away from the glass, that tugs insistently for him to open himself up to its power. But this is good too, in its own way, feeling that barely contained wildness outside himself and within himself and at his side all at the same time.

Even without letter his inner flame out to greet the storm the crackling potential in the air soaks into his skin, seeking his inner fire, and his inner fire flows and curls in response. The almost-visible vibration in the air slips down Zuko’s throat with each inhale, pooling in his stomach before leeching into his bones, singing along his nerves until he feels like he could snap his fingers and spark lightning across them. His inner fire strains to dance with that power and Zuko wonders if this is how you become someone who can channel lightning, by being able to let the storm in but never cutting your fire free.

It’s not a long storm for all its slow deliberateness—it’s not the season for endless monsoons anymore, they cleared that before Zuko came back which is simultaneously crushing and a bone-aching relief—and eventually the lightning is too far away to reach without flinging himself wholly wide. Zuko soothes his inner fire back, peeling his heat sense slowly back toward his center, shivering as his inner fire snaps and presses against his ribs, trying to wrap itself around and follow behind the lightning bouncing inside him. He concentrates on the slow rise and fall of his chest, trying to build gentle chains and walls around his fire by mastering his own breaths, wondering if there’s some balance point he can find within himself or if his only option is to find something large and flame resistant to reduce to ash.

When Zuko finally opens eyes he didn’t realize he’d shut, it’s to find Azula leaning against the glass, watching him, tawny gaze assessing. She raises a hand now that she has his attention, two fingers extended, drawing a small circle with just the curve of her wrist where normally she would use her whole arm. Sparks jump at her fingertips, white-blue, and with a curious look, she flicks them at his bare arm. Zuko twitches at the near-ticklish skip of the little static shock over his skin, watching in faint bemusement as it fizzles out as his fire grabs it.

Azula purses her lips, eyes lingering on his arm before she nods once, decisive, as if he just answered some question. She slips off the window seat and pads out of the room without a word, moving as silently as she came, and Zuko rubs absently at his bicep, wondering if he’s imagining the buzz against his fingertips.

Zuko can feel her leaving by the distance of her contained-explosion inner flame, the only wildness left in the room the crackling, half-foreign energy coiling inside him. Alone, with no witnesses—though who even knows what this would feel like to another firebender, what they might feel if they learned to use their fire sense that way—Zuko slumps back against the wall and finally lets his control burn away. The only other option is to set something on fire, which Zuko doesn’t trust himself to try right now just yet. And besides, Zuko knows how to chase behind his inner flame when it’s like this, how to go along as it spirals out and out, how to follow its lead into the bright, tangible wildness inside himself.

&#45;-

Sokka is struggling to move, the reality of not needing to fight his own body anymore still too fresh and sharp for him to wholly trust. Part of him can’t stop anticipating his limbs becoming not his own again, becoming someone else’s, even as he watches Hama being led away in bonds far too tight for bending.

The feeling—the memory, it’s a memory, it’s not happening—of his own body being used against him like that is stomach-lurching, aching in his joints and trembling through his muscles, and Sokka needs to get over it. And if he can’t get over it then he needs to indulge the depths of his horror later, because he has more important things to worry about right now than the way he still isn’t entirely sure that he can trust his own hands.

Sokka finally gets his feet into motion, stumbling over to where Aang is quietly urging Katara to sit, wincing because he might have actually wrenched something trying to fight against Hama’s bending, and that just makes him feel even more wild-eyed around the edges, and he needs to get it together because Katara is looking more than wild-eyed enough for all of them.

Aang seems to be coaxing slow responses out of her so Sokka takes a moment to just… appreciate the fact that his little sister is okay. To allow himself to truly understand and believe that she’s still present, maybe not doing *well* but still here and healthy enough to have the breakdown she seems to be on the verge of.

Spirits, Sokka doesn’t know if he’s ever been more terrified than in that moment of realizing that Katara was all alone with a sociopathic, powerful bender. It was uniquely horrifying for that to be all he knew, somehow even more so than when he found out that Azula had captured both Zuko and Katara. For as sickeningly awful as that had been—as it still is, to remember—Sokka had at least had ‘captured’ to cling to, the fact of impending danger that they might still be able to avert

All Sokka had tonight was an understanding of the magnitude of the threat Hama passed, and the screaming awareness of how acutely alone they had left Katara with absolutely no idea of what Hama might do with the isolation.

Sure, Katara’s a Master in her own right, can more than take care of herself. But Sokka knows all too well how the element of surprise can take down even the most adept warrior. And being able to bend the blood inside a person? Fuck, who would expect that? How can you prepare for something you didn’t even know existed?

Sokka flexes his hands open and closed, watching them intently, shaking out his shoulders and shuddering at the lingering sensation of his body moving against his will to do things he wouldn’t even think about doing, let alone act on. Spirits, but tonight has *very* thoroughly answered any questions Sokka still had about the boundaries of when, exactly, he appreciates being restrained.

And fuck, Sokka’s thoughts are getting out of hand. He hates even thinking about this in the same mental landscape he associates with Zuko, so he firmly shoves away all the distraction and distance his mind is trying to throw up between him and what just happened and forces himself to focus on Katara.

She has a shawl from some thoughtful villager wrapped around her shoulders and something hot has been shoved into her hands. The cooler mountain air that Sokka had found such a relief after the sticky heat they’ve experienced so far in the Fire Nation suddenly sucks at their warmth like the sharp winds that scream ahead of a surprise winter storm. Spirits, Sokka cannot *wait* for the sun to come up and burn away the last of this terrible night. He might actually be getting this whole ‘blessed Agni’s light’ thing, finally.

He’s never wished for the full moon to go away quite like this before, but he thinks they could all use a break for Yue’s blessing right now. He thinks she would understand.

Sokka hovers protectively over Katara’s shoulder, not wanting to interrupt until he’s feeling steadier since she’s nodding along to Aang’s low, earnest words. The gesture looks rote, automatic, but that’s better than numb or shocked or any number of other things she could be doing right now. Aang is crouched in front of her, hands anxiously tangled together but face calm, telling her that it’s okay, that she’s safe, that they’re fine, that it won’t happen again, that they stopped her, and Katara isn’t looking at anything other than her feet, but she’s listening.

Aang is eventually called away to help Toph or soothe villagers or something Avatar-y— Sokka is pretty sure they’ve blown their cover again pretty spectacularly, but he can’t be mad about this one—and Sokka slides over to join Katara on her log. Katara immediately curls up against his side, fitting just as well as she used to in the months after their mom died, and leaving him feeling just as helpless. He fusses, lacking anything else to do, tucking her closer, settling her comfortably under his arm and making sure the shawl is snugged around her and nudging her to take a sip of whatever is in her hands.

Alcohol, from the way she sputters and coughs. At least it grabs her attention.

“You’re going to be okay, Katara,” Sokka finally says when her coughing dies down, giving her shoulder a tight squeeze. Katara curls deeper against his side and Sokka wracks his brain because that didn’t seem to be the right thing to say.

“Sokka, she made me into a *monster*,” Katara whispers, choking on the words.

“Katara…”

“She turned me into what she is.” Her hands start to tremble, violent, and Sokka hastily reaches over to take her mug before it drops. “I can never forget! I know it now, how to—and even if I never use it, I *know*. I *did* it. It will always be there…”

“Katara, you aren’t—”

“And—I saw the villagers, you know. The ones who were in the mountain. And they—they needed healing. And I thought—” Her whole body heaves around a strangled sob. “But then when I tried to—I couldn’t—I *felt*—” She heaves in another way that has Sokka quickly scouting out places for her to vomit, if it comes to that.

“But you didn’t do—”

“Every time I try to waterbend,” Katara says, and Sokka tightens his grip around her in alarm as her tone suddenly goes low and steady and flat. “Every time, I can sense it. I can feel it, I can’t—it’s *there* now, and it—it makes me sick.” She holds up her hands, staring at them in horror. “I—Tui and La, I could be just like her.”

“No, Katara, you could *never*—”

“Yes, I could!” Her hands curl into fists and she glares down at the forest floor, unforgiving in her judgment, and Sokka feels like his heart is breaking at the way she’s turning her relentless sense of justice on herself. “She hates the Fire Nation more than anything. She wanted revenge for what they did to her and her family and her home. And she had so much power and she went off all alone and—and—”

“And took it out on the wrong people?” Sokka finishes gently.

Katara crumples forward, balling her hands against her chest and pressing her forehead to her knees as she takes fast, shuddering breathes just this side of outright sobbing. Sokka rubs what he hopes is a soothing hand over her back, taking a bracing sup from her mug—*wow*, definitely not even a drop of tea in this whisky—as he tries to quickly sort his thoughts and ignore the way her words cause the low, churning nausea lingering in his gut to churn a little harder.

“Katara, you…you aren’t like her. Sure, some of the things you said are similar, but that’s like saying that because I like sea prune stew and she did too, I’m on a path toward imprisoning people under a mountain.” Katara lets out a choked noise, and Sokka hastily continues. “All those things you said aren’t who you *are*. You’re more than hatred and revenge. So much more. And the fact that you can even say that about yourself in the first place means that you aren’t like her. Do you think she could look at her behavior and say any of it was wrong?”

Katara shudders, and if there was an answer in there Sokka lost it beneath the force of her trembling.

“And besides,” he adds, “You’re not alone. You have us, Katara. You’ll always have us. Do you think we would just stand back and let you become like her?”

“I’m a *bloodbender* now, Sokka! I’m *already* like her!”

“And Toph is a metalbender,” Sokka says. “That doesn’t mean she isn’t still an earthbender. And Zuko’s a heatbender.” Sokka…doesn’t think that’s such a secret, at this point, from all the little details he’s dragged out of Katara about that last day in Ba Sing Se. “He still has fire. You haven’t *lost* anything, Katara.” He keeps the circles he’s rubbing over her back slow and even. “You’ve gained knowledge. And maybe it’s knowledge you don’t want, and maybe it wasn’t worth trading your ignorance for. But knowledge isn’t inherently good or bad. Just like bending isn’t inherently good or bad. It’s all what you do with it.”

She makes a disgusted noise from behind the curtain of her hair. “How could *this* ever be good.”

Oh boy. Okay. Sokka can do this. He takes a deep breath, pushing past the lingering, instinctive revulsion of how his body was wrenched around from the inside and forcing himself to think. “What if there was a child running into danger, and no one was close enough to reach them, but you could bend and stop them?”

“I’d just use water.”

“What if it was the desert. And we’d already drunk all our water.”

Katara makes an annoyed sound, turning her head just enough to glare. “That’s a stretch.”

“Well, you put me on the spot here,” Sokka says, gently flicking at the fall of her hair and earning himself a surprised, watery laugh.

“I don’t know how to…it feels like my bending is tainted now,” Katara admits, and Sokka thinks that this is the true core of her fear and distress. “Whenever I try to bend, it’s just… And it was so amazing and beautiful and whenever I waterbended I felt…But now…”

“And now it sucks. But you’ll get back there, Katara,” Sokka says, making sure the total confidence he feels is in his voice. “You will. I promise you will, if you want to.”

“…But *how*?”

“Bit by bit,” Sokka says quietly, tucking her back against his side when she finally sits up with a shuddering breath. “Little steps. Just…acclimate yourself first. Sit near some water. Maybe put your feet in. Then be near Aang while he practices. Let your bending just feel or whatever. Then practice with him. And then just yourself. Don’t rush it, just…ease yourself in.”

“We don’t have time for that,” Katara says, reaching for the mug. Her second slug goes down much easier than the first.

“What we don’t have time for is for you to have a mental breakdown in the middle of a fight because you pushed yourself too fast before you were ready.”

Katara grunts, but doesn’t pull away and doesn’t push back against the words, turning the drink slowly in her hands. “…How do you know all this? How can you be sure?”

“Zuko,” Sokka sighs, vaguely wondering if his answer to that is ever going to be ‘all the time I spent in a library’ like Katara probably wants it to be.

“He—oh. I thought—It looked old.”

Sokka shrugs, unwilling to put a timeline on it because it’s not his timeline to share, and he doesn’t need Katara thinking it will take her years to get back to where she wants to be. “I don’t know how old it would need to be for him to not remember something like that. But he does, and he’s…” Not fine, no matter what he’s always saying, but… “He bends now, and it’s okay. So it can be okay for you, too. It'll just take some work.”

Sokka leans to take a peek at her face around her matted hair when she doesn’t reply. She looks miserable, which he supposes is a shade better than distraught.

“Good things take work, sometimes,” he says quietly, holding in a relieved exhale when she gives a minute nod. “And you know how to work hard, Katara. You’ve always worked so hard. This is just a different way to work on your waterbending.” He gives her another squeeze, quietly, desperately hoping that the things he’s telling her are true.

&#45;-

Katara is back on her feet and moving because she’s always been nothing if not resilient. She’s helping with bandages and administering plain food and sips of water to the newly freed villagers, finding ways to help even if she doesn’t feel up to bending yet. Sokka’s glad to see it, even if all he feels capable of doing this late in the night is grabbing the shawl she left behind and wrapping it around himself and trying to keep watch for any new danger. What if there’s an angry spirit around on top of all of this? Fuck, he doesn’t think he’ll be able to fully feel like they’re safe—or stop shivering—until the sun comes up.

Toph plops down next to him at some point in the endless stretch of darkness, and Sokka wordlessly offers her part of the shawl before remembering that she can’t tell and just throwing it around her shoulders because asking seems like too much effort. She grunts in surprise but tugs it around herself, one foot tapping restlessly against the ground.

“The Fire Nation is messed up, man.”

“No kidding,” Sokka agrees, scanning the dark tree line in front of them with eyes that feel dry and itchy from exhaustion even as nervous fear keeps his heart firmly in his throat. Yue’s light provides plenty of illumination to show that there’s nothing there but trees.

“Your boy better be fixing this shit, or else he’s not worthy of calling himself Crown Prince of this place,” she mutters, and Sokka blinks in surprise, both at hearing Zuko referred to that way and at someone voicing the idea that Zuko might be doing something specific, rather than the vague ‘there’s a plan’ that’s been all Sokka would commit to. Honestly, it’s…a bit of a shock to hear that any of the others actually think Zuko might have one, too, that they’re not just humoring him.

“I’m not sure that he does,” Sokka finally says, wondering if this is the kind of thing Zuko could even know about, to know that it needs fixing. “Call himself that, I mean.”

Toph snorts. “Pretty sure he is, if he came back here.”

…Fair. But then, they all just had a very rough first-hand lesson in people not being what they seem.

“Stop thinking whatever has your heart doing that,” Toph suddenly orders, elbowing him solidly in the side. “I know you insist on being sure before saying anything, but don’t be stupid about it. There are only so many things he couldn’t still do if he stayed away.”

&#45;-

Zuko jolts awake from a nightmare, kicking his way furiously out of the suffocating press of blankets and pillows and luxury. He’s surprised he even fell asleep in the first place so soon after the storm, but the energy of it had settled against his spine like it’s waiting to spark rather than jumping and playing like Zuko is used to, and his exhaustion had finally pulled him down.

Zuko sits on the edge of his bed, breathing heavily as he gets his heart back under control, nightclothes clinging damply to his skin. Agni’s tits, Zuko wishes for once that his mind would let him *rest.* He’s lived through Sokka’s rejection and Azula’s disgust and Uncle’s hatred a thousand times by now, and he’s so *tired* of it. But much as it weighs heavy over his shoulders, Zuko knows he can’t let it drag him down. And he won’t. All he’ll allow it to do is feed his grim resolve to see this thing through, to walk the only path left to him to the very end.

## Chapter 7: Truths Like Knives

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for some consumption of alcohol in this one

### Text

“I can*not* believe we’ve been sent away like toddlers. To go to the *beach*. Like we can be distracted by bright objects and shiny things.”

Zuko very firmly doesn’t point out the fact that Ty Lee is, currently, fascinated by the way the light is shining off her jewelry as they pull into the dock. Or that Azula may know how to project palpable menace in any room she enters, but if you take the time to actually look at her you might realize that she doesn’t come up to the shoulders of most of the soldiers in the palace guard.

“It’s outrageous,” she mutters, pointedly refusing to watch as their ferry approaches the beach. Zuko eyes the sand with open longing, his hands aching from how hard he’s gripping the railing. “As if those old *men* will manage to do anything but listen to the sound of their own voices without someone there to motivate them.”

Azula’s bored, flat stare is certainly an effective motivator to wrap up your point as quickly as you can without making a fool of yourself. Still, Zuko doesn’t think she’s particularly worried about *other people’s* efficient use of time.

She makes a disgusted noise in the back of her throat. “What could they *possibly* have to meet about without me?”

There it is, but Zuko shrugs as if he didn’t notice. “I’m sure we’ll find out when we get back.” Azula will get it out of someone within degrees if no one tells them outright.

She flicks him a quick, annoyed look. “Really, Zuzu, with the way you’re acting one might think you were perfectly happy being exiled to the beach.”

Zuko gives her a mild look, making a point of not reacting to her digging. He suspects that he has a very different perspective than she does on forcing his way into meetings he’s been barred from attending. “Ember Island can be nice.”

Azula wrinkles her nose. “Lo and Li’s house, though. Ugh. I bet everything *matches*.”

“Like you don’t appreciate some matching,” Zuko says dryly. Azula has coordinated her outfits for as long as Zuko can remember. Still part of him flickers to wary attention at her annoyance. Lo and Li have invested significant time and energy into Azula for as long as Zuko can remember, too. He wonders when she started resenting them for it.

“*Coordination* is different from *matching*, Brother, don’t be dense.”

Another shrug. Zuko isn’t going to argue that, he was never as focused on costuming and set design as she was. “It’s not like we could go to ours,” he points out.

Azula makes a noise remarkably close to a growl for someone whose face stays so flat, and Zuko flicks her another mild, considering look. He knows his lack of shared frustration is probably only making her more irritated, but he doesn't have much left in himself for  
getting particularly worked up by the whole thing. Zuko might tolerate being on the water better than he would have months ago, but that doesn’t mean he’s exactly at ease, even for such a short, familiar journey.

And besides, being sent away from the palace to spend days in the sun? Even if it’s some kind of power game or silent statement about his worthiness to be involved in politically important things? Zuko’s fine with this. The only thing still in Caldera he has to worry about is Uncle, and Uncle's probably not in any more danger with Zuko gone than with Zuko stopping by to yell at his back every few days.

“You’re trying to tell me,” Azula tries again, tone incredulous, “That you don’t feel like a child being sent to their room while the grown-ups talk?”

Zuko eyes his fourteen-year-old sister. “No one in this family gets to be a child.”

Azula scowls, visibly annoyed that he won’t give her the entertainment of rising to her bait, but finally lets it drop. She can’t exactly challenge that.

&#45;-

If Zuko’s going to be sent away for required relaxation, then he wants to at least take advantage of the enforced idleness to soak up the sun and bask like it’s been nearly impossible to do in the palace’s dark corridors. But Zuko’s never been to Ember Island and needed to use the public beaches. Their family house had its own beach that no one would dare step onto without permission where they could do…whatever they wanted, really, because supervision and monitoring weren’t exactly hallmarks of their upbringing. But Lo and Li’s house is on the public beach, and Zuko is suddenly finding that he can’t unwind in Agni’s light the way he usually can when he’s feeling quite so…exposed.

There are just so many *eyes*. Zuko’s hair is down in recognition of the relaxed setting— military-precise topknots may be the fashion in the capital, but the point of Ember Island is to pretend that your real life does not, in fact, exist—but he still feels like his scar is glaringly noticeable and obvious. And that self-consciousness worms up his spine, across his shoulders, undoing the work that years of communal bathing drummed into him.

It's not the same as the showers in the *Wani,* though. Zuko doesn’t know any of these people, and he can’t bring himself to fully take off his light robe even though he’s starting to get uncomfortably hot and uncomfortably jealous of Ty Lee, who is openly soaking in both the sun and the attention she's getting. As she should be, because they're at the beach, that's what you're supposed to *do.*

Except all Zuko can do is look at her ease, not replicate it, because he doesn't actually want anyone here looking at him, even if there are some nice shoulders on some of the boys she’s reeling in, and a whole lot of skin—though not nearly the right shade, Fire Nation skin can't darken like Sokka’s—that Zuko would admire if he were literally anywhere else.

But Zuko isn't anywhere else. He's here, with his sister and her friends, so he keeps his robe on and his focus on them. Azula’s splitting her brooding gaze equally between Zuko and Ty Lee, and Mai is raising an expectant brow at him from beneath her umbrella, and Zuko… doesn’t know what to do. His prior beach experiences have been ‘nearly drown each other' and ‘splash around in tide pools,’ or more recently ‘scour the hull,’ and none of those exactly feel appropriate to suggest to Mai, so…Zuko defaults to what he would do if he were here with Sokka.

“Ice cream?” Mai asks, as if she’s never seen it before. “Really?”

Zuko scowls. “It’s hot out.”

Mai rolls her eyes and shoves the brightly sprinkled cone back into his hands. “Then you eat it.”

“I already had one, though,” Zuko says inanely. And potentially stupidly. Was he supposed to wait to eat together? Or share one with her?

She flicks a pointed glance at his torso where it's visible beneath his robe. “Have two.”

Azula snorts from her blanket—blatantly eavesdropping—and Zuko glowers at them both before pointedly moving to the far edge of the blanket to eat his second ice cream while glaring at the beach around him. There are so many fucking *people*, lounging and swimming and chattering and flirting. It must be some kind of school break with the number of kids their age around. Zuko’s pretty sure that’s a thing that the schools do, right?

He doesn’t quite know what to do with the sheer volume of teens and near-total absence of adults, and he’s feeling rather…on edge about it, if he’s being honest with himself. Zuko hasn’t been around people his own age in any real numbers in…well, he can’t quite remember when. Mai and Ty Lee and Azula might count as ‘his age’ but he isn’t sure they qualify as ‘numbers.’ And it’s just been Sokka and a little bit of Jet, since Zuko’s grown up, and that doesn’t exactly give Zuko a template for appropriate peer-to-peer public behavior in the Fire Nation.

Azula suddenly lets out a soft ‘ah,’ her attention caught, and Zuko automatically glances up, following her eyes to the kuai ball net another group of teens is setting up. Ah. That *would* be nice. An outlet for Azula’s simmering frustration that she won’t admit to feeling, and some nice rules and roles and expectations for Zuko so he doesn’t have to think.

Azula looks back, catching his eyes and tilting her head in question, and Zuko is mentally weighing how nice a game could be against the need to actually interact with strangers when he pauses. No one here will know like Mai and Ty Lee not to let him and Azula be on the same team, and he can see that same knowledge sparking in her gaze, a slow smile curling his lips as his inner fire perks up with interest.

Zuko eyes the kuai court with new anticipation, openly grinning now. From the way it's tugging at his scar he doesn't think that it's a particularly nice expression and he doesn't exactly care. He hasn’t been allowed to be on Azula’s team since she was seven.

&#45;-

Zuko glances around the aftermath of the game, hesitating. Burning the net so no one could ever play again and claim a victory on their court was a very final touch, and Zuko is still barely bitting back an offer to find some salt for the earth as well. Though the impulse to tease is quickly drying up in the face of the fact that no one is saying 'no' to this objectively terrible idea.

"Are we sure this is a good idea?" Mai finally asks, outright skepticism in her tone.

“It’s a party!” Ty Lee enthuses. “It sounds great! What could be wrong with a party?”

Mai stares at her, eyes flat in that have-you-been-dropped-on-your-head way she has. “Yes. What.”

“If you have something to say, Mai, then say it,” Azula says while brushing some sand from her nails, innocent like an open pit trap.

Mai is conspicuously silent, and Azula slides her inquisitive, aggressive stare to Zuko.

He sighs. “Have you *been* to a party before?”

“Of course I have,” Azula scoffs. “There are fetes every month at the palace, dumb dumb.”

Zuko…refrains from pointing out that a palace fete—wining and dining and political agendas over canapes—doesn't sound like at all the same thing as a house party while someone’s parents are away, beyond the fact that both feature distantly acquainted individuals gathering in a relatively common space.

“Oh, we’re going to have so much *fun*,” Ty Lee says, her grin turning a little bit wicked. “Don’t you think? Those boys were *cute*.”

&#45;-

They arrive exactly on time because Azula really hasn’t been to a party before, not one that wasn’t a political event half-heartedly pretending to be a celebration. And even if she had, Zuko thinks they would still have arrived precisely on time. Azula doesn’t have time to play any games but her own.

Ty Lee’s enthusiasm—and outfit, probably, Zuko might not want to act on it, but he has *eyes* —carry them through the awkwardness of their early arrival, and Zuko hangs at the back of the group because Chan and Ruon-Jian don’t care about *him* being there. He watches Ty Lee flirt and Mai assess and his little sister do her best to not immediately alienate everyone around her and Zuko… almost wants to laugh.

Agni’s tits, for once Zuko might be the more adept of the two of them. And he might not love the idea of theoretically letting his guard down in someone else’s space like this, but there are enough similarities to music nights on the *Wani* and to Jin’s impromptu nights out that Zuko at least has *some* idea of how to act without making a fool of himself. Most importantly, he knows how to remove himself from the center of attention and find a nice wall to put at his back in all kinds of settings.

Zuko lets out a sigh that definitely isn’t relief when he finally presses his shoulders against wood paneling and can at least stop worrying about watching his back quite so literally. And it’s a good spot for minimizing anyone coming up on his blind side, too, while still letting him keep half an eye on Ty Lee—who might need some help as more and more people show up and drift toward her energy—and the other half on Mai where she’s chatting up a rangy looking guy whose nice pair of thighs do wonders to make up for his pretentiously disheveled hair.

Zuko considers that a moment, then absently touches his own awkward-length hair, glancing down at his legs.

“Really, Zuzu,” Azula says, pulling Zuko out of his contemplation. “You aren’t even going to try to fight?”

“Huh?” Fight…her? Here? Now?

She tsks in the back of her throat. “Someone is over there trying to capture Mai’s attention, and you’re not even thinking of a strategy, you’re just…” She waves a hand at him, encapsulating all her general disgust, or maybe all his general ineptitude.

Zuko tries not to be visibly amused and probably fails. “I’m not too worried about it.”

“Oh?” She tries for contempt and doesn’t quite make it. “I suppose I should have expected that your go-to approach to *all* your relationships would be ‘do nothing and stand in a corner and pout.’”

He eyes her bright jewelry and shining, perfect hair and position right next to him in the corner. “Forgive me if I don’t take relationship advice from you.”

Azula glares before tucking the expression back behind superior disdain, and Zuko makes a mental note to come back to that, after. What an unexpected nerve to suddenly strike. “At least I’m not so stupid that I'm risking my life because I can’t control my—”

“Azula.” Maybe it’s not an unexpected nerve at all. Zuko keeps his tone mild because this is so not the place to suddenly work this out. Nowhere in the Fire Nation is, really, but even the palace would be safer than this party surrounded by people they don’t know, who don’t know them enough to keep their mouths shut. Agni’s balls, Zuko wishes she would just let this go. He knows she won’t, not with what he’s been giving her, but it would be nice. “What are you trying to do here?" He asks. "You didn’t make a big production of coming here incognito just so you could fuck with me all night.”

Azula visibly considers the merits of fucking with him all night before falling back against the wall with a huff, crossing his arms and imitating his pose and managing to look just as relaxed as Zuko, which is to say, not at all. “I just…want to see what it’s like to be a normal person, for once.”

Zuko…didn’t expect to hear that in his entire lifetime.

“That’s what you did, isn’t it?” She examines her nails critically, angling them to look for chips before flicking her necklace straight. “Went off to go be someone else for four years.”

“It…wasn’t exactly like that,” Zuko says quietly. He might have been gone but ‘exiled Crown Prince’ is still ‘Crown Prince,’ and he knows that Azula is very aware of that fact.

“Close enough.” And from her perspective back in Caldera, going from ‘children of the Fire Lord’ to ‘child,' maybe it was.

Zuko takes the time to digest that, reshuffling a few things and trying to understand the new shape they could make. “So…what, you want to be a normal Fire Nation teenager at a party?" Whatever that means. "Are you trying to get drunk?” That’s…a spectacularly bad idea around so many people. “Flirt with a guy?” Azula scoffs in a way that means yes-but-I’ll-never-admit-it-and-neither-will-you. “Because if you need advice…”

“I don’t need *advice* from—”

“Because just saying, of the two of us…”

“Shut up, dumb dumb,” she orders, rolling her eyes and flicking him on the bare shoulder.

“You could ask Ty Lee for help, then.”

“I don’t need help,” Azula says, the words more rote than forceful as she eyes the crowd of boys not-so-subtly shouldering each other for Ty Lee’s attention.

“Sure.” Zuko holds back an eye roll. “Well, then you can plan your strategy with her, or whatever. Besides,” he adds, seeing that Azula still looks skeptical, “She might need some help soon.” The boys are starting to shove a bit too far into her space, in Zuko’s opinion, not that Ty Lee can’t put them in their place the moment she decides she’s had enough.

Zuko bites his tongue and waits, watching Azula mull that over and decide that it’s her own idea from the start. Once he sees the determination settling over her face, he slips away to give her the space to march over like she always intended to do so and was just biding her time. He's lost his nice spot in the corner, but he can make himself busy finding the food, maybe. Mai's been talking to that guy for a while and is starting to look dangerously bored. Food can’t hurt.

&#45;-

Zuko’s been aware of the girl—choker, darker red top than the others, hair short in a deliberate rather than disgraced away that would never fly in the palace—for a while now. Ever since Azula put a cup on her head in dismissal, really, but specifically when she started working her way around the room with an eye always on him. He’s hoping he can just I-don’t-even-notice-you-enough-for-this-to-be-pointed ignore her, but—

“I like to watch, you know.”

—Zuko can’t exactly ignore that. He eyes her askance as she leans one shoulder against the wall and tries to be subtle about edging away.

“Or being watched. If that’s more your thing.” Her eyes flick over to Mai, who Zuko *had* been watching as she continues to talk to Ruon-Jian, but not because of *that*.

“Uh…”

The girl smiles, apparently pleased to have flustered him, and leans in, following as he tries to shift away. “I can be down for whatever. I’m…flexible.”

What she is not is subtle. “I don’t…”

“Alone time is nice, too,” she adds before Zuko can figure out where that sentence is going. “I know Chan. He won’t mind if we use his room.”

Zuko’s pretty sure that Chan is the one that Azula set her eyes on, and the idea of competing with his little sister for use of the guy’s room, even as an abstract thought…Zuko has never wanted anything less in his life.

“Use whose room for what?" Mai suddenly asks, voice sharp enough to cut.

The girl turns to take Mai in, somehow managing to use the gesture to both convey mild amusement and to slide even further into Zuko’s space, like it’s her that belongs there and Mai that’s the interloper. She smirks a little as Mai’s eyes narrow, and Zuko…reevaluates his prior thought. He would prefer fighting Azula for Chan's room over whatever this is trying to be. “Just talking about mutual interests in a quiet place.”

“Mutual interests,” Mai repeats, flat.

“Hm, you know. Ways to spend our time. You can come too if you want.” The girl runs her eyes over Mai, and Zuko is simultaneously grateful that they’re off of him and bristling at having them on Mai instead and then confused about how he somehow went on the defensive. Mai doesn't need his protectiveness.

“You can spend your time fucking off,” she says bluntly, arms crossing in a way that lets Zuko know she brought at least two knives to the party.

The girl blinks, straightening from her chest-first lean. “Excuse me?”

“Did I stutter?”

“What makes you think you can talk to me that way? Do you know who I—”

Mai doesn’t care who she is, apparently. “What makes you think you can talk to us at all?”

“’Us,’” the girl repeats, incredulous. “He’s said more words to me in five degrees than he has to you all night.”

That…is technically true, and Zuko wants to just find a nice new corner for himself, please, except he’s stuck back against the wall with one of them on either side, hemming in him. Fuck, fuck, fuck.

“*Talking* doesn’t mean much,” Mai says. “Talk is cheap.”
