Zuko goes completely still in the shadows when he reaches out with his fire sense to dampen the next torch, to pull the darkness a bit deeper to slide between, and instead of open flame brushes against a familiar hold already wrapping around the same fire.

He slowly scans the shades of shadow and sparse light, moving just his eyes and keeping them slitted to avoid reflecting any stray moon- or torchlight. Finally, he picks out the shape of Azula clinging to the darkness between the wall and the huge, ornate columns that used to form the perimeter of this exterior walkway before it was closed over for security reasons decades ago during one of Azulon’s fits of paranoia.

Azula stares up at him for a moment, taking in his perch on the heavy, decorative beams that make up the rafters. Both of them hold their breath, waiting, until the silence drags on long enough with no sound but the murmur of fire for them to wordlessly agree that they’re alone. Then they each move onward on silent feet to continue with their respective business in the dead of night.

&#45;-

Fire Lord Sozin was Avatar Roku’s childhood best friend, and then his killer. Maybe you could look at it sideways and say that Sozin didn’t actively end Roku’s life, just passively let it happen, but…Zuko knows how his family works. He can’t imagine they’ve changed all that much in so few generations.

The information is interesting enough, in a kind of late-afternoon-chit-chat-over-tea way, or maybe as part of some pretentious post-dinner posturing in a smokey study when everyone is pretending that they’re all friends and not eager to claw the power and wealth from each other’s corpses at the first opportunity. It’s the kind of thing Azula likes to know and strategically share.

And the truth of Sozin’s attack on the Air Nomads isn’t exactly a world-changing revelation for Zuko, if it was supposed to be one, and he doubts it was to Azula either whenever she inevitably dug it up. Though she would hoard this secret, rather than share it. Zuko read too much in text scavenged from across the Earth Kingdom, saw far too many skeletons that were far too small in the Western Air Temple, to truly believe the Air Clans were amassing an army against the Fire Nation.

Zuko supposes it’s good in an academic kind of way to know that this information hasn’t been entirely erased by the diligent work of the Ministers of Education over the decades. But Zuko fails to see how any of this concerns him enough to warrant the risks of a secret message that anyone passing through that hallway could have come across, *especially* one hinting at any destiny that the Fire Lord didn’t first approve of.

Agni, if that servant had actually managed to beat Zuko to waking for once it could have been both their necks very literally on the line—though fire, realistically, was probably what Zuko would face. It wouldn’t have mattered that Zuko didn’t welcome the message if he was in any kind of position to receive it. And her…well, the Fire Lord knows what to do with inconvenient witnesses.

Zuko forces his hands to stay cool as he sets the scroll back down, tucking it and the others away where he found them and leaving some streaks in the dust to hide the information he came for, using the opportunity to gently touch the fragile paper and remind himself that the temple library is very full of very flammable things and that that’s an excellent reason not to let his anger spark.

But the cryptic-ness and vagueness of it all is infuriating, his inner fire restless and sharp-edged with it. Agni tits, the fact that all this shit that old men did one hundred years ago is supposed to be Zuko’s fucking future? That somehow it’s his *destiny* to deal with now, like he’s nothing but what his ancestors and his blood would have him be rather than what he would make of himself?

The resentment that shadows his steps out of the Temple has a familiar taste to it, clinging like smoke on the back of his tongue as he sets himself not back toward the palace, but toward Caldera’s prison tower. It will be early for a visit by the time Zuko gets there, and he isn’t exactly dressed for it. But then, it’s always early when Zuko isn’t supposed to be there in the first place.

The leash on Zuko’s frustration snaps the minute he steps into the room and his eyes land on Uncle’s familiar wide-shouldered silhouette.

“Why did you send me this,” Zuko hisses, inner fire lashing in his chest as he throws the fucking scroll through the bars. And the fact that *that* gets him his first reaction in weeks and weeks of trying, that Uncle finally moves to pick up the scroll as if he doesn’t recognize it, as if he doesn’t know exactly what it says, as if Zuko wouldn’t recognize Uncle’s hand and fixation on destiny after *all these years*—Zuko feels like he could turn these stones to *ash*.

“What was the *point*?” Zuko demands, driven to sharp, tight pacing across the confined space, because if he doesn’t move then he’s going to burn. “Are you just trying to get me in trouble? To waste my time? Do you know what fucking *day* it is?” He strangles a noise of frustration when Uncle doesn’t respond, hands fisted and raised and totally impotent and he could *scream*. “There was nothing *there*.”

Uncle shifts in that way of his, gathering his thoughts and your attention and making his words seem weighty and important. “Nothing?”

Zuko barely restrains himself from punching the iron bars and probably breaking his own fucking hand at that fucking teaching *tone*, which would just be *exactly* what he needs today of all days. Maybe *that’s* the fucking point!

“What, am I supposed to be shocked?” He snarls. “Is it supposed to be a *surprise* that Sozin let his friend die for political expediency? Is that supposed to change my worldview? Because if it is then I’ve got some fucking *things* to tell you about seven years ago.”

Uncle gives him a level look, unreadable. “I did not refer to Sozin, in this,” he finally says, tapping the scroll against the prison floor with infuriating calm. “But to your other great-grandfather.”

Zuko stares, and wonders if it’s time for him to just…leave. To just give up on this if Uncle isn’t going to give him anything to work with. To give up on *Uncle*, which—fuck, Zuko isn’t there yet, he isn’t, but Agni, why does this have to *hurt*. “You’ll have to be a little more specific, Old Man,” Zuko finally rasps out, the words shaking around the edges in time with his heaving chest. “I have four of them. Unless you’re about to tell me we’re even more Agni-born than we tell people.”

“No, none of your recent ancestors were born of one body,” Uncle says, ignoring Zuko’s sarcasm with the ease of long practice. “I meant on your mother’s side of the family. Ursa’s grandfather was Avatar Roku.”

“…What.” How…Why…Fuck, does Azula know? The things she could do with this…

“The combined heritage of Fire Lord Sozin and Avatar Roku runs in your veins,” Uncle says with earnest urgency. “That is why you are so conflicted over your own destiny, Zuko.” Oh. Is *that* fucking why. “It is in your blood to both destroy and assist the Avatar.”

Zuko doesn’t know what Iroh expects in response to that revelation—professions of gratitude? Tears? Pronouncements of changed ways?—but what finally comes out of the boiling mess in his chest is a flat, toneless, “…Are you fucking kidding me?”

“I am not,” Iroh says, as if he actually *believes* it. As if he isn’t just using the information to pull Zuko’s strings, placing new tiles on his pai sho board as it suits him. “And I have one more thing for you.”

“What,” Zuko snorts as Iroh reaches into the neat pile of blankets at the foot of his pallet. Always neat, even here, everything in its place. Including him. “About to tell me that Ozai isn’t actually…”

His words—words Zuko knows better than to even think about speaking aloud, let alone actually doing it, because they’re the kind of idea that can run regardless of its truth—trail off as Iroh passes something gleaming through the bars.

“…This is the Crown Prince’s hairpiece.” Zuko would recognize the sharp, bright gold from all the portraits he’s been staring at even if he hadn’t worn it himself for three years.

“Yes.”

“It’s been missing since…” Since the Agni Kai. Zuko had been wearing it when he was burned, had presumably still been wearing it when he was rushed to the healers, and then no one seemed to know, not that Zuko had been particularly conscious for that part of it. But Azula had told him about it. At length. She’d been furious, in her letters.

“Hm,” Iroh hums, lips curling in what might be the shadow of a smirk. “Has it?”

Zuko looks blankly at his Uncle, then down at the hairpiece, finally dropping his hand with a sigh. His fingers try to curl into habitual fists, the tines digging into his flesh instead. “What do you want?” Zuko just…needs it plain, for once. He’s too tired for any more of these games, too busy trying to deal with the ones he’s already embroiled in, the ones where he’s barely keeping his head above water. He just…needs to know if Iroh is about to fuck him over. Because this is another dangerous thing to give him, and Zuko doesn’t kid himself anymore that he can fathom why.

“Zuko,” Iroh says gently, gravely, hands open-palmed on his knees. Not quite supplication, but the echo of it. “You alone have the power to redeem our family, and the sins of the Fire Nation, by restoring balance to the world. *That* is the destiny that is before you. *That* is the greatness that awaits you.”

Zuko stares, waiting for more, and when he finally realizes that nothing else is coming, that that’s it, the sum total of all Iroh is going to give him—that *Zuko* is the sole savior of their entire fucking family and nation? That *Zuko* has to bear the weight of its sins? Of the *world’s* sins? Zuko, not Iroh, not Azula, not Ozai? Just him?—he turns on his heel and walks out without a word.

Silence, he’s learned from Iroh, can be just as loud as screaming.

Zuko is so numb with what he abstractly recognizes is an incandescent kind of rage that he doesn’t even notice until he’s back in his own rooms again that the headpiece has dug into his hand hard enough to cut. He slowly uncurls his fingers, joints stiff, watching his own blood pool in his hand and trickle along the edges of the crown.

He can’t. He can’t, he *can’t*. Zuko can barely walk the path he’s on now, the one he’s desperately trying to keep himself on, and now, *now,* fucking *now,* Iroh expects him to—

Zuko’s free hand hits the desk so hard that Zuko hears wood splinter, and he distantly wonders if he actually let Iroh goad him into breaking his fucking hand after all. Agni, Zuko can’t bear the weight of the entire world. Not on top of what he already carries, not alone. Not without drowning under it.

Zuko lets a rush of fire come to his palm, blood-streaked gold clattering to the floor as flame sweeps over his skin, burning away the blood and stinging with familiar pain as it sears closed the edges of the shallow cuts. They’ll probably scar, this way, but it’s far from the worst scar Zuko carries. And Zuko can’t afford to explain the injury to anyone who might see it.

&#45;-

Sokka shoves a mouthful of breakfast into his face and keeps his thoughts firmly to himself, thank you very much. Aang is furiously punching the air from a deep, wide squat while rattling through a too-fast explanation that he doesn’t have time to sleep because he needs to train, because if the Fire Lord can beat him in his dreams then he can beat Aang in real time, too, and Aang doesn’t even know fire yet shouldn’t he know fire? Just in case the eclipse doesn’t happen? What if the math is wrong?

Sokka feels like he’s sitting across the fire from a smaller, less composed, more manic Zuko which…honestly is a terrifying thought. The world can barely handle the one it already has.

But maybe Sokka can just…handle Aang mostly the same way?

“Maybe,” Sokka says, clearing his throat. “Some breakfast?” Aang gives him a blank look in between punches. “To—” sit down and calm down. “—support all that training?”

Katara scoffs something that sounds suspiciously like ‘your solution *would* be food’ but Sokka just shrugs. Aang has to slow down at least a little bit to eat if he doesn’t want to choke, right?

“…Yes, okay, sure,” Aang says, eyeing the pot over the fire and sinking a little deeper into his stance. “I can just—”

“Sit down and eat?” Aang hesitates. “Fuel and recovery are important parts of building strength and stamina,” Sokka points out, maybe doing a bit too much of a Zuko-wrangling thing as he manages to flex while taking his next bite. But it gets the point across.

“…Right. Right,” Aang nods, finally popping upright and wobbling over to take a seat. “Right. Okay. Yes. Strength and stamina. Good to have. That’s what training’s all about.”

Sokka keeps half an eye on Aang as the airbender accepts the bowl Katara offers, watching as he takes quick, rapid bites like eating has become a contest. The only thing keeping Aang from choking, as far as Sokka can tell, is his inability to stop fidgeting long enough to get a truly full spoonful into his mouth and the jittery pauses he keeps taking to shoot concerned looks toward Momo and Appa.

Sokka catches Katara’s eye, engaging in a quick, silent exchange of ‘*what’s going on,’ ‘I* *don’t know,’ ‘well do something about it,’ ‘no you do something about it.’* He clears his throat again, scraping up the last of his breakfast with forced casualness. “How are we doing, buddy?”

“Oh, you know, I’m, you know—”

“Fine?” Sokka finishes dryly, and Aang makes a little strangled noise and shoots him a guilty look, spoon *tap-tap-tapping* against the side of his bowl. Toph twitches.

Katara leans forward, keeping her face bright. “What if we…take things down a notch.”

“But shouldn’t we be ramping them up before battle?” *Tap-tap-taptaptap.*

“It’s important to center yourself and be calm,” Toph jumps in. “Learned that in the Earth Rumble. You just need to be still. Let the time to strike come to you. Don’t go flailing around looking for it.” The spoon stutters to a halt.

“What if we did some meditation?” Katara suggests. “You were going to show me the tiger monkey breath sequence, right?”

“I don’t know,” Aang frowns, fiddling with his spoon again but at least not banging it against anything yet. “I feel like I should really be doing things right now.”

“Breath control is super important, though,” Sokka says without being quite sure where he’s going to end up. “You need to be able to breathe right for all kinds of, you know…things.”

“…And what,” Toph says, propping her chin on her fist, “*Specific* things do you mean, that you need to be able to breathe right for? Care to elaborate.”

“Toph, not the time,” Katara says. “Sokka, ew.”

“What—no, I didn’t—”

“But *now* you’re thinking about it,” Toph grins, and Aang makes a slightly hysterical sound that could be a nervous giggle.

“Come on, Aang,” Katara says, rising to her feet with a sniff, nose in the air. “Let’s go meditate away from *some* people who don’t know how to *focus*.”

“I—I’m not the one—you know what—” Sokka drops his face into his hands and gives up. Spirits, he cannot *wait* to get Katara back for all of this, even if Sokka’s absolute mortification does seem to have momentarily derailed Aang from his all-training-all-the-time line of thought.

“Good idea,” Aang says, hopping to his feet and shoveling the last of his breakfast into his mouth. “Let’s go! Hey, maybe after we do some breath sequences, I won’t feel like the edges of me are unraveling!”

Sokka and Toph both blink into the silence as he skips away after Katara. Unraveling?

“…That can’t be good,” Toph finally mutters, finishing off her own breakfast with neat, almost dainty bites.

“No…” Sokka says slowly, “No it cannot.” Shit. Suddenly the days that they have left don’t seem like nearly enough time at all, not if they’re going to need to use them to stitch the Avatar back together.

&#45;-

Zuko is nowhere near the right frame of mind for the Council meeting that afternoon, though he would, in fairness, probably never be. Shockingly, skipping training and spending the entirety of the morning watching the way his blood dried on the Crown Prince’s headpiece somehow had not helped settle his thoughts.

Zuko might not be feeling exactly mentally prepared like he needs to be to sit for an entire meeting across from Azula and at their Father’s side, but Zuko knows how to pretend to be fine when he isn’t. Sharp-edged, prickling anger is a familiar weight on his shoulders, and Azula is the only one whose eyes linger for a beat longer than usual.

The Fire Lord starts proceedings with the typical roar of fire. Peaks of flame race in from the edges of the room to sweep up in front of the throne, finally simmering back to a low enough level to indicate that the Fire Lord actually plans to speak, today. “It is nice of you to join us again, Princess Azula, Prince Zuko.”

“You know I could never stay away, Father,” Azula smiles, full of teeth.

Zuko just dips his head in agreement or acknowledgment or however anyone wants to read it, attention split between the Fire Lord’s reaction and scanning the rest of the table. There are no new faces, and no missing ones, so he and Azula weren’t sent away because they might interfere with a tableside assassination. And no one has moved seats, so if there were any power plays over the past few days, they weren’t successful ones.

“I would expect nothing less,” the Fire Lord murmurs before raising his voice to address the whole room. “You all know that Sozin’s Comet returns to us this summer.” In eighty-four days. If anyone cares to be precise about it. “One hundred years ago, the great Fire Lord Sozin used this gift from Agni to eliminate the direst of threats to our nation, and to take the first steps in founding our glorious empire.” He pauses, yellow eyes flat and hard as they sweep the room. “A century later, we have a duty to finish my ancestor Sozin’s great work.”

Zuko feels himself go motionless, his breath catching as Azula’s inner flame snaps to attention against his heat sense, a contained explosion trembling on the edge of bursting free. *Oh shit.*

“The Earth Kingdom has long resisted civilization,” the Fire Lord proclaims, straight-backed and stern. “Within its borders bandits, pirates, lawlessness, and rebellion have been allowed to fester.” His lips curl at the edges, just a little, and Zuko’s heart begins pounding in triple-time. “That will end this summer. The power of Sozin’s Comet will allow us to crush the Earth Kingdom once and for all, to bring civilization to those lawless lands. We will protect the Fire Nation from their savagery and ensure that Agni’s light always shines on blessed ground.”

Zuko barely manages to claw back his inner flame, to keep from sending visibly anxious flares through the fire at his side. No one is calling the Colonies sacred ground, but if Agni’s light is always to fall on sacrosanct earth…Fuck. That’s not just military conquest and political rule. That’s…cultural cleansing? Agni’s tits, did the Fire Sages sign off on this? Is the Temple supporting it?

Zuko’s scar aches as he holds back a wildly inappropriate laugh at the idea that the Dragon Throne needs the Temple’s *support*, anymore.

It’s beyond dangerous to do so for even a second, but Zuko can’t help making eye contact with Azula across the table as their Father expounds on his vision, seeing the quickest flicker of his own ‘*fuck’* in her eyes before she shutters her expression.

“Our task today, as trusted councilors and advisors of your Fire Lord, is to establish our Nation’s plan. We have at the table knowledge of our military strength—” his eyes pause on Azula. “—our supplies, troops, and advances in weaponry—” his eyes linger on the Generals. “—and our enemy.” The Fire Lord’s gaze suddenly lands on Zuko and everything in him, even his inner flame, suddenly trembles on the edge of taut, shivering motionlessness as his Father’s stare seems to slice right through him. Oh, Agni. Oh fuck.

“So.” The Fire Lord’s gaze cuts away again, sweeping the room. “Let us begin.”

The Generals leap to be the first to outline a plan, the Ministers edging in where they can with logistics and finances and messaging, tempers and fire flaring as the collected Councilors leap at the opportunity to posture on such a grand stage. To be the architect of the Fire Nation’s eternal glory…there aren’t many opportunities for an honor like that in a lifetime.

Zuko does his best to listen, the overlapping voices harder than usual to pick out over the roar of the fire by his unscarred ear. He forces his face to show nothing but the sullen anger he walked in with, wrapping every bit of control he has around his inner flame so his distress and spiraling sense of panic and need to think, think, *think* doesn’t bleed into his fire. He’s so preoccupied with looking unaffected that he nearly flinches at the unexpected sound of his own name.

“Prince Zuko,” Governor Ukano says. “You have seen the Earth Kingdom firsthand in your travels, have you not?” Is there a dig in there? Zuko keeps his expression angry since he’s never been able to truly master Azula’s default bored contempt, even though he should probably attempt to not antagonize Mai’s dad. “What are your insights?”

Zuko’s eyes follow the man’s gesture toward the map inset into the floor before them all, and he makes a point of slowly looking from end to end of the painstakingly detailed contents as he scrambles to gather his thoughts, trying to sort out what he can share and what he has to share and what he can hold back without being too obvious about it. “Well…the population is quite unevenly dispersed over the Earth Kingdom. There are regions that are barely populated.”

He pauses, but no one interrupts with a snide comment or too-bland observation, or to pick up the thread of some idea, so he continues, silently cursing them for now of all times deciding to observe the respect due to his theoretical station. “These areas in particular are drought-stricken the past few years, which causes banditry,” he says, fingers tracing over the spots in question. “Together that’s leading many people to leave their ancestral lands. Ba Sing Se takes in any refugee able to travel to its gates. That’s the major population center, especially with New Ozai…underpopulated.”

Mai’s dad makes a face at that, and Zuko belatedly remembers where Governor Ukano is governor of. But that was the most political way Zuko could phrase ‘losing population by the second as people flee like jackalopes from a drowning ship.’ Things must be going either very well or very poorly for him to have been recalled to the home island.

“The Colonies are obviously also a major population center,” Zuko hurries to continue, trying to strike the perfect balance between blandly useless facts and insightful observation. “Their coastal access is key to moving resources throughout the Earth Kingdom, so they’re likely to always be major hubs.”

“And the local authorities are fine with this population movement?” The Minister of Housing asks, a tight frown barely visible beneath his substantial beard.

“Not…necessarily,” Zuko says slowly. “It isn’t sanctioned everywhere, but it also isn’t discouraged except in pockets of…stronger leadership. In general, local power tends to be concentrated among the wealthier merchants. The Earth King had significant power over major population centers, but generally isn’t overly concerned with the rural regions. And of course, all the major population centers are already under Fire Nation control,” he adds, tilting his head toward Azula who gives him a stately nod in return.

“The merchants fill in the gaps, and there are lots of pockets of resistance because of that. Not just against the Fire Nation, but against their own people.” He shrugs. “Everyone wants to gather enough power to create a breakaway state.”

“Despicable,” mutters a Rear Admiral, as if he didn’t get his position through a series of rather spectacular deaths in Agni Kais and one advantageous marriage. As if the Fire Nation’s didn’t begin with a series of warring states brought under central rule island by island, and only relatively recently in its history qualifying as anything that might be called united

Zuko refrains from pointing either of those things out, dropping his eyes back to the map and absently picking out all the places he has traveled to. Up and down the coast, through the interior, by ship and foot and ostrich horse. He doesn’t think they would be particularly interested in where to find a local fortune teller, and he wouldn’t dare comment on the best place to find healers along the coast. And they don’t need to know about the abbey, or how the upper crust of Ba Sing Se likes their tea. At least not until they start jockeying to be the permanent replacement for the interim governor.

“How insightful,” the Fire Lord murmurs, and Zuko barely manages to keep from visibly bracing himself at the tone that hovers just between genuine and mocking. “And what would you do with this information, Prince Zuko?”

Zuko manages to turn back to the map instead of falling off his cushion in surprise, skin prickling with awareness that all eyes in the room are suddenly trained on him again, eager for an answer. Well. Zuko always knew a loyalty test would come eventually. He supposes now is as good a time as any to get it out of the way. He was just expecting it to come through Azula, to be honest. And judging by her raised eyebrow and here-is-some-rope-to-hang-yourself-with expression, so did she.

&#45;-

Katara comes back from meditation time with Aang looking distinctly un-meditative, wearing a fierce scowl and with a stomp to her step and her hands in white-knuckled fists.

Toph cocks her head. “That good, huh?”

“He talks about balance *all the time*,” Katara growls, throwing herself down onto the grass. “Mental harmony and physical synchronization, but I suggest *a little bit of stretching—”*

“Alright,” Toph says, cracking her knuckles which is…more threatening than Sokka personally might have gone for, but okay. “My turn.”

Sokka silently passes Katara a flatbread, waiting for her chewing to look a little less savage before he hazards, “So…do you think he’s feeling any better?”

“Eh,” Katara grunts, shrugging with one shoulder and tearing off another bite.

The food seems to be settling her a little, at least, so Sokka risks another question. “How about you?”

She pauses mid-chew. “Huh?”

“You know, how do you feel about—” He waves a hand vaguely to encompass the near future and all that hinges on it. “—everything.”

“I’m ready to get this done,” Katara says, eyes flashing with determination, and something in Sokka relaxes that he doesn’t see a hint of the uncertainty that plagued her after Hama on her face. If it isn’t leaping to her thoughts—he can feel good about that.

“Yeah,” Sokka belatedly agrees with a sigh. It’s only been a few months, but he’s already exhausted by needing to think about how to break things down. The idea of needing to keep this up…He wants to *build*, wants to somehow put things back together better than he found them. And he will, he promises himself. Soon. “Do you think Aang will be ready?”

“Yeah,” Katara nods, pulling a face as she glances off toward the waterline where she left Aang. “He just…needs to get out of his own head.”

“He’s a philosopher monk. I don’t think they *do* that.”

Katara flicks a crumb at him but doesn’t argue. “Do *you* think he’s ready? You’re the one with the plan.”

“Oh, now it’s my invasion again?” He dodges Katara’s half-hearted smack, glancing around just in case Aang wandered over in the past few seconds. “Training-wise, yeah. I mean, he was already a Master bender at what, eight?” Katara snorts. “But mentally, he’s…young.”

“Because he *is* young.” And yet his sister…Sokka raises his eyebrows and doesn’t manage to dodge the next whack against his shoulder. “Shut up.”

Sokka lets Aang’s maturity and Katara’s awareness or not of the airbender’s longing glances drop in interest of the more pressing issue—because, unlike *some* people, Sokka’s mind does not live in the gutter. “We’re asking him to do a pretty grown-up thing.” Fuck, Sokka almost hates himself for saying it like that, all euphemistic and vague like the reality of it won’t be exactly the opposite.

“Has he let us down before?”

“Has he had to do something like *this* before?”

“Maybe not quite like this,” Katara allows. “But you haven’t protected him from every hard thing out there, Sokka,” she says, giving him a knowing look, and Sokka…can’t deny the effort, or the failure. “He’s strong,” Katara continues. “He won’t let the world down. He won’t let *us* down.”

“I just…it’s a lot of pressure for one kid.” Especially for one who, historically, ran from hard things. Though that might be unfair of Sokka. Aang’s had one hundred years to get over that tendency. And it’s not like Sokka isn’t aware of his own miles-deep streak of avoidance, and the fact that he’s learning to act anyway.

Katara seems remarkably unconcerned, too, which Sokka really wants to cling to. “All of us are just one kid, at the end of the day. But none of us are alone, right? That’s what you keep telling me.”

Sokka sighs. He hates when she uses his own words against him, but he can’t exactly walk that pep talk back now. “Right, right. I just…would feel better if he were a little...”

“Less frantic?”

“Yeah. That.”

“I think we’re all feeling that way to some degree,” Katara says quietly, finishing off the rest of her flatbread, and Sokka holds in a wince. “Don’t try to tell me you’re feeling all calm and collected about it.”

“…No.” Sokka most definitely is *not* feeling that. More like grimly resolute and vaguely full of a dread he can’t quite name, at any given time somewhere between nausea and something that feels like excitement but is significantly less comfortable.

“Do you think *you’re* ready?” Katara asks after a beat, bracing her forearms on her knees to give him her full attention. “I know we don’t—that you think—stuff. About Zuko and everything. But—either way, this is the hard part, right? This is where things could get…”

“Yeah,” Sokka agrees, able to fill in the end of that sentence all on his own. *Painful. Loyalty-testing. Dangerous in too many ways to name. Real*. *World altering.*

“And..?” Has he actually thought about it by now, she means.

“I’ve gone over the plan and all the backups so many times I could do it in my sleep,” Sokka says, tilting his head back. The sky is so clear and bright and blue and calm, like nothing world-changing could possibly be on the horizon.

“And if..?”

“I’ll be ready,” Sokka cuts in softly, closing his eyes and turning his face toward the sun, distantly surprised that his voice doesn’t reveal how the words make his chest feel hollow, unsteady. “There isn’t another option.” Even if he isn’t sure he’d be able to forgive himself for it. Even if he’s quietly, desperately hoping that it doesn’t come to that, that the fears that invade his dreams don’t play out, that his fragile faith won’t crash hard against the reality of war.

“…Sokka, what are you going to do if he’s there?” Katara asks, looking pained but firm, and he sighs. He should know by now that Katara won’t let him avoid talking about it, talking around it. He should know by now not to try. “What if he’s fighting on their side again?”

“Then he won’t have his fire like the rest of them,” Sokka says levelly, as if the larger part of himself isn’t even right now holding that truth like a scream in his chest, a shout of denial and fear and rage that regardless of how tomorrow goes, Zuko will be vulnerable in a place that has never allowed him to be anything but strong.

Katara kicks at his ankle. “You know what I mean.”

Sokka does. He blinks his eyes open, finally meeting the worried blue of her stare. “Then the plan still doesn’t change.” The words sting coming out of his throat even as Sokka understands why she’s making him say it, even as he’s fully aware of the way too many things left unsaid can turn surety and knowledge into precarious uncertainty.

“I just…I don’t want you to get hurt, Sokka.”

It’s too late for that. Years too late, for the both of them. “I’ll do my best,” he says, offering her a lopsided smile, the best he can manage right now.

Her shoulders slump, expression half-contrite. “Sorry to make you…I know you still think —” She waves her hand. “And I know we agreed to--I’m not trying to say he *doesn’t*, just…”

“Just that it’s good to be prepared,” Sokka finishes softly. “I know.”

Sokka broods on that thought while Katara works her way through another flatbread before the need to be alone with his thoughts finally drives him to grab of space sword and find an empty clearing. Nominally he’s training, but really Sokka is holding his sword in his hands, giving his body something to do as he forces himself to step through all his plans one last time.

Every plan, every contingency, every backup and variation, needs to be absolutely ironclad for what they’re all here to do—for what *Sokka* is here to do. And because Sokka is the leader, the inadvertent linchpin, the *Plans Guy,* each needs to be shored up firm and tight for the possibility that’s been sitting behind Katara’s eyes for weeks now: that Zuko might be on the other side of them. And against what Sokka is going to do if Zuko isn’t, too, a possibility that sometimes makes Sokka even more afraid. Because there are only so many places the plan can flex, and Sokka is acutely aware that it was never meant to be a rescue.

&#45;-

Zuko is trying to do…absolutely anything that will let him claw his way toward a single shred of perspective on the sudden upheaval that’s been so casually introduced into his life. He should maybe see Gao before the light fully fades, just to lose himself for a few moments in following the messenger hawk’s sharp lines against the sky and dreaming of all the words he doesn’t dare to send. It’s an indulgence—a risk—he doesn’t usually allow himself, but today...Zuko might need it today.

For now, though, he’s settled on one of the benches by the turtle duck pond, cutting a very conspicuous red-clad figure against all the soft green and pale stone and gentle browns. He’s making a show of meditating in the late afternoon light, though anyone who bothers to get close would probably immediately see that he’s far too worked up to be able to actually do anything meditative right now, much as he might need to.

If Zuko’s making a show of meditating, Azula makes a whole multipart production of strolling over to disrupt his calm. He bristles at the interruption, shoulders tight, fists clenched, a picture of annoyance as she silently and precisely digs at every single one of his sore spots. Agni forbid anyone think Ozai’s heirs capable of a civil conversation.

“Azula,” he snaps in barely acceptable tones when she’s close enough for him to only have to raise his voice a moderate amount rather than all the way, and she wrinkles her nose, tossing her hair in annoyance.

“Brother,” she bites back, and he lets out a small, relieved breath. Azula is far too clever with her lies for the certainty Zuko needs to feel right now, and he’s already far too focused on not letting himself become overwhelmed to trust his ability to parse through her words right now for the truth. This will make things marginally easier, even if the risks…fuck, Zuko can’t think about those right now.

Zuko lets the silence stretch until she finally reaches a reasonably conversational distance at his side. She flicks the open space on the bench beside him a dismissive glance before pointedly crossing her arms and glaring at the pond like she wouldn’t entirely mind another try at seeing if she could light the water on fire.

“This changes things,” Zuko mutters, flicking a piece of bread into the water, then another, ripping off piece after jagged piece.

“Does it, though?”

“The timing—”

“Is fine,” Azula cuts in, pinning him with a hard stare. “Nothing we heard changes that.”

“I’m sorry, were we just in the same Council meeting? If there’s going to be—”

“*There’s still time*.” Her eyes narrow on him. “Unless you’re forgetting what you’re here for.”

He matches her glare. “I’ve never forgotten.”

“Then we continue.” Her tone goes from icy to just cool as he flicks another piece of sharply torn bread. “The whole world isn’t ours, Zuko.”

“Maybe it should be.”

Her tone goes spider snake soft. “That sounds like forgetting, Brother.”

Zuko throws what’s left of his roll, watching the ripples in the pond chase after each other, ricochet off reeds and turtle ducks, crash together and break in new direction.

“No way out but forward,” Azula finally says into the silence, and Zuko for once can’t tell if it’s supposed to be a demand or a reminder.

“Light the way ahead,” he whispers, wondering if she hears agreement or something else.

Azula shifts her weight, pointedly reorienting her body toward the pond and suddenly speaking in her usual bored drawl, marking the end of the conversation. “Mai says you’re having dinner with her again tonight.”

Zuko glances up from the turtle ducks, wary at the sudden change of topic instead of her just walking away. “Yeah.”

“…Give me some bread.” Zuko wordlessly pulls an extra roll out of his pocket for her to shred. “Are you playing with her?”

“No.”

“Using her?”

“…Not like you mean.”

Azula flicks a piece of bread too hard into the water, glowering when the turtle ducks scatter in alarm. “Do you want her?”

Zuko sighs and doesn’t bother voicing an answer when she already knows. Azula isn’t one for pointless questions, and maybe in eight-five days he’ll have the mental capacity to figure out why, exactly, she can’t seem to let this go.

Azula hisses between her teeth at his silence, suddenly thrusting the shreds of bread back into his chest hard enough to rock him backward and then continuing to push until he has to grab for the bench to keep from falling. “Don’t mistake the first person to whisper something sweet into your ear as anything other than what it was, *Brother*,” she snarls, nails digging in through his tunic. “And don’t sacrifice any more than you already have for something you never had in the first place.”

Zuko bites his tongue, because this isn’t a battle he is willing to fight with her, refusing to reply beyond raising a hand to keep the bread from falling. Her eyes narrow, and he can see her debating whether to test his resistance before she shoves off him as suddenly as she lunged into his space in the first place.

He slowly straightens, resettling his robes and watching as she strides away, all stiff shoulders and blazing eyes and leashed fury looking for an outlet. And looks after her, gathering the crumbs in his lap and wondering how she’ll react to the first person to give her praise instead of punishment, to the first person that catches her eyes for reasons other than being an active threat.

Probably light them on fire, he thinks ruefully as he tosses the last of the bread into the water. Azula would never allow herself the weakness.

Aang screaming his way across the clearing and out the other side rather gives away Toph’s update a few minutes later when she strolls back into camp at a much more measured pace. “Didn’t work.”

Katara slowly turns away from Aang’s path to look back at her. “…You don’t say.”

Well…shit. They have a little over one more day to figure this out, and Aang isn’t exactly progressing in the direction Sokka had hoped for. He doesn’t know if his mistake was giving them too much or not enough time in the schedule, but either way, he’s pretty sure he messed it up somewhere.

Zuko is barely dressed for training—and he *needs* to light something on fire this morning— when someone knocks at the door, only slipping in at his call, which is *not* what anyone usually does with Zuko’s rooms. It’s a servant, but not his usual. A messenger.

Zuko is wary of another early-morning message, but this one seems official enough—and the messenger’s hands are bare against the paper—that he only pauses a moment before taking the scroll. It’s a notice that the Council is convening fifteen degrees after sunrise, today, instead of their usual afternoon session, and Prince Zuko’s presence is required.

Fuck.

Zuko barely remembers to dismiss the messenger before he dashes back into his rooms, already stripping off his training tunic and casting around for his formal robes. They usually get laundered during the day for the afternoon and shit, he’s going to need to improvise with the over robe, that is *definitely* a stain. If he tried to show up with that, Azula would set him on fire on principle.

Here’s the power play that Zuko had foolishly started to think would never come. Which means that all at once, things might finally be in motion that Zuko has been waiting and waiting on. Agni’s balls, he doesn’t know if he’ll ever feel ready for this.

&#45;-

The morning war council—because that’s what it is now, not that it was anything different before—is, somehow, even worse than yesterday’s. By some miracle, Zuko is able to keep his visible anger to the pissy, simmering kind that everyone’s used to from him, and not the completely unstable turmoil that he actually feels as the Generals outline precisely how they’ve taken Zuko’s knowledge and experience in the Earth Kingdom and twisted it into something horrifying, something so far beyond what he thought anyone could do with his words.

Agni, he tried to take the unexpected opportunity to show them a path to a swift end to the war, toward a new beginning, and instead…

“Well it *will* be fast, what they’re suggesting.”

“I can think of faster,” Zuko says darkly, glaring at the breakfast buffet for lack of better options right now to glower at.

Azula snorts as she selects a plate of dainty buns. “You of all people know that Father knows to look out for poisons in the night. And really—” Her tone turns sardonic. “Would you do something so *dishonorable*?”

“I don’t want to hear *anything* about honor when they’re in there suggesting—” He cuts himself off, unable to even give voice to it yet, like somehow that will make it final when there’s technically still time to change things. But Agni’s flaming dick, it makes him furious how to hear them all bluster about their honor when it doesn’t matter as if that makes up for their silence when it does.

“Watch yourself,” Azula murmurs as she strides away with a flick of her head to settle her already-perfect bangs.

Zuko knows. He knows. That he needs to watch the things he says out loud, and that the heart of his nation is a festering mess of selfish ambition. And that if this is how things are going to be, if this is the path that the Council will choose to reshape the world, over every other option available to them…well, then maybe that changes things for Zuko, too.

He knows, and for once he thinks he knows it before Azula, that doors would close with this that could never be opened again, ones that she might not care for but that Zuko *needs*. And he knows, where she doesn’t, that he can walk his own path if he has to, much as it makes his inner fire wrench to imagine it. Much as his inner fire has already twisted and writhed and tied itself into knots during the planning of it.

Eighty-four days until the Comet comes and the world changes, for better or for worse. But just one until the Black Sun, and Zuko’s never forgotten what he’s here for, or how much can change in just a few minutes used well.

He doesn’t need to be hasty, not yet, there’s still time. But a much more finite amount, now, to determine if the path he’s chosen for himself will be walked alone.

Breakfast is objectively delicious, one of Katara’s better efforts. She’s really getting a feel for the Fire Nation herbs they keep encountering. It still sits like a ball of lead on Sokka’s stomach, even as he forces himself to take bite after bite. He needs the sustenance, the energy and nutrients now more than ever. And honestly, if he could make this meal last forever and never have to think about what comes next, he would.

“Aang’s plan to not sleep until the invasion starts doesn’t seem sound,” Toph finally says over the faint sounds of Katara trying to cajole Aang into post-meal cleanup instead of extra pushups.

“I would agree with that.” Katara is saying something about wanting a bending partner and Sokka hopes that’s just an excuse. He thought she was doing pretty okay, the past few days.

Toph scrunches up her face. “How long before he starts hallucinating?”

Sokka eyes the way Aang is making kissy faces in Katara’s direction. “Not as long as we would like.”

Toph doesn’t have the patience to let the silence drag before she finally gets tired of waiting. “Come on, Snoozles. Me and Katara already tried.”

“I know, I know,” Sokka mutters. “Just…let a man finish breakfast first.” And figure out what the fuck he’s going to say while he’s at it. Katara tried the soothing approach and Toph tried the tough love. Sokka has about one-third of his bowl left to come up with something else to help the savior of the world save himself from himself, or else the entire invasion tomorrow is going to be dead in the water.

&#45;-

Zuko will give a prayer to Agni, later, that none of the torches flare out of control, caught as they are between the press of Zuko and Azula’s short tempers.

“Are you *trying* to bait him?”

“Are you *trying* to let him walk all over you?”

They glare at each other, jaws clenched, before spinning with matching huffs to stalk toward opposite ends of the refreshment tables. Zuko checks the time as he goes and wants to scream, or maybe flip the table, or smash it. Agni’s hot steaming shit, they aren’t even halfway through this.

Sokka finally manages to catch Aang’s attention in the late morning. One would think with how wired the kid is that he would notice his environment a little more, but he seems to be walking a dangerous kind of wakeful disassociation when it comes to his surroundings.

Sokka doesn’t give Aang time to wander off again once he has his focus, just grabs his arm and starts towing him off toward a more private place with a blunt order: “Heart to heart.”

“But—”

“Heart to heart,” Sokka repeats. “Now.”

“Fine,” Aang mutters, trotting a little so he’s walking alongside Sokka instead of being hauled after him.

They find a place up on one of the Black Cliffs, far enough away for privacy but still in sight of the girls in case of danger, with a great view of the ocean where it crashes against the cliffs. Sokka settles down on a nice-looking rock, getting comfortable as he eyes Aang because no part of him thinks this is going to be quick. “Want to talk about it?”

“No.”

“Too bad,” Sokka says easily, gesturing for Aang to join him. “What are you dreaming about?”

“Doesn’t matter.” Lack of sleep apparently makes Aang sullen and terse, on top of delusional. Sokka…is not unfamiliar with that.

“Come on,” Sokka presses, softening the demand with a gentle bump of his shoulder against Aang’s. “You can’t try to say nothing’s bothering you. Not when you’ve been freaking out for days. ”

Aang sighs, pulling up his knees to rest his chin on them, face pinched and frustrated. “It’s dumb. I meet the Fire Lord and I have no pants on.” Ah. That explains the shouting about laundry. “Or the Fire Lord gives me a math test and I forgot to study. Or I oversleep and I miss the whole invasion. Or…”

“Or?”

Aang hugs himself a little harder. “Or I’m on time for the invasion, but you all get hurt anyway.”

The dread in his voice suggests it’s much worse than just ‘getting hurt,’ and Sokka turns that over, trying to find his footing in this conversation. Spirits, Sokka’s had so much else to worry about that physical injury seems nearly abstract. But it shouldn’t be, it never is, and Sokka can see how for Aang, who isn’t focused on the entire picture but just his corner of it, the reality of that danger wouldn’t be able to be anything but immediately present.

It’s not a good fear. But it’s a *real* fear, valid and earned and sensible. And Sokka wonders again what it says about himself that he can start to see the shape now of where he needs to take this conversation having uncovered it. “Do you think that Katara isn’t ready?”

“No,” Aang says immediately.

“What about Toph?”

Aang snorts. “No.”

“So it’s me then?”

“No! Just…” He struggles to voice what he’s been running from for days. Sokka can sympathize. “You guys can all be ready. But what if it doesn’t *matter*? I’m alone for my part of the plan. For the—at the end.”

Sokka picks his words carefully, making sure that they’re words he actually believes. “We’re all part of a bigger thing, though. It’s more than just any one of us. And it only works if we do it together. None of us are going to be alone because of that, no matter who is or isn’t around us tomorrow.”

Aang makes a noise that Sokka doesn’t have any words for except ‘discontent,’ so he plows forward until he can get a reaction he can work with. “And we prepared each other, right? That’s what training is all about. So even if you’re doing something alone, it’s with me and Toph and Katara and everyone else behind you making it happen.” Aang doesn’t reply, but Sokka can at least finally read uncertainty in the way Aang tugs on his hair. “You don’t agree?”

“It’s just…I haven’t mastered all the elements.” Aang sounds like he’s admitting to some dark secret. “I learned water and earth so fast, and I don’t have any fire, not really…”

“Neither will anyone else, tomorrow,” Sokka points out, ignoring the way his stomach clenches with some mix of dread and anticipation at the idea of all those firebenders suddenly without their fire. “That levels the playing field. When the time comes tomorrow, Ozai is just going to be some guy with a fancy piece of metal in his hair.”

“He’s still going to be the Fire Lord, though.”

“I mean, the ‘fire’ part seems like a pretty significant perquisite—”

“He rules a whole country! All those people and soldiers and everything, he tells them all what to do and they listen. And I have eight minutes to get him to surrender.”

Eight minutes and thirteen seconds, but Sokka doesn’t think Aang will appreciate the correction. “You don’t need him to surrender, though,” Sokka says carefully. That’s never been one of the outcomes he’s chalked up as particularly likely, or particularly desirable in his darker moments. “We just need him to be…not ruling, when the eclipse ends.”

Aang hunches in on himself instead of replying, and Sokka runs his words back, treading cautiously now as he says, “That bothers you.”

“…He’s the Fire Lord,” Aang finally repeats, as if that explains everything. “He’s used to ordering people around. To being in charge. Why would he listen to me?”

*Because you won’t give him a choice*. Sokka doesn’t let that thought break free, though. “We’ve had to tell a lot of people in charge what to do in the past few months,” he says instead. He can appreciate that Aang’s views on the Fire Lord aren’t the same as Sokka’s opinions of Zuko’s father, and that now isn’t the time to try to change them.

“I guess,” Aang shrugs, picking at the strap of his sandal.

“We told the Northern Water Tribe how to defend themselves,” Sokka points out. “And Ba Sing Se. We told the Earth King how to rule. The Southern Water Tribe and all our friends are following the plan we made.” And isn’t that a bizarre thought, still, when Sokka spends too long looking at it. He doesn’t like to spend much time doing that. “You’re already telling people in charge what to do, Aang, and being listened to,” Sokka says gently. “This isn’t so different.”

“Except *you’re* usually the one doing the telling.”

Sokka snorts, saying dryly, “I borrow heavily from your authority.” He bites back a laugh when Aang looks startled that anyone might think he has any, adding, “But if you need to you can just imitate me and then you’ll be fine.” And if he says it briskly enough, maybe Aang will agree that that settles the matter.

“I can’t just be *you*,” Aang protests, which…is honestly kind of flattering. Sokka might not be quite as touchy about not being a bender as he used to be, most days, but it never hurts to be recognized.

Except it’s a bit inconvenient now, specifically, so Sokka can’t let it seem *too* impressive, not when it’s supposed to help things seem approachable. “Want to know what the trick is?” Aang perks up, nodding eagerly, and Sokka lets his pause become weighty as he leans in to whisper, “Fake it until you make it.”

Aang blinks. “What?”

“Bravado all the way through, buddy,” Sokka grins, clapping Aang on the shoulder. “If you seem confident then everyone else acts like you actually are. Great, huh?”

“…Huh.”

“It’s a tried-and-true strategy,” Sokka says, eyeing Aang’s stunned expression and continuing forward before he can reconsider. “And you know what? I learned it from Zuko.” Aang finally turns to look at him full-on in his surprise, and Sokka offers a half-smile back. “So. Just because someone has a fancy title, or a crown on their head? It doesn’t mean anything.”

Sokka holds his breath while Aang chews that over, trying to pretend—putting that strategy right into action—that he isn’t getting more and more nervous with each sidelong glance Aang steals. Aang is acting like Sokka just said he was considering going vegetarian, and Aang needs to figure out if he’s serious or not in time to put the shopping list together.

“Believe in yourself, Aang,” Sokka finally says, unable to let the silence drag any longer, not when he has no idea what thoughts Aang might be filling it with. “And if you can’t do that? Then remember that a lot of other people believe in you, too. Whatever gets you there. There isn’t one way you have to feel to be ready.”

Aang nods, biting on his lip but finally relaxing enough to let his legs drop into his usual lotus position, forearms leaning on his thighs. His expression is marginally less broody and marginally more contemplative when he finally glances over, which Sokka is going to take as a win. “What gets you there?”

Sokka takes a deep breath, hoping he isn’t about to undo all his good work, because Sokka’s approach to psyching himself up isn’t exactly cheerful and uplifting. “I know that it will be hard. And I know that I’ve done hard things before. And I’m still here. So I know that I can do them this time, too.”

Aang nods slowly, brow furrowing as he clearly tests out the concept to see how it fits. “And by the end of tomorrow, the hardest thing will be done,” he finally says, open relief in the words.

“…Yeah, buddy,” Sokka says, taking a deep breath and pressing his fingers to his knees to prevent them from curling into fists. “It will be.” Sokka wonders if it still counts at lying if he just desperately hopes it ends up being that way.

“Watch yourself.”

“*I’m* not the one who needs to watch it. What the fuck was that back there?”

Zuko and Azula both exhale hard, cutting their eyes away. Zuko lets the anger settle over his expression, covering anything else as Azula lets out a disdainful sniff, making a show of picking an iced tea from the available options and wrinkling her nose when Zuko randomly grabs a cup of something hot. He doesn’t want to drink it, he just needs something he can boil dry. Admiral Feng had started casting suspicious looks at her teacup in the degrees leading up to this break.

Azula’s voice is quieter after she takes a sip and deems the drink suitable, her lips barely moving. “If you don’t have the guts to do what needs to be—”

“That isn’t the issue,” Zuko cuts in, speaking into his mug to obscure the words. Ugh. Oolong.

“Isn’t it?”

“I know where this ends, Azula.”

“Do you?”

He flashes a quick glance toward her face. “There’s only one place it could.”

Azula concedes that with a flick of her fingers, expression twisting in mockery, words staying low. “And you think you can do it? Be part of it?” She drags her eyes over him. “Really, Brother, you can’t even handle it when a turtle duck dies.”

“Four years is a long time,” Zuko finally says, his eyes sweeping over the mostly-empty antechamber. Nearly everyone has made their way back inside.

st There’s a slight, telling pause. “I don’t mean indirectly, Zuzu,” she finally drawls. “The 41 doesn’t count.”

Zuko hisses low between his teeth at the words designed to put him off balance and back into his place, giving her a quick, slashing glare. “I wasn’t counting them,” he snaps, stalking away to join the meeting, for once not bothering to wait for her reply.

Sokka finds Katara practicing her waterbending at what seems to be her normal pace from what little he can tell about it. He’s relieved to see that she seems easy with her water again, even if she’s frowning a bit more in concentration than she normally would for something that Sokka is fairly sure is on the more basic end of what she can do these days.

“How’d it go,” she asks without turning, feet rooted and body swaying with the motion of her arms.

Sokka takes a moment to consider. Both of them walked away with no weeping and no punches thrown, so, could have gone worse. “You should go tell him that he’s ready,” he decides.

“What?” She says, blinking and releasing the water in her surprise, turning like full line of sight will help her hear better.

“Tell him that he’s ready,” Sokka repeats, wondering if he should take a big step back from the water when Katara’s brow tightens in confusion and no small amount of agitation.

“Didn’t you tell him that?”

“He’ll believe it if you say it.”

“…You don’t think it’s true?”

“It’s as true as it’s ever going to be,” Sokka says, shrugging. Sure, he would like Aang to be feeling more self-assured. Spirits, he would even take cocky. But at this point, reluctantly coming around to feeling resolute is more than enough.

Katara huffs, folding her arms in annoyance. “So you say it to him, then. Do your whole— manly talk thing or whatever you call it.”

Sokka sighs in exasperation., “We just did that. And it will mean more coming from you.” Katara eyes him suspiciously. “Why?”

Sokka gives her a look, slowly raising his eyebrows. “Do you really want me to go there?” Because he will *happily* start all that payback right now.

Katara stares a moment before her mouth forms a silent ‘oh,’ ducking her head against a sudden blush. “Don’t be telling me to tell people stuff,” she grumbles, tossing her hair like she can shake Sokka’s implication away. Good luck with that. He’s been living with her implications for weeks now. “I don’t want to hear it from Mr. Never Talk About Anything Important.”

“Hey now,” Sokka protests. Spirits, how does it always get turned back on him? Is this some secret thing little sisters learn? “Just because I don’t talk about it with *you—”*

“Oh, sorry, did I miss the part where you and Zuko filled each other in on all your plans and also your feelings?”

Sokka scowls, crossing his arms. Low. Blow. “Just go tell Aang how great you think he is.”

“I don’t see why you can’t—”

Sokka throws his hands up and lays it all out since *talking about it* is so important to her. “Because it means something different when it comes from someone you care about!”

“…Oh.”

Zuko finds Azula on the roof near the palace library, feet propped up on one of the gargoyles that dot the roofline on the older parts of the palace. She doesn’t seem to be bothered by putting her boots on one of Agni’s spirit-warriors, just looking thoughtful as she gazes up at the moon as it drifts between clouds like it isn’t anything to feel threatened by. It’s a nice thought.

“Enjoying the night, Zuzu?”

He leans against the wall where the second story joins with the first, shifting so that his shape won’t be visible to anyone inside the palace or out on the grounds, pressing into the shadows.

Azula’s eyes flicker over at his silence, little more than a bright glimmer in the darkness. “Octocat got your tongue? Spit it out, we don’t have all night.”

Zuko manages to get the words out only because he spent so much time rehearsing them. “I need to ask you for something.”

“Brother, I’m shocked. You never ask anyone for anything.” He can see the shape of her fingers lazily flicking through the air. “You’re a veritable island moving through life, Zuzu.”

“I’m serious,” he rasps, managing not to choke on admitting it.

A stretch of sharp silence, then her voice is hard, losing all its taunting edges. “What is it, Zuko?”

Zuko takes a deep breath and jumps in with both feet, trusting…honestly, he doesn’t know what he’s trusting to see him through to the other side with this. His own read on the situation, his own judgment, his ability to understand his sister, all of which are terrifying to rely on. “It has to do with tomorrow,” he starts, “I know Father put you in charge, and…”

Azula doesn’t react as he speaks, but she doesn’t stop him either. And at the end of it, when his words are all out and lingering in the darkness, she doesn’t say yes. But she also doesn’t say no, which really was the best that Zuko could have hoped for. He sighs now that it’s done, dropping his head back against the still sun-warm stone, briefly closing his eyes and gathering himself for what he still needs to do tonight.

Her voice stops him when he shifts to leave, though. “Are you going to see dear Uncle Iroh before the night is through, too?” Some of the mockery slides back into her tone. “Maybe yell at him some more?”

Zuko snorts quietly. “I hadn’t planned on it.”

“Finally giving up?” A flash of moonlight lights the idle curiosity on her face, like his answer doesn’t matter, before a cloud throws her back into darkness.

Zuko sighs, summoning something close to a wry little smile even though he knows she can’t see it. “I *do* know how to recognize a futile thing, Azula.”

“Eventually,” she scoffs. “Really, Brother, it took you years.”

Zuko sighs, not responding because he doesn’t want her to hear the lingering doubt in his voice if he does. It felt—still feels, in a raw, sluggish way—like ripping up some part of himself to acknowledge that it was pointless to keep trying there, at least in the time he had left.

And Azula isn’t wrong that it had been harder than it should have been to admit to himself considering Zuko had nearly four years of experience to drive home the fact that Uncle can’t read between the lines when it comes to Zuko. Not that many people can, but…Uncle looks at Zuko and doesn’t even realize there *are* lines to read between. Zuko thought it could be different, being back here, not being all they have to each other anymore, not being just a nephew anymore, but—whenever Zuko raged and shouted and seethed, Uncle still didn’t hear what Zuko was trying to say in the only way he could say it. Uncle just heard betrayal.

Zuko is aware that he is a miserable liar, which should make him a miserable actor. It makes him afraid, sometimes, that knowledge. Maybe he isn’t acting at all.

But finally, Aang is settled, and for once everyone else seems fine too, the rhythms of their breathing blending together to form a familiar little symphony that means *all is well* to Sokka’s subconscious.

## Chapter 9: The Best Laid Plans
