### Text

The Day of the Black Sun dawns clear and bright. The deep blue of night slowly gives way to gray and then red-tinged dawn as the sun briefly paints the sea in streaks of fire before climbing above the horizon. Sokka watches the sunrise, still cuddling Momo in his arms, and forces his heartbeat to stay steady as he remembers a different sunrise in the North, when Agni’s light heralded the start of a different invasion.

It’s the same participants, though. The same war. The same essential strategic position for each nation despite all the life that was lost before. Spirits, but Sokka means to change that by the time the sun hits the horizon again, as definitively as they possibly can.

Katara is the next to rise, pausing to give his shoulder a wordless squeeze before she sets about making breakfast. The sounds and rhythms of her rustling through the packs and starting the fire settle over Sokka’s rising nerves, a comforting familiarity that keeps the tides of his anxiety from cresting too high. Her movements are precise, crisp, steady, and Sokka lets out a little breath of relief when she bends water into their pot with absent confidence, feeling like the last piece of a puzzle just slotted perfectly into place.

Toph is next—she can never sleep through the sounds of breakfast being made, or maybe it’s the bodies moving around—looking sleep rumpled and dirt-covered as she spins the domed helmet she’s made herself in her hands, metalbended bracers already in place. She’s wearing a determined kind of eagerness that does more to ward off attention than her sparse armor, her posture silently daring anyone to ask her if *she* feels ready.

It isn’t long before Aang joins him, Momo squirming free to leap to his bare shoulder almost before Sokka registers his presence. Sokka does a double-take at the sight of him back in his orange robes, head freshly shaved and gleaming bright in the early morning light, blue tattoos proud.

Sokka takes in Aang’s tight grip around his glider and the bouncing energy in his step and can’t say the robes and the hair and the tattoos don’t feel right. “Feeling more like yourself?”

“Yeah,” Aang smiles, suddenly bashful as he rubs his head. “Feeling good.” He gives his glider a sharp twirl, jaw going firm. “And ready to take the Fire Lord down once and for all.”

“Well, *I’m* feeling inspired,” Toph drawls, and if she meant it to be sarcastic, she misses by a wide margin. “How are you going to do it?” She continues. “Airbending to really rub it in? Waterbending to soak him like a wet fire ferret while he can’t fight back? Earthbending because it's objectively the best? The Avatar state to show him whose boss?”

“I’ll see what feels right,” Aang grins, taking a few swipes at an imaginary opportunity with his staff. “But not the Avatar state.”

Katara glances up from where the rice is looking like it’s almost ready. “Why not?”

Aang straightens with a shrug. “It’s out of reach because my seventh chakra is still locked from Azula’s lightning.”

He sounds completely calm about it—thank anything listening—but Sokka can see Katara’s healer’s mind working. “…So you need a really good stretch?”

“Or to let go of all my worldly wants, desires, connections!”

Katara blinks, nonplussed, cutting Sokka a quick quizzical look, as if Sokka’s ever been an expert in that kind of mumbo jumbo. He’s going to take his cue from Aang here—after the past few days, if Aang is relaxed about it, then Sokka will be too. And while it’s not *ideal* to not have that card up their sleeve, it’s not like the Avatar state was never part of the plan to begin with, so it’s not like anything has fundamentally changed.

Sokka didn’t want to rely on something they couldn’t control. And maybe it’s for the best, considering the number of civilians that will be around, and the degree of destruction that generally accompanies Aang going all scary-glowy.

And it doesn’t matter if it isn’t for the best, because it’s too late to do anything about it anyway. With the shape of mist-hazed ships just beginning to form on the horizon and the sun steadily climbing, the clock is ticking. All they can do now is execute to the best of their ability, and all Sokka can do is hope that all his planning will be enough.

&#45;-

Zuko is cutting across the gardens, his inner flame pulsing to the sound of his boots against the paved walkways when a flash of just-over-the-caldera light against dark-washed armor has him slowing his stride, his breath hitching for a moment before he finds his rhythm again.

He maintains his pace to intercept Azula’s unhurried stroll, because even only knowing the parts of today's plan she’s deigned to tell him, he knows there’s no reason for her to be here except to find him. It’s too early still for anything else, Agni’s rising still tingling in his veins and degrees and degrees yet before her face is hidden from the world.

But maybe it’s not about him. Maybe Azula’s just restless. Neither of them has ever had much by way of patience for sitting and waiting, and the eerie quiet of the palace this morning doesn’t exactly lend itself to biding one’s time within the walls.

He lingers at the edge of the turtle dock pond and her high-kneed boots crush the grass as she pauses at his left shoulder, gaze sweeping with mild disinterest across the grounds like happening to stop at his side is purely incidental. Her armor is polished to a high sheen, deep black and blood red, a perfect match for the hair neatly framing her face and her immaculate lipstick. Her gold hairpiece gleams, sharp, picking out the color of her eyes. The picture of Fire Nation excellence, ready for battle.

Zuko is hyperaware of the fact that he’s geared for a very different kind of battle. His swords are a welcome weight across over his back like they haven’t been in weeks. His boots are comfortable, scuffed, and he chose his clothes for movement and speed and sturdiness. They might also be as deep black and blood-red as Azula’s, but Zuko knows he presents the picture of something else entirely.

She rakes him with a piercing look, taking in his outfit without even a flicker in her expression. “Subtle.”

“We’ve been over that,” Zuko murmurs, glancing down at the water where their reflection wavers and breaks as the turtle ducks paddle over in hope of breakfast.

“Yes,” Azula rolls her eyes. “I suppose you’ve never been one for an understated gesture when literally anything else will do.”

Zuko only barely manages to avoid looking pointedly at her head-to-toe color coordination, his inner fire wobbling with an incredulous kind of amusement. “You’re going down already?”

Azula shrugs, holding out her nails to examine them in the light. “I thought I would redo my nails while I waited.” Her eyes slash toward him. “You should consider joining, Brother, your cuticles are a disaster. It makes you look like a nervous wreck.”

“Noted,” Zuko says mildly, gaze wandering back to the water. “After,” he adds after a beat, the word soft. After all this.

“Hm.” He can feel her eyes trying to examine his face through the scar. “Is that a promise?”

Agni, that’s a loaded question if Zuko’s ever heard one. “It doesn’t only depend on me,” he points out, watching her reflection instead of her because this close, alone, with the degrees burning away…he can’t afford to slip now, even if he can feel the words pressing against his throat, wanting to break free.

Her eyes narrow slightly, darting toward the water to catch his gaze. “Don’t take too long to get to your place,” she finally orders, voice low with warning.

“I’ll be where I need to be,” Zuko assures her, the truth of it ringing through his tone, his posture relaxed and loose.

Azula stares, face unmoving even though Zuko can practically feel the intention to press that answer in the pulse of her inner fire against his heat sense. Finally, though, she just shakes her head, shifting to join him in looking at the turtle ducks. “I know it’s hard for you, Brother, but don’t do anything stupid.” She flicks a piece of imaginary lint into the pond. “I made your job easy. Even you can’t mess it up.”

Zuko barely glances at her, feeling a spark of annoyance in an almost perfunctory way. He can’t work up the energy to get truly incensed by her prodding when at least half his attention is siphoned toward worrying about what’s going to come. He isn’t good at playing out scenarios once too many variables come into play, not like basically everyone else he knows is, but Zuko knows that he could finish out this day sitting in front of the hearth as the sun sets, meditating on his renewed connection to Agni. Or things could go the way Azula clearly suspects they will, even though she isn’t saying it outright, in which case…

“Focus, Zuko.”

His eyes flick up, tracing the familiar sharp lines of her profile. “You, too.”

…in which case he isn’t sure that she'll ever forgive him. The thought is a squirming worm of cold through his gut, his inner fire trembling at the edges even though they’re an entire morning yet away from Agni’s touch on the world going dark. And it doesn’t bear thinking about, not when Zuko already knows he can’t let the consequences dictate his actions.

They part on some mutual unspoken signal, each moving again toward their respective destinations with the kind of crisp stride that says ‘fuck off’ as thoroughly as their expressions. They will both, he thinks, be wanting privacy to get ready in their own way to do things that can’t be undone. He hopes she’s strong enough for it like she thinks she is, like she’s never truly had to be before. He knows better than to hope for himself.

&#45;-

Sokka is grinning so wide that his face is starting to ache around the edges. Watching the Southern Water Tribe ships pull into shore, seeing those familiar shapes and sails coming *toward* him, like he hasn’t seen in nearly three years.

Sokka can barely contain himself, bouncing on his toes as lines are thrown and nimble figures jump to secure them on the jutting piers that Toph casually—and conveniently— raises for them. And then the ships are offloading, a tide of Southern Water Tribe blue interspersed with greens and browns and familiar faces, more than Sokka had expected to see, enough to make his favorite plan start to thrum with potential in the back of his mind.

*Okay*, he tells himself, watching Toph get swept up into an enthusiastic greeting from her Earth Rumble friends. *We can do this*.

“Sokka,” Hakoda says, greeting him with open affection and a warrior’s arm clasp that has Sokka smiling even wider. “Katara.” He opens his arms, folding her into a hug—that she visibly decides to allow before hugging him back.

“Did you find everyone?” Sokka asks, scanning over the figures milling around the beach, trying to count and check names off his mental list at the same time.

“We did,” Hakoda says. “And can I say,” he adds dryly as the Foggy Swamp contingent disgorges from a ship, “What *interesting* friends the two of you have made.”

“Oh,” Katara says, looking straight at Sokka. “You don’t know the half of it.”

Sokka feels embarrassed heat creeping up his neck, ducking his head to hide his flush and catching her eye when their Dad glances away to stick out his tongue at her. Now is *not* the time, for at least two very significant reasons, even if part of him still enjoys the flash of familiar teasing, the quick moment of levity before Sokka has to box all that aside again.

“So,” Bato says, sweeping in from nowhere to throw an arm over Sokka and Katara’s shoulders, which Sokka notices Katara accepts with significantly more grace than their Dad’s hug. “Are you ready to tell the entire assembled invasion force about the plan? We got everyone here.”

…Right. That.

Sokka’s heart drops at the reminder, all his neat plans and contingencies and just-in-cases suddenly tangling in his mind as he even begins to think about explaining them to a crowd. “Do I have—”

“Yes.”

He sighs. “Fine. Let’s go this over with.”

“What admirable enthusiasm,” Bato grins, clapping Sokka on the back. “Cheer up—it’s going to be a day for the history books!”

&#45;-

Zuko is up on the roof even though he usually doesn’t do this in daylight anymore, not since he came back at least. But he can’t feel anyone around with his heat sense, or at least not anyone who could see him, and it’s easier to shake the itchy feeling of being watched up here than it is on the ground.

And if Zuko isn’t ready to distance himself from Agni’s touch yet, to leave her warmth and put himself beneath cold stone before he needs to, then that’s between him and all the people who don’t know he’s up here anyway, as close to Agni’s light as he can get himself. He’d rather precisely track Agni’s passage across the sky up here than through the fuzziness of stone and earth. And if he reaches out with his fire sense, straining like he can somehow anchor the sun to the earth when the time comes if he wills it hard enough, like he can yank Agni back the few critical degrees necessary to pass behind the moon unscathed—well, there’s a reason he’s up here where no one can see it.

He tracks Agni’s passage by sight, too, across the cloudless sky, in the shifting shadow of the caldera chasing the golden arc of Agni’s light like some premonition of what’s to come, in the path the sunlight makes across a certain prison tower, creeping into the follow of stone it sits within, creating dark pits of windows and throwing almost-unnoticeable shadows on seemingly smooth surfaces where the rock is uneven, pooling like liquid fire along each gilded ledge.

Zuko flexes his hands, concentrating on the clench and release of muscles, on the strength of his fingers, on the heat pooled in his palms and the soft metal pressed between them. It feels good to turn his bending toward something like this, something small and contained and precise and almost like play, something so unlike what he is going to need to do all too soon. It feels good to fill his body with his fire, knowing that soon he will have eight minutes and thirteen seconds of icy cold to get through.

Zuko might have felt that chill before, edged in darkness and in the depths of fever, but feeling metal shift under his hands, seeking his body and his fire moving in sync in such a tangible way does more to steady him than any hazy recollection of clawing his way back to the light ever could. It’s a firm reminder that that is in the past, something more solid than memory to hold on to settle him for what’s to come, until he feels a little less wild around the edges, until he can believe that he’s once more wrapped in and grounded by his purpose and resolve.

Zuko glances down at the shape emerging from his heat-warmed hands, the shape he’s been teasing around for half the morning now. He’s vaguely startled to see that he’s become maybe even halfway decent at teasing out delicate shapes and graceful edges from the lump he has to work with. But then, the past few weeks—shit, the past few *days*—have certainly been stressful enough that Zuko’s desperately needed the outlet to keep his mind focused and his emotions off his face.

Zuko can admit to himself, looking at what he’s made before pressing an imperfect edge back down, that he isn’t exactly just idly burning off excess fire anymore, isn’t just distracting himself the way he would in the teashop. Or rather, that he’s distracting himself in a way very *like* how he would in the teashop, a way that dances around but never directly touches a very specific purpose.

He’s making something specific today much as he’s trying not to focus on anything at all right now, and as he pulls at the excess metal, trying to draw out a specific pattern before he catches himself at it again, his mind drifts back to his brief time in that forge. Agni, but he wishes he had retained more there, or from Piandao all those years ago, so he didn’t have to spend so much on focus-grabbing trial and error now when his focus needs to be so unwavering and sure on everything else.

It’s getting harder and harder to keep this part of himself quiet, though. And Zuko wants this to be perfect. Zuko can accept all sorts of imperfect things for himself, but Sokka doesn’t deserve anything but the absolute best that Zuko can give him.

At first Zuko thought he was making a sculpture or some kind of small statue, but none of those had felt *right.* And now he can see as it starts to take shape that it’s something else entirely, something small and strong. Something that could maybe be part of a bracelet, or a choker, or an earring. Something that could maybe lay claim in a way that others would be able see, like the mark of Zuko’s hands never could.

Zuko considers that he’s being particularly presumptions in making this, as if all he’s going to need to do is muster up an apology and give Sokka a token of his regard. Zuko considers that he’s being particularly stupid in making *this,* of all things, for a Water Tribesman. Even if the South doesn’t do that, because Zuko is well-aware that Sokka’s been to the North and that he isn’t dumb.

Or maybe it’s just Zuko’s subconscious being its usual blunt self and having as little patience for slow realizations as Zuko generally has for anything else.

Ideally Zuko would have more to show for himself the next time he sees Sokka. He had hoped to have more, because he can’t seem to stop himself from hoping these days even knowing how much it hurts. And maybe he will. Nothing is set, after all. Nothing is done, yet.

But Azula is so rarely wrong—even if Zuko *needs* her to be wrong about this, with a kind of desperation he won’t quite look at, with the kind of desperation he knows means she’s right. She wouldn’t go to lengths like these on just a hunch.

With a sigh, Zuko tucks the metal carefully away, because there’s no use getting himself caught on those kinds of thoughts now. He raises his hands automatically to check the swords on his back before turning his attention back to Caldera, to the calm ridge of the crater’s edge and the cloudless blue sky and the steady passage of Agni’s light.

He will find out soon enough, one way or another. Now, Zuko tucks away any kind of wanting as carefully as the pendant-to-be, letting it all sink down to the center of his resolve. He takes a deep breath, holding the sea-tinged air in his lungs and letting his inner fire spiral out underneath his skin, reveling in the feel of it full of readiness for what’s to come and twisting around the thin possibility that maybe none of it will have to happen at all.

&#45;-

Zuko can’t stay on the roof forever, not unless he wants Azula to start wondering enough about where he is to figure it all out early. He slips back into the palace when he can’t stand being still any longer, wandering the empty halls until he finally slows to a stop in the portrait gallery again. It’s close enough to where he’s supposed to be for Zuko to just seem belligerent and sullenly defiant, which no one will find particularly unusual, rather than something else that would require him to be put back into his place.

Zuko is examining the only portrait of his mother that he’s found in the palace when he hears it, jolting out of his contemplation of the shape of his mother’s face, of the way her hands sit on his and Azula’s young shoulders. The warning bell rings up over the crater’s edge, quickly rising, the air so unnaturally still that it feels like even the weather is waiting to see what comes.

Zuko holds his breath, waiting for the double note that would signal a false alarm or a test, or the drumbeat that would announce a storm. But instead, the warning is picked up much closer to the caldera, then from the top of the ridge, then from the palace itself, until the very air seems to vibrate with the call to arms.

*Fuck*.

Zuko closes his eyes, indulging for just a heartbeat in a surge of frustrated, exasperated despair. That fucking *idiot*. Zuko doesn’t know if he’s ever met such a smart, brilliant person who could be so *stupid*. And it’s only now, as they’re dashed, that Zuko realizes just how large a part of him had been hoping that Azula was wrong, or lying after all, that he wouldn’t…

Zuko opens his eyes, cutting off the thought before it can twist its way to its useless end. Zuko knows not to waste energy with hoping, not when there’s action to be taken, and especially not when the actions are forced on him by others.

But no. Others might be walking their own paths, might be closing off turns he hoped to take and opening up doors best left closed. But they are not forcing Zuko to act, even if Zuko can look at the choices available to him and know that they aren’t really choices at all.

Zuko crosses to the tall, thin windows that light the gallery, quickly hauling himself up into the corner that lets him get a good angle over Caldera if he leans out enough to clear the decorative filigree. He looks even further up to the sky, though, instead of the city, straining to see anything past the volcanic ridges, and his inner fire wrenches with a mixture of relief and instinctive fear when he finally picks out a distinctive shadow gliding across the brightness of the sun. At least Sokka isn’t being totally foolish.

Zuko takes a deep breath, sparing one last glance back toward the portrait, meeting flat, painted eyes and tucking this away too alongside the other parts of his resolve. He can feel how each piece, so strong on its own, sits in such fragile balance relative to the others, like only a single misstep could send it all crashing done.

Zuko takes a deep breath, and jumps down to set into motion what needs to be done.

The battle is going…okay. Well, even. Honestly, beyond what Sokka could have hoped for. Contingency after contingency falls away as they clear checkpoint after checkpoint—getting through the Gates, the underwater ships actually working, gaining purchase on the beach, the tanks crawling up the steep roads of the outlying city with no pit traps or impassible terrain to deal with.

It’s like everything that could have gone wrong is going their way instead, and Sokka might start thinking about benevolent spirits if he believed in that shit. The Fire Nation soldiers are mustering against them in numbers on the lower ends of Sokka’s estimates, and seem more unprepared than Sokka expected compared to the ones he encountered in the Earth Kingdom —cushy interior postings, maybe? Even the firebenders are manageable with so many benders of their own, and with the Southern Water Tribe warriors having so many years of experience against firebenders in far more flammable conditions than this.

The soldiers are falling back beneath the invasion force like they’ve never faced organized, mechanized resistance before, and Sokka allows himself a brief surge of ‘*maybe this is* *actually going to be smooth sailing’* before he drags himself back into planning mode, scanning for weakness in their lines, checking for anyone getting too excited and too far ahead of the main force.

Sokka’s almost relieved when the towers along the ridgeline begin firing on them from above. Here, at least, is one of his backup plans that can go into action. He barely even needs to raise his hand before Hakoda is already in motion, sprinting toward the rear of the force with Sokka at his heels, Appa swooping down, a heart-stoppingly immense figure in his armor as he skids to a stop.

Sokka can’t help the fierce swell of pride he feels as he vaults up onto Appa’s back, helping Katara pull up their Dad. The three of them together are going to shut these towers down, in Water Tribe blues and wolf helms and moon-sigil armor so there can be no doubt about exactly who’s taking the fight to the enemy’s door.

Sokka almost feels like he could do anything right now, everything around him slotting perfectly into place, everything visible before him with the kind of clarity that only comes when your adrenaline is up and your mind is calm and the world seems to move in slow motion around you. He and Katara work seamlessly to clear their tower with the kind of unthinking synchronization he used to dream of back home, Sokka covering her back and funneling soldiers her way as tentacles of water lash through the tight corridors. It feels good, to destroy a Fire Nation watchtower. And to do it *fast.*

Speed is good, today. Speed means—please, let it mean—that this invasion is going as cleanly as it can possibly go. And speed is necessary. Sokka’s mental clock is pinging at the back of his awareness with each minute that passes with Aang infiltrating the interior ahead of the ground forces. If Aang encounters too little resistance, if he goes too fast—

Too much speed—that opens up space for error.

“Dad!” Katara screams, sprinting across the surprisingly wide, rocky plateau that tops the mountain. Sokka is on her heels, spinning around to look for danger and forcing himself to truly confirm that the enemy is subdued, that Hakoda cleared his tower before he went down, even as everything in Sokka wants to sprint with her.

“Katara, I’m fine, I’m fine,” Hakoda pants, wincing as he raises an arm toward her, clearly reconsidering trying to sit up. His face is pale, drawn tight, body tense in that this-hurts-a-lot-and-maybe-it-will-go-away-if-I-pretend-it-doesn’t way that Sokka is familiar with.

“You’re *not*,” Katara snaps, fumbling for her waterskin.

“You’re definitely not,” Sokka confirms as he takes in blood and charred skin, feeling his gorge rising at the sight. Sokka’s calm fractures at the edges like he can’t afford to let it. He needs to stay focused, needs to stay in control. One person’s injury, no matter how important that person is, can’t matter enough to derail the plan.

“Cover me,” Katara orders, falling into her role in this battle with a look of fierce concentration.

“Done.” Sokka turns his back on them through pure force of will, scanning for danger and along with Appa and sparing a quick moment to be grateful that Katara is here, that she didn’t protest not having a frontline position. She’s the only one of them who can play this role—who can let Sokka know that he did everything he possibly could to minimize casualties—and still be trusted to hold their own in the rearguard to preserve their retreat. He just wasn’t sure if she would see it that way.

Finally, Hakoda makes a sound of…relief? And Katara lets out a sigh. “That’s as good as it's going to get for now,” she says, voice tight, but after so long helping her at Aang’s bedside Sokka can parse the difference between worried and grim. Sokka sags in relief as he glances back to see Hakoda leaning carefully upright under her support.

“This will hold,” Hakoda says, gingerly testing his range of motion, skin showing pink and fragile through the rends in his tunic, the vulnerable stretch just below the edges of his armor.

“But not well enough to fight,” Katara cautions.

“No,” Hakoda agrees, looking at Sokka, eyes serious. “Not on the front lines.”

“Okay, okay,” Sokka says, mind working as he adjusts plans and launches contingencies. “This is fine. I have a backup plan where—”

“Sokka.”

He trips to a stop, hiccupping over his words to keep them in.

“We don’t need a backup plan,” Hakoda says with that mixture of gentle and firm that screams ‘*Dad*.’ “We need you to lead the battle now.”

“But—”

“I believe in you. This is your plan, Sokka. The men will take heart. They’ll rally around you.”

Sokka gapes for a moment, voiceless, before turning to Katara like she’s going to volunteer in his place. She just shrugs, nodding her agreement and tilting her head to show that she’s still comfortable with her piece of the plan if they split up. Which Sokka did have a contingency for, and he knows she remembers it, so… “Okay. Okay. I can do that. I will do that.”

“I know you will,” Hakoda smiles, reaching forward to clasp his forearm.

Katara musters a fierce grin for him. “Make us proud.”

Sokka nods, recognizing a dismissal when he hears it and taking a deep breath, shoving himself forcefully back toward his battle calm with each beat of his heart. He sprints to Appa’s side, finding handholds in armor where he’s used to grasping fur and yip yipping them back toward the army—toward *his* army. Spirits, Sokka scrambles to push away the lurch that gives him, clinging to that sense of cool-calm-collected that he had only five minutes ago.

“Sokka!” Bato breaks away from the men as Sokka lands, sprinting over in that half-crouch of an experienced warrior used to navigate battlefields.

“We need to reform before they can deploy any resistance,” Sokka says as he slides down Appa’s armor, mind full of his glimpse of the landscape as they came in toward the invasion force, the terrain and the enemy and the invasion force trying to push through both. “Let’s get a wedge formation and hit them fast and hard.”

There are nods all around from those who hear, the order echoed without question down the lines and Sokka tightens his grip on his sword instead of going weak at the knees at the way they all respond to his command. That trust…He will do them all proud.

“Sokka?” Bato asks, voice low, and Sokka gives him a quick glance and a reassuring nod. They both know that Hakoda was supposed to come back with him, and he can see the tension leave Bato’s shoulders at the assurance, the renewed focus in his eyes.

“Ready?” Sokka glances around, pausing and taking a deep breath as Bato steps up behind his right shoulder as if Sokka were the Chief. “Remember, hit them fast. We don’t need excessive casualties, we’re giving Aang space and cover.” There are murmurs of understanding all around, the quiet clatter of weapons shifting and adjusting as people psych themselves up. “Good.” Sokka takes another breath. “Let’s end this.”

He almost stumbles back from the force of the fierce shout that greets his words, and then the wedge is charging forward, Sokka in the lead. His sword is comfortable in his hands, battle-calm like armor around his shoulders. He has plans queued up and ready to deploy, muscles ready to fight, thoughts clear and focused on top of the blend of fear and excitement bubbling in his chest. His voice surges with the others as they charge uphill, and a steady beat of *Zuko,* *Zuko, Zuko* pulses at the back of his mind that he can’t ignore and can only match to the cadence of his strides, each taking him one step closer to the palace and answers and the end of it all.

Caldera is empty and it’s freaking Sokka out. Even with the warning bells sounding as they were sighted approaching the beach and the time it took them to gain a foothold on the ridge surrounding the city and then breach the defenses into the city proper—there’s no way the populace should have been able to evacuate so quickly and thoroughly that the invasion force doesn’t see even a hint of anyone beyond their own soldiers on the streets.

Sure, the citizens could be hiding inside their homes, could have retreated to some kind of defensible rendezvous points throughout the city. Sure, none of Sokka’s oh-shit triggers have been switched yet, but…it still doesn’t feel right.

Sokka knows they need to press their advantage, though, that they don’t have time for him to step back and analyze and assess, that the whole point of all that planning in the first place was so he wouldn’t have to. They’re starting to really race against the clock. Caldera’s citizens probably withdrew toward the center in response to the attack, that’s all. Or maybe— what if Zuko—

Sokka doesn’t get a chance to finish the thought, wherever it might have ended, because they turn the next corner into a wide plaza and trebuchet fire. *Here’s* that resistance. Okay, right, this is—this is fine. The soldiers must have abandoned the perimeter to marshal their defenses around the interior. Or maybe it’s a counterplan to suck the invasion force into the confines of the city and then attack it from both sides.

Perfect. Sokka can work with that.

“Earthbenders! Cover and counterattack!” Shields of stone shoot up from the ground, Sokka hunkering down next to Toph and whipping out his map, the one he painstakingly copied and filled in and cross-referenced and checked against every book in every library in Ba Sing Se. If they’re *here*, then the possible avenues for a pincer movement…Sokka glances up at a sudden commotion, breaking into a relieved grin when he sees Katara helping Hakoda join the line. Good, that means the rearguard isn’t encountering any trouble. And Sokka could use another opinion before redeploying into a preemptive defensive formation.

“I’m glad you’re here,” Sokka says as Katara and Hakoda join them, trying not to let his relief out too strongly because it’s too early for that. “I could use another set of eyes.”

Hakoda grunts as he sits down on a hunk of rock Toph obligingly stomps out of the ground for him—battle seems to make Toph unusually agreeable. “I’m good enough for that, at least,” he says, leaning carefully forward to study the tattered piece of paper.

“How are things?” Katara asks, hand hovering anxiously over her waterskin even as her face is set in tense focus.

Toph hurls a boulder over her wall, a mighty crash and chorus of screams following shortly after. “Fine.”

“We’re doing okay on time,” Sokka expands, absently tightening his half topknot, half wolf tail thing. He should have shaved his hair this morning like Aang did. “We can afford to hunker down here a bit and really cause a distraction. It seems like they were trying to meet us here—” he traces the plaza on the map, looking at the broad avenues leading into it from three sides. “—so we can probably expect some kind of counterattack from here, and…”

“Here,” Hakoda finishes, tapping the street in questions. Sokka nods and grins, relieved, because he’d thought that too. Perfect. He glances up to talk to Katara about shifting from the rearguard in case the field of battle swings around them, hesitating to find her staring up at the sky.

“Katara?” He looks up automatically. Is she looking at the moon? It’s finally started to turn from a pale ghost, barely visible against the white-blue of the sky, to a dark orb that makes Sokka shiver. He isn’t used to seeing Yue looking so…ominous.

“Is that…Aang?”

Sokka blinks, then twists around to follow her gaze, finally picking out the rapidly approaching figure that is definitely coming in on a glider. Fuck. Aang either did spectacularly well and wrapped things up without them even needing the eclipse—in which case…Sokka won’t really know what to say—or else things are about to go very, very wrong.

Sokka starts lining up his emergency plans before Aang finishes swooping down to join them. “Please tell me you’re here because you’ve got great news to share.”

Aang’s mouth is pressed in a tight line. “No one was there.”

Sokka’s glad he’s already kneeling, or else he might have stumbled in his shock. “What?”

“The city, the palace, it’s all empty.” Aang’s knuckles turn white around his glider. “There was no one there, not in the throne room, not anywhere.”

“…So this whole thing is a counterattack, then,” Toph says, her hands staying tight and controlled and precise as she launches another boulder.

“They knew we were coming,” Sokka says slowly. Which he does have a contingency for, but fuck, now he’s realizing that he should have had five more. He was *really* hoping he wouldn’t have to use this one. Shit, how did they *know*? Not that their group was exactly subtle coming across the island, between blowing up factories and capturing evil waterbenders, but for them to know that an *army* was coming…

Sokka glances up, about to ask about counter-counterattacks versus a series of elaborate feints to draw the enemy out, only to see Katara biting her lip, looking at him, and Aang staring determinedly down at his feet.

Sokka’s chest goes cold, his spinning thoughts stuttering to a stop as he belatedly registers the tension. Fuck. Just fuck absolutely everything. “Say it,” he forces out, low so that Hakoda can’t hear even from so close. “Whatever it is, say it.”

Katara’s nostrils flare, jaw clenched and arms crossed. “Did he know?”

“I never told him a thing about it,” Sokka whispers back, feeling grim and ferocious with his need for them to believe it.

Katara and Aang glance at Toph, who scowls but tips her head into a tiny confirmation. Truth. Sokka grits his teeth and doesn’t protest. He understands it even if he hates it. And right now, he needs their doubts to settle more than he needs proof of their trust.

Spirits, this is going to hurt tomorrow.

Please, let it be the only thing that hurts tomorrow.

Aang frowns down at the ground again, addressing the debris-covered paving stones. “But is there any way he could have—I don’t know. Seen something? By accident, or—” A deep breath. “Maybe you left the room and he—”

“No,” Sokka cuts in. “No. Never—we didn’t—no.” Zuko was never alone with his stuff, just like Sokka was never alone with Zuko’s. They had so little time together, neither of them had ever wanted to waste any of it by being apart.

“But he knew you were planning something,” Katara says.

It’s not a question, but Sokka forces out the “…Yeah,” anyway. It’s hard to say, even knowing that they all know the answer already.

She won’t quite look at him. “He could have told them, then.”

“If Zuko knew, he found out some other way,” Sokka snaps, voice low. “I’m not the only one who talked to him in Ba Sing Se.” Katara starts, biting her lip again. “And Zuko wasn’t the only one from the Fire Nation who was there, either.”

“It doesn’t matter,” Toph cuts in, hurling a boulder with more visible frustration than Sokka has seen from her yet today. “It doesn’t matter *how*, or *who.* Either way they knew. So what do we do now?”

“Do we retreat?” Aang asks, shoulders tensing like he might try a solo attack on the entire Fire Nation if they say yes.

“No,” Sokka says immediately. “Even with—everything. We can’t waste this opportunity.”

“So we search,” Katara says, eyes flicking back toward the map Hakoda is still studying with far too much focused intent in the midst of battle to not be straining to hear.

“They can’t have cleared out the city entirely,” Sokka says, thinking out loud and firmly ignoring the little waver that creeps into his voice over the fact that they’re still with him on this, that even with—that they still trust him enough for this. “They didn’t have enough time, not unless they started, what, a week ago? Longer?”

“So if they evacuated,” Katara starts slowly.

“It must be to somewhere in the city,” Sokka finishes. Because they didn’t see any fleets of boats fleeing the island, or hear about groups of people moving as they crossed the Fire Nation, and the sheer rock faces aren’t exactly hospitable enough to hold an entire city’s worth of people.

“Underground,” Toph puts in, expression shadowed by the broad brim of her helmet. “It’s a mountain island. They’ve got space to go down and that’s about it.”

Sokka turns the idea over in his head, liking the shape of it. “It *is* a volcano. There could be a lot of natural tunnels down there to start with, right?”

Katara blinks “There could be?”

“It’s like Roku’s island, remember all those tunnels?” He shrugs at her blank look. “I read up on volcanoes,” he explains, “We kept running into them.” And here's a third one, even if it’s dormant.

It is dormant, right? Fuck, it would be just their luck to deal with another one exploding on them.

“That’s still a big place to look,” Aang says, but not like he’s really disagreeing. They *do* have a track record of discovering things beneath the ground, right? And given the time they have, it’s their best chance when the only other option is to do a building-by-building search of the city.

“Toph?” Sokka says. “Get the earthbenders on it. Anyone who knows what to do, round them up. New priority.”

“On it,” Toph nods, cocking her head and doing her almost-listening thing before dashing off with a shield of rock between herself and the Fire Nation soldiers.

Sokka rises to his feet, looking out at the city and straining his eyes like maybe he’ll spot some structure or bend in the road or dip of the cobblestones that suggests Secret Tunnels. Caldera spills out below him from here even as it seems to rise up around him on all sides, and for a moment Sokka feels a surge of vertigo warring with claustrophobia. He can maybe see why Zuko always seems to find his way to high places, if he grew up surrounded on all sides by this.

“Do we have time for this?” Katara asks quietly, speaking from just behind his shoulder.

Sokka glances toward the sky where Yue is steadily moving to block Agni’s light and give them all a once-in-who-knows-how-many-centuries opportunity to change the world. “We’ll make it happen.” They have to. Sokka has a head full of contingency plans, but none for a failure quite like this.
