## Chapter 23: The Shape of Mercy

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for a bit more than canon typical violence in this one

### Text

Zuko is grounded and centered, inner fire coiled and ready for Katara’s wary greeting the next morning when she walks over to find him already at her cook fire, flames lit and tea steeping. Katara’s been willing to cede lunch and dinner to the others, but she’s made a sharp —and repeated—point of claiming breakfast as her own domain. Zuko knows he’s poking at blasting jelly lighting the fire, let alone having tea going, particularly after yesterday. But he’s starting to think that dancing around things with Katara might not be the way to go.

“I know who killed your mother,” Zuko says before Katara has a chance to vocalize the outrage he can see forming on her face. Her mouth snaps shut. “I can’t retake Ba Sing Se. I can’t bring anyone back who’s gone or make it so no one got hurt. But I can bring you to the man who took her.” He reaches for the kettle when Katara just stares. “Tea?”

Katara finally moves at that, her steps careful and deliberate as she chooses a seat across the fire. Her expression is somewhere between suspicious—really, she takes after her father— and guilty as her gaze flicks between his face and his no-longer-injured arm and the teacup he’s holding out to her. Zuko doesn’t take it personally. “Why are you telling me?” She finally asks, eyes narrowed. “Why not Sokka?”

Zuko considers Katara’s overflowing rage and Sokka’s quiet sadness, so deep that it could almost seem distant. “Sokka doesn’t need it.” Not the same way, at least.

Katara frowns, looking like she isn’t sure whether to be insulted or protective or something else entirely.

“Everyone grieves differently,” Zuko says before she can decide to be mad. “If I have the chance to take out the person who killed my mother, I will.” If she’s even dead. If that wasn’t just a distraction. Agni’s balls, Zuko truly wishes some days he could ask Azula about it. But then, there wouldn’t be much point. He already knows Azula wouldn’t think it mattered either way. Dead or gone, she still wasn’t there.

“So you think what I need is revenge,” Katara finally says, eyes hooded, face as unreadable as hers ever is. “And what, somehow that will make things better? I’ll just get over it and we can go be one big happy whatever this is supposed to be?”

“I think,” Zuko says, “That having a choice is better than not having one at all.”

Katara is quiet for a long time, then she slowly reaches out to take the mug of tea, her fingers neatly avoiding his own. “Fine. What do you know?”

&#45;-

Sokka is yawning, sitting up in bed with the blankets pooled around his waist, and Zuko can’t help but smile at his sleepy scowl, at the way it transforms into something soft and pleased as Zuko slips back into the room, a cup of tea and a quick reheated griddlecake in hand.

“That’s sweet of you,” Sokka says, voice still hoarse with sleep.

Kind of. It’s a true shame when Sokka’s looking like this, all loose and happy and soft, but, “I’m going to ruin the mood again.”

Sokka pauses with his mug halfway to his mouth, eyeing Zuko through the tangle of his loose hair. It’s just begging to be finger-combed, and Zuko kind of wished he’d kept his mouth shut for a bit longer. His hands itch. “Worse than yesterday?”

“…Probably pretty much the same.” It’s the same general topic, so…

Sokka’s quiet a moment, then he grunts, shoving half the griddle cake into his mouth and washing it down with a slug of tea as he claws his hair back from his face. “Alright,” he sighs, straightening. “Hit me.”

Zuko hesitates, aware of Sokka’s past ability to participate in conversation this early in the morning. “Want to wake up first?”

Sokka shoves the rest of his breakfast into his mouth, mumbling around it, “I want to do a lot of things other than this. Let’s get it done.”

…Fair enough.

Zuko leans a shoulder against the wall, arms crossed as he contemplates his boots. He’d have to take them off to get back into bed, and he isn’t sure that he would reliably be able to resist the distraction if he does. He regrettably doesn’t have all that much time, which…he didn’t exactly anticipate. “I know who killed your mother.”

Sokka freezes. “…What.”

…Not a great tone. “I told Katara.”

“You—why—” Sokka closes his eyes, scrubbing his hand roughly over his face. “Back up.”

“Yesterday Katara said that I needed to make things right.”

“She has no right to—”

“And this is something I can do, Sokka,” Zuko says firmly, evenly, stopping the hot flow of Sokka’s words. “From what you said last night—there’s only one person it could be.”

Emotions flash across Sokka’s face, too fast for Zuko to be able to pick out any one of them. “You know them,” Sokka finally says, words low. It’s not an accusation but it still manages to feel like one.

“I know of him,” Zuko corrects. There were few in the Fire Nation willing to be known by Zuko the way Sokka means, after his banishment. Zhao was an outlier, in that.

A divot is forming between Sokka’s browns. “And now what. We go after him?”

Zuko’s inner fire gives a nervous twist. “*Katara* goes after him.”

It takes Sokka a moment, then, “*Alone?”*

“I…offered to join her?” Zuko hugs his arms a little tighter across his just when Sokka just gapes, mouth working, silent. “She said yes,” he adds on.

Sokka looks like he isn’t sure that he isn’t still asleep. “You and Katara are going to go… alone? Together?”

“That…seems to be the idea, yeah.” Zuko isn’t quite sure how it happened, to be honest. He just didn’t like the idea of her setting off with half the knowledge she probably needs and far too much emotion to be clear-headed about it.

“…And you’re okay with that?”

Zuko gives a lopsided shrug. “If it will help her.” If this can form some kind of common ground for them to stand on, more than just mutual care for Sokka. If Katara wants to go on her own mission into the Fire Nation, Zuko certainly isn’t in a position to say no.

Sokka’s eyebrows come crashing down. “If this is some kind of self-sacrificing—”

“It’s not,” Zuko interrupts, catching Sokka’s eyes to make sure he hears it. “I want to help if I can.” He wants to get to some place where she can at least feel genuinely neutral about him, and not the clear effort she’s putting in for Sokka’s sake. “And this is something I can do.”

“How—what—how does it *help?”*

…How would finding the person who did something awful to you and making sure that nothing like it could ever happen to anyone else ever again *not* help? Is this one of those Water Tribe things? “It’s up to her to decide what helps her or not, right?”

“But—*why*—” Sokka sputters. “It’s dangerous and risky and so close to—and what if someone gets hurt! What if—”

“What if it’s exactly like Boiling Rock?”

Sokka snaps his mouth shut, rocking back, looking stung, and Zuko yanks back the urge to immediately rush to soothe the damage.

“I’m not saying you shouldn’t have done it,” he says carefully. “Just—is it *that* different? Both of you have something that you need that will help you. Something you think is important enough to be worth the risks.”

“It’s not the same,” Sokka grumbles, with so much belligerent obstinance that his relation to Katara suddenly shines.

“Why, though,” Zuko presses. Is this some kind of sibling thing that he just…doesn’t get, because Azula and Zuko aren’t normal siblings, just like they aren’t normal anythings?

“We were trying to rescue someone, not kill them!”

…It’s not intentions mean anything when it comes to risk. “You don’t know that Katara will kill him.”

“You don’t know Katara,” Sokka says, face tight as he tugs his hair back into a wolf tail.

“Maybe,” Zuko allows. Sokka certainly knows her more. But Zuko thinks—hopes—he knows more about killing than Sokka, and what it takes to do it.

Sokka ties off his hair and then immediately flops back on the bed, covering his face. “It’s already done, isn’t it? She’s going.”

“I think so.” Zuko bites the inside of his cheek, trying to read Sokka’s body language with his face hidden and most of him hidden in the jumble of blankets. “I didn’t expect her to move so fast,” Zuko admits, earning a snort from Sokka. “Are you…mad at me?”

Sokka peeks through his fingers to catch Zuko’s gaze. “No. I’m—frustrated. But I’m not mad.” Zuko makes a face, because Sokka doesn’t exactly *sound* not-mad, and Sokka sighs, dropping his hands. “I wish you had told me first.”

That’s…fair. “I’ll tell you if you want,” Zuko offers, resisting the urge to say that Katara asked first. It was more of an oblique challenge than an ask. And he and Sokka aren’t supposed to have to be asked in order to share things anymore.

“I don’t want to know,” Sokka groans, turning his head into the bed. “What I already know is enough.” Which would be the other reason Zuko hadn’t wanted to tell him first but…maybe he should have offered it anyway? Is that…a *boyfriend* thing to do?

Zuko waits, not really sure what to say so opting to say nothing, until Sokka finally sits up with another sigh, slugging back the rest of his tea and accepting the second griddlecake Zuko offers him after a moment of eyeing it, like maybe he’s aware that Zuko waited until after the hard conversation to reveal the rest of the food.

“Thanks,” Sokka mumbles around his mouthful, mustering a wry expression. “I guess I should have known you wouldn’t be able to stop going out hunting for things.”

“Habit,” Zuko says, his shoulders relaxing at Sokka’s teasing even if it feels like the humor isn’t fully there yet.

Sokka smiles, a quick flicker before he pauses halfway through another bite. “Where’s Katara now?”

“She said something about talking to Aang about Appa.”

Sokka stares a moment, then shoves the rest of the griddlecake into his mouth, scrambling out of bed. “We better hurry then.”

&#45;-

They find Katara and Aang in the middle of their own strained conversation topside, which Zuko thinks Katara could have really helped to head off by bringing some tea with her, too, given how long it takes Aang to usually wake up for their morning training. Zuko hesitates, reluctant to get between their tense stares even as Sokka approaches with enough its-too-early-to-be-graceful stumbling to make their presence known.

Aang and Katara don’t glance away from each other, though, their rapid-fire torrent of words filling the air too fast for Zuko to follow with the way the constant wind up on the cliffside buzzes in his scarred ear no matter how much he tries to shake it away. Zuko much prefers the forests up here.

“—not like I’m going out attack innocent people!”

“—who can judge another—”

“—I can judge actions just as well as anyone—”

“’Just as well’ sounds like something a freedom fighter would say!”

Zuko glances over when Sokka makes a low noise, his shoulders hunching uncomfortably even as Katara draws herself straight and sharp with offense. Zuko peeks at Aang, who’s looking a mix of guilty and resolute and not at all like he shares any of Zuko’s confusion about why both Water Tribe siblings are stung by that comment specifically. Zuko…will just tuck this away to figure out later. He has his own opinions of the Earth Kingdom’s so-called freedom fighters, but he remembers one of those early letters from Sokka. He thinks there might be a story here.

“—you don’t need to—”

“—this is my thing—”

“—but why can’t you bring us*?”*

“I agree,” Sokka jumps in, and Zuko’s inner fire gives a nervous flutter as Katara and Aang’s eyes swing toward them. “Why leave your firepower behind?”

“I’m bringing it,” Katara says tartly, and Zuko just…gives a little wave when everyone turns to him, his brain trying to sort out too many sets of interpersonal relationships at one time to offer up anything else.

“The monks always said that vengeance is a temptation that’s overcome by forgiveness as a community, not as—”

“Forgiveness is earned, not owed,” Katara snaps, arms crossing over her chest.

Aang lets out a sound of frustration, turning to Sokka with some appeal on his face. Zuko isn’t surprised when Sokka just shrugs, though, because Zuko’s heard him express the same sentiment enough times to know that Sokka isn’t going to disagree with it now.

Aang frowns and turns to Zuko, who can only offer his own shrug, scratching the back of his neck. “Currently earning it,” he points out. Not that he’s still entirely clear on what he’s being forgiven *for*, but he’ll feel that out later.

Agni’s balls, he really hopes it’s not going to be his general existence or sleeping with Katara’s brother. Those would be rather…ongoing problems.

Aang throws up his hands, spinning back toward Katara and trying a new tact. “What would your dad say?”

Zuko sucks in a slow breath between his teeth, wondering if Aang realizes what he’s opening the door to with that. The Southern Water Tribe’s fleet has a reputation for taking no prisoners because there aren’t any left alive to take, and Zuko can’t tell if Katara and Sokka’s quick glance means that they’re aware of the rumors or not. “Let’s leave fathers out of it,” Zuko suggests. That’s always the best approach, in his opinion.

Aang slumps, kicking at the ground, a picture of discontent. “I’m not going to try to stop you,” he finally mutters. “You can take Appa. It’s your choice. But I don’t agree with you doing it this way.”

Katara sighs, her shoulders softening, and Sokka must take that as some kind of signal because he steps back, gentle urging Zuko to move away with him and give some semblance of privacy to Katara and Aang. Or maybe to get some semblance of privacy themselves as Sokka steps into him, slinging an arm around his shoulders and tangling his fingers in Zuko’s hair and resting his cheek against Zuko’s.

“Did you have to start this,” Sokka murmurs, but without any real rancor, so Zuko just wraps his arms around Sokka’s waist, feeling the rise and fall of his breathing and enjoying the gentle pressure of Sokka’s hand in his hair.

“You wanted me to have a better relationship with Katara, right?” Zuko smiles when Sokka huffs out a reluctant laugh.

“Yeah, but not through going on another life-endangering field trip,” Sokka mutters, like he wasn’t the one hurt the most from the last one. “You’ve already gone on enough of those.”

The past four years of Zuko's life have been one life-endangering field trip. “I didn’t realize there was a quota.”

Sokka rolls his eyes, pulling back to make sure Zuko can see it as if Zuko doesn’t know it just from the tone of his voice and his general demeanor by now. “Just—shut up and come back safe, you suicidal idiot,” Sokka says, tugging Zuko into a kiss that cuts off Zuko’s protest about pots and kettles and makes the words taste nothing but sweet.

&#45;-

Suki comes up to the campfire later, yawning as she peeks into Sokka’s pot of half-empty, definitely over-steeped tea that’s long since gone cold. Toph, though, pulls up short, giving a little stomp before approaching with open wariness.

“What’s going on,” Suki frowns, glancing around as she registers Toph’s caution.

“Where’s Katara,” Toph demands. She tilts her head, face set with concentration. “And Sparrowkeet.”

“Katara,” Sokka says, words precise, “Is going on a little trip with Zuko.”

“…Hunting for some meat again?”

“Something like that,” Sokka mutters.

“I didn’t realize His Royal Highness was the accomplished hunter, of the two of you,” Toph says after a moment.

Sokka glares, which is completely useless.

“Since, you know. He never actually caught anything.”

“He caught something a time or two,” Sokka says, and he must be going crazy to be both rising to Toph’s teasing and trying to defend Zuko’s ability to take Aang captive at the same time.

“What,” Toph shoots a sharp grin in his direction. “You?”

…Okay. Sokka will allow, as Suki lets out a snort of laughter, that he really walked into that one.

“Why are you so grouchy,” Suki asks, making a face as she gets her first mouthful of over-steeped cold tea. “Feeling left out?”

Sokka gives her an annoyed look, because he *isn’t*, it’s not about feeling left out, he just… wishes Zuko and Katara were both here, where he could see them. Or that he was with them. Where he could see them. “I don’t particularly want to endanger my own life, no,” he finally grumbles, aware of how testy the words sound.

“Hm. So you don’t want to train, then?” Suki raises a challenging eyebrow. “I was going to say we can brush up on your fan skills, but if you’d rather safely pine for your boyfriend instead…”

Toph lets out a snort, and Sokka sputters, pulling himself upright. “I’m not *pining,* I’m just —” Sitting by the campfire brooding over the last pot of tea Zuko made him before going away, quietly longing for him to be back again.

…Fuck.

“Do you even have makeup?” Sokka asks, switching tack. Does she even have *fans*?

“We can do it without makeup,” Suki says serenely.

“You wear makeup?” Toph cuts in, leaning forward with interest. “Does Zuko know? Wait— does he wear makeup too?” She pauses. “Does everyone wear makeup?”

“I’m not telling you anything,” Sokka grumbles.

Toph flicks a pebble at him. “Suki, you’ll tell me all about it later, right?”

“You bet I will.”

Traitors. Traitors all around him. Spirits, Suki and Toph together are terrifying.

Zuko is ambivalent about sky bison as modes of transportation. They’re easy to steer—as long as they like you—and the upkeep seems straightforward. But flying wholly unsecured inside a glorified wooden fence barely high enough to lean on isn’t exactly suited for more than basic maneuvers, and Zuko’s finding that this particular sky bison is far too vocal. Every rumble and grumble and groan that Appa makes resonates through his entire body and has Zuko tensing in alarm, years of ship life training him to respond to sudden changes in the vibration of his craft.

Still, Zuko’s coming around to the idea. Partly because it’s kind of a revelation, to stretch out his heat sense and feel the way they’re moving through the air on the equivalent of a contained wildfire. And Zuko always appreciates being able to lay out under Agni’s light, especially closer to the source than he generally ever gets.

But mostly he’s starting to understand the appeal because Appa can come when called, which is *incredibly* convenient as they sprint out of the outpost, the map they want and a few decoy ones in hand. Katara is leading them toward a sheer cliff face, and Zuko’s reluctant to suggest that she doesn’t know what she’s doing with something as basic as gravity, but he’s just on the verge of pointing out that throwing themselves off a cliff might not be advisable when Appa surges up from below, rumbling in greeting and tilting to catch Katara as she leaps into the saddle in a mostly-contained tumble.

Well. War balloons certainly can’t do that.

Zuko sprints to the cliff edge, grunting as he hurls himself across the gap, swinging his legs forward and spotting his landing and it’s just like going rooftop to rooftop, except his landing spot is moving, so it’s more like going tower to deck on the *Wani*. Zuko lets himself tuck into a roll just like he would there, his momentum carrying him forward to flip over his shoulder into a low crouch that mirrors Katara’s.

She kneels upright, hands low and wide. “Yip yip,” she says, arms sweeping up as Appa banks away from the cliffs into a low glide, hugging the sea and the shroud of mist that Katara wraps around them to obscure the sky bison’s pale shape in the moonlight.

“We’re away now,” Zuko finally says, tracking the fading pinpoint of the tower’s light with his fire sense more than his eyes.

Katara grunts and lets the mist melt away, pulling the loose ends of her scarf off her neck now that she no longer needs it to cover her face. “You have it?”

“Yeah.” Zuko keeps his own mask around his neck, tucking away the other maps to examine later and laying out the one detailing the latest distribution of Fire Nation naval forces, the ink smudged in places it’s so fresh.

Katara leans over for a look, her jaw tightening as she takes it in. “And you can read it?”

“Yeah, it’s military shorthand.” Zuko takes a moment to orient himself between the lines and squiggles and sharp shapes that represent different cruiser types and commanders, supplies and enemy sightings. He traces his finger across the paper, looking for one symbol in particular and trying to swallow back the nausea that kicks low in his gut when he sees just how thinly spread the Fire Nation navy is.

He knew the North was a huge blow, but this is worse than it should be. They’ve had months to begin rebuilding. The latest factories can pump out a mid-class cruiser in a week. If they haven’t been…Zuko thinks of factory explosions, of fortunes rising and falling in the Council over resource allocation and production numbers, of how readily the plan to burn the Earth Kingdom was accepted. He glances up at the full moon and considers that this gamble of the Fire Lord’s could be more of a last-ditch effort than anyone would ever admit out loud.

“Here,” he finally says, finding what he’s looking for, letting his finger trace the shape of the coastline.

“Whale Tail Island,” Katara says, staring a moment before moving toward Appa’s head to take the reins. Zuko braces himself against the wall of the saddle as Appa turns, making sure they’re fully done with all tilting and direction changing before he makes his cautious way toward the front of the saddle.

“How fast does Appa go,” he asks, not taking offense to Katara’s sharp, questioning look. Everything she’s done since the campfire this morning has been sharp. “So we can estimate our arrival time.”

“We’ll get there when we get there,” Katara mutters, staring between Appa’s ears before relenting. “We don’t really know. It depends on the day, and what he’s had to eat, and the weather, and…” She pulls a face. “Sokka has it figured out.”

Zuko nods and doesn’t say anything. He knows better than to suggest that it might be a good thing for them to have planned enough to have it figured out themselves when Katara’s so clearly spoiling for a fight. Still, he recognizes the pulled-too-tight quality of Katara’s silence, the too-sharp quality of her movements, the restless way she fiddles with the necklace at her throat, settling it and resettling it as the waves pass beneath them. Sometimes it helps to have a different kind of outlet.

“Do you want to talk about it?” Zuko pitches his voice to be barely louder than the wind around them and the waves below, something easy to ignore if she wants to.

“About what,” Katara demands, slashing a look over her shoulder.

“Whatever’s on your mind. You keep—” He gestures toward his throat, keeping his face impassive as Katara’s fingers clench around the pendant, her eyes just this side of a glare.

“It’s not bothering anyone.”

Zuko sorts through potential responses. “I didn’t say it was.”

She eyes him, the examination bordering on uncomfortable by the time she finally says, “Why do you need to know?”

“I don’t *need* to know,” Zuko says. And he already knows the bones of it from Sokka, if he did. “But if you want to talk about it. You can. A burden shared is a burden…not held just by you anymore.” He doesn’t think he messed that one up so badly. “Sometimes it helps.”

Katara is silent for a long time, face dark, and just when Zuko thinks it’s time for him to shift back and withdraw she suddenly speaks. “It started with the black snow.”

Katara tells him like it’s been bubbling just below the surface too long for her to keep it in, and Zuko shifts to make sure his unscarred ear can catch the words. In some ways it’s similar to Sokka’s story, starting out on the snow, the falling rain of ash, the sudden realization, the panic among the adults. But where Sokka was old enough to understand at least conceptually what was happening, to want to fight, Katara didn’t get it until she was running to find her mom, being told to flee, to hide, to be quiet, to shut her eyes and make no noise no matter what she hears and find her dad the first opportunity she can.

It’s different, Zuko thinks, to intellectually know the details of what happened and see the aftermath and feel the pain of being too late, than it is to have Katara’s visceral reality sitting in your mind, the raw experience of watching it happen and needing to stay quiet and knowing for a fact that her mother died because the Fire Nation was looking for her.

Zuko isn’t surprised that Katara takes her bending so seriously. And Zuko suspects that Sokka doesn’t fully realize all that Katara heard and just how much she remembers from that day.

“It was a very brave thing to do,” Zuko finally says when Katara’s words run dry. An instant death sentence, if his math is right. Policy had changed across the military by that time, but particularly for naval forces, the Fire Nation didn’t try to keep waterbending prisoners anymore.

“She was very brave,” Katara agrees, his acknowledgment of the sacrificing seeming to have drained some of the tension out of her even if her face is still set with purpose. It’s a quieter resolve now, the kind that burns low and constant in the center of your chest instead of high and urgent in your throat. Her eyes cut over to him after a moment, guardedly curious. “Was yours?”

That’s…a question. “I don’t know,” Zuko says slowly, contemplating the wood grain on the perimeter of Appa’s saddle. “She was just gone one night. I went to bed and the next morning she just…wasn’t there. And then she wasn’t ever there.”

Katara frowns. “Illness?”

“No. I mean, maybe. But—literally gone.” Zuko shrugs, restless. “I think she woke me up in the night to say goodbye? Sometimes I think I just dreamed that, though.” It would be on par with the rest of his dreams.

Katara twists around, frowning. “She just…left?”

“Probably not,” Zuko says, glancing away from her incredulous stare. “Grandfather was dead in the morning, too. And Father was Fire Lord instead of Uncle. So.”

A long silence, then, “What..?”

“Happened? I think she poisoned Grandfather.” Zuko remembers her always smelling like herbs and tinctures and burn cream. “Azula thinks she smothered him with a pillow,” he adds. It would have been more dangerous, with a firebender. But then, fire comes from the breath.

“But—what—*why*—"

“No one’s ever told me,” Zuko shrugs, tilting his head back to look up at the stars. “She felt she had to, I guess. Maybe if she didn’t something worse would have happened. Maybe…she just had enough.” Everyone breaks eventually, Zuko knows. No matter how strong they think they are.

Dad finally approaches Sokka about halfway through the day, which…well, Sokka doesn’t know if that’s sooner or later than he expected, because he has no idea what Dad and Katara have been talking about.

“Where are Katara and the Prince,” Dad asks frowning around like they might suddenly pop out from behind a column together.

Sokka sets the bag of herbs he’s prepping for lunch down with a sigh. “…Can I just tell you not to worry about it?”

“…Like I shouldn’t worry about you breaking into any more prisons?”

Okay, well that’s just—Sokka isn’t going to *do* it. Sure, he thought about it, and he has some ideas, but he isn’t—Zuko wouldn’t—ugh.

“Where is she,” Hakoda presses.

Sokka sets his shoulders. “Doing a thing she feels she has to do.”

Hakoda shifts, studying Sokka’s face, but Sokka isn’t going to give this away, not until she comes back. It’s Katara’s thing, for one, and Sokka might not agree with how she’s going about it, but years of showing a united front in the face of parental disapproval have trained him well. And maybe more relevant, Sokka doesn’t know how their Dad would react. He remembers the well of grief that Hakoda had to climb out of after the raid. He isn’t eager to rock that boat again, no matter how much Hakoda seems to be in calmer waters these days.

Hakoda eventually settles back a little, gently prodding. “And it’s a thing she needed to do with…the Prince?”

Sokka shrugs. “Apparently.” He’s trying not to be frustrated by it. Zuko’s part of the team now, which means he isn’t just Sokka’s, which means it’s a good thing that he’s building his own connections and running off on his own adventures. Something he can’t do if Sokka tried to hold him back and keep him safe, something Sokka wouldn’t do just like Sokka wouldn’t let Zuko tell *him* to sit on the sidelines. But knowing it doesn’t make the waiting any easier, because knowing it isn’t the same as feeling it, and…fuck, Sokka’s going to need to work on this one. Maybe he should go talk to Suki.

“And…you’re okay with that?”

Sokka feels himself freeze a little, before he catches it. “…Why wouldn’t I be?”

Hakoda opens and closes his mouth a few times, rubbing a hand along his jawline as he searches for words. “Was the Prince in Ba Sing Se with you all, too?”

“He wasn’t *with* us, exactly,” Sokka says carefully, wary of the apparent non sequitur and the fact that *Sokka* definitely knows isn’t actually a non sequitur at all. Does Hakoda? Shit, is this why Zuko’s been so tense? “But he was there.”

“Hm.”

Sokka doesn’t love the revelation that sound seems to imply.

“You wanted to tell me something back in Chameleon Bay,” Hakoda finally says. “It got cut off by the battle and the Avatar.”

Sokka holds his breath, hoping this question will veer off in another direction but knowing exactly where it’s going.

“Did it by any chance have something to do with a certain firebender?”

“…Yes.” Spirits, Zuko’s going to lose his shit. Or maybe not, with the pressure of trying to keep things under wraps off his shoulders. Sokka would wonder what gave them away if he wasn’t fully aware that they weren’t exactly all that good at subtlety to begin with.

“Sokka—”

“*Please* don’t go all protective threatening manly parent over this,” Sokka cuts in, nearly begging. Because then Zuko will *really* lose his shit.

“I wouldn’t *threaten*,” Dad frowns. “But a father wants to have a serious talk with anyone who—”

“Katara already did it,” Sokka says over top of him, trying to head this off before it can begin. “Katara did it, and I didn’t need it then and I sure don’t need it now. And I *will* know if you do it anyway,” he adds when Dad just frowns at him. Zuko would probably climb a pillar and never come down again. “And I *will* be pissed.” Just in case that needed to be additionally clarified.

“Someone needs to ensure that any prospective partner has the right intentions,” Dad insists.

“That someone is me, considering I’m the one who knows him best,” Sokka snaps.  
Fucking *intentions*. Why does everyone want to have it all figured out from the start? Like it's wrong to just want to *be* with someone, and know they want it to, and work it out from there? “And if you’re going to act like I can’t judge it for myself, then like I said. Katara already did it.”

Dad doesn’t look satisfied with that. “It should be someone with—it’s not something the youngest should have to take on.”

“Well there wasn’t exactly anyone else, was there,” Sokka says with more than a bit of bite.

Dad clamps his mouth shut, rocking back as he takes the criticism. The silence only lasts a moment, though. “He seems rather…jumpy.”

Sokka grunts. Hakoda would have primarily seen that part of Zuko, and it’s not like Zuko’s exactly a low-key person to begin with.

“And wasn’t—” Dad’s brow furrows. “Bato told me something about a Fire Nation Prince chasing you and your sister around the world?”

Sokka suddenly finds the ends of his wrist wraps very interesting.

“And…that was the Lightning Princess he was fighting back in Boiling Rock? His sister?”

Sokka sighs, closing his eyes. “Just…say what you want to say.” He’ll deal with the interrogation if it gets it out of Dad’s system before Zuko gets back.

“How did the Prince come to join you all? To be at Boiling Rock?”

“It’s…complicated.” Plans and defections and commitments that actually looked like betrayals. “He wants to help Aang. He wants to end the war.” And what more Zuko wants than that doesn’t feel like Sokka’s to tell, or to speculate on.

Hakoda studies Sokka’s face, eyes intent as Sokka tries not to visibly squirm away from his gaze. Squirming does *not* say ‘mature adult who has this handled and doesn’t need his dad to get involved.’ “Do you trust him?”

“Yes,” Sokka says immediately.

“With more than just yourself? With your sister? The Avatar?”

“Yes,” Sokka snaps.

Hakoda grunts. “Does he respect you?”

“Yes.”

“Treat you well?”

Sokka just glares.

“Does he make you happy?”

“*Yes.”*

“Would he walk away if you told him it was over?” Sokka snaps his mouth shut, staring. “Would he let you walk away if you wanted to leave?”

Sokka leans back, eyeing Hakoda askance. He wasn’t expecting…he doesn’t know what to say to that. The mere idea of it makes him want to flinch, but Sokka’s gut reaction is that Zuko wouldn’t press where he knew he wasn’t wanted. Or fuck, even where he *thought* he wasn’t wanted, if there was ever a reason to question it.

Except Zuko also isn’t one to just walk away without trying, or to watch Sokka leave without understanding why. And Sokka doesn’t know what that answer is going to do to Hakoda’s evaluation of Zuko, when Hakoda's already so openly cautious.

Hakoda finally sighs, waving the question away as Sokka’s silence draws out. “Just…think about it.” He ignores the face Sokka makes with the ease of long practice. “And I’m…glad for you.” He clears his throat. “That you found someone that makes you happy.”

“Me, too,” Sokka says, firm, ignoring the lingering skepticism he can hear in Dad’s words. He’ll take the statement, and work on making the sentiment catch up.

“But it isn’t going to be easy,” Dad cautions, and Sokka doesn’t bother holding back a snort.

“Trust me, I know,” he mutters. He’s more than aware that the Crown Prince of the Fire Nation—even a former one—and the son of the Chief of the Southern Water Tribe don’t have much space they can share together in most people’s eyes. But Sokka also knows that views can change. And that between him and Zuko? They have more stubbornness and determination to figure out how to make things work.

They fall on the ship like a storm, dropping through the darkness from Appa’s back onto the deck. Zuko lands heavy-footed and tall, the tremors of his landing ringing through the ship’s structure like he spent nearly four years learning how to master, pulling every eye toward his shadow-wreathed, black-clothed, masked form.

Zuko lets sparks kindle along his fingers, fits and bursts of flame that build, grow, coiling toward his palms like a vortex. He feels a sharp burst of satisfaction as the soldiers and firebenders on deck step forward with shouts of alarm and warning, the technical crew breaking for cover—he and Azula practiced that move for *weeks* one summer on Ember Island, so it would be perfect for the dramatic stage battle in *Love Amongst the Dragons*.

It’s undoubtedly eye-catching and different enough from Caldera Standard to be alarming, the perfect distraction for the absolutely massive tidal wave that suddenly sweeps across the deck, rising up from both sides of the ship and curling down enough like claws that it makes Zuko’s heart pound even though he’s expecting it. Then the wave is surging back toward the ocean, hurling bodies overboard, water receding *up* instead of down to writhe around Katara’s feet.

Zuko admires her flair for the dramatic even as he makes quick work of the ropes holding the lifeboats, sending them hissing and rattling down into the water. This was Zuko’s demand. Every Fire Nation sailor needs to be able to stay above water in their lighter standard armor for at least two degrees, measured by the summer solstice at Caldera. Everyone in the water should have plenty of time to get to the boats assuming they’ve maintained their fitness, and with the ropes cut instead of lowered, no way to get back up onto the ship.

Zuko waves Katara forward, taking them through a maintenance hatch rather than the main stairwell toward the command tower. It’s not what they planned but this ship is bigger than the *Wani*, and Zuko’s familiar enough with the way Fire Nation engineers operate to know that this tight passageway will connect to a broader access route that should run the length of the ship. From there it’s just a matter of picking the right place to drop out and make a run up the interior stairs—hopefully with the forces marshaling to defend the route at their backs.

Zuko’s relieved that Katara doesn’t question the adjustment, instead shadowing him with tight focus. They can’t afford the extra noise of a conversation with the way sound bounces around the ship, and Zuko’s counting on the element of surprise, especially since he doesn’t need to kindle a light that a passing firebender might notice to guide them through the intense darkness. Zuko can follow the heat of the cooling pipes that run into and out of the engine room, and Katara can follow the flow of the water itself. He distantly, deeply hopes that she isn’t going to need it—he doesn’t want to have to bleed off the heat from a pressurized spray of near-boiling water tonight, if he can help it.

Zuko’s vaguely surprised, in a corner of his mind that has room for these kinds of things, that they’re working so well together. They barely need to bend beyond what it took to get them onto the ship, moving swift and silent, evading sweeps and patrols, barely needing to speak to know when to pause, when to go, especially as light begins to seep in and they finally react to gesture and body language and sudden stillness.

Every step winds tension tighter and tighter around Zuko’s shoulders, though, especially once they drop back into the halls. It’s all going nearly too well for something not to go wrong. But then, maybe Katara has a different kind of luck than Zuko, too.

They reach the landing at the top of the command tower on near-silent feet, Katara whipping around the corner with barely a moment’s pause. She hurls out a globe of water that bands over the lone guard’s mouth, muffling his panicked shouts as Zuko lunges forward on the heels of her attack, reaching with his heat sense to yank the man’s inner flame low, catching him as his eyes roll back to carefully lower his limp body to the floor.

Katara ghosts forward, calling her water back and setting herself up alongside the door to the command room, Zuko mirroring her position a beat later. She holds up her fingers, Zuko taking steady breaths in time to her countdown, stoking his inner flame and feeling his adrenaline singing as his fire expands in his chest, spills out down his limbs, presses up against his skin.

Then Katara’s last finger folds into her clenched fist and she’s stepping back, Zuko inhaling as she sweeps up tentacles of water and exhaling in time with her strike. She launches forward into a high kick, water surging and metal screeching loud enough to set his scarred ear ringing as the door folds and then flies off its hinges under the force of her assault. Zuko throws himself forward after it, coming in low to sweep under any counterattacks and immediately leaping into his own flaming kick to force any opponent onto the defensive.

Zuko sees the silhouette of an armored body fall back into a standard block. He reaches with his heat sense almost before his feet find the floor again, already flowing into his next strike before the man even manages to fully form the fire dagger in his hand.

Slow, and a terrible choice for distance combat, Zuko notes, automatically adjusting for longer range attacks, and then adjusting again when the dagger abruptly goes out, the man’s hand spasming open as he loses hold of his fire. Zuko nearly stops to stare, at the last moment sliding sideways instead, opting for evasion rather than stillness. If this is a feint—no one *actually* this bad at firebending would be put in charge of anything, let alone the Southern Raiders—then it’s a weird one, but Zuko’s seen plenty weirder from desperate men.

Except this man—the Commander, Zuko finally notes, good—doesn’t react, doesn’t move with him like Zuko expects. Instead, he just stares at his extended hand, trembling, then at his arm. Then he looks to the doorway, eyes wide, choking on a cry before thudding to his knees so suddenly that his unsecured helmet—which is against regulation, that’s why you secure it —clatters to the floor, rolling to come to rest at Katara’s feet.

…This is also not what Zuko expected.

Zuko steps back, uncertain, keeping his fire ready as he takes a quick glance to see Katara staring the Commander down. Her face is tight, icy eyes blazing in a way Zuko is unfortunately familiar with, her hands poised in front of her, stiff, angled, fingers bending at a nearly unnatural angle and the Commander’s arms slamming down into the floor in response.

…In *response*. The man’s entire body is shuddering as he strains and fights and doesn’t move an inch until her finger twitches, allowing him to raise his head. Allowing him with her *bending*.

Agni’s flaming cock. *Fuck*. Is this—can she just do this, whatever the *fuck* this is, because of the full moon? Or has Katara had this in her back pocket the whole time?

Zuko suppresses a shiver with a careful breath, letting his anxious inner fire expand in his chest and trying to focus back on the mission. For now, at least, this is just an asset. Another tool and another piece of proof that Katara is a prodigy like Toph with her metalbending and Azula with her lightning. Why not Katara too? And if Katara decides to use this against Zuko now that it’s out in the open, whatever it is—well, Zuko supposes they’ll find out how much he really needs to move to work his heat.

But fuck, he hopes that never happens. Hopes he’s not wrong in thinking it wouldn’t, in thinking that however much Katara might not trust him or like him or whatever her issue is, she still doesn't want to actively hurt him like that. Agni, that would crush Sokka, and Zuko doesn’t know that he can solely rely on that, but he knows it doesn’t count for nothing with her.

“What is—what’s happening,” the Commander pants, veins popping in his neck as he strains and goes nowhere. “What *is* this?”

“We ask the questions here,” Zuko says, stepping forward to draw the man’s attention, picking back up where he’s supposed to be and making sure not to interrupt Katara’s line of sight in case she needs it. Shit, Katara had said she would handle restraints and Zuko could take the actual interrogation. It’s his fault for not asking questions about her methods.

“I won’t tell pirate scum anything,” the Commander spits, in a rather fine show of bravery under the circumstances.

Zuko thinks it’s more than a little bit of bluster. “Katara?”

She obligingly does…something that makes the man cry out. It’s good to know that she can improvise in the moment, but Agni’s steaming shit, this is…probably going to give him nightmares him, when Zuko finally has the time to have a breakdown over it.

“I would think you’d have a little more sense than to insult your captors,” Zuko says, checking the light and shifting to be most ominously backlit. “We aren’t asking much. All I want is for you to think back. You remember your last raid on the Southern Water Tribe, right?”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” the Commander grits out, screaming low in his throat when Katara…crunches him, without needing to be prompted. Zuko keeps his face as impassive and cold as he can make it.

“Don’t lie,” Zuko says, letting fire spark off his fingertips in warning. “You’re only making it harder for yourself.”

“I don’t know!”

“Do you need to jog your memory?” Zuko almost wishes Azula were here for this. “How about you look at her. That should remind you.”

Kate makes a quick, tight little gesture, the man’s head craning back, his too-wide eyes rolling as she steps into the moonlight and pulls down her mask, baring an expression of cold rage that slowly melts into shock as she searches his face. “That’s not him.”

Zuko steps back in surprise. “What?”

“I would never forget that face,” Katara says tightly. “It’s not him.”

Zuko stares a moment, then forces his expression to neutrality, turning back to the Commander. He feels sick to his stomach to have done this without cause, even knowing the Southern Raiders’ reputation. They’ve been allowed too long of a leash for too long, practically their own fiefdom within the larger naval structure, and their Commanders have always been known for inspiring more fear and resentment than loyalty. There’s a reason this one responded with a fire dagger to a surprise attack. Zuko can work with that.

“If you aren’t who we want,” Zuko says, crouching down to the Commander’s level, still keeping his back to the light. “Then you must know who is.”

“You’re crazy! I don’t know anything!”

Zuko holds up a hand, letting his own dagger flare to life in his fist. “You don’t know who you succeeded?”

The man blinks. “Yon Rha?”

“Yon Rha,” Zuko repeats slowly, casting his mind back over years of gossip and taunting letters and dockside news. “Yon Rha, who retired with fewer than the expected honors four years ago to a village on the Southern Tip to live with his mother who he hates?”

“…Yes?”

Zuko looks to Katara, dismissing the man and his gaping. “I know where he is.”

“Let’s go,” she says, fierce, and Zuko can see the warrior’s determination she must have inherited from her mother in her face.

When Aang crumbles a flying boulder into pebbles and then sprays them back with enough force that even Toph is impressed, Sokka considers that maybe it’s worth having a little chat with the airbender. Aang might be visibly brooding ever since they woke up this morning to find Zuko and Katara not returned like they were hoping, but Sokka’s expecting them back at any moment. Really, any moment now. They *will* be here. They will.

And if Aang greets Katara like this? Well. Aang tried to smooth the way with Zuko to the best of his abilities. It might have been something of a disaster, but Sokka can still try to return the favor, hopefully with better results. And Sokka’s suddenly realizing that he has years more experience than Aang does in managing the worry and anxiety of knowing someone you care about is away, out of your line of sight and potentially in danger at any given moment.

Aang is moving through an airbending kata when Sokka finally finds him in one of the rooms that always makes Sokka feel a bit dizzy with its lack of walls and seemingly random array of pillars. Gusts of air twine and dance and rip through the room, coming off the gorge and carried by the wind and breaking around the columns. Leaves dance along in a more intricate pattern than Sokka can keep up with, Aang in the middle of it all, moving in slow, steady counterpoint, keeping it all in harmony.

Sokka settles in to watch, absently patting Momo when the lemur scampers over and obligingly pulling out a little packet of dried fruits when Momo grabs at his pocket. Sokka tries to predict where the flow of leaves will go next, on the verge of feeling like he’s about to get the hang of it when Aang finally brings himself to a rest. Aang takes a moment of stillness, then straightens out of his stance, spinning his staff in his hands a few times before finally acknowledging Sokka.

“Any left for me,” Aang asks, glancing over his shoulder.

“Momo is a ravenous monster,” Sokka says as he tosses the remaining fruit Aang’s way. “But I managed to save you a few.” He watches Aang eat a moment, giving Momo a few ear scratches. “I don’t see you practicing your airbending like that as often.”

“I do,” Aang shrugs. “There’s just so much else to learn. But it’s nice to do it again here.” He casts a quick, wistful smile around the space. “This place was made for it.”

The random array of pillars suddenly makes a bit more sense. “Is it…calming?”

Aang gives Sokka a sideways look and his staff another spin. “Is there something you think I need to be calm about?”

That’s a trap if Sokka’s ever heard one. “Not…necessarily.”

Aang’s staff comes to a stop. “Heart to heart?”

“Heart to heart,” Sokka confirms.

“You didn’t think Katara should go either,” Aang bursts right out, air briefly swirling around his feet.

“Not alone,” Sokka concedes, wondering if that was a natural gust. Probably not. “No.” “Then why do you have anything to say about it now,” Aang grumbles.

“Because I’m her brother,” Sokka points out. And not trying to be her boyfriend, he thinks, watching Aang blush when he eventually fills in the end of Sokka’s sentence. “It sucks,” Sokka adds. “But…we can’t be part of everything.”

“We’re supposed to be a team,” Aang insists, stubborn. “What’s the point of that if we all go off alone when it matters?”

“Not everything is a team thing, though,” Sokka points out. As the Avatar there are some things only Aang can do.

“Like rescuing your dad?” Aang asks with a tartness he must have picked up from Katara.

“Yeah,” Sokka says after a beat. “Like that.” Not what he was thinking, but…sure.

“That’s total crap,” Aang says, openly annoyed “Like it wouldn’t have been helpful to have a waterbender around on an island? Or Toph? The Fire Nation makes everything out of metal! Katara broke into a prison ship before!”

…That would have been great, actually. “We did okay.”

“Sometimes the big picture doesn’t matter if you forget all the little things along the way,” Aang fires back. “You matter, Sokka, and your stuff matters, and so does Katara’s, and—”

“…You’re important, Aang,” Sokka says quietly, trying to disperse some of the frustration snapping through the air, trying to understand why his stomach is twisting so hard at those last words. “Maybe not more than the rest of us, but in a different way. And that means there are some risks that I can take and that Katara can take that you can’t. Especially when it’s not your responsibility to fix.”

Aang fixes him with a deep frown. “Except part of friendship is sharing. And you’re not a good friend if you only share in the good parts.”

“Okay,” Sokka concedes slowly. “But friendship is also about looking out for each other, too. You can’t expect us to not look out for you.”

“Sometimes you look out for someone by letting them learn and experience and do the things they want to do,” Sokka sighs. A hard lesson, for a big brother. “And Aang—Katara isn’t someone who’s going to be happy holding herself back to stay safe.”

“Sharing burdens and holding someone back aren’t the same, though,” Aang protests, face set with stubbornness. “And I’m not *asking* her to hold herself back, I just—she’s about to face one of the hardest choices of her life, and she’s going to make it all alone. We should *be* there for her.”

“And Zuko knows what it’s like to make hard choices,” Sokka adds on. Big ones, the kind that impact entire nations.

Aang chews on his lip, rubbing a hand down Momo’s back as the lemur hops over to him. “I guess so,” he finally says, grudging.

“You just wish you could be there with her?”

“Yeah,” Aang sighs, glum.

“I feel the same way, buddy,” Sokka admits. “But they’ve got each other’s backs. And if anything goes wrong, Zuko will be there to look out for her.” And vice versa, he hopes.

Zuko is immobile, breathless in awe of Katara’s bending, of her mastery over the rain and the thousands of tiny icicles that pepper the ground but don’t touch Yon Rha. The full moon is set, but Katara is still overflowing with power. She’s like an implacable spirit as Yon Rha pleads for his life, Tui and La made manifest, and seeming just as indifferent to humanity. Zuko’s inner flame flares in response, recognition and wariness and respect giving it fuel as it swirls in his chest and for a wild moment Zuko wonders if Agni was really the only spirit to bless her people with her flesh and blood.

“Please!” Yon Rha pleads. “I—take my mother! An exchange! You—you can do to me what I did to you!”

“…I always wondered what kind of man could do what you did. I understand, seeing you now.” Her voice could flay, and Zuko’s distantly surprised not to see red spilling across Yon Rha’s skin. “Someone who is weak. Pathetic. Empty. Death would be too kind for you. You deserve the life you’ve made for yourself.”

“Thank you,” Yon Rha gasps, voice trembling. “Thank you, your mercy—”

“It isn’t mercy,” Katara spits. “I’ll check on you. You might not see me, but I’ll see you. And if your mother is ever less than perfectly happy? Then I will take the price from your flesh.” The ice trembles in warning across the ground, a thousand razor-sharp, vibrating knives. “You will make yours happy since mine can no longer be.”

Zuko shadows her as she backs away, keeping himself to a silent, intimidating presence that she very much doesn’t need and struggling to keep his face hard instead of letting his admiration shine through. That was…masterful. The way she built the fear, dangled the possibility of death, opened the door to a false kind of hope, and then laid down her sentence with a threat she never actually has to follow through on. He doesn’t know if even Azula could have done it better, but she would definitely appreciate the choice to let an enemy live out the agony of the rest of their life in a trap of their own making.

“Did I do the right thing?”

Zuko glances up, wiggling upright from where he’d been dozing in the corner of Appa’s saddle

after carefully steaming his clothes dry, trying to snatch as much rest as he ever can under Agni’s light. Zuko takes in the weary slump of her shoulders, the hair beginning to wisp out of its tight binding, the black robes loosened to help them dry, flapping in the wind to reveal the blue of her dress underneath. A true blue, not the periwinkle of the North. The color that would have marked her as the last bender of the Southern Water Tribe.

“Only you can decide that,” Zuko finally offers, shoving his own matted hair back off his face. Agni, what he wouldn’t do for a nice shower now. Or a bath where he didn’t need to keep one eye on the door for someone wandering in. …Sokka would probably jump at the idea of a bath.

Katara glances back, and if her eyes are a bit red-rimmed Zuko isn’t going to comment on it. It could just be the wind. “What do you do? When that happens.”

He sighs, dropping his head back and wondering if there could ever be an answer to that. “… Pick the one where you can live with yourself after. And then if there are still choices, the one where if someone is going to hold you accountable for it, you can mostly look them in the eye when you tell them about it.”

Katara tugs at the scarf still draped around her neck. “That’s…bleak.”

Zuko hums, closing his eyes and tilting his face more fully toward the sun. “So’s the world,”

“Would you have done it?” Katara asks after a moment. “What I did?”

“It doesn’t matter what I would have done,” Zuko says. “It was your choice, not mine.” And he isn’t going to tell her when she’s still so uncertain over it that he wouldn’t have. Zuko is aware that he and Azula learned early and often that they had to operate in different ways than everyone else.

Katara grunts. “Thank you,” she finally says. “For giving me the choice. I couldn’t have done it without you.”

Zuko cracks an eye open to catch the flip of her hair as she turns back forward. Being thanked…Zuko doesn’t know how to take that. Katara twists around, face suddenly animated with curiosity. “You believe in destiny?”

Zuko can feel his scar tugging, with the face he makes. “I believe it’s a load of shit that people use to justify the things they want to do to others. Or that they want you to do for them.”

“…Huh.”

“…Sorry,” he mutters, belatedly remembering that she’s into that kind of thing.

“You and Sokka both,” she says, shrugging. “No need to apologize.”

Zuko doesn’t know if he agrees with that, not with all the Fire Nation has done, all that he’s done. But he won’t fight her on it right now, at least.

Zuko doesn’t expect the tension to loosen from his spine at the sight of the others waiting for them. It’s like seeing the whole crew—even the adults hovering at the edges—was all he needed for his body to actually believe it can release the last of its adrenaline, as much as it ever does.

Katara tumbles neatly off Appa’s back the minute his six feet touch down, calling greetings to the others and making a beeline for where Aang is hanging somewhere in the middle distance between the adults and the others. Zuko watches from his perch for a moment, checking that there isn’t any anger between them. Tension, uncertainty, an uncharacteristic hesitance, yes. But that boiling, defensive frustration of Katara’s seemed to have gone dormant, for now at least.

“You going to come down? Or are you planning to take a nap up there?”

Zuko glances down to see Sokka staring up at him, his grin bright in the afternoon light. “A nap would be nice.”

“Like you can sleep with the sun out.” Fair. “What have you been up for, thirty-six hours?”

“…Something like that,” Zuko says. “The math’s too hard right now.” He’s feeling a little too fuzzy to convert that into degrees, between sleeplessness and the adrenaline crash and the happy ripple in his inner flame over coming back to Sokka waiting to greet him.

Sokka’s eyes crinkle with amusement. “Is getting down too hard too?”

Zuko mock-glares, then vaults down with far more showiness than is necessary just to make a point. Which is probably exactly what Sokka wanted judging by the way his grin grows. “No.”

“Good,” Sokka breathes, his smile softening as he scans Zuko for injury before wrapping his fingers into Zuko’s loose cowl, stepping close. Zuko automatically drops his hands to Sokka’s waist to steady him as Sokka leans in, seeming to enjoy the moment of being body to body despite the fact that Zuko can*not* be smelling good right now before tilting his head up for a kiss. Zuko gives it to him without thinking, his breath catching and thumbs tracing the undersides of Sokka’s ribs until the brush of Sokka’s tongue across the seam of his lips has Zuko remembering where they are.

Zuko jolts back, hands loosening around Sokka’s waist even if he can’t entirely make himself let go, his eyes flying first to Katara, who’s still talking to Aang, and then to Hakoda, who’s watching his daughter. But…for how long?

“So,” Sokka says, tugging lightly on his collar to grab Zuko’s attention back. “I’ve got some news.”

Zuko eyes him, most of his focus still on Hakoda. He’s reluctant to pull away from Sokka when he’s standing loose and strong and solid against him, but Zuko‘s also beginning to feel an unwelcome self-consciousness wrapping its way up his spine.

“He knows.”

Zuko snaps his full attention back to Sokka. “What?”

“My dad,” Sokka says, a smile still quirking his lips but eyes starting to go tense with worry. “About us.”

Zuko makes some kind of gurgling noise as his brain just…turns off.

“He figured it out himself,” Sokka says, rueful and apologetic, tugging lightly on Zuko’s cowl again when Zuko doesn’t react. “Zuko?”

“He—is that—are you—do I—”

“It’s fine,” Sokka says quickly, the words…Zuko understands them, but he doesn’t *understand* them. “It’s fine,” Sokka repeats. “It was good. We’re good. You and me. Him and me. All good.” Sokka bites his lip, expression turning anxious. “Are you okay? I know you didn’t want to say anything…”

“I’m fine,” Zuko says automatically, blinking when Sokka flicks him in the shoulder and actually managing to process the question. “I…guess. Yeah.” If Sokka’s fine, if Hakoda isn’t mad…Zuko isn’t sure how comfortable he is with Hakoda knowing when Zuko’s still so unsure of where he stands with the man—fuck, of where he *wants* to stand—but…it’s one less thing Zuko needs to worry about.

Even if he needs to read up on Southern Water Tribe courting practices as soon as possible, fuck, what if he offends Hakoda on Sokka’s behalf without even realizing it.

“I’m glad you made it back in one piece,” Sokka says, the words along with the hands smoothing over his shoulders pulling Zuko out of his thoughts.

“Me too,” Zuko says, letting his fingers slowly climb the ladder of Sokka’s ribs. He wants to fold himself around Sokka and just…breathe to the rhythm of his heart while he readjusts his mental landscape and confirms to himself that he does actually feel better. But as Zuko looks over Sokka’s shoulder he sees Aang finally walking away from Katara, approaching the two of them.

Zuko reluctantly eases back, opening up the space for someone else to talk to him, the protesting flicker of his inner fire turning into a happy little flip when Sokka shifts with him, turning toward Aang but hooking one finger with deceptive idleness into the belt of Zuko’s overtunic. Zuko’s own hand flutters, trying to decide where it should rest until Sokka wordlessly grabs his wrist and sets Zuko’s hand decisively on his shoulder. Zuko stills a moment, processing the casual togetherness of standing next to Sokka this way. Then he lets his arm relax, grip turning more natural as he settles Sokka a little more solidly against his side. This…if this is the kind of thing that comes with people knowing about them, Zuko’s more than fine with it.

Aang’s smile is a mix of relief and a quiet version of his usual cheer as he approaches. “Katara said you helped her find the man who killed her mom.”

“Yeah,” Zuko confirms after a beat, moving this thumb in a slow, comforting circle against Sokka’s shoulder when he feels Sokka tense under his arm.

“And that she didn’t hurt him.”

That…depends on your definition of hurt. “She didn’t injure him, no.” Sokka’s finger twitches where it’s looped through Zuko’s belt at the distinction, and Zuko reaches back with his free hand to press a quick touch to Sokka’s loose fist.

“Thank you,” Aang says, face going serious before he bows, straight-backed and neat and hands forming the everlasting flame as if Zuko had just concluded a bending lesson.

Zuko blinks, fumbling to automatically return the gesture. “What for?”

“For being there for her. For helping her find the path of forgiveness.”

Zuko manages to hold back from sharing that he isn’t entirely sure that what Katara did was meant to be forgiveness at all. He doesn’t think Katara knows either. “She made the choice on her own.”

“And you were there for her,” Aang smiles. “And together you both saw that the path of violence is never the answer.”

Sokka’s elbow lands against Zuko’s rib almost before Zuko processes Aang’s words, Zuko swallowing his tongue as he chokes on a noise of disagreement.

“Let’s get dinner ready for them now that they’re back,” Sokka says with a shade too much brightness.

“Good idea,” Aang says, skipping away, Zuko and Sokka both looking after him and making no move to follow.

“Sokka.

“I know.”

“*Sok*ka.”

“I was here, too.”

“*Sokka*.”

He sighs.

“What’s he going to do when he faces the Fire Lord,” Zuko asks, turning to Sokka, hearing the edge of something like pleading in his voice. “Sokka. What—”

“We’re going to figure it out when we come to it,” Sokka interrupts, eyes still on Aang’s back. “And we’ll do what needs to be done.”

Zuko can’t stop the way his hand automatically tightens on Sokka’s shoulder, anchoring, holding on, trying to hold off the premonition that what Aang might think needs to be done and what Zuko knows needs to happen could end up being two very different things.
