Sokka lets out a surprised laugh as his back hits the wall, something light and bright fluttering in his chest, so big he can barely breathe around it. “I can be persuaded.”

Zuko’s eyebrow shoots up, pausing a moment before he slowly reaches out, his expression full of silent question. Sokka holds his gaze, lips parting on a soundless gasp and eyelids fluttering as Zuko wraps Sokka’s wolf tail around his fist and applies a gentle, insistent pressure to tilt Sokka’s head back. “Oh?”

“Very convincing,” Sokka says, arching to press himself against Zuko wherever he can, Zuko's laughter vibrating through him, for a moment just as good as that brief second of riding Zuko’s hard thigh. “I’ve been persuaded.”

“Easy,” Zuko murmurs, an accusation Sokka doesn't mind in the slightest as Zuko loosens his hand and makes space for Sokka to slide down to his knees—*easily—*running his hands up and down Zuko’s thighs, smiling up at him when Zuko lets out a happy, eager little sound. They grin at each other for a moment like idiots, Sokka drinking in the laughter still lingering on Zuko’s face as Zuko braces his forearm against the wall, resting his forehead against it, his free hand wandering over Sokka’s shoulders and cupping his jaw and hopefully digging into his hair once Sokka gets going.

Sokka kneels up, giving Zuko more access and pressing his face against Zuko’s abs, inhaling the clean scent of sweat and spice and smoke. He drags his hands up to bracket Zuko’s erection, pulling Zuko’s pants tight against him in a way that makes Zuko’s breath catch, then just teasing along the edge of Zuko’s bulge until Sokka can feel the tiny, almost-suppressed tremors shivering through him.

Sokka is contemplating whether he wants to get right down to business or really draw out the teasing—with so many people around there’s been surprisingly little time to *touch*—when Zuko goes utterly motionless beneath Sokka’s hands, his fingers tensing against Sokka’s head without digging in.

Sokka pulls back, alarmed, looking up to see Zuko’s head turned, cocked like he does when he’s trying to hear something in his unscarred ear. Sokka holds his breath to listen—if someone is close enough to be heard then they don’t have much time to make it look like they weren’t doing exactly what they’re doing—and feels a sharp wash of horror down his spine as he realizes that the rhythmic thrumming he’s been distantly registering growing louder and louder is *not* the sound of his own rising heartbeat.

“Wha—”

An explosion rips through the air, the entire Temple shuddering on its heels. Sokka instinctively ducks his head, grabbing Zuko by the hip with one hand and yanking Zuko’s foot out from under him with the other, shoving Zuko into a throw and twisting as they fall so they land on their sides against the wall.

They both tuck themselves in tight as another blast sounds out, Sokka trying to press his back to the wall and pull Zuko even closer into the thin shelter it provides. Something crashes in the depths of the Temple and they throw their arms up, covering their heads as pebbles and dust shower down.

Sokka twists around as the pebbles stop falling, Zuko’s hands urging him to stay low as he cranes to look toward the canyon in time to see the tail end of something gigantic and dark rise through the lingering late-Spring fog. “Fuck,” he breathes, a cold wash of terror stabbing through him. Sokka spent enough time trying to figure out how to dispose of an airship to recognize it from any angle.

“Azula,” Zuko says, grim and tight in Sokka’s ear.

Another blast—projectiles? Firebending?—echoes through the gorge, screams ringing out this time along with it. Fuck, the others—it’s too early to gather for lunch. They would have been dispersed around the Temple, which is good from an avoiding-being-hit standpoint and fucking terrible from a coordinating-a-defensive-effort perspective.

“We need to—”

“Yeah,” Zuko says, springing to his feet as Sokka scrambles upright, both of them hugging the wall. “Do we know where—”

“No.” And *fuck*, Teo and The Duke were going to go exploring which means they could be anywhere. He can only hope that everyone remembers to move toward the main plaza, even though they’ve never discussed facing an aerial attack before. Spirits, *why* did they never talk about it? Like the fucking Fire Nation doesn’t have plenty of airpower, and know exactly how to attack the Western Air Temple?

“Go,” Zuko urges, his eyes on the gorge and the swirls of smoke mixing with the fog. “Get the others ready to run.”

Sokka hesitates. “What about you?”

“I’ll be there,” Zuko assures him, face tight with focus. “I’ll buy us time.”

Sokka mentally maps out the path he needs to take, but he doesn’t go just yet. “Is there a plan?”

“No,” Zuko says with blithe unconcern, clapping Sokka on the shoulder and taking off.

“Oh,” Sokka says to himself, “Good.” Spirits.

Sokka’s feeling more than a little hysterical as he finally takes off in the opposite direction, sprinting as fast as he can when he can’t be sure of his footing. If Zuko’s buying them time, then Sokka can’t waste a single second.

&#45;-

Zuko knows the Western Air Temple. The early days of his banishment were seared into his memory by pain and strangled fear and bone-deep horror at the truths of his nation’s history that none of them witnessing it could ever speak aloud. Zuko knows this place, better than the others and certainly better than Azula and the Fire Nation forces marshaled against them.

And he knows that the Temple isn’t going to stay here for long if the bombardment continues like this, the sound of at least three ships ringing through the interior.

Zuko sprints through the hallways, jumping gaps in the floor and scaling stairless interior towers, making his way upward as efficiently as possible before dashing back toward the canyon. He bursts out into one of the highest plazas that jut out into nothingness and immediately has to throw up a spray of fire to deflect shards of rock and vine and earth that fly through the air, another bombardment setting his scarred ear ringing.

Zuko narrows his eyes against the smoke and debris, scanning the gorge and finally finding the silhouette on top of the lead ship. It’s far away, but Zuko would recognize that straight-backed figure anywhere, recognize the way she turns toward him like a messenger hawk about to dive. Her tawny gaze locks on him and for a moment both of them are still, waiting, Zuko’s inner flame blazing to his call, building and building until it's raging against the confines of his skin.

Then Azula snaps into motion and blue fire screams down, ripping into pavers and pillars, ricocheting off his block bare inches from his face to tear off chunks of ceiling. The smell of singed rock and nearly-singed clothing fills the air, rising and rising as the fire keeps coming until the floor suddenly tilts under Zuko’s feet, breaking apart behind him, taking away his retreat.

Not that he was going to use retreat anyway. He sprints for the lip of the plaza before that crumbles away, too, body humming with readiness. The plan was always to go forward. --

Sokka and Katara are covering the other’s retreat toward the interior, Haru and Teo leading the way with their knowledge of the Temple’s corridors when the fog suddenly lights from the inside with dual red and blue fire. Sokka’s heart stutters, knowing that somewhere above him Zuko is fighting his sister. His body trembles with the urge to run forward, to find him and help him and fight at his side.

But Zuko said he would be there, and Sokka can’t doubt that, not when he knows that Zuko’s done wilder things, not when he knows that Zuko is relying on Sokka to do this. *Planning* on him to do this, even if Zuko would never put it that way.

Sokka finally throws himself into the tunnel, Katara at his side and Toph brings the wall down after them with a resounding crash. Aang and Chit Sang kindle fires in their hands, flickering orange light making the usually open, breezy hallways seem close and oppressive. Suki does a quick headcount before giving Sokka a sharp nod. Then it’s a matter of running, winding their way in and up, Toph shoring up the hallways as they go as shudders and crashes continue to roll through the Temple, their pace as fast as Appa can maintain on the ground.

Sokka’s thinking they might actually manage to slip this net when Suki suddenly skids to a stop in front of him, throwing out a hand to catch his and Katara’s momentum as they both pull up short, skidding on loose stone and debris.

“Wha—”

A low moan shakes down another rain of earth and dust, Appa’s rumble of protest sufficiently answering the question. Sokka shoves his way forward, trusting Suki and Katara to hold the rear, coming to the front to find Appa groaning again in reluctance, Aang anxious at his side, both of them staring down a tunnel barely bigger than Appa is.

“Toph, can you make it bigger?”

“*This* one,” Toph says, hand slapped to the wall, face tight with concentration.

“But it doesn’t get any wider up ahead,” Haru cautions, glancing to Teo for confirmation.

“We’d have to rearrange it all as we go.”

“We can’t risk that,” Hakoda says, staring up as if he can see through layers of stone toward the structure of the Temple. “If we have to move walls all the way through…”

“We might bring it down,” Sokka finishes. They might as well just blast their way out, at that point. With three earthbenders they might be able to do it, but—that’s a lot of rock and stone, and not a lot of space to shift it.

“…We go back, then,” Suki says, glancing into the darkness behind them.

“Not all of us, maybe,” Chit Sang suddenly says quietly. “Airships aren’t nearly as maneuverable as a sky bison.”

“I’m not leaving him,” Aang says immediately, fist tightening in Appa’s fur.

“And he can’t carry everyone,” Sokka points out, dread settling in his throat, because Sokka ran these numbers weeks and weeks ago during the Day of the Black Sun and he knows exactly what combination of bodies will fit on Appa’s back.

“He doesn’t have to carry everyone, though,” Hakoda says gravely, taking a deliberate step back. “Just those who need to go with the Avatar.”

“No,” Sokka says immediately. *No.*

“Sokka.”

“I—we just got you back,” Sokka protests, hating how choked the words come out, hating that his mind is throwing up just how many people would need to stay behind with Hakoda and how many could go with Aang. “I—we can’t leave you again.”

“I’m not going away,” Hakoda says firmly, his pale eyes serious as Sokka forces himself to meet his gaze. “And you aren’t leaving me. But you need to stay with the Avatar. And the Avatar needs to stay with his air bison.”

“We can provide a distraction if we can get topside fast enough,” Chit Sang offers, exchanging a glance with his friends. “Draw at least one of the ships away. Keep it occupied.”

“I know a fast way,” The Duke pipes up.

“And I can help with any rock falls we encounter,” Haru offers.

Sokka hates it, but his mind is already working, dividing them and assessing their respective mobility and offensive and defensive capabilities. “Going all the way back—”

“This is an exterior wall,” Toph interrupts, giving the wall in question a thump. “It’s close to where they dug into the mountain, so we wouldn’t take anything down if we blow it out.”

“Appa out there with all those airships, though,” Aang says, pressing anxiously against Appa’s side.

“What if he had some armor,” Katara says. “Like the stone armor you used in Ba Sing Se.”

“But not full-body,” Sokka adds. “So we can still go fast.”

Toph purses her lips. “I can do that.”

“Then it sounds like a plan,” Hakoda said, the words decisive but his gaze on Sokka.

It does. Fuck. “Alright,” Sokka says, matching Hakoda with his decisiveness and shoving down the protest writhing in his chest. “Everyone going on Appa, get ready on his back. Katara—help Toph bust us out of here.” He jogs for Appa’s saddle, trying to think through the anxious little voice screaming at the back of his mind that Zuko isn’t here, that they’re deviating from the plan and Zuko doesn’t know. That Zuko is supposed to be around and isn’t, just like in Ba Sing Se, except this time there’s no part of Sokka that could accept leaving Zuko behind as an option.

&#45;-

“It doesn’t have to be this way,” Zuko calls, even as he spins into a tight, sharp kick that forces Azula to finally flip off her lookout tower down onto the surface of the airship, the metal plating trembling under her impact.

“What other way would you have it be, Zuko?” Azula asks, clipped and narrow-eyed as she punches out a fluid, rapid series of fireballs. “You can’t have it both ways.”

Zuko grunts, dancing across the sloped sides of the airship, using his agility as much as his bending to avoid her attack.

Azula watches him move, barely adjusting her feet as she tracks him, eyes narrowed. “You can’t play both sides.”

“I’m not,” Zuko growls.

“Then you’ve made it abundantly clear the side that you’re on.”

“Azula—”

“Actions speak, Zuko,” Azula snaps, a brief flare of anger and sparks before her face goes cold and impassive. “And unlike you, I don’t need to learn more than once. I’m not going to take a rat viper back into my fold.”

“I haven’t betrayed you,” Zuko says, firm, fire crackling in his hands, ready to throw.

“Just everything you claimed to stand for.”

“That’s not true,” Zuko protests, desperately clinging to every breath spent exchanging words instead of fire, even furious, hostile, outraged accusations.

&#45;-

They burst out of the temple into the gorge in a spray of stone, Aang shoving a cone of air out ahead of them to clear Appa’s way as they fly the first few seconds blind, everyone with their heads tucked low. Except for Sokka, who can’t help scanning, looking—finding.

“Oh.” That’s…unexpected. But not surprising. “There he is.”

&#45;-

Zuko and Azula both throw themselves low as the side of the temple explodes, the force of it rocking the airship beneath them. They immediately turn toward the sound and the unmistakable shape of a sky bison tearing through the air, Zuko instinctively finding Sokka on his back as Appa streaks toward them.

“Isn’t it?” Azula spits, rolling neatly back to her feet. “Then what is this, *Brother*.”

“It’s not a betrayal,” Zuko says, hearing his words crack with urgency as he turns his focus back toward her, rising up into a ready crouch.

She snort, disgusted. “I’m not an idiot,” she says, her face twisting before going abruptly, coldly blank. “You always did have a suicidal streak, Zuko. I never realized it was quite so literal. And for quite so little in return.”

Zuko expects the attack that forces him to sink low into his block, relying on the strength of his legs to keep him from sliding too close to the edge as he makes himself a smaller target. He does *not* expect to pick his head up and see Azula nowhere in front of him. He goes motionless, uncertain, before casting his heat sense wide, quickly finding the barely-contained explosion of her inner flame *below* him.

Zuko scrambles to the edge, skidding down the sloped wall of the airship in the direction he can feel her in, finally catching sight of her crouched neatly on the lookout tower of one of the other airships that must have maneuvered below them. To flank Appa, Zuko realizes as he catches himself on a maintenance railing, leaning out over the gorge to see. And Azula must want to be part of it.

Well. Zuko did say he was here to buy them time. And he’s made harder leaps than this before.

Zuko hurls himself out into space, landing on the new airship in a spray of fire that deflects the precise arrow of blue flame punching down toward him. He spins his shield into a tight funnel instead of letting it disperse, swinging it toward her and sprinting in its wake to close the distance between them.

Azula doesn’t precisely run, but she doesn’t wholly stand and fight, either, and Zuko can’t help but think that somehow he’s playing into her hand, wasting time even though that’s his goal too, because he’s never known her to be this noncommittal otherwise. He dodges and blocks flames, throwing his own in return, punches and kicks, both of them flipping around railings and darting between the high and low ground, boots skidding across the curved tops of the airships.

“You’ll have to be better than that, Brother,” Azula says, a dismissive flick of her hand dispersing the covering flame Zuko used to shield himself as he dropped to a new airship after her.

He glares, legs flexing as this airship lowest in the formation rides a sudden gust coming out of the gorge, launching his next attack in rhythm with the updraft he knows is coming next. His feet slide with tight control over the metal sheeting, knees absorbing the sudden roll of the ship and translating the force into his fire. Zuko knows the wind patterns here far better than she does, and he’s spent far more time accounting for the movement of the ground beneath him training on the *Wani* than Azula ever would have.

He feels a burst of grim satisfaction when she has to flip back instead of holding her block or dispersing the flame, wobbling slightly on her landing enough that she turns the motion into a smooth roll, coming up onto one knee, eyes narrowed. “Trying to toss me off the edge, Brother?”

“Azula—”

“Well I think you’ll find,” she snarls, both hands bursting into jagged blue flame. “That I am not someone you *throw away.”*

&#45;-

“Can we—”

“We need to—”

“*Duck,”* Suki screams, everyone throwing themselves down except Aang as Appa banks sharply away, groaning with anger as a flaming ball of something flies by, the force of the turn pressing Sokka flat even as he feels himself sliding toward the edge of the saddle.

Sokka forces his head up as they level out to see three massive, dark sharps arrayed in front of them, two ships cutting off their maneuverability, driving them toward the third where Sokka can see blue and red gouts of fire ripping over the surface. Herding them toward Azula. “Aw, fuck.”

At least Zuko is there too.

&#45;-

Zuko grabs onto a strut as the airship banks, taking a quick moment to spot himself relative to Appa and the other ships and the Western Air Temple.

Not good, he realizes as the ship levels out. Appa’s barreling toward them, and he could zoom right over the ship if Azula weren’t positioned exactly where she is, eyes pinned on the sky bison’s approaching figure and lightning beginning to crackle around her fingers. Even if the Avatar survived the lightning, there’s no way the sky bison would be able to do anything but fall. Fuck.

Zuko flips back up to rise to his feet directly across from her, mirroring her braced, rooted stance, Appa at his back now. Azula raises an eyebrow, face set with mocking challenge as she continues the precise motion of her arms, extended fingers carving a neat circle in the air and Zuko can *feel* the sudden crackling potential against his fire sense as it begins to coalesce between her hands.

Zuko sets his breathing and his feet, holding her sharp gaze as he grounds himself, hands curved in readiness, inner flame coiling from his stomach, branching away from his chest to twine down his arms, forming an unbroken line from fingertip to fingertip so that when her hand suddenly snaps forward, two fingers extended and white-blue lightning igniting, Zuko is ready to catch it.

The force of it sets every hair on his body on end. It screams down his arm and through his gut and then back up as he launches into the swirling patterns of redirection, faster than he’s ever done before. Agni, Azula’s lightning feels just like one of her hugs—utterly shocking and more than a little painful, dangerous enough to set your pulse pounding. The Fire Lord’s lightning might have been all clawing hatred, but Azula’s is fast and tight and *cold* in a way that makes Zuko’s bones ache as he sends it coiling back up his left arm and off his fingers to explode toward the rear of the other airship.

The redirected strike lands with a wrenching scream of metal and soldiers, the airship suddenly careening downward as one of its rudders crumples. Zuko watches the falling ship and the way Appa veers toward suddenly open space, heart in his throat until Azula *snarls*, jerking Zuko’s attention back around.

He sets his feet, shaking the lingering sparks from his hands and as Azula turns on him with slow, deliberate intent, his inner fire suddenly flaring with apprehension as he takes in the look on her face. The Avatar, Zuko realizes, might have just dropped to second on her list of targets for the day.

&#45;-

“Swing wide!” Suki shouts, scanning the sky above them.

“Not too wide,” Sokka calls, eyes trained on Zuko as his firebender suddenly begins skidding and sliding and *jumping*, Zuko was doing all that before, but not this urgently, and not this —“Oh, shit.”

“What?” Katara asks, grunting as she hurls out a tentacle of water to knock a projectile off course, throwing her entire torso behind it since she can’t risk rising off her knees.

“Azula’s chasing him.”

“Wasn’t that already happening?”

“He was chasing her, before.”

Katara turns, craning her neck to see the royal pair, a grim kind of determination settling over her features, blue flame reflecting in her eyes. “We can chase him too. Right?”

There’s a moment of tight silence, then they all spring into motion, orienting themselves around the new mission. It’s no longer about getting out and trusting Zuko to meet them, it’s about meeting Zuko before they can get out.

“Toph, can you move your shield?” Suki asks, leaning over the side of the saddle to eye the interlocking stones.

“If someone tells me where to move it,” Toph says, arms steady in front of her despite the work she’s been doing this whole time to hold the protective shield in front of Appa’s head.

“Aang,” Sokka says, slithering forward, staying low. “How long is Appa good for?”

“With this many people?”

“Right,” Sokka mutters. Fuck. Not nearly as long as Sokka would like. He takes a deep breath before squaring his shoulders. “Alright. Shadow Zuko, but don’t get so close that the firebenders on the ships can fire on us.”

Aang frowns. “But don’t we need to get close enough that Zuko can reach us?”

Katara and Suki answer at the same time: “He can jump.”

&#45;-

“Why don’t you stand and *fight*,” Azula growls as he weaves under and over railings, sliding ahead of her latest attack. The air is growing dry around them, thin, their fire blazing long enough and hot enough to boil away the lingering fog.

“I don’t want to fight you, Azula,” Zuko calls back, coming to a wary crouch on top of the maintenance railing. From here he can launch himself up back toward the high point of the airship or flip himself back if the second ship comes along this side.

“You never do,” she snorts, raking him with a disgusted look.

“But I will if I have to,” Zuko finishes, a warning as his inner fire coils in his palms, in the back of his throat.

“Well, Brother,” she says, stepping off the high point of the airship to land on the maintenance walkway at his level, eyes fixed on him the whole time. “You can’t run forever.”

&#45;-

They finally manage to get achingly close, enough to make out distinct expressions, to see the details of the bending forms Azula and Zuko are using against each other. Sokka can barely breathe through the words locked in his throat, swallowed back because there’s far too much happening for him to risk distracting Zuko by calling out. But Spirits, they’re close enough to fucking *hear* them.

“Really, Brother,” Azula drawls as Zuko skids back despite his block, wavering a moment before turning the momentum into an absolutely nauseating flip down to a new part of the airship. “It’s like you’re determined to be inept. You finally get the technique, and you’re too scrawny to pull it off against a real firebender.”

Zuko’s head lifts into a familiar glare, but his reply is lost as Appa suddenly banks sharply away, back toward open space as the other airship tries to come down on them from above.

“Left! Left!” Suki screams. “Less left!”

Toph growls, hands rigid as her stone shield takes a barrage of fire. “Be a bit more specific next time!”

&#45;-

“I didn’t know that Mai and—”

“*Don’t speak their names.”*

&#45;-

They try coming in from below next, since Zuko’s apparently so willing to hurl himself from airship to airship, or airship to cliff wall to other airship in a move that nearly stops Sokka’s heart. Katara’s using ropes of water to divert attacks, grim with concentration, trying to conserve every drop. They’re nearly in range when the air above them suddenly boils with blue and red flame, and in a scramble of feet it’s suddenly fucking *Azula* who’s closer to the edge as she drives Zuko back toward the center of the airship.

“Pathetic,” she huffs, the tense lines of her body at odds with her tone, and Appa drops away because close enough to hear means close enough for her to blast them. “No wonder Father always said you should have been drowned at birth.”

&#45;-

“Drowning would have suited you,” Azula continues as she stalks deliberately up the ridge of the airship after him, Zuko focusing most of his attention on the movement of her shoulders and hips, readying himself for her next attack. “Since you love water so much more than fire.”

“It doesn’t have to be one or the other,” he grunts, dropping low and forward into a block so her attack sheets off into the air above him, burning away fog and nothing else.

“Don’t be naïve, Zuko,” Azula says. “It’s alive or dead. You can only be one.”

&#45;-

“Now, Katara,” Sokka urges, fingers digging into the edge of Appa’s saddle, the only outlet he’ll allow for the anxiety banding around his ribs.

“Are you sure?”

Not in the least, but they don’t have the time left for Sokka to be sure. “Do it.”

“But Zuko—”

“He can make it,” Sokka says firmly, injecting every piece of faith he has in Zuko into his voice as Aang calls out a warning, “Here it comes!”

All of Katara’s water retreats toward her and for one terrifying moment they’re totally defenseless as she stands tall at the back of the saddle, all her focus on the ship Zuko and Azula are dancing over. Then the updraft hits them, breaking around Appa with Aang’s help even as it buffets the airship into a turn to compensate, exposing its rudders.

Katara’s water slams forward. There isn’t enough over this distance to tear anything apart, but they’ve all developed an eye toward breaking apart Fire Nation machinery at its vulnerable points. The rudder screams as it bends under the force of her attack, the airship lurching into a hard, sharp turn that has Sokka’s heart frozen in his throat, his eyes fixed on Zuko as the entire craft lists sideways.

&#45;-

Zuko throws himself low, slamming a hand down so he lands in a controlled sprawl instead of hitting the roof with his whole body and losing his ability to brace against the slick metal. His arm is bent, flexed, toes digging in as he rides out the bucking of the ship, angling his body so the force of the turn presses him down, so the air can’t get beneath him and tear him away.

Azula’s higher up the slope of the airship, though, where the force of the turn is stronger, caught too high and now fighting to get her body low. Zuko watches, inner fire tight, as she strains to make her body obey her will, as her faces twists with rage. She slashes her eyes up, hitting him for a breath with a furious glare. Then she abruptly shifts back, away from Zuko, turning her momentum *into* the airship’s spin and throwing herself into a graceful, arcing flip out into the gorge.

Zuko stares, scrambling to keep his eyes fixed on the already-gone space in the fog where he last saw her, straining out with his heat sense but encountering nothing but dense, cool, dampening mist. His inner flame wrenches low in his chest and he clenches his jaw, forcing his breathing to stay steady and deep because he needs to get out before he can allow himself anything else.

Zuko reaches out again, anchoring his heat sense around the ball of heat that is Appa, the familiar not-flame that is Sokka, calculating spin and trajectory and distance, riding out one last turn before following Azula’s lead.

He leaps out into the open air, pinwheeling his arms, straining for every bit of distance he can as he hurtles toward Appa, spotting his landing as he gets close enough to see through the fog and ignoring the shouts rising from Appa’s back as they finally get eyes on him. Zuko concentrates on his landing as Suki hauls Toph back, Appa suddenly banking inward as Aang tugs on the reins, the motion enough that Zuko readjusts at the last moment to spot the high edge of Appa’s saddle instead of the broad expanse of his fur.

Zuko’s breath explodes out of him as he slams into the wooden saddle edge chest first, every muscle in his body clenching as he tries to keep his legs from swinging back out and pulling his body into space. Then hands are on his forearms, his biceps, anchoring him, wrapping around his shoulders, clawing at the back of his clothes, and Zuko is being hauled up, with an assist from Appa as the sky bison takes a sudden dip that gives Zuko a moment of weightlessness to finally clear his hips into the safety of the saddle.

Zuko falls forward as gravity reasserts itself, crashing down in a mess of limbs. He tries to rise up to avoid crushing whoever is beneath him, almost immediately sprawling out over the saddle again as Appa abruptly swoops. Zuko grunts, bracing himself up on his forearms and deciding to just stay down here for now, scanning the remaining airships and seeing nothing but steel, and then the Temple, and nothing more, where—

“Fin and tooth,” Suki mutters from somewhere behind him. “What will it *take* with that girl.”

Zuko snaps around to follow her gaze, finally picking out Azula clinging to the sheer rockface, one hand hanging loose and sparking blue like she hasn’t quite given up on the idea of attacking. He can’t tear his eyes away from her tawny, cold glare, his heart beating so fast in his throat it might burst through, unable to look away even when they fly far enough that Zuko can’t see anything more than flickering fire and the dark shape of her alone on the wall.

&#45;-

“Holy shit,” Sokka laughs as they swoop away. “Holy shit.” He finally sits up and wiggles out from where he’s been half-underneath Zuko, running his hands over his firebender, looking for injuries. “You’re okay? Is everyone okay?”

They do a roll call, everyone sounding off, miraculously unscathed beyond scrapes and bruises, ending with Zuko’s belated, “I’m not injured.”

“Are you sure?” Sokka says, even though he’s run his hands over every part of Zuko it’s decent to touch and hasn’t drawn out even a flinch. “I saw—it looked like—”

“I’m not wounded,” Zuko repeats, sighing as he shoves himself up to sit against the edge of the saddle.

Sokka frowns. That motion was heavy, with little of Zuko’s usual grace, and Sokka’s getting familiar now with Zuko’s ability to evade. He can hear the difference between ‘I’m okay’ and ‘I’m not injured.’ He taps Zuko with his boot, a quick, light brush against his ankle to draw his attention, letting all his questions fill his face.

Zuko hesitates, glancing with a flash of visible discomfort around at the others. He offers a little half-shrug, eyes flicking back toward the gorge—which Sokka realizes he’s been staring at ever since he made it into the saddle—before landing back on Sokka. Zuko makes to speak a few times before finally mouthing ‘*later?’*

Not physically injured, then, but maybe not okay. Sokka slowly nods his agreement, watching the way Zuko slumps back in something that might be relief or might just be the end of his ability to engage, his eyes going mostly closed with exhaustion even as tension continues to sit in his hands and shoulders and legs.

Sokka keeps his boot pressed gently against Zuko’s ankle, offering silent support as he thinks about what it might mean for Zuko to need to fight his sister so soon after Boiling Rock. Was this the first time he dealt with her like this—not as someone he’s in individual conflict with, but as a Princess bringing the forces and power at her disposal against him?

Sokka thinks of what they overheard, too, and considers that with Azula, the fighting rarely seems to happen just with fire. She was wielding words as well, and Sokka remembers how deep those can cut, how it can make you feel weak and gasping for breath even though you're physically untouched, how Azula seems to have a particular talent for making you feel like she’s stripped the skin from your bones with just a sentence.

Except…Zuko doesn’t seem to be tense with anger or resentment like Sokka would have expected if that was the case. It’s more…worried-tight, bringing Sokka suddenly back to the quick, anxious sweep of Zuko’s eyes over his body back at that abbey, to the memory of Zuko crouched over Iroh in that no-name town.

“Are you sure you’re okay?” Katara asks, pulling Sokka out of his thoughts as Zuko twitches at the question and lifts his head up from the edge of the saddle like it takes actual effort.

“As much as you could expect,” Zuko offers after a moment, shoving a hand through his hair, grimacing when it comes away streaked with soot and dust.

“I guess,” Katara says dubiously. “So that…that was your sister.”

“Yeah,” Zuko sighs, head tipping back again, and Sokka eyes Katara warily, wondering where she’s taking this because he knows she’s more than aware of who Azula is.

“…Was she…?”

Zuko peeks at Katara when she doesn’t finish, and Sokka really hopes this actually non-combative, voluntary conversation happening between them doesn't take a turn. “Was she what?”

Katara bites her lip. “Was she particularly angry?”

Zuko tilts his face fully toward her, confused. “I mean. Out of sorts, I guess.”

Aang twists around, looking aghast and Toph lets out a snort, which Sokka thinks is a little ridiculous. They were both below the palace with him. They both heard what Azula said, and the total calm with which she said it.

“Out of *sorts*,” Toph mutters. “Shit balls. I’d hate to see her really angry, then.”

“Yeah,” Zuko agrees seriously, totally missing Toph’s sarcasm. “Me, too.”

“Is she like that with everyone?” Suki asks after a beat, brow creased.

“Not really,” Zuko shrugs, and Sokka thinks that it takes a level of personal venom to come at Zuko the way she did. “But—you’ve all met her before. It’s not like you don’t know?”

“We’ve fought her but…she’s hunting us,” Sokka points out, adding on when Zuko just looks at him blankly. “She kind of hates us.”

“And you’re her brother,” Katara points out.

“…And?”

“And…she just shot lightning at you,” Katara says slowly, like maybe Zuko isn’t remembering.

“I redirected it,” Zuko reminds her. “So it worked out.”

Sokka snaps his mouth shut around his immediate reply to the idea that anything back there just ‘worked out,’ and forces himself to actually think about what Zuko is saying. That it worked out, which means…what, that there was something to work? Or is it just a turn of phrase? Because Sokka knew that Zuko had his thing with storms, obviously, and he’s all too aware that Azula can generate lightning of her own. But he didn’t know a firebender could redirect lightning like that. And he doesn’t know if *Azula* would have known that, either. And if she did know that it was something Zuko could do—would she expect him to? Would she think that Zuko could pull it off under those conditions? If she didn’t…Fuck, if she *did*…

And if Zuko knew that she knew…

“So,” Aang says slowly, grabbing Sokka’s attention before he can get trapped in that circular line of thinking forever. “Does that mean she always says things like that to you?”

Zuko blinks. “Like what?”

“…Like that you’re pathetic,” Toph offers.

“Regularly,” Zuko confirms.

“Or that you should have been drowned.”

“It comes up surprisingly often.”

“Or that you’re scrawny and weak.”

“I mean.” Zuko glances down at himself. “I haven’t been at a normal fighting weight in a while.”

Suki finally speaks into the silence. “You have an interesting relationship with your sister.”

Zuko looks around at everyone staring at him with varying degrees of concern and upset. “… I guess?”

“Nontraditional,” Suki tries.

“…Sure?”

“Some might even say hostile.”

Zuko scratches the back of his neck, glancing toward Sokka with a quick plea for rescue in his eyes. “I mean. It’s not like she’s tried to assassinate me.”

“I think we might be running into some cultural differences here,” Sokka suggests before Katara can recover from her sputtering to dig into that, because Sokka *knows* Zuko isn’t going to want to peel back the covers on that particular mess of Fire Nation custom right now.

“I’m not sure that it’s cultural,” Aang says, looking concerned.

“It better not be cultural,” Katara finally mutters, scowling when Sokka waves her to silence. Sokka doesn’t know most days whether he hopes that these kinds of things are just part of Zuko’s family or of the Fire Nation more broadly, but it’s not like Zuko exactly has the perspective to tell them which it is, especially not exhausted like this. Even if Sokka were entirely comfortable with Zuko’s assessment of acceptable sibling conduct. Which Sokka isn’t, and which he needs to find a way to ask about, because Zuko’s finally unwound enough for the edge of his hand to find Sokka’s between their bodies, but his head has turned back toward the gorge and Sokka doesn’t think he’s checking for pursuit.

Sokka’s starting to feel what he thinks is the hard edge of realization that Azula might be a very large, very vulnerable spot for Zuko in a very different way than Sokka originally understood.

“Not to cut short this impromptu sociological exercise—”

Zuko frowns. “What?”

“—but…where are we going?” Suki finishes. “Do we have a rendezvous point? A place to set up camp?”

Silence falls over Appa’s saddle except for the steady, constant sound of the passing wind as everyone looks around, because they might have all fled to the Western Air Temple as the closest safe ground they could find after the failed invasion, but none of them had ever discussed leaving it.

Finally, Zuko stirs, his hand tensing slightly around Sokka’s before he quietly says, “I know a place.”

There’s a pause, then Aang shrugs, grabbing up Appa’s loose reins. “What way?”

Zuko looks up at the sky, then cranes his head to peer down at the ground below them. “West.”

“Toward the Fire Nation?” Katara frowns, and Sokka shares her concern. They aren’t exactly an inconspicuous group, and he doubts they can pull off another successful incognito traveling attempt within enemy territory.

“Toward Ember Island,” Zuko confirms, and Sokka isn’t quite sure what to do with the mixture of dread and longing that flashes over Zuko’s face at the words.

## Chapter 25: Glass Houses

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for sexual content in this one

### Text

They fly in silence for the most part, except for brief bursts of quiet murmuring. No one voices any questions about where he’s directing them, or what exactly Ember Island is. Which simultaneously sparks a spike of worry and a burst of confused pride in his chest, that they trust him enough to just go along with a plan they don’t even know the barest details of beyond ‘west,’ just because Zuko’s the one to suggest it.

It feels like a risky—or intimidating, maybe—level of faith, even if after Azula this morning, Zuko can’t exactly say he *wants* more questions and prodding and close examination.

Her rough edges are definitely getting rougher. And Agni, she hadn’t looked herself. All that open rage…Zuko can’t stop thinking that he critically underestimated just how much Azula has been leaning on Mai and Ty Lee. And that realizing it only after he’s faced her without them isn’t exactly a realization that does anyone a bit of good.

Agni’s balls, hadn’t Mai and Ty Lee been gone from Caldera for years before Azula went out to collect them this past summer? How had she managed to even get that far on her own if this is what she’s like without them?

His inner flame twists, cold and sharp behind his solar plexus, settling hard against his lungs. Maybe because Azula never truly thought she was alone, before.

&#45;-

Sokka shifts his boots in the fine sand, automatically testing his footing as he cranes his neck to take in the huge, weather-worn mansion rising out of the jungle. The palm trees and vines seem to be fighting to claim every bit of earth that isn’t sand or pavers or courtyard, the only thing seeming to save the whole house from being swallowed up by vegetation the fact that it was built on such a rocky part of the cliffside.

Sokka’s never seen one before, but he can’t imagine this is anything other than a rich person’s vacation home. “You know a place, huh.”

Zuko grunts at his side, and Sokka gives him a quick, sharp glance. He can read the tension and restless kind of resentfulness in that noise, even if the others don’t seem to register it. Sokka eyes the vacation home, and then his rich person again.

…Right.

“I don’t know,” Aang says, looking around the private beach that’s in full view of the nice private house. “How do we know the people who live here won’t come back?”

“No one lives here anymore,” Zuko says shortly.

“Well, the family might have maintenance people, or—"

“They don’t,” Zuko cuts in, voice suddenly bleak. “The family doesn’t exist anymore.” Aang stares, nonplussed, until Zuko shakes himself and turns sharply away from the house on the ridge toward the sheltered cove. “Let’s set up camp.”

Toph frowns, surprised. “We aren’t staying in the house?”

Zuko doesn’t turn back. “…It’s best to wait until morning to explore.”

Sokka glances between Zuko’s rigid posture and the sky. It’s getting on in the day, sure, but this close to the equator this close to summer there’s still plenty of sunlight left to explore by. Still, setting up camp does take time, especially on sand, so it’s not the worst excuse Sokka’s ever heard. And Sokka certainly isn’t going to be the one to suggest doing anything other than what Zuko wants right now, not when Zuko is moving with such sharp purpose, Sokka belatedly jogging a few steps to catch up and the others stropping along behind like a regular old parade as Zuko leads them to…something.

“This is a good spot for a campfire,” Zuko mutters, face shadowed as he stops in front of the clear remains of an old bonfire, covered in sand but still visible in its circle of rocks. A half-ring of driftwood logs have been dragged around, presumably seating for whatever produced the fairly impressive seats-to-bottles-of-wine ratio Sokka unearths when he gives the sand a little kick.

“Are we sure people don’t come here,” Aang asks dubiously, poking at the remains of the fire and dragging out the burned edge of…a canvas? “It looks like someone was messing with stuff from that house.”

“It’s fine,” Zuko says, digging with hit boot to the left of one of the logs and uncovering a corked bottle, quarter-full when Zuko grabs it. He turns it in his hands a moment, face set in a scowl, before tossing it to a surprised Suki and stalking back up to the tree line with a muttered, “I’ll…Supplies.”

Sokka eyes the bottle, then Zuko’s departing back, ignoring Katara and Aang’s questioning looks and the way Suki’s eyes dart between Zuko and the house. Sokka has a very good idea of who was burning things in the bonfire. He just doesn’t quite know what to make of the fact that there's clearly sitting room around the fire—and enough empty bottles—for more than one.

&#45;-

Sokka is less tending to the fire and more having fun with the way driftwood seems to do interesting things to the flames, drawing out sparkles of green and disconcerting licks of blue, when Zuko finally makes his reappearance. Not with the foraging Sokka expected, but with a neat sack of rice, a net bag of fruit and root vegetables, and a distinctive jar of what Sokka knows has to be chili paste.

“So,” Sokka says, sitting back on his heels and giving Zuko a mild look of question, because the set of Zuko’s shoulders is way too prickly for much else. “Supplies, huh.”

Zuko shrugs, still scowling as he begins to sort out his haul into their currently very sparse stash. “These are supplies,” he grumbles, shoulders hunching up to his ears. Definitely too prickly.

“Did you go to the market?” Katara frowns, and Sokka *clearly* needs to give her remedial lessons in firebender defensiveness.

“Yeah.”

“You just made some purchases,” Sokka observes, trying to pull Zuko’s attention back to him.

“I didn’t *steal* it,” Zuko says, testy, which…was so not what Sokka was trying to imply.

“Going into a market feels like a risk,” Suki says, brow furrowed. “We can’t afford to stand out.”

“It’s a tourist town,” Zuko snaps. “There are always new people. No one stands out.”

Suki crosses her arms. “How’d you pay?”

“I exchanged some stuff from inside,” Zuko says, throwing down a bag of moon peaches rather more forcefully than moon peaches usually need.

“And *that* didn’t stand out?”

Zuko gives her a flat look. “It’s a gambling town, too. There’s a gambling boat that circles the island.”

“But,” Aang pipes up, because Spirits, obviously what this conversation needs is more people for Zuko to set himself against. “Isn’t taking from the house the same as stealing? Even if you gave the merchants something, you didn’t give them something that was yours.”

Zuko snorts. “Hardly.”

Sokka interrupts before Zuko feels goaded into biting something out that he’ll really regret, or revealing things he clearly doesn’t feel ready to talk about quite yet even though he brought them here. “Let’s just…get dinner going.”

Katara gives him a surprised look, and Sokka is aware that he's usually the first one to shout out about someone blowing their cover. “But—"

“Returning the food at this point would stand out more,” Sokka points out, which makes Katara settle back even if Aang looks distinctly dissatisfied. “So…let’s just use it.” He glances around, at Zuko’s ongoing tension and everyone else’s various stages of discomfort. “We can pick this back up in the morning,” he suggests reluctantly. “We’re going to need to resupply again soon enough.”

Zuko keeps his head down other than to offer the barest nod, avoiding everyone’s eyes and continuing to sort out the supplies as the others acquiesce. Sokka watches him out of the corner of his eye, going back to feeding driftwood into the fire and wondering if literally anywhere else might have been a better place to go to ground than what Sokka is fairly sure is the literal shadow of Zuko’s past.

&#45;-

Sokka’s suspicions are confirmed the minute they push the creaky, slightly off-kilter doors open the next morning to walk into a dusty, sun-filled entry and Sokka comes face to face with a portrait of a man who *has* to be related to Zuko. The portrait is sun-faded and weather-beaten, framed by a tattered velvet curtain, but Sokka can still see a gentler, more worn version of Azula in the woman painted at the man’s side, and Sokka doesn’t know if he’s more disconcerted by that or by the fact that apparently, he’s intimately familiar with the sharp line of the Fire Lord’s cheekbones.

The others tumble in, oohing and ahhing over the tapestries and the wall hangings and ornate architecture, and Zuko comes up to Sokka’s side, staring at the painting with white-pressed lips, utterly immobile. Sokka holds his breath, waiting to see what Zuko will do and barely controlling an audible noise of relief when Zuko finally blows a hard breath between his teeth and twitches one of the curtains off its hook, the fabric sweeping in a puff of dust to cover the man’s half of the portrait.

“We can go back outside,” Sokka suggests when Zuko just continues to stare moodily at his mother. Sokka’s itching with curiosity about this place, but he’s itching more with the need to do something to soothe the tension from Zuko’s shoulders.

“It’s fine,” Zuko says, tight and very clearly not fine in the least. But the option is out there, and Zuko turns away from it and toward the interior, leading the way down the central hallway off the atrium.

They walk past sitting rooms and receiving rooms and parlors, and Sokka quickly runs out of names for all the different kinds of rooms by the time Zuko finally strides into a space full of dusty chairs and scattered knickknacks and sunlight—so one that looks exactly like all the others, as far as Sokka can tell. Except Zuko goes right up to the wall to shoulder open a section of paneling that Sokka doesn’t even realize is a door until it’s opening to lead them out into a broad courtyard, flanked on all sides by the wings of the house and with none of the vegetation fighting through the paving stones that Sokka would have expected.

“This is a good place for firebending training,” Zuko says, arms crossed, the first words since they left the entryway and said more to the sky than anyone in particular as he tilts his face toward the sun. Spirits, Sokka really wishes the others weren’t here right now. He wants to pull Zuko into a hug so bad his arms are twitching with it, and he knows that Zuko won’t accept it as long as he's in this mood unless they’re alone.

Aang takes a deep, purposeful, firebending-y breath, turning around the space and then imitating Zuko to tip his face toward the sun. “This is great,” he says, so full of enthusiasm that Sokka almost misses the quick flash of worried gray eyes in Zuko’s direction.

“The walls are all faced in stone,” Zuko offers after a beat, shoulders relaxing a fraction. Or maybe it’s just the wind pulling at his clothes. “And the roof is lacquered for fire resistance.” “Fancy, fancy,” Suki murmurs, eyeing the roofline with interest.

Zuko gives what Sokka is coming to think of as his I-don’t-know-how-I’m-supposed-to-take-that shrug. “It’s a standard part of most noble homes, even if they don’t have a bending bloodline.”

“So this is a standard Fire Nation aristocrat’s home?” Suki asks, tapping the smooth stretch of stone along the wall. Sokka wonders how they made this look all one piece without earthbenders.

“I guess.”

Suki traces her finger along a mark that might be the stone’s natural variation, or weather, or ash. “Did this one have a bending bloodline?”

Zuko makes another one of those little hisses between his teeth before biting out a sharp, “Yes,” and Sokka gives her a warning look, trying to glare her into shutting the fuck up right now when she clearly already knows the answers.

Suki subsides, flicking Sokka a quick, opaque look that might be an apology, and Zuko fractionally relaxes when no more questions come, tipping his face back up to the sky again. Which maybe is the real reason he’s relaxing, as Sokka watches Zuko somehow shift without ever seeming to move to be fully facing the sun.

The time in the sun—or maybe the lack of needing to think, or the other’s upbeat chatter— does enough that when Toph suggests more exploring, Zuko doesn’t protest. He just shrugs, more of an I’m-resigned-to-whatever-comes shrug, with a bit of his I’m-humoring-this-because-it’s-not-worth-talking-you-out-of-it. Which isn’t a bad mix considering where Zuko's head was last night, even if Sokka would really like to see something better than ‘not as bad as it could be.’

Except Zuko pauses as the others begin to move back inside, glancing back for Sokka and tilting his head in what looks like invitation. So maybe, despite Zuko's tension, it's not quite as bad as it seems.

&#45;-

Sokka can’t quite pin down his weird hesitance as they move through the formal rooms. He’s definitely feeling Zuko’s mood, but he isn’t *hesitant* about it. And it’s not being in a Fire Nation home, because he's mostly just cuious about that, or even the oddness of moving through a space that manages to feel simultaneously totally abandoned and totally put together, with all the precise arrangements of furniture and vases full of long-dead flowers and statues still best-positioned to catch the sunlight.

No, Sokka eventually realizes. It’s not any of that—it’s the fact that Sokka can’t manage to picture Zuko in any of these rooms, even knowing that he used to be in them. Just like Sokka’s struggled so many times to picture Zuko with him in Water Tribe gatherings, or on Appa’s back, or anywhere outside of a teashop in Ba Sing Se, and isn't this space supposed to be Zuko's? Shouldn't it be easier than anything to imagine him here?

It does become a bit easier as they move into rooms that have clearly been touched since they were last left, where furniture has been toppled or smashed, curtains torn, windows broken in, knickknacks broken and scattered. Sokak isn’t quite sure what that says about his mental conception of Zuko, except that Zuko certainly seems more comfortable here, too, finally sifting through the detritus and turning pieces in his hands and doing more than staring with a familiar blank scowl on his face that Sokka hasn't seen in months.

A sudden “*Oh,”* has Sokka glancing up from where he’s crouched next to Zuko, watching him poke at the remains of some kind of ornate, carved box

“What,” Toph asks, testy, stamping a foot on the wood flooring and scowling when none of the others continue moving or reply. “*What?”*

“There’s a painting,” Aang finally says, and Zuko makes a little grunt of realization in the back of his throat.

“Of *what*,” Toph huffs.

Katara shifts, glancing around the room in clear, sudden discomfort. “Zuko.”

“Why do you need him?” Toph grumbles. “You don’t know what it is? Then why are you all —”

“No,” Aang cuts in quietly. “It’s a picture of Zuko. And…”

“Azula,” Zuko supplies, still sifting through the shards on the floor. Sokka doesn’t trust *that* disinterested tone.

“…And?” Aang tentatively asks again, grabbing Sokka's attention.

“Lu Ten,” Zuko says, finally rising to his feet and absently extending a hand to help Sokka up, which is nice and sweet and makes Sokka's heart flip over a little, even if Sokka thinks he’s the one that should be helping Zuko right now. “My cousin. He’s dead,” Zuko adds after a moment.

“Well shit,” Toph finally mutters, breaking the sharp silence. “You could have told us it was *your* house, Zuko.”

Zuko frowns at her. “...Whose did you think it was?”

Toph scowls. “Still.”

“Besides, it’s not mine,” Zuko shrugs, like his face isn’t on a painting on the fucking wall. “It’s the Crown’s.”

“That feels like a technicality,” Suki mutters.

Zuko shrugs again, already moving on to the next room, and Sokka gives the painting one last quick glance—he can barely see it, between the sun fading and size and length of the room—before following after, wondering if the distinction Zuko just made between what’s his and what’s the royal family’s—or the Crown’s? Is there a difference—is a lot more significant than Zuko’s let’s-just-all-move-on-from-this shrug implies.

&#45;-

The others explore with new eyes after that, and as they all move more and more into what would have been the family’s private quarters, it becomes easier and easier for Sokka to see Zuko in these spaces. He isn’t entirely sure, still, what a young Zuko was like, but Sokka thinks he can build out a shape of him, one that he recognizes, in the scuffs on the walls at a child’s height and the singed edges to the doorframes, in the slowly-collapsing piles of moldering scrolls and the chipped collection of cheap-looking theater masks.

They disperse more and more as they explore, Katara lingering over the furniture and Suki over the artwork, Sokka gravitating toward the portraits, staring at people he doesn’t know and what has to be a young Iroh until finally, he finds what he didn’t realize he was after until he has it in his hands—a little picture of Zuko alone, face serious and stiffly formal and eyes big and bright. Sokka wonders if the impression of wide-eyed innocence is just because of Zuko’s youth, or from the lack of scar settling an ever-present scowl over his face.

“How old were you in this?” Sokka asks, gently blowing dust off the small painting.

Zuko drifts over, peeking over his shoulder. “Five? Six?”

“It’s cute,” Sokka says, tilting the painting into light and gentle tracing the glint of gold in Zuko's hair, the layers and layers of robes.

“It was itchy," Zuko huffs, thoroughly unimpressed.

“I didn’t even know they could make fancy boots that small,” Sokka muses, earning himself a breath of laughter.

“That thing took days,” Zuko grumbles, sounding like the memory of it still makes him cranky.

“Worth it,” Sokka says, making a show of admiring the little painting. “Because here you are now, memorialized for everyone to see you as a little prince.”

A sudden snort from the hallway that sounds suspiciously like Suki, and then Toph drawls something that sounds suspiciously like it's about Zuko's little prince and Katara lets out a squawk from down the hall and Sokka is going to do everything in his power to never find out what she said.

“I wasn’t much of a prince back then,” Zuko mutters, pointedly turning back to Sokka and clearly also deciding not to enter that conversation as Toph wanders off again, cackling.

Sokka valiantly tries to help him get things back on track. “Didn’t you grow up with all the training and etiquette and whatnot?” Toph certainly did. Sokka can see it in flashes even when she’s glorying in tossing it all aside, and Zuko isn’t exactly consciously trying to abandon it.

“It wasn’t as much of a focus then,” Zuko says, staring at the painting. “It isn’t really as big of a deal when you aren’t that close to the succession. Back then it was Uncle, and then Lu Ten, and then it would be his children and he wasn’t all that far off from getting married, really.”

Sokka tries to envision a world in which Zuko was just, what—a court functionary? A minor political figure? “What would you have been then, when you grew up?”

“A general, maybe. Or an ambassador. Whatever the Fire Nation needed.”

That, at least, sounds like it stayed the same. “Do you ever think about it?”

“Of what,” Zuko snorts. “What would have happened if Lu Ten hadn’t died and Uncle took Ba Sing Se, returning home in triumph as Grandfather continued to reign until he peacefully handed the crown to Fire Lord Iroh, with my father becoming some minor court lackey and my mother still alive to see me and Azula growing up to be the perfect age for political marriages that would solidify Fire Nation rule and the new peace without tainting the line of succession?”

Sokka stares.

“No,” Zuko says dryly. “I don’t think about it much.”

O…kay. “How old were you when he died, again,” Sokka asks, wondering if so much could really hinge on one person’s death or survival.

“Ten.”

Ten is the age, apparently, for worlds getting turned upside down. “That must have been hard,” Sokka finally says. “Grieving and needing to learn a new role at the same time.” By the time Sokka realized he needed to do both, the grief had become something more manageable, something duller and achier that you could breathe throughif you had to.

“Like you wouldn’t believe,” Zuko agrees with a sigh, an admission Sokka doesn’t think he would have gotten even a few weeks ago. “I just…had to cram it all in. What to say and who to say it to and what you couldn’t do and…Azula got it so *easily*, but I was the one who *had* to get it right, so I…”

“Played a role?” Sokka suggests, thinking of that pile of theater masks.

“Except someone gives you a script for that,” Zuko grumbles.

“Oh, you never got that one?” Sokka says, nudging Zuko and letting his tone fill with teasing, trying to pull Zuko out of the thoughts tightening his face before he starts brooding. “Because you certainly could have been following one for ‘Prince in Exile’ when we first met.”

Zuko is conspicuously silent.

“…Zuko,” Sokka says, leaning back to search his expression, caught between delight and disbelief. “No. You weren’t. You weren’t, were you?”

“Well it’s not like anyone *tells* you how to do it,” Zuko grumbles, tart. “And anyone and their mother used to be able to declare themselves a king in the Earth Kingdom, so there are plenty of plays about it.”

“*Zuko*,” Sokka laughs, grinning as Zuko finally cracks enough to roll his eyes and then huff out a laugh along with him. “What did you expect, a rule book?”

Azula’s ‘new firebender finally registers water’s ability to put out flame’ phase had been… memorable.

“Good thing you know how to climb,” Sokka finally says.

“We both do,” Zuko agrees. Azula had made sure of it, the rest of the summer. Sometimes Zuko thinks that’s one of the only reasons Azula let Ty Lee stick around long enough to decide she actually wanted to keep her.

“When was the last time you were here with her?”

Zuko sighs. “A few months ago. Before the eclipse.” He can feel Sokka go still with what he assumes is surprise behind him. “They wanted to get us out of Caldera, I think.”

“Why?”

“Just…politics. Planning.” Zuko ended up a little too distracted to really care much about the why of it, after.

Sokka grunts, wiggling a little to settle Zuko more firmly underneath his chin. “You didn’t stay here, though. When you were back.”

“No.” Zuko doesn’t think passing out on the beach counts. “We did come by, though.”

“Reliving some memories?”

Zuko snorts. “We needed some shit to light on fire.”

Sokka’s chest shakes at his back with a little laugh. “You burned that painting in the bonfire?”

“Like you didn’t already know that,” Zuko says, rolling his eyes, leaning into it when Sokka presses a smile against his hair.

“Guessing and knowing are different things.”

Zuko hums in agreement, closing his eyes as the sun angles in a new direction off the waves, feeling…oddly lighter, for having shared a little.

“There was lots of alcohol, too,” Sokka says after a moment, giving Zuko a light nudge with his chin.

“We mixed it up a bit on the old ‘build a sandcastle and wreck it’ game. Though,” he muses, “we did wreck someone’s actual house. It was much more fun.”

Zuko grins at Sokka’s noises of shocked disbelief, laughing as Sokka nudges him with increasing urgency, going, “Zuko, you’re joking, right? Zuko? *Zuko*?”

## Chapter 26: Casting Stones

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings for brief discussion of canon-typical homophobia

### Text

Zuko knew he never should have let Suki and Sokka go into the market, no matter how persuasive they were about the benefits of sending them so Zuko could focus on training with Aang. Even loaded down with tradeable goods and strict instructions on prices and reasonably passable Fire Nation outfits that had Sokka raising his eyebrows at the amount of skin on display—Zuko had just shrugged, he can’t imagine fashions have changed all that much in a few months—Zuko should have never let anyone go without him along too.

Because Suki and Sokka come back with all the supplies they were supposed to get, at exactly the prices they were supposed to get them for. And a flyer.

“The Ember Island Players,” Katara reads out.

Zuko cringes so hard the campfire nearly goes out.

“What is it?” Aang asks, glancing with interest between Zuko and nearly-dead fire. “Some local game?”

“It’s *theater*,” Sokka enthuses, with far more eagerness than Zuko ever thought Sokka would have for the topic.

“It’s hot garbage,” Zuko grumbles, his inner flame as he relights the campfire rather too cheerful for how sulky he wants it to be.

“The flyers were everything,” Suki explains. “Everyone seemed really excited.”

“Whatever,” Toph says, with the level of dismissiveness the Ember Island Players deserve. “Who wants to go to a boring show anyway?”

Suki grins and turns the flyer around. “Not even a show about us?”

“The Boy in the Iceberg,” Katara reads, barely finishing the words before Sokka snatches the flyer out of her hands.

“A tale of heroism, action, adventure, and romance,” he proclaims, clearly striving for something grand.

“When's the show?” Toph demands. “We can make time.”

“We have a training schedule,” Zuko protests. Which doesn’t even grab *Sokka’s* attention, which just—ugh. To be ignored for the *Ember Island Players*. To have Sokka interested in theater and have it be the *Ember Island Players.*

“It could be fun,” Katara is saying.

“It could be great,” Aang enthuses.

“It *will* be trash,” Zuko grumbles, glaring at the fire. Why is it burning so fucking *merrily*.

“We could all use a break,” Katara adds, putting on a serious face. “Overwork, you know. Healers warn about it.”

Zuko transfers his glare up as Aang makes a show of rubbing at his aching back and drooping as much as he can while still bouncing with excitement. “We don’t have time to take leisure breaks,” Zuko grits out. Not so close to the Comet, and when did *he* become a voice of reason. He eyes Sokka, suspicious.

“You and Sokka took a leisure break last night,” Toph point out, and Zuko just sighs as Katara smacks Toph in the arm with a hissed, *“We said we weren’t going to talk about that!”*

“My buddy,” Sokka says, clapping Zuko on the shoulder and waiting until he reluctantly looks up. “My dude. My man. Consider the benefits of a night of relaxation for the next day’s training. Consider—a night of *theater.*” He grins, open and excited. “That’s your favorite, right?”

…Oh.

Zuko tries to formulate a reply, to play it cool in front of the others, to point out that the Ember Island Players hardly count as theater. But he’s too caught up in all those ‘my’s, too bowled over by the fact that Sokka’s trying to make this happen for *him.* Too stuck on Sokka seeing the poster and thinking of Zuko, thinking that Zuko would *like* it.

And Sokka looks so happy and eager as he convinces the others, and maybe a little bit anxious at Zuko’s ongoing silence, and, well—

Looks like they’re going to see a play tonight.

&#45;-

“These seats suck,” Toph mutters, kicking her feet pointedly against the wooden balcony railing. “I’m not going to be able to see anything from up here.”

“We’ll tell you what’s going on,” Katara assures her.

Zuko snorts. “You don’t want to hear it anyway. The Ember Island Players ruin everything they put on.”

“Come on,” Sokka says, clearly amused. “How can they ruin something that is—” He angles the playbill toward the light. “’A true accounting based wholly and entirely on the tales of the people who were actually there’?”

Zuko eyes him sidelong. “You’ll see.” Sokka might think Zuko is being prissy with his standards. Sokka has never had to listen to the Ember Island Players butcher the entire *Phoenix and the Dragon* trilogy into one three-act performance.

“I think it will be great to see ourselves on stage,” Aang says, like if he says it firmly enough Zuko will be convinced.

“And there are snacks,” Sokka says with a pointed nudge. “So.”

Zuko rolls his eyes but obligingly passes out the packets of fire flakes he purchased outside the theater, settling back down between Sokka and Katara and suddenly hyperconscious as the lights begin to dim of the hard seat arm between them and the warmth of Sokka’s leg brushing against his own.

He can at least enjoy this, he tells himself, before the first act starts and his night is ruined by overwrought, poorly plotted thematic development. And Zuko does enjoy the sound of Sokka humming happily beside him. The chorus of coughs from Aang, Katara, and Suki, significantly less so. There’s a rather conspicuous lack of spice tolerance between the three of them for them to be eating in public…

“Really, guys,” Toph says, chomping delightedly. “It’s like you’ve never had fire peppers before.”

Suki gasps for air, wiping tears from her eyes. “They’re a bit rich for Kyoshi Island to trade for.”

“Hm,” Toph allows before shrugging and tossing back the rest of her fire flakes. “Well if you don’t want yours, pass them over.”

Sokka makes a noise of outrage around his mouthful when Katara shoves her barely-eaten flakes over to Toph instead of him, only settling back when he finally notices that Zuko is silently laughing at him.

&#45;-

Sokka realizes things might not go exactly as expected right about when the play opens with on-stage Katara swanning dramatically over the edge of a boat, talking about needing a man in her life to give her purpose. On-stage Aang appears—

Real-life Aang hisses, “They have me as a *girl?*”

“Something wrong with being a girl,” Suki asks with dangerous sweetness.

&#45;-and stage-Katara looks him up and down. “Or a boy will do,” she chirps, while stage-Sokka reels in a fishing line to reveal—“Or a sandwich!”

“Why would I fish for a sandwich,” Sokka frowns as the audience breaks into laughter. “That doesn’t even look like a fish sandwich.”

“Why do I look like a middle-aged woman,” Katara whispers, eyes already narrowed on the stage as stage-Katara cheers along as Aang promptly blows up a ship, the audience laughing again at his exaggerated “Oops!”

“…Oh,” Zuko suddenly says behind him, sliding down a few inches in his seat. “Fuck.”

“What,” Sokka presses, but Zuko just gives him a sideways look.

“You’ll see.”

Well that doesn't sound fucking ominuous.

“At least they gave Sokka a receding hairline if I have to be an old lady,” Katara grumbles, and Sokka can’t help his gasp of outrage, or the protective hands he places on his perfectly full head of hair.

&#45;-

Sokka sets aside the whole hair issue once the first act gets rolling and he realizes that even if they’ve done him a grave injustice, his character has all the best jokes. And he can’t help laughing at stage-Aang’s continued tagline of “Oops!” as he cheerfully upends markets, wrecks cabbage carts, sinks more ships, and generally brings mischief and chaos in his wake.

Sokka is leaning forward to get the best view, Katara reluctantly engaged even though she keeps sniffing in annoyance whenever her character speaks, and if Aang is still grumbling and muttering on Toph’s far side it’s at least quiet enough not to be too distracting.

Zuko, though, stays sitting back, which Sokka didn’t entirely expect—he thought Zuko was into this whole theater thing, even if he seemed to be relentlessly critical of this particular troupe. But Zuko was also relentlessly critical of an amateur puppet theater production, and nearly every play Iroh ever mentioned to him. Sokka figured relentless criticism was just what Zuko liked about the whole thing.

But Zuko just somehow seems to sit straigther and straighter in his seat whenever his character is on stage: talking about his honor, forgetting to eat because something reminded him of his honor, wandering into traps looking for his honor, barely able to bend because he can’t stop talking about his honor.

Which, sure, is a bit *much,* but Sokka can’t contain a fit of giggles when stage-Zuko walks off a dock while searching for his honor in the clouds, the actual Zuko next to him giving his leg a sharp, pointed smack. Zuko scowls at Sokka, looking embarrassed and annoyed and all-around prickly, and Sokka can’t help thinking it’s a cute look on him.

“You know I’m a fan of your single-minded focus,” Sokka whispers, nudging Zuko back with a smile, silently encouraging him to lighten up when he just huffs and goes a little pink in response, because, well—it might be a bit of a caricature, but it’s not like it’s entirely made up. Right?

&#45;-

Sokka’s on board with *The Boy in the Iceberg* right up until the moment Jet comes on stage— way taller than he actually was, broad-shouldered and stout and not looking much of anything like the actual Jet except for the way the actor somehow manages to ooze a seductive magnetism that has stage-Katara swooning. And then stage-Sokka.

Sokka goes still—conspicuously still, fuck, fuck—as Katara stiffens on Zuko’s other side. Stage-Jet settles between the siblings, nibbling on one neck, then the other, feeling up both as the audience oohs and whoops.

“I *am* the oldest,” stage-Sokka says, pulling a grinning, slouching Jet toward him.

“Well, *I’m* the smartest,” stage-Katara pronounces, pulling Jet right into her breasts.

“Remember,” stage-Aang chirps, fists planted on his--her?--hips. “Balance is all about sharing!”

“And I care about balance very much,” stage-Sokka shouts before grabbing Jet back and hauling him into a smacking kiss. Shit.

The audience roars in surprised, scandalized delight and Sokka slides down a telling inch or two in his seat, pointedly looking forward and aware of Katara doing…the exact same thing on Zuko’s other side. Fuck.

“…Ah,” Zuko says between them, like he’s just had a quiet little revelation.

&#45;-

Sokka perks up, a little hopeful for the distracting powers of theater when stage-Aang swoons over the mysterious, seductive, powerful Blue Spirit in one scene, and stage-Zuko lets stage-Sokka escape in the very next because he started a monologue on his honor and forgot to lock the prison door.

“Should I be worried about the competition?” Sokka whispers, earning himself an elbow to the side. “So distracted you couldn’t even lock the door.”

“Maybe I thought my ‘strong and mighty, yet shockingly tender and corporeal arms’ would be enough to keep you,” Zuko says back, which…would have been a fair assumption.

&#45;-

“I love you,” stage-Sokka proclaims as he stares longingly up at Yue as she goes off to do ‘moon business,’ “More than I love a meat sandwich!”

Sokka cringes from the declaration, somehow managing to feel simultaneously embarrassed and vaguely guilty as Zuko glances over at him. “Should *I* be worried,” Zuko whispers, raising an eyebrow as stage-Sokka cracks a sandwich-eating joke that has the adults in the audience hooting and the real Sokka flushing.

“I don’t even *like* sandwiches that much,” he grumbles. The South isn’t exactly full of bread.

Zuko snorts softly. “Don’t worry,” he says, dry, “I know you hold me and food in equally high regard.” Sokka’s mouth works in silence. “No need for a declaration,” Zuko adds primly.

&#45;-

Sokka has his first true moment of thinking he maybe doesn’t understand Fire Nation theater when the audience hoots and cheers as the first act comes to a dramatic close with a Spirit-possessed Aang stomping through a model of Agna Qe’la, crushing houses with a trademark “Oops,” before using a doll version of Zhao as a club to bash every Fire Nation ships bobbing in the harbor, the curtain swinging closed on the implication of ongoing destruction as stage-Aang pronounces that he’s here to save the day.

“I…” Sokka says into the stunned silence blanketing their little balcony as the lights come back on, excited chatter rising from below as the smiling audience streams toward concessions. “What?”

Zuko grunts, arms crossed over his chest, his silence significantly more critical than stunned as he eyes the stage. “Zhao was a fuck up who gambled and failed,” Zuko says, as if *that’s* what has everyone else dumbstruck. “They gave him better than I expected.”

&#45;-

“But was it really—”

“Aang, they’re exaggerating. This whole play is exaggerating.”

“But Katara, they’re exaggerating *truths*. Right? What is that's actually how they see me?”

Sokka opens his mouth to hop in and immediately slams it shut again when Katara pins him with a quick glare over Aang’s shoulder, shaking her head sharply before refocusing on Aang.

“You know the Ocean used you as a conduit for its anger,” Katara says carefully as Sokka eases away. He’ll trust her judgment that more voices aren’t what’s needed in that conversation right now. “And you know the Fire Nation fleet was sunk.”

“I know that, Zuko and I talked about that, but—”

“What do you remember? Of what happened?”

Sokka slips around the corner as their voices fade behind him, wondering if not forcing Aang to talk this out sooner was really the right choice. Sokka couldn’t imagine finding the words after the North when everything felt so fragile and stretched thin, and then in the hectic flight from Azula and the terrifying search for Appa there had never seemed to be the time. But maybe he and Katara were just kidding themselves that there ever *would* be a good time for it.

Just like there never seemed to be a good time to mention Jet, which Sokka *wants* to say doesn't even matter. But Katara's eyes had been sharp even in her focus on Aang, and  
now Sokka’s practically sneaking away—even if Katara sent him away—like avoiding this is important, like a few more moments of not needing to meet her eyes and confirm that yes, they both did in fact make out with Jet is really going to make a difference, like it's something *he* cares abotu instead of just something *Katara* might care about, and—fuck.

Toph and Suki are on the hunt for more food, but Zuko is easy enough to spot in the crowd, pausing for Sokka to catch up before peeling off into a side hallway. And Zuko knows the playhouse quite well for someone who professes to hate it, wordlessly bringing them up to one of the sparser little balconies off the back of the top floor, away from the concessions and souvenir vendors. It’s a little run-down and mostly unlit and the perfect place for hiding, which is…exactly what Sokka wants right now, actually.

“So,” Zuko says, hopping up to sit on the railing. “Still think they can’t ruin it?”

Sokka finds a spot to lean next to him. “The jokes are solid and the plot is decent,” he finally says, lips quirking when Zuko snorts. “But reality kind of sucks, sometimes.” One corner of his mind is already working on what he’s going to say when Aang comes to him seeking to confirm that yes, the North was really that bad. Though maybe Aang will go to Zuko. It sounds like they already talked about it. Maybe Katara is the confirmation...

“No argument,” Zuko shrugs. “It’s not the best Uluzon style I’ve ever seen. The costuming is a bit too subtle, but…”

Sokka…has no idea what Zuko is talking about, but he patiently listens as Zuko works through his first act criticisms of the presentation, pacing, and prop departments, finally offering some tepid approval for the play’s effective use of satire within the constraints of the given plot structure, whatever that means.

“Why did the audience react so strongly when I kissed Jet,” Sokka wonders when Zuko’s words finally run dry. This play seems shockingly suggestive for an audience full of children, but seemingly the one thing Zuko didn’t find to criticize was the raunchiness.

Zuko purses his lips. “Comedic theater in the Fire Nation style generally involves a degree of interaction with the audience. Uluzon style is more scripted in that sense, but the tradition is thought to have originated from—”

“No,” Sokka interrupts. “I mean…everyone, you know, whistled and stuff during the whole play, sure. But they did it more in that scene?” Maybe Sokka is just imagining that...

“Oh,” Zuko says, shrugging. “Because it’s not legal.”

Sokka blinks. “What?"

"It's not legal," Zuko repeats, frowning like he's thinking about the set design again, which— what?

"With…someone from the Earth Kingdom?” Except that doesn’t make sense, because the Colonies—

Zuko snorts, shaking his head. “The Colonies would be in trouble, then.”

Sokka stares at Zuko’s nonchalance, distantly feeling the blunt end of a weather worn spinter as his fingers tighten against the railing. Sokka *has* to be misunderstanding, with Zuko acting so casually, because…Sokka and Zuko always react with the same level of concern to the things in their lives. Fuck. “So…what do you mean?”
