“Yeah,” Zuko says, sounding like he’s reminding someone that the sun rises in the morning and sets at night. “They start the summer.”

“When,” Sokka presses, waving an apology when Zuko startles at his sudden urgency. "Sorry, but—when?"

“When what?” Zuko asks, backing away a half step and glancing between Sokka and Aang like whatever they have might be catching.

“When do the monsoons come,” Sokka repeats, struggling to keep his voice even. “They start the summer?” Zuko nods again. “When does that happen?”

“May,” Zuko says, openly confused, and Aang makes a strangled noise that might be a laugh under some other circumstance, and Sokka…Sokka wants to go right there with him. “What’s going on?” Zuko asks, somewhere between confused and worried and frustrated. “Why are you both freaking out? Monsoon season hasn’t started yet, and it seems like it's going to be mild this year anyway.”

Aang unfolds upright, barely reacting when both Sokka and Zuko flinch from the sudden motion. “Monsoon season starts the summer in the Fire Nation, right?”

Zuko gives him a sideways look. “I…just said that.”

“Summer for the Southern Water Tribe and the Earth Kingdom starts at the end of June,” Sokka says faintly, vaguely surprised he can get the words out when he’s feeling this aburptly numb.

“And the Air Nomads,” Aang says, briefly closing his eyes.

“…Okay?” Zuko looks to Sokka for some kind of explanation, glancing back down the beach like maybe he thinks he needs to bring the others.

“I thought we had time,” Aang says, low and dull, and then again, “I thought we had *time*,” repeating it again, voice going more and more upset and frantic with each repetition.

“We still might,” Sokka cuts in, trying to head off whatever is happening with Aang, because Zuko's already looking like he’s on the verge of bolting for more help and Sokka's feeling pretty upset and frantic himself and they all just—need to stay calm. “We don’t know, right? It’s not—we don’t know for sure, it’s just an idea, it could—”

Aang is shaking his head, sharp, hard enough that he nearly dislodges Momo. “*Roku* told us, he said 'by the time summer comes again.'”

“Fuck. *Fuck*.” *By* the time summer comes again, and if that means May in the Fire Nation…

“Guys, what’s going on?” Zuko asks, sharp and short enough to crack through the shell of numbness that wants to settle over Sokka.

“The Comet comes by summer,” Sokka begins, pulling up short when Zuko just huffs.

“Yeah,” Zuko says, looking at him like…that should be obvious?

“We didn’t—we thought we still had two months,” Sokka says slowly, carefully, watching Zuko go suddenly motionless with understanding.

“…What?”

“But if Roku is Fire Nation and the Fire Nation summer starts in May then maybe it’s actually…weeks.”

“*A* week,” Aang says, dropping his face back into his hands.

Zuko just stares. “…You guys don’t know the date of when Sozin’s Comet comes?”

&#45;-

“How did none of you know!”

“How did *you* know!” Katara sputters back, so frazzled she’s wringing water out of her hair by hand, trying to soothe Aang at the same time and accomplishing neither.

“Astronomy?” Zuko says, gaping at the others and responding about as much as Aang to the soothing Sokka is trying to do, which…probably says just as much about Sokka’s current state of mind as about Zuko’s. “General knowledge of one of the most significant events of our fucking lifetime? You knew when the eclipse was happening down to the second! You’re all—into the moon and stars! You seemed pretty fucking good with your celestial timing!”

“We were making sandcastles yesterday,” Sokka says, unable to stop the realization from falling out. “We just spent the morning wave whomping.” Spirits, all that *time*, all the messing around they’ve been doing, all of them failing to stick to a schedule Sokka didn’t even know fucking needed to *exist*.

“I thought it was some kind of earthbender zen thing,” Zuko says, folding his arms over his chest but leaning fractionally into Sokka’s hand against his lower back, his expression caught someplace between distraction and a more familiar sharp-edged scowl. “I’ve never done a big planned mission with you before, I thought you just—I thought you were just trying to be calm!”

“What’s earthbender zen,” Sokka asks after a beat, because he could…really use some of that right now. Probably they all could. Months and months—fucking *years,* for Aang— potentially all for nothing because of a cultural misunderstanding over the *seasons*?

"It’s...probably more applicable to combat situations,” Toph says. "It's about neutral—" She pauses, considering. "You know what? Not relevant. I'll tell you later."

“Right," Sokka says faintly. "Okay."

“I thought—I thought you guys had a process,” Zuko says, nearly pleading, and Sokka wants to tug Zuko into his arms right now—for himself as much as for Zuko—but he can tell Zuko isn’t in a place where he can handle being touched like that right now, not in front of the others. “I was trusting the process!”

“Okay,” Sokka says, taking a huge breath, then another, reaching for something that feels disturbingly like his battle calm. Zuko isn't the only one getting rattled, and Sokka can at least try to calm the situation for all of them. “Okay. We can—we can deal with this. We can—let’s just make a plan. That’s…a good place to start.” Sokka…*really* needs a fucking plan right now.

Aang makes a noise somewhere between one of those awful laughs and a pure breakdown. “Do we even have time for that?”

“Everything starts with a plan,” Sokka says, firm, determined, forcing his shoulders down and his fists to unclench and his spine to straighten and feeling like every single moment of faking it until he’s made it in his life is coming down to this. “Now. Where’s the paper?”

“In your bag,” Katara says, turning toward their packs and spinning back around when Toph snaps out a hand and hauls her back toward Aang, which…is probably a good idea right now.

“I’ll get it,” Toph says, stomping up the beach, sand shooting out around her feet with more than just the force of her steps.

“Alright,” Sokka says, taking a deep breath and shoving aside all the clamoring thoughts about anything other than what they’re going to do next, pressing his hand to Zuko’s back a bit tighter and nearly sagging when Zuko reaches up after a moment to anchor onto his shoulder. “Okay. Let’s just—start with saying everything we know.”

&#45;-

As plans go, Zuko isn’t sure that the Avatar’s shaky confidence is really getting built up by having Aang go again and again against a dummy Fire Lord. Sure, Aang’s bending looks crisp, his transitions between elements nearly seamless. But again and again, their pacifist Air Nomad can’t seem to bring himself to smash their dummy villain’s melon head.

Zuko wants to light that fucking melon on fire.

Zuko doesn’t know if he’s making everything worse by not saying something—of fucking course *not* saying something would be the problem, after so many lessons in learning to keep his mouth shut—just like he has no idea if he’s trusting the process not enough or too much right now. So he’s just…doing his best not to let his panic rise enough to become visible, as Toph tries to couch Aang through how to break a melon.

“You just—see? Just—firm strike. Like this.” Toph throws out a basic punch, her hand smashing out the other side of the fruit. “See? Now you try.” Sokka obligingly slaps a fresh melon onto the dummy and gathers up the fallen pieces, chasing Momo away from the bits that fall rind-side down. Sokka’s going to offer him a piece of melon soon. Zuko can tell. Sokka knows he’s panicking, even if no one else does.

Aang takes a deep breath, determination settling over his face as he sets his feet and sinks into his stance, muscles coiling, eyes narrowing with focus as he exhales hard and throws his punch and—goes wide, technique textbook perfect.

“…I think,” Sokka mumbles around a mouthful of melon, eyeing Aang’s frozen form. “That it’s more about hitting him *in* the face.”

“Guys, I don’t know,” Aang says, arm swinging down as he slumps forward, legs still solidly rooted.

“Let me rephrase,” Toph offers. “It *is* about hitting him in the face.”

“I just—it doesn’t feel *right*,” Aang says, and Zuko feels the trickle of dread creep slither the back of his neck that he’s been trying to hold off ever since the beach, the one he’s been trying to tell himself he doesn’t know for sure he needs to feel.

“I mean,” Sokka tugs at his wolf tail. “You did miss. So.”

“No, I mean—the punching at all!”

“I guess it’s a bit melodramatic,” Toph allows. “Bending his face in works too.”

Zuko nearly drops his own face into his hands at that, not the least surprised when Aang steps back, almost mouthing along as the words spill out of Aang’s mouth. “No, the violence! I’m an Air Nomad, my whole life I was taught that hurting another living thing was never the answer, and I just—I don’t see why it suddenly is now.”

“I don’t think he’s just going to sit down and talk it out with you, Aang,” Katara says gently.

“Maybe! You don’t know that!”

“I’m really sure he's not going to sit down and talk it out,” Zuko mutters to himself, and Sokka shoves a piece of melon into his hands—there it is—before saying, louder, “I think we’ve got a pretty good idea, Aang.”

“Maybe he just needs time,” Aang suggests, and for a brief moment, Zuko wonders if the Avatar has dissociated from the situation so hard that he’s now referring to himself in the third person. “Maybe with time he’ll want to talk. Why does it need to be *now*?”

“…The Comet,” Zuko says, wondering how he needs to give this reminder. “Which is definitely coming. Soon. On a schedule.” That’s…how Zuko is given to understand astronomy works. Agni’s balls, maybe Katara should look Aang over.

“Yeah, but…does the Comet matter?”

Zuko stares, then rubs at his good ear, wondering if the…light breeze up here is somehow creating too much background noise, because he fundamentally doesn’t understand Aang’s question. He glances over at Sokka, his inner flame twisting in confusion see Sokka thinking hard, as if Aang made any bit of sense, which…what?

Enough of this trusting the process shit, Zuko decides as he breathes himself through a flare of panic. Zuko does *not* trust this process anymore. Not without understanding it.

“The Fire Nation conquered the Earth Kingdom already, when Omashu and Ba Sing Se both fell,” Aang is saying, tone reasonable. “So the war is already over, right? So what harm will waiting until after the Comet do? Don’t I have time to just…come around to it?” That last bit ends up sounding more than a little distressed and anxious, which is just perfect because that’s exactly what Zuko's feeling right now too.

“…You think,” Zuko says, slowly, carefully, precisely, Sokka snapping to attention in his periphery. “That Fire Lord Ozai. The grandson of Sozin. Arguably *not* next in line to Azulon’s throne, but sitting on it anyway. Would have the once-in-a-century power of the comet bearing his most well-known ancestor’s name at his disposal and is going to—what? Sit at home during it? Maybe play some pai sho? Brew a really nice pot of tea?”

The silence is resounding, except for the slow drip of juice from the rind still in Sokka’s hand.

“I just want to make sure I got that right,” Zuko adds, hearing the edge in his own voice, feeling his inner fire crawling under his skin.

“I mean,” Sokka finally says, frowning when Zuko’s eyes snap toward him and Zuko—shit, he needs to get himself under control, he’s just—Agni, he hasn’t felt his inner fire flaring and boiling like this in months, and it would be easier to rein it back if he knew who, exactly, he was most angry with. “When you put it in those terms, it does sound rather…”

“Naïve?” Zuko suggests, the words clawing up his throat and bursting free, smoke acrid on the back of his tongue. “Like wishful thinking? Like—” He manages to clamp his lips together before he says ‘like pacifist Air Nomad ostrich horse shit,’ shoving the piece of melon into his mouth to keep the words in, but Zuko thinks Sokka probably picks up the subtext anyway from his wince.

Fuck. Zuko is most angry at himself. For managing to bring his plan up to this point but never even thinking that he might have to account for this. For still keeping Azula's trust when she isn't even here, she wouldn't even *know*, to the point that he's...doing exactly what Sokka did in Ba Sing Se. Failing to give enough information for the others to even realize they need to talk about something. All his hard work, all the bridges he knowingly burned, all his determination to walk the path in front of him, all his talk of *partners,* and did he ever give Sokka the chance to be one with this?

Agni, he can't believe it's really going to come down to this, to the reality of the Avatar having day to get over being a a twelve-year-old pacifist, a fact that Zuko’s known since first escaped the *Wani* without killing a single one of his captors.

Stupid. Just…stupid, and willfully blind, and dangerously focused on only himself. This is why Azula always says to leave the plans to her.

“Well, if the Fire Lord isn’t going to do any of that,” Katara finally says. “Then what’s he going to do? Do we know for sure that it’s something awful, or are we just assuming?”

“Yes,” Zuko sighs, his inner fire twisting in his chest as he forces himself to look down all the things he thought were shored up and managed, the balance that finally seemed possible for his three most important things, and see that maybe they’ve all been about to fall this whole time.

“Because,” Katara continues, “Maybe he—”

“Yes, Katara,” Zuko cuts in, louder this time and hating the way her face freezes on the edge of something like hope. “I know for sure.”

“You know what the Fire Lord’s plan is?” Suki clarifies.

“I know what the Fire Nation’s plan is,” Zuko corrects.

“…Are we going to want to sit down for this?” Sokka asks, sounding weary and resigned in a way that Zuko…intensely sympathizes with.

Zuko startles when a pillar rises up behind him—behind everyone—at just the right height for sitting. “Tell us,” Toph orders, taking a pointed seat.

Zuko sets himself down and braces his boots against the rocky ground and does. He keeps his voice as neutral as possible, reaching for a clinical kind of distance even as he hugs his arms over his chest and wishes Sokka's seat were a bit closer to his. It’s easier to stare up at the sky than at anyone’s eyes as he tells them about the armies and the new airships and path they’ll take over the Earth Kingdom. Of the vision of an empire that will always know Agni’s touch, the light and flame of Agni cleansing the earth. When wielded by the right hands, of course.

Zuko is highly aware of Agni at his back as he lays it all out. He wants to reach for that connection, wants to take assurance in the ever-present tie and comfort of his inner flame in his chest but he just…can’t, right now, as he articulates exactly what the Fire Lord plans to do with that same power. He wants it to all just be…ravings, delusions, a bad dream, a test that Azula set for him that he’s failing over and over and over again. But he knows it’s real, as real as the fire in his veins.

“I tried to…I don’t know. Make it better,” Zuko finally says, low, frowning down at the ground. “There was a full Council meeting—” Sokka jerks a little, beside him. “—and they outright *asked*, and so I tried to point out the…cleanest path,” he finishes, wincing as he hears himself say it.

“Cleanest?” Katara frowns.

“Just…” Zuko doesn’t know if he can voice it, in front of an Air Nomad. “The least resistance.”

“And the least death and collateral damage,” Sokka says, understanding.

Zuko nods, sharply aware that the kind of calculus that lives in the back of his mind isn’t something all of them would even think of, let alone look to.

“And…instead they went for the maximal death and destruction option,” Suki says quietly.

Zuko can feel his lips twist into a humorless smile despite himself. “You could say that’s something of a signature of this Fire Lord’s reign.”

&#45;-

Zuko is a tight ball of barely contained…everything by the time dinner rolls around. Prickly and jagged and biting out sharp comments and Katara keeps shooting Sokka these significant glances, like he’s supposed to do something about it, and making meaningful jerks of her head and mouthing ‘do something’ when she thinks Zuko isn’t looking just in case Sokka’s too dense to miss all the rest.

But Sokka can see the warning signs Zuko is putting out. If he tries to unravel one thread of Zuko’s control before Zuko feels ready, Zuko won’t be thanking him for it after.

Fuck, Sokka feels like he barely has himself under control. He’s still feeling the full impact of all the day’s revelations hanging over him, like he’s only been able to absorb the biggest, hardest facts and all the little truths and implications are going to hit like a fucking avalanche later. Sokka can’t believe that anyone could ever conceive of something like this, let alone plan and execute it. And the idea that this has been in place since before the eclipse…Spirits, that Zuko’s been carrying this with him and counting down the clock and still been able to *function* and not have the horror of it burst out of him. That Zuko’s been able to just go along with their play and banter and naps and goofing off and side quests and hasn't been screaming about it from the start. Sokka…fuck, he doesn’t know if he could have done it. But Zuko’s just been…exactly like he always was, driven and determined and focused and sweet and caring.

…Spirits, Sokka doesn’t know where he’s going to find the mental space to think about what the implications of that might be.

Sokka’s brooding stutters to an abrupt halt when Zuko suddenly shoves to his feet, neatly and precisely setting down his empty bowl, movements so sharp they border on violent, before striding off into the evening, eyes fixed on the sand the whole time.

Sokka stares after him, worry a tight knot in his chest. He wants to go after him, but he can’t think of a single thing to say that might make any of this better except to walk through the plan that still feels far too thin. And Sokka wants to be there if Zuko needs to talk about his emotions instead, but Sokka knows that pushing Zuko in the wrong moments doesn’t result in him opening up. Except when it does, explosively, and maybe that’s what both of them need, to just let it out and shout and stop trying to put on good faces for everyone else and—

Aang bursts to his feet, his meal only half-eaten as he stares after Zuko.

“Aang,” Sokka says, not even sure if he's trying to warn Aang off or encourage him or give him advice as Aang rather resolutely takes Momo off his shoulder and sets him down on the sand.

“I should talk to him,” Aang says, voice firm.

“Now might not be the best time.” Not when Zuko’s edging toward the kind of grim focus Sokka is more used to seeing from him in battlefields and impossible situations. If Zuko is feeling like his options are slipping away, the Avatar chasing after him isn’t going to make him feel less hemmed in.

“It’s my fault he’s upset,” Aang says, which Sokka…doesn’t necessarily agree with, but Aang’s still going on so Sokka bites back the protest. “I can’t just—” Aang shakes his head, abandoning whatever he was going to say to take off after Zuko.

Sokka stares after him, too, anxious, because Zuko is so clearly *not* in a mood to pull his verbal punches right now. But Suki gives Sokka a look like he should give them space when he makes to get up and…maybe Aang needs to talk to someone right now who’s always been able to focus on the fact that Aang is the Avatar first and everything else second. Maybe it’s Aang that Zuko needs to let it out in front of, not Sokka. Maybe Zuko’s brand of brutal realism and Aang’s resolute idealism will result in something better for both of them, something that will help each of them get into the headspace to do what needs to be done when the Comet arrives.

Maybe.

&#45;-

Zuko generally thinks fondly of this particular beach, but right now he would really love for it to have some different geography. He itches to find a high place to throw himself against and just…take a moment to get away from it all. To get *above* it all. But the rockface is too exposed, the foliage in the trees too sparse for how big he is these days, and Zuko’s grimly contemplating climbing the hill to get onto the roof of the house when he hears footsteps behind him, determined and fast and way too light to be Sokka.

“What do you want, Aang,” Zuko asks, missing a neutral tone by a long mile as he turns, putting Aang just into the edge of his periphery as he eyes the far side of the cove. Too far in that direction and he’ll start running into the other private beaches, but that also means other houses and other rooflines, though none quite as high.

“You’re mad at me,” Aang says.

*Yes.* “I don’t know what you want me to say,” Zuko says instead, exhaustion hanging heavy on his shoulders.

“You’re upset because of me, and I don’t want you to be.”

Zuko wants lots of things. A few months shouldn’t have made it so hard for him to remember how dangerous that is. “The situation is upsetting,” he grits out, trying to exhale heat and inhale calm and his inner fire just biting at the underside of his skin instead.

“It’s just, I’ve been raised my whole life to believe—”

“I know, Aang,” Zuko cuts in, taking another slow breath through his teeth to even out his tone. “I know what you were raised to believe. But you’re the Avatar.”

“I don’t stop being an Air Nomad just because I’m the Avatar,” Aang insists.

“No?” Zuko could have drowned under being the Crown Prince the way the Fire Lord needed him to be, most days. Sometimes it feels like he could still drown under the need to set aside his wants for what the Fire Nation needs. “What if it means choosing between ending the war or not? What if being an Air Nomad instead of the Avatar makes the balance even worse.”

“I’m not just *an* Air Nomad. I’m the *last* Air Nomad.” Zuko winces, trying not to hear an accusation there that he doesn’t think Aang intended. “How can I restore balance if I sacrifice my people’s beliefs in the process?”

Zuko can practically hear Azula’s voice in the back of his head making rather pointed comments on the value of idealism outside of philosophy scrolls. He refrains from sharing. “Being an Air Nomad is about more than just nonviolence, isn’t it?”

“Yeah, but…people already see me as this—this force of *destruction*. I’m supposed to be restoring balance to the world, not just ending the war. Part of that’s not letting my people’s traditions die out, and people are *scared* of me. The Air Nomads preached friendship and peace and nonviolence and everyone out there thinks that I run around destroying cabbage merchants for fun!”

Zuko feels himself go immobile, locking himself down against the cold anger trying to crawl up from his gut. “…Is this about the Ember Island Players?”

“No! But—it was based on true accounts, right? If that’s what people think of me, then how can I be the Avatar? How can I tell others to choose peace when I choose violence?”

Zuko whirls around, anger and disbelief finally overriding his desire to remove himself from this conversation. “The fucking Ember Island Players got to you? That fucking *play*? Fucking —true accounts selectively picked to create *war propaganda?* Agni’s balls, Aang.” Zuko turns away, sharp, feeling sparks biting against his fists. “Have you *heard* of Kyoshi?” Aang’s face is distraught, but his jaw is set, stance firm. “I just don’t see how things can be set right by doing more of what set it all wrong in the first place.”

“How about by stopping more bad things from happening!”

“But I would just be contributing to the violence,” Aang protests. “Don’t we need to truly break the cycle for things to change? For the war to end and the peace to be real?”

“*Or*, you can break the cycle by breaking the person driving it! One man, Aang. It’s *one* man, and all of this can end and things can be *better*.” Zuko hates how his voice cracks as he fights through the thickness in his throat, dangerously close to pleading even as his words just seem to make Aang even more determined.

“All lives have value, Zuko,” Aang says quietly, resolutely. “Where does the path end, when a person starts deciding who’s worth sacrificing for the greater good?”

Zuko wants to scream. Isn’t that what being a leader is all about? Doing whatever is in your power to protect your people, no matter how much it hurts? “Ozai doesn’t deserve your consideration, Aang,” Zuko finally bites out, the name harsh in his mouth.

“Everyone does,” Aang says firmly. “There isn’t any one of us who is above anyone else. Who am I to judge and place myself above another?”

Zuko’s spending so much energy holding out his incredulous ‘*the fucking Avatar?’* that other words burst out almost before he realizes he’s going to say them. “How about me,” Zuko says, voice scraping in his throat. “Can I judge the Fire Lord? As his former heir who saw how he intends to rule? Or how about as the grandson of the man he arranged to have killed so he could gain power? Or the son of the woman he had murdered to cover it up? Can *I* judge?”

Aang frowns, taking a half-step forward. “Zuko, I—”

“Or how about as his own fucking *son*,” Zuko hisses, because he can’t make himself stop now that he’s started. “Who had to grow up with him and knows exactly the kind of *care* he metes out to others? Am I allowed to judge the Fire Lord, Aang?”

“Zuko—”

“Or maybe you just care about the Spiritual stuff, since you’re the Avatar. All those worldly concerns are beneath you, right?” Zuko spits, sparks flying on the words. “If you don’t care about that, maybe you’ll care that he’s bastardizing the ways of the Eternal Flame. That he brings shame on Agni by justifying horrors in her name, by perverting her will and twisting her laws and burning off half the face of his underage Agni Kai opponents and claiming to do it with her blessing. Do you care about *that*, Avatar? *When am I allowed to judge*?”

“...Zuko,” Aang breathes, eyes wide with horror as Zuko heaves for air, trying to rein in the fire raging through his chest. “What—he—your father—?”

“*The* *Fire Lord*.”

“Sorry, sorry—the—the Fire Lord, he—on purpose?” Aang’s eyes are locked on Zuko’s scar like they've never been before, like it’s something fresh and new and horrifying. “It…I always thought it was a training accident.”

Zuko slowly forces his fists to open, flexing the familiar tightness from his joints. “…You didn’t know?”

“No!”

“…None of you knew?” Zuko tries again, the concept feeling strangely slippery.

“How would we?” Aang asks. “Is it—is it a thing?” His voice goes tight with alarm. “Does this *happen* in the Fire Nation? Is this some kind of—”

“Because Sokka knows,” Zuko cuts, and Aang snaps his mouth shut, rocking back, clearly processing. “And Toph knows,” Zuko continues, “And Jeong Jeong, and probably every Earth Kingdom General, and any merchant that trades with the Fire Nation, and I bet the Southern Fleet’s heard it by now too, and the Colonies have at least rumors, and—”

“*I* didn’t know,” Aang says, shaking his head. “I didn’t—no one ever said anything to me.”

“…Fine,” Zuko finally said, wondering what else is just slipping past the Avatar’s notice as he moves through the halls of power, what else no one is thinking to tell him. “But Aang—if you didn’t before, you know what kind of man the Fire Lord is now. Him staying in power, that just—that isn’t an option.”

Aang’s face is sympathetic—Agni’s tits, Zuko *hates* sympathy—but even as he nods, he still says, “Killing the Fire Lord isn’t the only way to get him out of power.”

“It is. Trust me.” Zuko and Azula have certainly thought about it enough to know how all those scenarios play out. “With the support he has—with what he wants to do with it? He needs to be put down.” There is no world in which Ozai couldn’t claw his way back to the throne, through politics or Agni Kai or assassination. A Child of Agni is needed to defend the Eternal Flame, and there are so few of them left.

“No living thing should be put down,” Aang insists. “No one deserves that!”

Zuko could scream. Zuko *wants* to scream, like he hasn’t in a long time. “Some of us don’t have the luxury of getting to stay above it all, Aang,” he snaps instead, wondering at the cruel twist of fate that could have him practically back in that little room at Boiling Rock, on the other side of this conversation with Mai. “And those of us on the ground? We know that sometimes you need to get your own hands dirty. There won’t always be someone else around to do it for you.”

&#45;-

They’re all trying to make concrete, real plans, now. To get actual timelines together and wrap their heads around the scope of what needs to happen when, and what needs to *not* happen, and what the team is going to have to do to make all that happen—or not—the way they need.

They’ve been at it for…Sokka doesn’t even know how long. Zuko would know, with his firebender’s instinct for the sun, but Sokka’s been entirely consumed by focusing all their collective brainpower into lists and plans and contingencies. It isn’t going poorly, exactly, but Sokka also can’t entirely tell himself that it’s going *well*.

They have the ‘when’ firmly locked down—too fucking soon, for Sokka’s taste—and a solid sense of the outline of things—the airships that need to be stopped, Ozai leading the charge, Azula consolidating power at the palace. But the ‘how’ of it…

“Any plan that leaves the Father Lord alive is going to fail,” Zuko snaps again, and Sokka suppresses a twitch. Again.

“How can any plan that hinges on murder be a success,” Aang protests—again. “The Avatar is supposed to be a symbol of unity and balance. How can we start a new era of peace with the Avatar murdering the leader of the Fire Nation?”

“Really successfully!”

“Zuko,” Sokka sighs. “Aang.” They’ve been over this, in one way or another, more than a few times already.

“How can you draw out this war to save your own conscious,” Zuko says, plowing forward anyway. “How clean are your hands when your inaction results in hundreds—thousands— more dying who didn’t have to?”

“Zuko…” Sokka tries again, hearing the chiding edge on his tone. Fuck, he sounds like Katara.

“How is this *any* different than the North?”

“*Zuko*,” Sokka hisses.

“*What?”* Zuko snaps, glaring a moment before sucking in a hard breath and visibly reaching for calm, gritting his teeth. Though Sokka, at least, can read the accusation clear in that glare —that they’re here now because they coddled Aang too much along the way, because they were too naïve about the world, because they didn’t have the guts to imagine the kinds of questions that needed to be asked.

Or maybe that’s just Sokka’s own sense of guilt speaking.

“I really think you’re underestimating the value of symbols, here,” Katara says after a moment, all of them apparently deciding to soldier on as if they’re having a level conversation, which…is fine by him. “Yes, it’s idealistic. But maybe that’s what the world *needs*. Something bright and hopeful and positive to rally around.”

“The war has had plenty of heroes,” Zuko says, scrubbing his hands over his face and Sokka barely resists the urge to knuckle at his own gritty eyes. They’ve all been at this far too long. “On both sides. The only ones who don’t end up with their hands just as dirty as the rest of us are the ones who end up dead.”

“It doesn’t have to be that way, though,” Katara insists. “Things can change—isn’t that what we’re trying to do in the first place? Change things?” She glances around, fist clasped at the hollow of her threat. “How can we ask others to be different and—and to *forgive*, if we don’t try ourselves first?”

“Letting Ozai live isn’t an act of *forgiveness*.”

“It could be the ultimate forgiveness,” Katara pushes back, and Sokka nearly fumbles his ink, his hand spasms so hard. Shit, they might need separate cookfires tonight…

Zuko just pins her with a steady, cold glare, though, which…honestly might be scarier than if he were blowing up. “If Aang says he doesn’t have the right to judge the Fire Lord, then Aang doesn’t have the right to forgive him, either.”

Katara meets Zuko scowl for scowl. “And if you sacrifice your ideals for expediency whenever things get hard, what's the point of even having them in the first place?”

“There isn’t any,” Zuko says bluntly. “Ideals are for people who haven’t learned how the world works yet.” Sokka nearly chokes, hearing *Zuko* say that, one of the most doggedly idealistic people he knows. “And it’s great that Aang gets to hold onto his and gets to care about what everyone thinks of him. But the rest of us just have to do what needs to be done. We don’t have the luxury of clinging to principals at the expense of everything else.”

Sokka shivers at the almost rote quality of Zuko’s words, like it’s something he's heard over and over and over again. Fuck, it probably was, because that’s not how Zuko *acts*. “Zuko,” he says carefully, trying to pick his words carefully. “Putting your responsibilities ahead of your personal wants—that’s an ideal.”

“It’s a duty,” Zuko corrects, as if adhering to duty isn’t also an *ideal*. “Accepting a role comes with obligations, and if you don’t want them then you shouldn’t be acting like you can fulfill the role. And once you accept it, you do what you have to do, and you make the best out of whatever pieces you’re fortunate enough to be left with.”

“That’s a bit bleak, Sparrowkeet,” Toph murmurs, feet buried in the sand. “Roles aren't predetermined. They aren’t set.”

“And it’s not all one or the other and nothing in between,” Katara huffs, clearly trying to rein in her frustration. “Even if you’re all about roles and duty and whatever, what people think matters. Isn’t that part of it all?”

“Don’t lecture me about perceptions and what people think, Katara,” Zuko snaps. “What do you think the Phoenix Emperor *is*? My whole life has been nothing but fucking perceptions.” And pretenses, Sokka mentally adds on. The kind that everyone buys into as long as no one pokes too hard. And power built on relative position, all just waiting for one sharp jab to bring it all down…

“And you didn’t run around dressed up in a costume and mask because you thought symbols didn’t matter!”

“The Blue Spirit was a *disguise*,” Zuko says, and Sokka thinks that’s splitting hairs a bit too finely, can see the same thought on Suki’s face. “And no, you don’t fight an idea with your own delusions. You cut through the performance and spectacle, and you erode faith in the very concept of it so completely that there’s no hope that it could ever be resurrected again, until the very idea of holding onto it is nothing but shameful stupidity and you would be embarrassed to admit you’d ever even *thought* about believing it, let alone actually believed. You destroy an idea by sowing doubt.”

“And symbols can do that,” Katara says determinedly, as Sokka blinks down at his notes. That was…very specific. Much more so than ‘one sharp jab.’ He isn’t quite sure how to capture it with the other suggestions.

“Not fast enough,” Zuko says, shoving his hands through his hair. “Look, I get that it’s hard. I’m not stupid, I know it isn’t easy, and it’s going to suck. But this is the fastest end,” Zuko says, his voice cracking over a note of naked pleading. "It's been a century already. How much more can we take?"

“Is that all that matters, though?” Aang frowns, wrapping his arms around his knees. “Doing it fast? Not doing it right?”

“*Yes*,” Zuko says, which Sokka can see he clearly didn’t expect. “*Nothing* is right in war! So you do the thing that ends the war the fastest. You don’t drag it out to make yourself feel better at the expense of everyone else!”

*Oh*, Sokka thinks, a little burst of understanding breaking through his exhaustion. There it is. That familiar idea that Sokka remembers from letters and conversations on Zuko’s ship and words exchanged on ice. That *ideal* that probably drove Zuko to leave Caldera after the eclipse, and that sent him back to the Fire Nation in the first place. He saw a path to end things as quickly as possible, and he’s been chasing it with the single-minded intensity that Zuko brings to everything, regardless of what it did—does—to him, because Zuko’s ideals don’t include making himself feel better at the expense of everyone else.

Spirits, Sokka feels sick for what Zuko's been trying to carry this whole time on his own shoulders. But at the same time, Sokka remembers more than just that from the letters, the conversations on Zuko’s ship, the words exchanged on the ice. He remembers that Zuko thought about the end of the war intensely and deeply and passionatley. But only parts of it.

“What comes after?” Sokka says, bracing himself against the growing tightness in Zuko's expression as Sokka keeps speaking. “Ending things as fast as possible,, that’s great, but what if it ends fast and the underlying problems are still there?”

“What underlying problem?” Zuko scowls, sounding distinctly pissy. “The Fire Nation?”

“You know that’s not what I mean,” Sokka says, managing to keep his tone even. “If the underlying problems are still there—if people aren’t willing to set revenge aside to move forward…”

Zuko sets his jaw and glances away, unable to argue with what they wrote to each other months and months ago.

“What’s fastest in the short term might not be the best in the long run,” Sokka says carefully.

“So what?” Zuko presses, his full attention suddenly wholly fixed on Sokka. “You agree? Let the Father L—Fire Lord live and hopes he’s so grateful he was spared from something he didn’t even know was coming that he comes around to the Avatar’s side? Maybe he’ll be Aang’s new best bud, too. Maybe they can come back to fucking Ember Island together and have a nice vacation together!”

Sokka raises his eyebrows, Zuko glaring a moment before letting out a noise of pure frustration and dropping his head into his hands. Sokka eyes the shuddering tension along Zuko’s shoulders, the very precise nature of his still very ragged breathing, considers how much Zuko clearly loved coming to this place no matter what his family is now. Flashes of fear are already leaking through Zuko’s sharp-edged anger and Spirits, Sokka doesn’t know how eroded Zuko’s sense of balance needs to be for Zuko to keep verbally slipping up like that while advocating for killing the Fire Lord, but he doesn’t think they’re going to be able to keep this up much longer.

Suki must see the same thing, because she clears her throat into the ringing silence after Zuko’s words. “Maybe we just…take a step back.”

“To where?” Katara mutters, her open frustration mirroring Zuko’s.

“Well,” Suki shrugs. “We *are* supposed to be planning.”

“The goal is a pretty fundamental part of the plan,” Zuko grumbles from behind his hands.

“Or you’ve been talking about a solution,” Suki suggests. “One of many.”

“And what are the others, then,” Zuko asks, sliding from furious to irritable, which…Sokka will take right now. They’re all cranky, to say the least.

Suki hesitates—because it’s clear what she thinks even if she hasn’t said it—and glances around the circle, eyes settling on Toph. Who somehow must realize, because she offers a little shrug. “The first thing you learn in the Earth Rumble is not to leave an enemy standing who can come at your back.”

Suki nods after a moment, then turns her gaze to Aang. “You know what I think,” he sighs.

Sokka fidgets when her clear hazel eyes land on him. “I think that we don’t have the time to come up with something other than taking the Fire Lord out,” he admits, avoiding everyone’s eyes. He wants to, for both Zuko and Aang’s sakes, but if they’re talking *days* to plan *and* execute…

“The Avatar kills Ozai,” Zuko says with brutal simplicity next. “There’s your resolution and your symbol all in one.”

“…Zuko, what if you just made him unconscious?” Katara says when Suki looks to her, and Sokka shares a quick look of confusion with Suki at what feels like a total non sequitur as Katara keeps looking thoughtfully at Zuko. Aang looks alarmed. “Or teach Aang how to do it,” Katara adds, which doesn’t seem to clarify anything for Zuko even as Aang relaxes before suddenly frowning, apparently just as confused as the rest of them now that it’s clear Katara isn’t suggesting knocking him out.

“…Teach Aang how to knock out the Fire Lord?”

“Whatever you did on the Southern Raiders’ ship,” Katara says, looking increasingly excited for the idea. “The bending. With the guard? You knocked him out before you even touched him.”

Zuko goes still, face shuttering behind his usual scowl, and Sokka has a pretty good fucking idea that Katara isn't talking about Zuko knocking anyone out with a fire blast.

“I saw it,” Katara continues when Zuko doesn’t respond, like maybe Zuko will protest that she didn’t. “Why not just teach Aang how to do that? Or Tui and La, do it yourself. It doesn’t have to be Aang who fights him.”

Zuko’s expression flickers before settling into a frown, too fast for Sokka to read. “It won’t work.”

“What is it?” Aang asks, his expression teetering toward something close to hope. “What won’t work? Why not?”

Zuko glances at Sokka, a quick flash of gold that Sokka might not see if he weren’t already studying Zuko’s face so closely. “…It’s kind of like heat bending.”

Katara raises her eyebrows. “Kind of?”

Zuko promptly flounders, which Sokka fully understands considering what Zuko last did with this particular piece of his bending, and what he’s suddenly being asked to think about doing with it instead.

“What’s it like, Sparrowkeet,” Toph asks, even and steady, curious but not too intent, somehow hitting just the tone that lets Zuko’s shoulders unwind. Sokka gives her a quick, assessing look. He hadn’t realized Toph knew the trick of that.

Zuko shifts, some of his typical reticence around sharing seeming to rise back up now that he isn’t fighting, but after a moment he crosses his arms over his chest and sighs. “It’s…people are warm,” he says, pulling a face like he doesn’t like his own description. “Firebenders have the most apparent inner flame.”

“…Okay,” Katara says, clearly much less used to Zuko’s style of teaching than Sokka and Aang, who are both waiting patiently.

“And…firebending can do things like make flames bigger.” He makes a little gesture and a piece of fire streams forward to sit cheerily on a rock, flaring higher when Zuko raises a finger. “Or put them out.” He closes his fist and the flame disappears without even a puff of smoke.

Katara slowly sits back. “…You put out the guard’s inner flame?”

“That’s—” Zuko gives a quick, sharp shake of his head. “It wasn’t really—I didn’t put it out.” He shoots an anxious glance toward Sokka. “I just…dimmed it.”

Katara frowns at the little spot of ash on the rock. “Would you even know if you did?”

“Yes,” Zuko says, the word tight, hollow.

*Oh*. And here’s the reason Zuko’s so categorically refused to take risks with Sokka’s inner flame thing, when he approaches it with his firebending rather than waterbending forms. Sokka’s heart aches, that this is something that Zuko clearly *has* done before, yet another thing he’s been carrying as if his job was to spare everyone else the weight. Sokka can see the realization rippling through the others, along with various shades of shock and upset and unsurprise, and fuck, does he wish they hadn’t just been arguing over the immorality of taking a life. Zuko tips his head forward, hiding behind his bangs, and Sokka shifts to the right, sliding a few inches closer, enough that Zuko would only have to shift his knee a little bit to touch Sokka’s leg, practically holding his breath in the long moment before Zuko does just that.

Finally, Suki speaks. “I don’t see why that wouldn’t work, though. It seems kind of… perfect.”

“Sozin’s Comet amplifies firebending,” Zuko says quietly, still mostly frowning at the ground but shoulders loosening slightly as the focus stays on logistics and the practicalities.

“So wouldn’t it amplify your heat whatever too?”

“…He would fight it.”

Sokka…doesn’t know what to do with that particular tone. If it was just them, Zuko would be wrapped in a hug right now. But they’re not, so he adds ‘firebender cuddles’ to his mental checklist of things that need to get done before the end of the day. That probably needs to be done every day just to cover his bases.

“It would be like fighting for control of a flame,” Aang says, understanding dawning over his face.

Zuko nods, flicking up a quick look. “Except an inner flame so intrinsically belongs to a firebender that if you aren’t exponentially stronger…”

Right. Well. Sokka can fill in the rest of those blanks just as well as everyone else can.

“Firebenders have the most *apparent* inner flame,” Toph abruptly says, bare feet braced against the sand. “That’s what you said. *Most* apparent.” Sokka suddenly finds himself and Zuko going still in a…very similar way. “So what about non-firebenders,” Toph presses. “Do they have an inner flame too?”

Sokka holds his breath as Zuko takes a slow, deliberate inhalation. “They have something.”

“And do they have any defense? Like a firebender does?”

“They can learn,” Zuko says, tight like he knows the answer isn’t enough, shoulders hunched again and fuck, if *Toph* of all people suddenly starts acting wary of Zuko…she doesn’t sound it, but she sure as shit doesn’t sound happy, either.

“…And how’s learning going for Sokka?”

Sokka ignores Katara’s sudden hard inhalation and Aang’s startled jolt, clearing his throat and striving for something as close to normalcy as he can get, feeling just…beyond awkward, to be talking about this with anyone other than Zuko, something that feels so intimate and personal and just for them. “It’s…fine.”

Toph grunts, but it’s not a lie so she has nothing to call him on. “Any other firebenders doing this thing?”

Zuko offers a shadow of a shrug. “Not that I’ve heard about.”

“Good,” Toph grunts, sitting back. “We’re going to have some words, Zuko, after all this Comet business.”

&#45;-

This has been…the longest day of Sokka’s life, and it's only just past noon. And yesterday felt like the longest, and the day before that…he has a feeling tomorrow is going to be even longer, and again, until the Comet finally comes and goes.

He stares at the notes laid out before him, shoving his hands through his hair and barely biting back a growl of annoyance when they get caught on his hair tie again. He tugs it loose, wincing at he feels strands pulling and breaking, shoving his hair back as it falls loose and rubbing at his scalp. It’s significantly less soothing than when Zuko does it for him.

“Anything else,” he asks, giving it up and gathering his hair back into its tie. “Is that it?”

Zuko grunts, the sound devoid of anything except exhaustion. “Is that not enough?”

Fuck, it better be. “I just don’t want to miss anything because we didn’t think it through,” Sokka sighs, carefully setting down his brush.

Zuko lets out a noise that might be a laugh, if it weren’t so utterly drained. “Sure wouldn’t.”

Sokka wonders if he’s imagining the ashes of Zuko’s plan somewhere in that laugh. It clearly relied on Aang more than Zuko has been realizing he can, which…just makes Sokka feel sad. Which doesn’t feel like enough, but sad is about all Sokka can manage through the numb, fascinated kind of horror he experiences whenever he looks at the notes he just spent hours drawing out of Zuko’s head.

Sokka already had a healthy appreciation for the political savvy Zuko doesn't seem to think he has, but Spirits. All of this had just been locked away in there, coexisting with Zuko’s day-to-day thoughts. All these political players and their motivations, the awful things people will do and have already done for power, horrible contingency after horrible contingency, all delivered with total pragmatism, as if needing to know all this in order to survive is just how things are. As if anyone with sense would know how all those pieces will shift and react to each other after the eclipse, how the players will respond to the Boiling Rock escape, what will rush to fill the vacuum of Zuko’s absence.

“Not much of a vacuum, really,” Zuko had said, and Sokka couldn’t find even a hint of bitterness in his tone. “I’d been gone for nearly four years. It’s not like anyone was sure of me enough to really start working me into things.”

“It seems like you’re pretty sure of them,” Sokka pointed out, tracing his thumb over pages and pages of notes.

Zuko shrugged, looking…sad. “Azula is the one who knows it all. She’s better at this stuff than I am.” Said with such unhapiness that Sokka thinks he means far more than just what’s drying on the paper in front of them. This web of motivations and ambitions and weaknesses and plans upon plans upon plans, everyone trying to be the spidersnake at the center. And Zuko, who is…comfortable in this even as he clearly doesn’t like it. Who can speak about pulling levers and strings and shifting allegiances as if he’s done it before.

A nest of dragons, Aunt Wu had said, not a family. One that doesn’t care about what it burns. Sokka's known he hasn't truly grasped what that's meant for Zuko yet, not fully, that there's so many layers to it Sokka might spend years learning. But he thinks he's getting a good, long look at what it means for someone to grow up like that, with all this.

“Spirits, Zuko,” Sokka finally says, resisting the urge to shove the stack of papers away, like that will get him any kind of distance from their contents. “This…sucks.”

Zuko draws in on himself even more, looking away, everything about his body language locked down, tight. “I know.” A breath that doesn’t quite manage to be steady. “I’m sorry.”

“It’s not your fault,” Sokka protests, barely even sure what Zuko is trying to apologize for. "Zuko, it sucks for *you*."

Zuko just grunts in response, not exactly sounding like he agrees, and Sokka ducks his exhausted head to catch Zuko's eyes, taking in the unhealthy pallor to his skin, the deep circle under his unscarred eye, and add in the defensiveness and fracturing prickliness and avoidance that’s lingered even once they left the others...Spirits, Sokka feels like he’s well beyond his emotional limit right now, and he's at least used to sharing his ideas, his experiences, his thoughts. Zuko is decidedly not, and Sokka can barely even imagine what it must be taking for Zuko to still be going right now.

“Can I have a hug?”

Zuko freezes at the question, uncertainty in every line of his body. “What?”

“A hug,” Sokka repeats, twisting his hands together against the urge to reach. Maybe he’s misreading this, but fuck, even if *Zuko* doesn’t need it, now that Sokka's dragging himself out of his thoughts, Sokka really, really could use one for himself. “Can I—it’s been…rough. And it would be really nice to just—”

Whatever else Sokka might have said is lost as he nearly gets bowled over by his firebender, Zuko throwing himself into Sokka’s lap so hard that Sokka needs to slam a hand down behind himself to stay upright as Zuko octocats around him, face tucked into the curve of Sokka’s neck, his entire body nearly vibrating.

“…Like this?” Zuko finally breathes out, shaky.

“Yeah,” Sokka says, swallowing down the lump in his throat. “Perfect.” He wraps his arms around Zuko in return and slowly, inch by inch, feels him start to unwind from sharp-edged imminent explosion to quietly, anxiously miserable puddle. Which…matches Sokka rather well, actually.

“What if Aang can’t do it, Sokka,” Zuko finally whispers, low and scared, scar rough as he turns his face more firmly against Sokka’s shoulder, trying to tuck himself even further under the curve of Sokka's arm. “What if the Fire Lord wins?”

“Then we keep fighting,” Sokka says through the stab of pain in his chest at how fucking *young* Zuko just sounded, like he was voicing a fear that’s lived within him for years and years.

Zuko chokes on a tight, frustrated noise, hands fisting against Sokka’s back. “You only get so many chances.”

“We get as many as we make for ourselves,” Sokka says, making his voice firm and resolution. “And I’m good at making plans.”

“Yeah?” Zuko says, a little wobbly.

“Yeah.” Sokka runs a slow hand down his spine, gently urging him to unwind. “I got you, didn’t I?”

Sokka more feels than hears the exhalation that might be something of a laugh. “Was that a plan?”

“I let my subconscious work on it for a while.”

“Hm.” Zuko’s hands slowly uncurl to press flat against his back. “I’m glad it worked.”

“Me, too,” Sokka murmurs, pressing a kiss against Zuko’s hair and refusing to think of a future where he can’t crack this one, too. Zuko’s doing more than enough of that for both of them, even as he’s clearly trying to keep those thoughts at bay. And Sokka will just have to work extra hard to help him, because Zuko puts far too little stock in hope and far too much in sacrificing it all for the greater good, for Sokka’s comfort.

Sokka glances up at the house on the cliff above them, thinking that it isn’t particularly surprising that Zuko turned out that way. It seems like it was the only thing Zuko was ever taught, by all the people who were supposed to teach him love and safety instead.

&#45;-

“When was the last time you slept?”

Sokka accepts the mug of tea Katara offers, gratefully inhaling the steam and wincing slightly as he takes a sip. Clearly, Zuko didn’t make it. “I…recently?”

“Real sleep,” Katara says pointedly. “Not just a nap.”

“…It’s been a while.”

Katara’s brow furrows with concern, as if her own eyes aren’t red from too much rubbing the tiredness away. “We need you fresh, Sokka. All of us.”

“I know, just…” How can he *stop*, when every second that passes is one second closer to the Fire Nation trying to fucking burn down the Earth Kingdom? And being able to do it?

“I get it,” Katara sighs, taking a seat beside him, watching the waves for a few moments. “There’s more on your mind than just planning, though.”

“I’m worried about Aang,” Sokka admits. Spirits, he hates how this whole thing feels like… taking sides. But he can’t help but feel like the clock is ticking down on whatever wake-up call Aang needs in order to prevent the world from rather literally burning.

“Give him time,” Katara finally sighs, the words edged with her own concern.

“Time is a limited resource right now.”

“I know. But that’s not the only resource we have.”

“What, the power of friendship?” Sokka thinks about and discards the idea of rolling his eyes. It just feels like far too much effort right now.

Katara apparently has the energy to flick him hard in the shoulder. “I was going to say the Avatar state, or something like that. But sure. The power of friendship works too.”

It turns out Sokka does in fact have the energy for an eye roll for that.

“He’s going to find the right path, Sokka,” Katara continues, serious again. “And yeah, maybe he needs to meditate on it and talk it out and worth it through, but we *do* have the time.”

“'The right path,’” Sokka echoes. “For him, or for the world?” Spirits, but Sokka hates all this…spirit stuff. *Destiny* stuff. That the fate of everything might come down to one kid’s choices over the next few days no matter what the rest of them do. Sokka doesn’t know if he’s ever felt so small.

“Why not both?” Katara asks after a beat. “You’re the one who always finds every possible contingency and exception and outlier there is to find,” she says, fondly exasperated. “Why does it have to be one or the other?”

“I don’t know if Aang is really looking for that option,” Sokka says quietly, fiddling with his mug. “He seemed pretty set.”

Katara gives him a surprised look. “You don’t think Aang wants what’s best for everyone involved?”

“I think sometimes you have to sacrifice a bit to gain somewhere else, in order to find it.”

“Some things aren’t worth sacrificing,” Katara finally says, pulling up her legs to rest her chin on her knees, staring out over the water. “Some things are so important that you can’t give them away.”

Sokka mirrors her posture after a moment, taking a sip of his almost-bitter tea and thinking of all he would do to keep his people safe, Katara and Aang and Toph and *Zuko*, Suki, everyone back home, everyone who should be home and isn’t. Of everything he would do for them. Of everything *they’ve* done for *him*. And of the times it's felt like it was being done *to* him, rather than for him.

“Sokka, there’s always a bigger picture you can point to,” Katara eventually says. “You’re the king of rationalizing the things you want for yourself—”

“Hey!” Sokka…isn’t actually sure if he’s offended by that, or just overly seen. He *does* have a shred of self-awareness over how he’s acted in the past year.

“—I know you know that. So eventually there has to be some things you aren’t willing to compromise on. Right?”

“Is that what you do?” Sokka asks after a long moment, eyeing her profile. “Refuse to compromise?”

“…Too much, maybe,” Katara says, face briefly shadowed before reaching out to give him a firm shove when Sokka can’t hold back a noise of exasperation.

“I’m sorry, but don’t compromise at all, but not too much—”

“Maybe it's about who you want to be in the world,” Katara cuts in, glowering a little and giving his shoulder another push so he has to brace himself against the sand to keep from toppling over. “And if you get what you want but you hate yourself on the other side of it, how much does getting what you want really matter?”

“But it’s never just about you,” Sokka sighs, slugging back the rest of his tea and grimacing at the grit at the bottom. Definitely not brewed by Zuko. “Other people are impacted by what you do.”

“Someone else is always impacted,” Katara agrees, “But Sokka, it’s impossible to plan for every single thing that might happen, and that might happen because of that, and then because of that—you might as well try to predict the future.”

Sokka gives her a sideways look. “I thought you were into that stuff.”

“And I thought *you* weren’t,” she huffs. “Should I start calling you Aunt Wu?”

“*Wow*, Katara*,*” Sokka mutters, physically leaning away from the idea. “I’d at least be Uncle Wu.”

They both stare at each other for a moment, expressions trapped someplace between affront and annoyance. Then Katara lets out a noise suspiciously like a laugh. “Sokka,” she says, face utterly serious and voice only a little wobbly. “Your wedding would be *beautiful*.”

Sokka pulls a face. “Ugh, no—”

“Think of the *clouds*—

“How about we don’t ever think about that.”

“—you could do it on the rim of a nice active volcano, what a venue—”

“Okay, very funny.”

“—I’m sure she can tell you exactly how to dress to make your marriage as auspicious as possible—”

“Did I ever tell you Aunt Wu grew up in the Fire Nation?” Sokka cuts in, smirking when Katara’s giggling suddenly chokes off into a shocked gurgle. “Near the palace, actually, it sounded like.”

“…Sounds like she knows all about Caldera then,” Katara finally says, eyes wide with mock innocence as another snicker breaks through. “Really, the perfect person for you for you considering your—”

Sokka jabs her right in her ticklish lower rib, setting off a *real* burst of laughter. It's a temporary victory, though, as Katara quickly finds the spot on his foot that makes his whole body twitch, face triumphant, and Sokka can’t let *that* stand, and it quickly devolves from there.

It is, Sokka can admit as he dives to somehow pin Katara’s arms but have his own free, one of their more juvenile tickle fights. Which might not be an ideal use of time and energy, but as Sokka shoves a retaliatory handful of sand down the back of Katara’s dress since there’s no snow to be had, he considers that he might be more than half-delirious at this point and really, he should just give himself what he wants right now. Even if that means taking a gamble on being able to reach the spot right under Katara’s shoulder blade and losing because he gives her an opening on the sensitive back of his right knee and sends him flailing to the sand to get away.

Eventually they both run out of steam, panting on their backs, eyeing each other in wary truce. Sokka pointedly blows a chunk of loose hair out of his face and Katara lets out a little giggle that might just be this side of hysterical, not making any attempt to do anything about her own hair. Sokka barely holds back his own maybe-laugh looking at the way it’s straggling over her face. It’s like all his skin has been stretched too thin the past few days and finally it's back to the size it should be, his whole body tingling with the release of having a moment to just…be stupid and dumb and silly with his sister.

Katara gives him a little nudge with her foot to catch his attention, bumping against his shin, which is decidedly not ticklish and therefore within the grounds of the truce. “Really though, Sokka,” she says, voice still a bit breathless. “Maybe this whole thing is about thinking smaller, sometimes.”

Sokka raises his eyebrows, trying to work the sand out from under his wrist wraps without unwinding them. “We’re talking about an end to a century of war and the fate of all the nations.”

“Or we’re talking about one man.”

Sokka grunts, but…can’t exactly deny that fact. “Thank you for the lesson in moderation, Lady of the Blown Up Factory.”

Katara’s foot lands much more solidly against his shin, even as she gives a prim little sniff. “You’re welcome, Lord Who Thinks He’s Responsible for Everything.”

Another moment of silence, then they both snort out a laugh, half-heartedly shoving sand at each other.

“Really, though,” Katara says once they calm back down again, both of them looking up at the clear blue of the sky. Sokka can barely believe that something as perfect as this is what’s heralding something as dire as the Comet. “How are you?”

“Other than tired and being unfairly attacked by my own flesh and blood?” Sokka huffs, aiming for a joke, but Katara just gives him a serious look.

“Other than that.”

“I’m fine,” Sokka says after a beat, more than a little surprised at how quickly she is tossing aside their levity. “As much as can be expected, I guess. Why?” She makes a neutral little hum, her healer’s hum, eyes examining his face like he’s a patient trying to conceal his symptoms. Sokka scowls back. “Why, Katara?”

“How long have you known about Zuko’s…inner flame stuff.”

Sokka briefly considers trying to play dumb and immediately discards the idea. Zuko himself offered this secret up, which means Sokka doesn’t have to defend it anymore. Still, Sokka can’t quite hold her eyes as he shrugs and digs at the sand between them. “…Ba Sing Se.”

Katara considers that for a long moment, finally saying, “That’s a big secret for you to keep for him. His scar—” she catches his hard glance and waves it away. “—I don’t know, and I’m not asking. I’m just saying his scar, his family stuff, whatever, that’s one thing. But bending like that, it’s...”

“It’s what?” Sokka asks, fighting to keep his voice even, trying not to jump toward immediate protectiveness or defensiveness or whatever it is that’s beginning to gather in his gut.

“It’s not the same. It’s…I get that he tells you things he hasn’t told the rest of us, and that he’s sharing stuff with us too now, but—”

“I don’t run around telling everyone we meet about your bloodbending,” Sokka cuts in, because whatever is going to follow that ‘but’ Sokka is pretty sure he isn’t going to want to hear.

Katara winces, looking distinctly uncomfortable, but soldiers forward. “I’m never going to accidentally bloodbend someone unconscious.”

“Neither is Zuko,” Sokka points out. Sokka might not get the intricacies of bending, but he hasn’t been living the past year with three bending masters for nothing. Zuko might not have known quite what the result would be that first time when he shielded Sokka from the heat of fever, but Sokka knows from the way Zuko talks about it that using his firebending this way is very much an active thing.

Katara glances away, biting her lip, and Sokka is relieved when she reluctantly heeds the warning in his voice. “As long as you’re comfortable with it.”

“I am,” Sokka says. “With both of you.” He raises his eyebrows at her startled look. “I trust both of you,” he repeats, lips twisting into a wry smile. “It’s part of being a nonbender in a world of benders, Katara. People can do crazy stuff to you and around you and you just… need to take it on faith that on any given day some earthbender doesn’t decide to crush you with a rock.”

“…I never thought about it that way before.”

Sokka is aware. “That’s because you never had to.” But for Sokka, the idea that someone could theoretically hurt him and there’s only so much he can do to stop it isn’t a new one. And it’s only worth thinking about so much, when at the end of the day, he also knows that anyone can be hurt by anyone. Bending not required.

&#45;-

The wedding to Aunt Wu may be officially off, because Sokka will freely admit—not that anyone feels the need to ask—that all his planning and contingencies and notes and schedules utterly failed to account for one fairly major possibility: That Aang might up and disappear in the middle of the night, leaving nothing behind but a set of fading footprints in the sand.

&#45;-

No one can find Aang. There are plenty of kids dressed in Air Nomad outfits—that stupid fucking *play*—but none of them are *their* Air Nomad. Katara is openly freaking out about the possibility of kidnapping, particularly after Toph admits that she can’t hear his heartbeat no matter where on the island Zuko took her.

Which doesn’t have to mean anything, right? There are lots of situations where Toph’s bending won’t work, lots of perfectly valid, Aang-is-still-alive reasons. Like Aang just not being on the island anymore, as Suki reluctantly points out that private and public boats leave the docks every day, and Zuko just closes his eyes, face set in a cold, quiet fury that might be alarming if Sokka weren’t too busy trying not to freak out himself over the fact that Aang’s footprints stopped well above the waterline.

“Anyone got ideas?” Sokka finally asks, throwing himself down onto the sand. “I was using up all mine for the final showdown.”

“We find Aang,” Zuko grinds out, arms crossed tight and hair whipping in the wind as he glares out over the water.

“That feels like more of a goal than a plan, at this point,” Suki sighs.

“His spirit companion is still here,” Zuko bites out. “We use Appa. Or we use him for transport, he’s faster than any public ferry.”

“Where would we go, though,” Sokka asks, picturing the map in his mind. Fuck, if Aang left by boat he could truly be anywhere.

“We can ask if he was seen at the docks. And we can go to all the most popular points along the ferry route, and the bigger port towns where someone might get a private vessel, and—”

“Won’t that give away that he’s missing, though?” Sokka interrupts, really hoping that Zuko knows where all those things are because Sokka sure doesn’t.

“And anyone who took him would just say they haven’t seen him,” Katara says, voice tight with worry, arms folded just as tightly as Zuko’s.

The only way Sokka can think to describe what happens after is that the entire conversation devolves. All of them are loopy with stress and tiredness, tight with worry none of them can fully acknowledge, and each increasingly wild suggestion seems to just spark someone else to a new level of irritation.

Except for Zuko, who stays grimly, resolutely focused—“we can’t storm the Spirit world, we have no way to get in without the Avatar”—and almost brutal in his bluntness—“there’s no point preserving the secret of his location if we can’t use it, and right now it’s working against us, not for us”—in a way that makes Sokka tiredly think he’s finally seeing out in the open the ruthless pragmatism that sent Zuko back to Caldera in the first place.

“Why not just speed the battle up at this point?” Zuko is saying, the campfire seething along with his words. “If it gets Aang to come back, great. If it doesn’t, then Aang still isn’t here and we need to strike early.”

Sokka tugs on his wolf tail like he can physically pull the tiredness out of him, trying to make his brain work, trying to sort out that idea and hold it up against their time and their resources and their capabilities, to see if this is maybe the thing that will let them stop being paralyzed about what to do next.

“Brothels *always* have the best information,” Zuko says in response to some comment from Suki. “And they can spread it, too.”

“It’s not like Aang’s going into brothels,” Katara says, shifting restlessly on the sand. “And what would we even spread?”

Zuko shrugs. “What will make the Avatar come running?”

The others go silent, trying to come up with an answer, and Sokka distantly thinks that they were lucky that this version of Zuko wasn’t who chased them across half the world all those months ago. This Zuko who seems focused and practical to the edge of ruthlessness, which isn’t to say the Fire Prince wasn’t those things the first time he crashed into Sokka’s village and into his life. But this is a Zuko who's sure of himself and his goals in a way he wasn’t a year ago, in a way that puts Sokka in mind of Azula’s terrifying brand of getting things done. And is that really such a surprise, considering everything Zuko’s told him these past days? Considering Zuko and Azula grew up in the exact same environment, were shaped by the exact same hands?

As Sokka watches Zuko trying to cling to what control he has left over what’s going on—“if we can get to the Earth Kingdom, I know a guy”—he can’t deny that a piece of what's in Azula must live in Zuko too. Tempered by far more caring than is probably good for him, and a fierce sense of duty and responsibility and honor—no matter what Zuko keeps saying about the state of his—but…Sokka still thinks he can see the ways that other part of Zuko much more like Azula than not could have flourished, in another life. Or fuck, maybe even in this one, if Zuko ever decided that different things mattered, that the world of people deserving his care should drastically narrow. It's a thought that settles in Sokka's chest along with firm resolve and quiet commitment to make sure Zuko never has reason to doubt all the ways that his caring is appreciated by all the people around him, to do everything he can to make himself the best partner he can be.

&#45;-

“You again,” June drawls, slamming down her empty beer mug and casting an eye over the rest of the crew. Zuko can see Suki looking around in interest on his right, an arm extended to keep Toph back with the others clustered behind him, all of them staying close as they take in the roaring pub and the coins exchanging hands as June’s arm-wrestling opponent is helped off by a bouncer. Her eyes flick back to his face. “New haircut.”

Zuko takes in the skull pin fastening her loose topknot and the bright tattoos on her arms. “Yours is the same.”

June raises her visible eyebrow, face half-hidden behind her bands as she rakes him with another, longer glance before looking at Katara. “You have your girlfriend with you this time.”

“She’s not my girlfriend,” Zuko snaps.

“I promise,” Katara says, taking a pointed step back.

“She’s really not,” Sokka adds, the line of his body suddenly pressed close along Zuko’s back as he curls an openly familiar hand over Zuko’s shoulder, thumb stroking lightly across Zuko’s back out of June’s sight, which Zuko…will tuck aside to feel shivery over later.

June lets out a bark of laughter. “You live a dangerous life, kid,” she says, a gleam in her eyes as she takes in the crew again. “You’re missing a few faces.”

Zuko resists the urge to growl. Growling never made anyone want to be his employee in the past, he reminds himself. He doubts it’s going to start working now. “Isn’t that your specialty?”

A slow grin slides over June’s face as she leans back in her chair, body lazy and eyes sharp. “How much you got?”

&#45;-

“Gone,” Sokka repeats. He can feel his lips shaping the word and his tongue moving and his breath giving it force, all of it working together, but what comes out still makes no sense.

“That’s what I said,” June snaps, giving her paralyzing smell-beast a pat.

“Dead?” Katara asks, something awful trembling in her voice.

June gives her a moderately-less annoyed look. “I would have said dead if I meant dead.”

“A shirshu can find human remains,” Zuko explains, frowning at this particular shirshu in question.

“A shirshu can find *any* kind of remains,” June corrects proudly.

“So…not dead,” Sokka says, bringing them back to the problem at hand. “But the shirshu which can find anything can’t find him.”

June purses her lips. “Are you sure he existed?”

“You saw him yourself!” Katara bursts out. “Of course he exists!”

“Girl, I’m a bounty hunter. I don’t see anything if you pay me right, and this kid—” She tilts her head toward Zuko, who sighs. “—and his creepy old uncle paid me real well.”

“He’s not a creep,” Zuko mutters,

June gives Zuko a long, flat look that has *Sokka* shifting uncomfortably. “Were you the one he was creeping on?”

Zuko stares a moment, then concedes the point with a wave of his hand, giving her one of his habitual, thinking glares. “Wait here.”

“Kid, I’m not some—”

Zuko flips her a gold ring that has Suki’s eyes bugging out as she gets a glance at it. “We have a job for you. Wait here.”

June scowls, but also holds the ring up to the light, and it must be valuable because she doesn’t walk away immediately, pausing a moment—*really* valuable, maybe—before finally saying, “You’ve got a lot of sass for someone in need.”

“I’ve got a lot of jewelry,” Zuko corrects, turning on his heel and striding out like he knows exactly what’s going on, Sokka trailing after with the others because he would really like to know, too.

&#45;-

Zuko is thankful that Katara at least waits until they’re back outside to let the questions burst out of her. “What’s going on? You’re acting all…”

“Fire Prince-y,” Toph supplies.

Zuko decides to just ignore that…accusation? Compliment? Whatever. “If Aang is gone, then we can’t waste time looking for him.”

“But—”

“The shirshu would be able to find him,” Zuko continues, grinding out the words, needing her to understand. Needing them all to. “It can find people across oceans. If Aang is gone, then…”

“Then it’s some Spirit mumbo jumbo,” Sokka mutters, sounding distinctly unhappy about it.

“Probably,” Zuko agrees, shooting him a quick, sympathizing look. With the Avatar, it’s as good a bet as any.

“So what do we do instead?” Toph asks. “Just roll up to Caldera and start bashing heads and hope the Fire Lord comes out?”

Zuko wouldn’t personally depend on that hope. “If we can’t rely on Aang, then we need to find other allies to fight with us.”

“Who?” Sokka asks after a moment. “Most of ours are still in a Fire Nation prison.”

“All my Warriors are,” Suki confirms.

Zuko takes a deep breath and sets aside the question of whether they should have spent less time training and more time executing jailbreaks, setting what he hopes is a reassuring hand on Sokka’s lower back just in case Sokka is asking himself the same things. “My Uncle.”

Suki stares. “…The creepy old man the bounty hunter was just talking about?”

Zuko flicks her an annoyed look but doesn’t engage. “Yeah.”

“I like Iroh,” Toph offers, and Zuko blinks, trying to remember if he was aware that Uncle knew Toph. “I’d stop a world-ending invasion with him.”

“I’m not opposed,” Sokka says, with the care of someone holding onto plenty of opposition. “But why now? You didn’t try to find Iroh before.”

No, Zuko didn’t. Not when he was still stinging from the reality of being left behind, of risking his life and his plans to orchestrate a rescue that wasn’t even needed. Not when his inner fire was still in knots over the fact that Uncle was too busy placing tiles on the pai sho board to even notice that Zuko was playing too instead of just being buffeted along by other players.

But now? Zuko can grimly acknowledge that desperation is a powerful motivator, and that he’s feeling the kind of back-to-the-wall need that strips away things like fear and pride and doesn’t leave any room for caring about who was using who to do what in the past. The kind of need that forces a person to set aside the possibility of betrayal and the idea of forgiveness and face head-on the fact that Uncle has always been playing his own game.

So maybe he’ll understand that Zuko was, too. And maybe he’ll be willing to join this one for its end.

“Zuko?” Sokka says, and Zuko jolts, realizing that he’s been lost in his thoughts. “Why now?”

Zuko takes a deep breath and plays one of the last tiles he has, one that might lead to nothing, but could change the whole board if he plays it right. “Because I’m pretty sure he’ll have an army.”

&#45;-

Sokka eyes Zuko’s weird balance of sharp-edged fear and grim Crown Prince-ness and feels like he’s an idiot for asking, but he isn’t exactly running at full capacity for clever and gentle openers at the moment. “Are you okay?”

“No,” Zuko says bluntly as he finishes tying down his pack, ignoring the shirshu’s questing snout.

“Are you not okay for any specific, particular reason,” Sokka presses, because if this is the last bit of time alone they’re going to get until who knows when, he’s going to sure as shit take advantage of it.

Zuko cuts him a look as he checks the swords strapped to his back.

“Other than the general situation we’re in,” Sokka amends. “Because we’re about to try to see Iroh again, and we’re talking about fighting the Fire Lord, and that’s…a lot.” A lot of father figures, specifically, which have never seemed to be Zuko’s favorite thing. “And if I can help, I’d like to do that.”

Zuko stays stiff for a moment, head half-bowed, before suddenly letting out a little sigh, barely a puff of air but enough to crack the tight restraint he’s been holding himself under. “I just…I haven’t seen Uncle in a long time.”

Sokka makes an encouraging noise.

“And the last time I saw him, he thought I betrayed him.”

Ah. “He loves you. I’m sure he’ll forgive you anything.” It’s a little hard to say, considering Sokka’s thoughts about Iroh’s kind of love, but he can step back from his own feelings about it to recognize that he isn’t exactly an unbiased observer, or in any way possessing of all the facts when it comes to this.

“I don’t need his forgiveness,” Zuko mutters, tight and low and raw in a way that rings true, but also not. Zuko doesn’t need it, but Sokka can see that he wants it, more than he’d like to admit.

“What do you need, then?” Sokka asks quietly, wondering if there’s any way that what Zuko thinks he might need forgiveness for matches what Iroh might think he needs to forgive.

Zuko smiles, grim and humorless. “I need someone to defeat the Fire Lord.”

Sokka hesitates. Katara had danced around it. They’ve all been dancing around it, really. But Zuko hasn’t been picking up what everyone else is putting down, and Sokka doesn’t know if that’s just because he doesn’t notice, or because he doesn’t want to. “What about…you,” Sokka finally says, carefully watching Zuko’s reaction.
