“It can’t be me,” Zuko says, dismissing the idea with a flick of his hair so immediately that for a moment Sokka doesn’t know what to say.

“I think you’ve grown a lot more in your bending than you’re giving yourself credit for,” he finally says, mentally lining up every example that he can think of.

Zuko stares a moment, then huffs out something that really isn’t a laugh. “Thanks,” he says, scrubbing his hands over his face. “But it’s not about believing in myself or whatever. It isn’t an option, and if it was then Azula would be the one doing it. And she doesn’t think she’s in position yet, anyway.”

“…What?” Sokka has very much lost the thread of the conversation.

“Someone needs to defeat the Fire Lord who isn’t one of his heirs,” Zuko sighs. “Starting a new reign different than the previous ones is a bit harder if you’re coming to power the exact same way.”

“But it can still be family,” Sokka says slowly. “A brother?”

“Yes,” Zuko says, flicking a brooding glance back in the direction of the Fire Nation. “Aang would have been best. He’s outside the Fire Nation entirely, he’s the Avatar, but—yes.” Spirits, if it isn’t a fucking week for revelations. Sokka’s gone through enough by now to know that he’s teetering on the edge of a rather big one. Though this isn’t so much a revelation as something Sokka has been perfectly happy to trust Zuko to hold onto until Zuko feels able to share. Sokka just didn’t expect it to come up now. “This…is the plan?”

“Yes,” Zuko says, gold eyes level.

“Your plan?”

“…Partially?”

And Sokka can imagine who’s filling in the other half. He takes a deep, steadying breath. Okay. Fuck, okay. That…that’s not really shocking, at this point, even if Sokka is still missing far more pieces than he would like. “Will you tell me what it is?”

Zuko eyes him a moment. “Long or short version?”

Sokka glances at Appa already ready to go and the bounty hunter giving her shirshu’s harness one last check, his shoulder briefly throbbing in remembered numbness as the animal turns in his general direction. “Short.”

“Fire Lord Ozai isn’t the Fire Lord anymore.”

Sokka blinks. The short version is…much shorter than he expected. Almost more a goal than a plan.

Though maybe it just sounds that way because Sokka isn’t thinking big enough. He carefully turns that thought over as Appa launches into the air and Zuko climbs into the shirshu’s saddle like someone who's done it before—because he has—and leans down to haul Sokka up—which makes Sokka’s stomach swoop in memory of being tossed over Zuko’s shoulder, helpless from the shirshu venom and pressed against him for the first time, which all in all is just…incredibly poor timing.

Because Zuko needs his support, now, not his daydreams. And because as the shirshu sets out, Appa trailing overhead, Sokka is considering that what might be a goal for him could just be an…intermediate step, for Zuko. A piece in a larger process. After all, Zuko is nothing if not single-minded and determined in pursuit of a goal, even over the course of years. And capturing the Avatar was always just an intermediary step for Zuko, too.

Sokka is starting to recognize the landscape, Zuko already gone stiff in front of him, as the shirshu pulls up next to a familiar wall that Sokka had honestly hoped to never see again.

Particularly broken like that.

“This is the spot,” June announces, pulling the shirshu to a sharp stop, the beast’s snout questing through the air even as it pants.

Appa’s landing a judicious distance away is almost enough to cover Zuko’s resigned little sigh and muttered, “Fucking of course,” as he looks up at the Outer Wall of Ba Sing Se.

“Where is he?” Zuko asks—demands—as he jumps down to the ground after Sokka with about half the stiffness which is…really unfair, honestly. Sokka steps deliberately out of the shirshu-tongue range in the guise of stretching out his legs, looking around and seeing… nothing but them.

“Inside the wall,” June says with a jerk of her head. “Close enough with the way Nyla’s acting.”

“I don’t see anything,” Suki says, scanning from the top of Appa’s saddle.

“I don’t hear anything,” Toph adds, stamping a foot against the ground.

June shrugs, looking bored. “I guess you’ll have to look for him then.”

Zuko rounds on her, glaring. “I thought a shirshu is supposed to be able to lead you right to its target.”

“Nyla *can*,” June bites back. “But I’m not stupid enough to bring her into Fire Nation controlled Ba Sing Se, even if you all are.”

“We paid you to bring us to my Uncle,” Zuko grinds out, hands curling into fists. Sokka isn’t sure whether to shift closer to show a united front or away to give Zuko room.

“And you’re here,” June says, voice going hard. “You just need to use those legs of yours a little. They look strong.”

“We *hired* you so we don’t *have* to use our legs.”

“You hired me because you’d have no clue where to even start if you didn’t,” June says, matching Zuko glare for glare. “And now you do. So I *suggest* a little gratitude.”

“She said close enough,” Katara says, voice carefully soothing and neutral as she sidles into June and Zuko’s stare-off. “We can camp tonight and look in the morning. Between Toph and Appa it won’t take any time at all.”

“Your girlfriend’s got a good idea, kid,” June says softly, hand hovering over the whip at her belt. “Might want to listen to her. Wouldn’t want a ruckus that makes the Fire Nation troops come looking.”

“You’ve only done half the job,” Zuko insists, stubborn, eyes narrowing like he’s considering the odds, and Sokka wouldn’t necessarily give that threat the same weight June clearly does after seeing the way Chit Sang and the others reacted to Zuko.

June snorts. “At least three quarters,” she says, shifting in the saddle so that the shirshu’s questing, can-shoot-its-poison-tongue at any time face is suddenly aimed toward the group. “And what are you going to do anyway, cut this into pieces,” she drawls, flashing the gold ring between her fingers

Zuko inhales for a reply that Sokka anticipates will be at truly impressive volume when Toph makes a sudden, quick gesture.

“Good idea,” Toph says as the ring flies out of June’s hands, face hard and challenging as she makes a show of casually metalbending it into pieces and flicking a chunk back to June. “There. Three-quarters payment for a three-quarters job.”

June stares blankly down at the neat three quarters of a ring in her hand, lips parted in surprise.

“We wouldn’t want word to get around the Earth King that you don’t deliver on payment rendered, after all,” Toph says with such sweetness that Sokka can only assume it’s some kind of threat.

June purses her lips, then tucks the ring firmly into a pocket, eyeing Toph, then Zuko. “Interesting friends you’ve picked up, kid. Good luck.”

Then the shirshu turns on no signal Sokka can see, bounding away in a spray of dust and earth that feels rather unnecessarily, to Sokka, leaving them in the shadow of the Wall in the falling light.

“I hope you didn’t care about that ring,” Toph says after a beat, tossing Zuko a little quarter-curve of gold.

Zuko considers it for a moment before tucking it away into a pocket. “It was Azula’s.”

“…Ah.”

Sokka wakes to fire. The sudden roar of it, flaring light and intense heat jerking him from sleep. Zuko is somehow already on his feet even as Sokka scrambles upright, phantom pain in his side that he knows isn’t real throbbing in time with the way the fire seems to breathe beneath the crackling, like it’s a wild, living thing prowling around them.

Appa is bellowing in protest, the others shouting in alarm as they find their feet, ready to fight. Suki has a pair of knives in her hands, Sokka instinctively finding his boomerang as Katara readies her water skin and the earth begins to rumble under their feet. Zuko hisses out an angry breath and shoves his hands wide, and Sokka can *see* the way the flames ringing them shudder and twist as Zuko fights whoever is holding them for control.

Zuko steps back with a gasp, though, eyes narrowed as the flames roar higher. A strong firebender with this Fire Nation patrol, then, to hold the circle against Zuko.

“On three,” Sokka calls, the others nodding a confirmation. “One,” he says, just loud enough to reach the others over the sound of the fire. Zuko unsheathes his dao, giving them a quick spin. “Two.” Sokka can see Zuko’s intent and shifts to give him space to meld fire with swords, inhaling to give the final count—

“Hold!”

Sokka and Zuko both draw up short as the command rings out from beyond the circle of fire, Zuko whipping his swords into a wary defensive position as Sokka reaches out to snatch Katara’s arm and hold her back. Because that voice—and the fire surrounding them is banking down to a ring of embers, narrow enough to easily step over.

“Crown Prince Zuko,” the voice says again from the darkness as Sokka tries to blink away the bright spots in his vision. “We did not expect to see you here.”

Sokka strains into the darkness, Zuko frozen with disbelief best him. “Is that..?”

“Master Piandao,” Zuko breathes, the tips of his dao coming to rest on the dirt, and Sokka feels his knees go momentarily weak with relief that they aren’t being attacked, and that Piandao is someone Zuko would greet with such surprised pleasure.

The ring of embers winks out, and Suki barely has time to finish biting out a curse about her night vision before Zuko is bringing their campfire back to life, drawing it unnaturally high and bright to spread the light wide over the figures that step forward out of the darkness.

“…What,” Katara says, tight and hard as she locks eyes with Pakku.

“Are you fucking kidding me,” Sokka mutters as he takes in fucking Jeong Jeong, who must have been responsible for the fire.

“What a lovely night for a reunion,” King Bumi cackles, casually bending himself a nice throne to sit on and thoroughly ignoring the exasperated looks he gets from his… compatriots? Friends? What are all these Masters doing here? “I can’t wait to catch up.”

Toph cocks her head, then bends herself an even more elaborate throne. “It *is* a lovely night,” she agrees, all upper-crust primness in her voice. “Are we all acquainted, then?”

“Seems like it,” Suki murmurs as she glances around at the mix of mutual glaring and wary standoffishness and Zuko and Piandao smiling at each other off to the side.

“What are you all doing here,” Sokka asks, unsure where to direct the question and finally settling on Piandao as the one he prefers to interact with out of the bunch.

“And who are you all,” Suki adds.

Piandao gives Sokka a thoughtful look before clasping his hands behind his back in that lecturing pose that makes Sokka’s hand instinctively jerk for a set of paper and a brush to take notes. “We are members of an organization known as the White Lotus.” Zuko grunts, like a blow to the gut he’s been bracing for just landed. “Our society was founded on ideals of philosophy and beauty, and we adhere to those ideals to this day.”

“…So what,” Toph finally says, openly skeptical. “You’re all here to check out the Ba Sing Se art museums?”

Pakku scowls, looking like he just bit into a sour apple berry. “Members of the White Lotus are committed to the balance of the world.”

“You’re doing a great job of that,” Katara says, voice tart like she’s eating off the same bush.

“That’s all great,” Sokka says slowly, trying to reconcile Master Girls-Can’t-Bend-and-Stay-In-The-North with world balance and border-spanning secret societies. “But why are you all *here*.” In the shadow of Ba Sing Se’s broken Wall, specifically

“We could ask the same question of you,” Jeong Jeong growls.

“Especially with such an important member of your group missing,” Bumi adds, leaning forward on his throne. “Where’s Momo?”

“…With Aang,” Sokka says, unwilling to unload the whole of the last few days when he’s still trying to grasp that all these people, Kings and Generals and trusted advisors, might have been working together this whole time in the background with Sokka and the others none the wiser.

It…doesn’t exactly make Sokka inclined to trust, not until he has a moment to think through the implications, at least.

“Ah, good then,” Bumi says, settling back. “They’ll be alright as long as they have each other.”

A beat of silence, then Zuko shifts his attention back to Piandao. “We’re here looking for my Uncle.”

The sword master’s face is neutral, as unreadable a Fire Nation expression as any Sokka has seen. “Why?”

Zuko’s finger taps once against the hilt of his dao before stilling, like he doesn’t even want to fidget in front of this audience, which tells Sokka all he needs to know how Zuko’s level of trust, too. “We need his help.”

“…Come,” Piandao says after an endless pause. “We will take you to the Grand Lotus. It was he who called us all here.”

Sokka frowns, opening his mouth to point out that meeting the head flower or whatever isn’t what Zuko said. But nothing comes out as Sokka suddenly realizes that maybe that *is* what Zuko asked for, just not in those words. And a quick glance at the nearly-grim tightness of Zuko’s face says his firebender realizes it, too.

“This is the Grand Lotus’ tent,” Pakku announces, indicating a large white pavilion.

“It does look grand,” Suki mutters, eyeing it and the surrounding neat ranks of tents with open skepticism.

“The flap is closed,” Sokka points out.

“Observant as ever,” Pakku says, and Zuko doesn’t even know this guy and already is pretty sure he hates him. “Now come, I will show you to where you can stay tonight.”

Zuko frowns and pointedly doesn’t move his feet. “Piandao said you would take us to the Grand Lotus.”

“Piandao did not say we would wake the Grand Lotus in the middle of the night,” Pakku scowls. “You can talk to him in the morning.”

“Lot of reinterpreting the deal going around tonight,” Toph mutters under her breath, tilting her head like she’s waiting to see how Zuko wants to play this.

His first instinct is to press, to say that the Grand Lotus will want to be woken up for him, to meet the air of superiority this Northern Tribesman is putting out with proof that Zuko has power here, too. Except…Zuko isn’t sure that he does have power. He isn’t totally confident that it's Uncle on the other side of that tent wall. And even if it were, he isn’t totally confident that it’s true anymore, that Uncle would want to be woken for Zuko.

So he stays quiet and lets Pakku usher them to a much more sedate tent, where they’re promptly left to their own devices outside the patrolling guards. That, at least, feels familiar.

“Wonder how many of those tents out there are empty,” Suki says as she glances around the space they’ve been given, identical to all the rest.

“Hold on,” Katara says as they drop their packs and bedrolls down. “Are we really just going to wait the night?”

Zuko glances up to see everyone looking at him, belatedly realizing that…this is still his mission, apparently. At least until they officially find Uncle. And they’re all waiting for him to make a decision.

“Zuko?” Sokka prompts, the furrow that’s been etched between his brows all night digging a little deeper.

Except the silence stretches as Zuko can’t seem to come up with any words. It feels like the specter of all the ways he failed to be a Good Nephew is suddenly at his back, trying to find a grip on his skin even though Zuko rejected all that months and months ago, said it wasn’t for him and was never going to be, that he could hold up this side of his most important things another way, so why is he suddenly feeling so strangled by all the ways he failed to live up to something he never wanted in the first place?

“Fuck waiting,” Toph finally says, folding her arms. “Let’s just go talk to him. We got Sparrowkeet, he’ll see us.”

Zuko nods, but he can’t quite push back the wave of uncertainty that hits him again, his surety that Uncle will always make time for him bumping up against the reality that Zuko doesn’t necessarily know Iroh as well as he thought. Agni’s balls, Iroh isn’t just *in* a secret society, he’s *leading* it. Which…fuck. That doesn’t happen overnight or in a handful of months. That happens over *years.* At least a few of which Zuko spent thinking Iroh was just his sometimes-bumbling, well-intentioned, good-natured, tea and pai sho and opaque wisdom Uncle. And instead, he was…this.

And suddenly Zuko doesn’t want to see Uncle, not at all, not when he feels like he can barely think with the way his inner fire is straining to press up against the sudden tightness banding his chest.

“Zuko?”

“Let me just—check—I think I left—” Zuko doesn’t even try to finish the excuse, he just breaks for the darkness outside the tent, pointing himself away from all the bright pockets of fire and heat he can feel pressed against his outflung fire sense, every step loosening the knot of anxiety over his ribs even as he knows that running from this isn’t actually going to solve anything.

Sokka figures that Zuko isn’t exactly planning to come back the minute his firebender bolts, and he’s nearly through his mental countdown before going after him—Zuko…clearly wanted the space he was taking—when Katara finally figures it out.

“Where did Zuko go?” she asks, rubbing at her eyes and glancing around like maybe he’ll be in one of the corners and she just didn’t notice. “Shouldn’t he be back by now?”

“And what did he have to get again?” Suki yawns.

Sokka rubs at his gritty eyes. The tiredness is really starting to get to them. “Away, no, and nothing,” he answers in order, leaving it to them to sort out which answer goes with which question.

Katara straightens a little when she gets it, staring. “…Should we look for him?”

“I can’t feel his heartbeat,” Toph frowns, her other foot smacking firmly against the ground as she drops it off her upraised knee.

“The guards must have seen him,” Suki says, pushing herself upright. “They’re all around the perimeter. He can’t have gone far.”

“It’s fine,” Sokka says, waving them back down. “I know where he is.”

“What? Gone?” Katara snaps, a too-soon kind of fear making her voice sharp.

“No,” Sokka sighs, shoving himself to his feet as his mental clock ticks down to zero. Spirits, he would really like to get at least a nap in before morning. Maybe he can talk Zuko into one. “Hiding.”

&#45;-

Sokka stares up at the jumble of rocks along the base of the Outer Wall. It’s too dark for him to pick out the outline of a body, but Sokka knows how Zuko works. This is the highest thing around outside of the Wall itself, and significantly more scalable. Still, Toph couldn’t hear his heartbeat, and the camp is right up against all that stone…

Sokka pivots toward the stand of trees bracketing the other side of the White Lotus encampment. “You going to come down?” Sokka gives the tall, slender trees a considering glance in the silence. “Because I can come up.”

Zuko’s voice floats down from way up in the treetops. “…There aren’t good handholds on these trees.”

“Are you saying that I’m not a good enough climber?”

Another long series of heartbeats, then Zuko suddenly drops into view, hopping right out of one of the closer trees to land in an easy crouch like the sight of him falling isn’t something that briefly makes Sokka’s heart leap up into his throat.

“No,” Zuko mutters, as awful at lying as ever.

“I know how to climb trees,” Sokka protests. He is *great* at climbing things! He can climb with the best of them.

“How many good climbing trees are there in the South?” Zuko points out. Which is…a fair point. Most of the ones near the village got taken down for timber long before Sokka remembers.

“You want to find a spot I can climb to, then?”

Zuko considers a moment, then nods and gestures for Sokka to follow, grabbing his hand when Sokka gets close enough. Sokka gives Zuko’s fingers a careful squeeze, exhaling his relief. Whatever’s bothering Zuko, it can’t be too bad if he’s reaching so easily for physical contact.

They end up settling on a maybe-insultingly low branch—Sokka will consider whether to take issue with it later—with Sokka firmly tucked against the tree trunk and Zuko somehow managing to look completely balanced as he sits in front of Sokka, swinging one leg off the branch, half-hugging the other to his chest. Sokka takes up Zuko’s hand again the minute he’s sure of Zuko’s balance, rubbing his thumb in slow circles over Zuko’s wrist as he studies Zuko’s profile as best he can in the moonlight filtering between the leaves. “You want to talk about it?”

“…I don’t know if I can face him,” Zuko finally says, voice quiet enough that Sokka needs to strain to hear it even as close as they are together. “I thought I could. I know I *need* to. I will, I just—I don’t know if I can.”

“Why not?” Sokka asks, trying to hold back his own opinions on the matter as he sorts through all the ‘can’ and ‘will’ and ‘need’ in Zuko’s words.

“I’m not who he thought I was,” Zuko says, with an incredulous, strangled look that Sokka can read even in the dim light.

“He wasn’t who you thought he was either, though,” Sokka points out.

“No, but—” Zuko bites off the rest of his protest, but Sokka can guess. No, but Iroh doesn’t need Zuko like Zuko needs him. No, but Iroh thought he was seeing all there was of Zuko and Zuko always knew there was more to Iroh. No, but Zuko cares about betraying members of his family unlike the rest of them.

Or maybe that’s just Sokka’s uncharitable interpretations.

“Why do you want from him,” Sokka finally asks. “Not armies or help or anything to do with the Comet. Just—you and him. Zuko and Iroh. What do you want from him?”

Zuko is quiet for a long time, long enough that Sokka would think he isn’t going to answer if it weren’t for the way Zuko’s fingers are fidgeting against the back of his hand. “I want to be able to trust him,” Zuko finally whispers, and fuck if Sokka’s heart doesn’t feel like it's breaking for him, just a little.

“What happens if you tell him that?” Sokka asks when his voice feels like it will come out steady, giving Zuko’s hand a squeeze instead of using his grip to haul Zuko into a hug.

Zuko’s fingers still, the angle of his head turning uncertain. “I don’t…I dont know.”

Sokka finally clears his throat when the silence draws out, Zuko’s scarred eye a thin gleam of gold in the moonlight as he glances up. “What happens if you don’t?”

&#45;-

Sokka stays with him until he nearly falls out of the tree from nodding off, so Zuko unceremoniously hauls him down and urges him back to their tent and ignores the barley-awake supplications to stay that slur into a wordless murmur as Sokka’s head hits the pillow and exhaustion drags him back down.

Zuko’s tired too, but he’s used to that, more than he’s used to being well-rested. And he’s restless, beneath the tiredness—another familiar state—too much to lay down beside Sokka and let his mind turn. He slips back out into the cool night air, taking slow steps toward Uncle’s tent this time instead of back toward the trees. He can feel the possibility of Agni on the horizon, even if the height of the Outer Wall will extend the night. Morning is too close now for more hiding.

Zuko is just settling into a seiza when he feels body-sized movement against his heat sense— it’s been spilling out all night, Zuko feeling far too much wariness to call it back in this camp full of Master benders, only some of whom he can call allies—and it’s not long before steps are padding behind him and Katara plops down at his side, knuckling sleep from her eyes.

“Why aren’t you sleeping?” She asks through a yawn.

“…Can’t.” People don’t usually ask.

“Are you okay?”

Zuko considers that. “I’m not hurt.”

“Okay, even *I* noticed that one,” she mutters, shaking herself to something more like alertness. “What’s wrong? Want to talk about it?”

Zuko gives her a sideways look. “The Water Tribe really likes to talk about things, huh?”

She looks startled for a moment, then offers a rueful smile and a shrug. “Sokka does, at least.”

Zuko hums, a flash of fondness breaking through his anxiousness even as he begins trying to sort his thoughts. *Does* he want to talk about it? Zuko already knows what Sokka thinks, what Sokka’s suggestion is. He doesn’t know that he needs more advice, or that he has the mental capacity to deal with it right now if it’s contradictory. But Agni, it’s like everything is just boiling up inside him and he can’t keep it down, can’t keep his worries and fears in line no matter how much meditative breathing he tries.

Maybe it’s not worth keeping them in anymore, if it’s distracting him this much from everything else.

“What if he hates me?” Zuko finally says, the words practically bursting out of him.

Katara starts, like she’d begun dozing off again in the quiet. “Your—your Uncle?” Zuko can only nod, everything in him still now that he’s put the words out there. “Why would he hate you?”

“He thinks I betrayed him,” Zuko says, his inner fire giving an unhappy twist at the words. “He thinks that the last thing I did for him was betray him for my—for the Fire Lord.”

Katara purses her lips, giving him a curious look. “But you didn’t, right?”

Zuko gives her a sideways look. “Does it matter? You thought I betrayed you, too.” And Zuko’s pretty sure Uncle's already taken himself on his self-revelation field trip.

“Did you?” Katara asks again, voice steady and no hint of reproach in her words even if Zuko can’t help feeling it like an accusation anyway.

“Does it matter?” He pushes back again. “If it looked like I did, that’s what people see.”

“Yes,” Katara says immediately, with so much conviction that Zuko can’t do anything but want to believe her. “Whether you actually did something to someone matters. Way more than what people think you did, or what it looked like.”

“But if Uncle thinks I did something to him…”

“Well does he think that because you did do it and just didn’t mean to? Or does he think it because he doesn’t know all the facts?”

Zuko…supposes that depends on just how much loyalty Iroh thought he was owed, a question Zuko doesn’t feel as equipped to answer as he did before walking into the White Lotus’ camp.

“Your intentions matter,” Katara says, face serious. “So do your actions, and maybe you hurt him without meaning to, and not meaning to doesn’t make the hurt go away. But what’s in your heart still *matters*.”

“Hurt is still hurt, though,” Zuko finally says. It’s not like the pain suddenly didn’t happen just because you’re looking at a scar from a new angle.

“It is,” Katara agrees, clasping the pendant at her throat. “But do you really think it won’t matter if your Uncle is hurting from something he just thinks happened, instead of something you actually did?”

Maybe. She seems so sure, but Sokka’s found plenty of moments to quietly and carefully point out that bad things done for good reasons are still total shit things to do. And Zuko isn’t a particular fan of selectively applied morality. If that applies to Azula, then it applies to Zuko too, or else there’s no point in having rules in the first place if they bend so easily.

Agni’s tits, Zuko doesn’t even know how to start applying any of that to this situation anyway, because he’s starting to think that he followed too well in Iroh’s footsteps without realizing it. If Iroh was in the wrong for having plans and schemes and secret allies and not telling Zuko about it, then isn’t Zuko in the wrong too for having the same? And if Uncle is to be forgiven because he cares, despite the pain he caused, doesn’t that entitle Zuko to the same forgiveness? And if none of what either of them did was okay, but Zuko doesn’t see any other way his own piece of it could have gone—is it alright to just move past the fact that it happened and focus on what comes next?

Zuko sighs, rubbing at his eyes before sending a mostly-asleep-again Katara back to bed. He doesn’t have any answers, and now really isn’t the time for an existential crisis. Aang is already having one of those for all of them. The rest of them need to act.

&#45;-

Uncle wakes with the sun, even if the camp is still dark in the shadow of the Wall. Zuko can hear the movement inside the tent is trying to talk himself into calling out, or at least standing up, when Uncle steps outside with a teapot in hand and rocks to a halt. Zuko lets his inner flame rise to fill his chest and meets Uncle’s shocked eyes, suddenly conscious of what he must look like—travel-worn, tattered clothes that used to be nice, his hair shaggy and loose, tired and mussed and fuck, he probably has forest grit on him from climbing trees, and Sokka doesn’t usually leave hickeys but knowing Zuko’s usually luck he’s probably wearing a necklace of them.

Well. It’s too late for a first impression, on so many counts.

“Uncle,” Zuko says, hearing the formality of his voice as he finds the start of his script and bows forward, the grass damp with dew nearly brushing his forehead. “I—”

Zuko swallows the rest of his carefully planned speech as hard, strong hands suddenly grab his shoulders, pulling him upright. For a heart-stopping moment, Zuko can’t tell if Iroh is turning him away, pushing him back, can only feel the fingers digging into his shoulders, wide and strong and not familiar, not Sokka’s. But in barely a heartbeat the grip shifts and Zuko finds himself wrapped in thick, sturdy arms, pressed tight against Uncle’s comforting, solid bulk as the teapot drops forgotten to the grass.

Uncle is kneeling down on the ground too, which isn’t how Zuko thought this would go. Hugging him, which…Zuko hadn’t dared to even think about hoping for.

“Zuko,” Uncle breathes, his voice full of wonder, his arms tightening even more and head tilting against Zuko’s as he glances toward the sky like he can’t quite believe he’s not dreaming. “My Zuko.”

“You’re okay,” Zuko gasps, tension he could barely even acknowledge he was carrying suddenly loosening so sharp and fast that he can barely breathe through it, lodging in his throat and making his words come out tight and thin.

“Nephew. My Zuko. You are safe,” Uncle is saying, over and over, the words shaking with emotion, and Zuko sags as he registers the pure relief in the statement, his script and his control evaporating in Uncle’s hold.

“I went back and you were *gone*,” Zuko chokes out, the words spilling out as he tries to hold back the hot sting of tears, to try to breathe calm into his inner flame. Uncle makes a low soothing noise, rubbing a slow hand over his back, but Zuko can’t seem to stop himself now that he’s started. “I didn’t know where you were. I tried. I tried. But I got to your cell and you weren’t *there* and I didn’t know.” He heaves for air, tripping over half-remembered terror that he never had time to let himself feel. “I’m sorry, I tried but I didn’t *know*.”

Uncle makes another calming noise, gently rocking him like he’s a child crying over a broken toy, and Zuko can’t even pretend that it doesn’t feel like cool water after days in the desert to let himself sink into it. “Deep breaths, my boy,” Uncle murmurs, waiting for Zuko to suck in a shaky inhale, then another. “Deep breathes. Everything is fine now. Deep breathes. When was this?”

Zuko swallows hard, managing to gasp out, “During the eclipse. I went to break you out but you already…”

“Ah,” Uncle rocks Zuko a bit more, which feels almost like he’s gently shaking loose the rope of anxiety that’s been knotting up Zuko’s spine all night. “I did not know to wait for you.”

“I could tell,” Zuko says, the words coming out sharp and the accompanying spark of frustration is enough for Zuko to pull away to sit on his heels again, swiping at the wetness around his eyes and avoiding Uncle’s gentle, searching, concerned, worried, *Uncle* gaze.

“Forgive me, Nephew,” Uncle says, “For not realizing I should.” A fond smile flickers briefly through the…the regret?—settling on Uncle’s face.

“I—” Zuko snaps his mouth shut, nonplussed. “I should be the one apologizing, not you.”

“There is nothing to apologize for, Nephew.”

“There *is*, I—” Zuko lets out a hollow laugh, scrubbing his hands over his face. Agni’s balls, he practiced his script over and over, words about duty and family and all that Uncle’s tried to do for him and all Zuko's given him in return, all the times Zuko’s pulled back when he knew Uncle was trying to reach out, and now he can’t quite bring himself to say it. “I—”

“There is nothing to apologize for,” Uncle says, more firmly this time.

“You—in Caldera, you wouldn’t even *talk* to me,” Zuko bursts out, different words than he planned, raw and vulnerable and he *hates* it, hates the way Uncle’s face goes all sad but he can’t stop himself, can’t stomach the idea of keeping this in anymore. “I kept coming and you wouldn’t—you just sent cryptic notes, and—I didn’t know what to *do*.”

“I was not angry with you then, Zuko,” Uncle says quietly. “I was sad. I was worried that you had lost your way.”

“Well, I hadn’t,” Zuko snaps, inner fire flaring with defensiveness and irritation, and Sokka would probably think this is messed up too that the familiarity of it is nearly a comfort. “You just—”

“I just what?” Uncle asks, but Zuko just shakes his head. They aren’t on the *Wani* and Uncle isn’t all he has and things don’t have to be this way anymore. Zuko’s been telling himself that all night, but Agni’s tits, on the *Wani* he choked back his words and let loose his fury and what is he supposed to do now when all the words that want to break free feel angry? “What, Nephew,” he presses, expression encouraging as he searches Zuko’s face. “I will not be upset. Not when I finally have you back before me.” And he says it with such genuine evenness, instead of neutral-but-actually-something-else for maybe the first time since Zuko can’t even remember when, that Zuko can’t help but continue.

“You wouldn’t *talk* to me,” Zuko says, glaring at the ground somewhere between their knees. “You wouldn’t *listen.* It felt like you just wanted me to just—I was never going to be a tea server in Ba Sing Se, Uncle. I just wasn’t. It’s not a bad path, but it was never going to be *mine*.” And trying to make himself fit had felt like peeling away parts of himself bit by bit, day by day.

“No,” Uncle says after a moment with a sad kind of smile, brushing the hair back from Zuko’s face and cupping the side of his head and after a tense moment, Zuko relaxes into it, the unfamiliar familiarity of it. “I suppose I always knew that it was too much to hope for, for you to be happy with such a simple life. I know I have not always chosen right, but I have only ever wanted your happiness, Nephew.”

Zuko drops his head forward, for now shoving aside the urge to snap that *simplicity* had nothing to do with it, deciding to just let himself believe Uncle’s words, at least for a bit. To see how they feel, that Zuko’s happiness could matter to Uncle above everything else that’s tangled and confused between them. Zuko closes his eyes and leans into the strength and care in Uncle’s touch as he tries to reorient his world around that belief, wondering if understanding and forgiveness and the thin possibility of future trust can wait. Wondering if for now, just belief can be enough.

Zuko manages to get himself together over the familiar rhythms of a cup of tea enough to feel like he’s on steady ground again. Not drinking it, of course. But watching Uncle make it, absently tracking the rising heat with his bending, feeling the way Uncle’s fire is pushing that heat higher. It’s the first time Zuko has felt another firebender working with heat before, and Zuko lets himself get lost in feeling it through his heat sense, focusing on the intricacies and technical details and delicacy of Uncle’s touch until a cup of jasmine is pressed into his hands and he’s automatically inhaling familiar steam.

“It is good to see you well, Nephew,” Uncle says, amusement crinkling his eyes as Zuko familiarly fails to take a sip.

Zuko nods, clearing his throat and trying not to sag around the evidence of Uncle’s caring. He thinks he’s done more than enough breaking down for one day. Agni’s balls, it's barely past dawn. “You, too.”

Uncle takes a sip of tea, studying Zuko all the while. “May I ask what you have been up to, in these past months? I am told you did not arrive alone.”

Zuko opens his mouth, unsure where to even begin—with Ba Sing Se? Caldera? Azula? With when Uncle had the time to hear anything about how Zuko arrived?—then hesitates. “Can—” He takes a deep breath and starts again. “Can I ask you first?”

Uncle looks faintly surprised, but his nod is easy as he settles himself more comfortably. “What would you like to know, Nephew?”

Zuko glances around, taking in the white and dark blue fabric, the lotus motifs and stylized designs that he’s sure are somehow lotuses too, if you look at them right, and Uncle looking very comfortable in the middle of it all. “What is all this? You’re…a Grand Lotus?”

“Ah. Yes.” Uncle puts on his life-wisdom face. “The Order of the White Lotus is a society founded on principles of—"

“Philosophy and beauty,” Zuko echoes. “Yeah, we heard. But—what do you *do?”* Because Toph’s art museum suggestion sounded pretty on the mark to Zuko, if he ignores the soldiers.

Uncle examines Zuko’s face for a moment, some of that careful neutrality falling over his expression, and Zuko straightens a little, bracing himself. “We seek to return the world to balance.”

Zuko does his best to digest that. It could mean…so many things. “Were you—did—” Uncle waits while he sorts himself out. “How long?” Uncle hesitates, confused. “Did you only come with me for them? This? Did you only come with me for them? This? Because it was easier to do all this away from Caldera?”

“No, Zuko,” Uncle says immediately, back straightening. “I came because I wanted to help you. I have *always* wanted to help you. To keep you safe.”

“Safe,” Zuko echoes, feeling wild, semi-hysterical laughter catching in his throat. Agni’s balls, how much less safe could he have been? “But you were doing all this—Lotus stuff at the same time.”

Uncle nods, face going thoughtful again. “It was important work that I was lucky to be able to bring with me.”

Bring with him. Suggesting he was doing it ever since the Agni Kai. Suggesting he had *before* the Agni Kai, which…well, Piandao is here. And Jeong Jeong deserted so easily, which suddenly looks very different in this light. But for Uncle to have had this in Caldera… he still hasn’t said when it started, and Zuko isn’t sure if it would be better or worse for the Dragon of the West to have found his way to this only a few years ago, or for him to have always been working against the throne.

Would Zuko have been more safe or less, if the White Lotus was never involved?

“The White Lotus sent us to Ba Sing Se,” Zuko finally says. He’s almost positive it’s true, but it’s still a relief to see Uncle’s nods. “The White Lous set up our life there?”

“They made sure we would have a toehold in the city,” Uncle corrects, and Zuko thinks of Jet, with his rickety apartment that barely had space for the three people trying to live in it let alone their occasional fourth. A toehold in a city like Ba Sing Se isn’t nothing.

“Would you have stayed there?” Zuko asks, his inner fire tight and restless when Uncle just gives him a questioning look, so fucking *mild* about it. “You’re Grand Lotus now,” Zuko says, eyes flicking around the tent. Three times as big as any of the others and just for Uncle —the title clearly means *something*. “Did you give it up? Or were you Grand Lotus back then, too, and Mushi was just—just *cover*.” In more ways than Zuko ever realized. “Was I just supposed to live a simple life while you led *three* of them?”

Uncle opens his mouth to speak, expression starting to go tight, but Zuko’s inner flame is burning hotter and hotter, the words tripping out faster and faster, and he slashes Uncle to silence with a tight jerk of his hand. “What does the Grand Lotus even *mean*? Philosophy and beauty and balance? Those are just *words*. And Agni’s balls, if it mattered to you so much why didn’t you *tell me*?” Zuko hears his voice crack over the question, struggling not to sound like a plaintive child. “Did you think you couldn’t trust me,” Zuko presses, searching Uncle’s face and feeling another bubble of hysteria at the idea of just how mutual that might have been. “Did you think I wouldn’t *care*?”

“Zuko,” Uncle finally says, sadness breaking through his neutral mask. “You were always so singular in your cares. I did not want to push more than you wanted onto you, or more than you were ready for.”

“I *learned to brew tea*,” Zuko nearly shouts, fists clenching empty around his disbelief. “I sat through pai sho games and formal dinners and I *played the fucking tsungi horn* because *you* cared, what do you—how was I supposed to be *ready* if I never knew it *existed*?” Uncle’s face is folding around something like pain and maybe regret and Zuko can't—doesn't want— to make himself stop. “Was it—did you not think I could help?” Zuko presses, feeling a little desperate. “I know I was still a kid, but—” But he was old enough to be given his own command, his own mission, his own Agni Kai, a voice that sounds suspiciously like Sokka whispers in the back of his mind. And Zuko is seventeen, now—and a voice that sounds like his own points out that he hasn’t been a kid in a long, long time.

“Nephew,” Uncle says, neutral mask gone now even if his open emotionality is just as difficult to face. “I am sorry for not speaking sooner. I never knew that you would be interested.”

Zuko struggles to process that, barely registering the apology as he tries to understand what kind of interest he could have shown without tipping himself over into open treason. “…Did you think I was that much Ozai’s creature?”

“I think that you were single-minded in your purpose.” A careful statement that isn’t a ‘no.’ Zuko knows all about that. “And you were already growing up so much faster than you should have needed to.”

Well. At least Zuko can comfort himself with the fact that he was *convincing*, even to someone he lived cheek by jowl with for years. It’s not like Zuko wasn’t already aware that Uncle didn’t look below the surface when it came to him, and if it hurts to have it confirmed, the ache is at least dull and familiar rather than new.

But maybe Zuko is being unfair. Maybe Uncle was right to hold back his secrets—to still hold them back—painful as it is to force himself to consider.

Because Zuko isn’t so sure that he would have been able to say yes, if this were extended to him four years ago, or three, or two. Fuck, he doesn’t know that he could say yes *now*. Because returning balance to the world is a noble cause, a necessary one. But Zuko still doesn’t know what interest this international secret network of powerful benders and Masters and leaders of nations—with the former Crown Prince to the Fire Nation and Dragon of the West at its head—is taking in the Fire Nation throne.

Zuko might be here to ask them to take a very particular kind of interest, one that he isn’t entirely sure he can control but one that he has to open the door to anyway with circumstance forcing his hand. But if it was a year ago? If Zuko was still trying to claw his way back home, before any of them definitively knew the Avatar still lived?

Zuko’s heard Uncle’s opinions of Azula. How could Zuko have said yes, if the offer was just for him?

“Would you have ever told me?” Zuko finally says, aware that he can’t quite bring himself to ask what he really wants to know, what he doesn’t know if he can handle pulling into Agni’s light—*or would you have just kept using me until my usefulness ran dry?*

“I always wanted to,” Uncle assures him, the words landing flat against the slowly tightening ball of Zuko’s inner flame. “I always planned to, when the time was right.”

“And when,” Zuko says carefully, looking down at his tea, “Would that have been?” When *could* it have been? Would Uncle have ever said something to him if the Avatar hadn’t come out of the ice? Or would the right time have always been just on the horizon?

Agni, it’s almost too much to think about what might have happened if Zuko had known. Could he and Sokka have found their way to each other sooner, more openly, with less heartbreak on both sides? Could he have chased after Aang to keep him safe and protect him, used the *Wani* to bring the Avatar to waterbending Masters and safely to the Earth Kingdom’s shores rather than put him in chains?

“I wanted for you to feel stronger in yourself, Zuko,” Uncle says gently. “It is no simple thing, to join an Order such as ours, or even to ally with it. I did not wish to press you into something that you would not have chosen for yourself.”

“Maybe,” Zuko says after a long moment, “I would have been stronger if I knew I wasn’t all on my own.”

“I was there,” Uncle protests, face drawn. “I was always there.”

“Were you though?” Zuko feels the way his hands want to shake, to be pushing this, feels the adrenaline making his inner fire thin and jagged around the edges. “When you were dragging me around ports looking for pai sho tiles, were you there for *me*? When the Avatar escaped the first time and you just made some tea, were you there for me or for the White Lotus?” Zuko shoves the hair back from his face, wishing he could just pace and stomp and *move* his way through this. Fuck, he keeps asking but does he really want to know? “Every time you reprimanded me in front of Jee and the crew, were you there for me?”

“I—Zuko, you were learning,” Uncle says. “Learning is important, and just like with firebending, correction is a natural part of the—”

“I was captain!” Zuko cuts in, incredulous. “It might have been a fucking joke that I had it, but it was still *my* command! And that either meant something or it didn’t.” And it’s so blindingly clear which it was, for Uncle, even more now than it already was before.

“It was never my intention to make you feel unsupported, Nephew,” Uncle eventually says, quiet, brow furrowed as he slowly turns the teacup in his hands.

“But was it ever your intention to support me?” Zuko asks, hearing the extra rasp to his voice as if he actually has been screaming.

“I have always wanted what is best for you,” Uncle says, voice firm and absolute and sure and not quite answering the question, and Zuko wonders for a moment if Uncle is even aware that he didn’t.

“And what if what was best for me was going back home?” Zuko asks, staring down at his own cup. “What if it was succeeding in my mission? Resting my honor?” Becoming Crown Prince in more than just name, with everything that would have come with it, from actual authority to back up the perception of it to a world bigger than just the confines of the *Wani*.

“Zuko, I wanted you to throw off the chains you had been taught to live with. I wanted you to become your own—”

“But what if it that’s what *I* wanted for myself,” Zuko breaks in before he has to listen to however that sentence was going to end. “I’m not saying I do, or I did, but what if that’s what I chose?" Zuko says, forcing himself to drag his glare up to Uncle’s eyes. "What happened then?"

“I could *not* see you break yourself for that man,” Uncle says, words suddenly coming hot and fierce, his hand cutting sharp through the air before he jerks himself back under control.

“But I never knew that I had any other option,” Zuko says, feeling suddenly exhausted. Agni, how many different ways does Zuko have in himself to say this?

“You could have always turned to me, Nephew,” Uncle says, voice even again in a way that Zuko suddenly wants to shake and crack and split open so he isn’t the only one here skating on the edge of his control. “I was always there with advice.”

Zuko nearly laughs. “Did it ever seem like I understood it?” He asks, not bothering to try to hide his incredulity. “Agni’s balls, if you had something to say I wish you would have just said it.”

Uncle shakes his head, expression going kind and wise and knowledgeable and Zuko’s inner flame is rising sharp and wild in his throat. “Self-discovery is an important and valuable process. Only you could determine who to be, Zuko, I could not tell you that.”

“Unless it was Lee, right?” Zuko snaps, feeling the words come out barbed and caustic. “Then you’ll tell me every day.”

Uncle draws up short, hurt and uncertainty flickering at the edges of his expression and *fuck*, this isn’t—this isn’t what Zuko wanted. He can’t find it in himself to keep the words in now that he’s started, but hurting Uncle back was never part of the script and Zuko can’t help but feel a sharp stab of regret as the silence draws out that he let it get to this.

“I didn’t want to do it like this,” Zuko finally says, voice low, suddenly feeling the mostly sleepless night dragging at his thoughts. Agni, he’s getting too used to good rest with Sokka. “Yelling and shouting and—I *am* different. I have changed. I *self-discovered* and I’m stronger now, and I didn’t—I don’t want to be back to *this* like we just stepped off the *Wani*.”

“Nephew,” Uncle says after a beat, matching Zuko’s quietness. “I always want you to be able to express yourself to me. Even if what you are expressing is anger.”

Zuko glances away, unsure how to respond when it seems like that’s all he’s ever had inside himself to show.

“I am proud of you, you know.”

Zuko jerks, startling so hard his tea sloshes over his fingers as his eyes fly to Uncle’s gentle, earnest face.

“You are right. You have changed, Zuko. You have grown so much, and so fast. More than I could have ever hoped for,” Uncle says, lips curling into a sad smile. “But also more than I ever wanted to ask of you.” He sighs, expression going…wistful? “Some days it feels like it was only yesterday that I first held you the night you were born. So small but already fighting, screaming your fury at the world. I would not say that ever changed,” Uncle adds, sounding *fond* about it, “And it can be hard for an old man to admit, sometimes, that his child has grown.”

Zuko swallows hard, so overwhelmed he feels numb with it, his inner fire nearly still as he tries to—to *process*, to understand and to hear and to—Uncle said—does that mean—

“And I can only hope that one day you will forgive me for being slow to see it,” Uncle continues, voice going heavy but his eyes staying steady on Zuko’s face. “I hope I will have the chance to make it up to you. The habit of freely offering of oneself—it is not an easy one to build, after a lifetime of not.”

“I know,” Zuko says, finding his voice again even as he feels thrown all over again by the fact that he *does* know, part of him totally unsure what to do with the fact that he knows exactly what Uncle is talking about. “But that doesn’t mean you can’t, you just—you need to want to, and just—start small, and realize that it’s okay, and then do it again, even if it feels like it’s going against everything you know, because you can’t do it all alone and you want the other person to be part of your life and you need them to know that, and you want them to know how much you value their—" Zuko nearly bites his tongue as he finally registers the words tripping out of his mouth.

“Ah,” Uncle says after a moment. “Indeed.” He takes a sip of his tea. “And how is Master Sokka these days?”

Agni burn it. “Good,” Zuko says, blushing and forcing himself to meet Uncle’s eyes, nearly throwing the words down like a challenge as he wills his gaze to stay up. “He’s good.”

“I am glad to hear it,” Uncle says serenely, inscrutable as ever, but…Zuko thinks he means it. “I look forward to whatever you might one day wish to share with me about him.”

Zuko…has no idea what to do with that, and after a moment he just takes a sip of his tea for lack of anything any better response, tasting it go down honey-sweet in what Zuko knows is a travesty to proper tea making, just the way Uncle knows he likes best.

Sokka is itching with the need to get his hands on Zuko by the time he finally catches sight of a familiar set of shoulders weaving between the tents over to their little clearing. Waking up this morning and realizing that Zuko wasn’t there, that he was with Iroh—even a round of training with Master Piandao hadn’t been enough to fully capture Sokka’s focus, which Piandao had noted, pointedly and dryly, before telling him to go tend to his blade while Piandao sparred with Suki instead.

“Zuko,” Sokka calls, something in his chest leaping when Zuko’s head snaps toward the sound of his voice.

Sokka hastily sets his sword aside and hurries over, scanning Zuko from head to toe on the way and relaxing when he sees that Zuko looks tired and maybe like he’s been crying— which has Sokka's adrenaline wanting to spike—but not like he's currently, actively upset. His shoulders are loose, gold eyes focused and a smile curling the corner of his mouth as he approaches Sokka to greet him with a quiet, almost shy, “Hey.”

“How’d it go? Good? You’re okay?” The words spill of Sokka in a rush as he closes the distance between them to brush Zuko's bangs back, studying his face and making a note to do things like this more often when Zuko's eyes flare with surprise before tilting in pleasure as Zuko turns into his touch, pressing a quick kiss to his wrist, the ease with which Zuko offers it its own assurance.

“I’m fine,” Zuko says, lips tilting, inviting Sokka into the joke. “It was…good.”

“You feeling better?”

“Yeah.”

“Good,” Sokka says, grinning in relief. “Good. Do I need to crack any skulls for you?”

Zuko winces. “Please do not cack my Uncle’s skull.”

“Noted,” Sokka says, aiming for levity to cover the little burst of what might be disappointment. That’s a good thing. It makes Zuko happy, and Sokka is more than happy about that.

“Will you be joining us in training, Prince Zuko?”

Sokka and Zuko both jolt at Piandao’s voice, Zuko freezing a little and Sokka taking a step back in response ashe registers their position—Sokka cupping Zuko’s jaw, Zuko’s hands settled low in Sokka’s waist. There aren’t many other ways to interpret that and Sokka abruptly realizes that *Iroh* being fine with him and Zuko doesn’t mean every Fire Nation citizen in this camp will be, even if Iroh’s the one in charge.

Zuko clears his throat, offering a picture-perfect bow. “I would be honored, Master Piandao.” A Prince replying to a respected teacher, *not* someone scared and trying to avoid reprisal, and Sokka feels the hard spike of readiness in his chest slowly ease.

Piandao’s eyes flick between them. “Maybe Master Sokka will be able to focus now, too.” Zuko cuts him a sideways look, and Sokka flushes. Sure, he was a bit *distracted*, wondering if Zuko was okay, but there was no need to *announce* it.

“Probably not,” Suki says, with the weary wisdom of experience, and Sokka blushes even harder as Zuko ducks his head, a smirk lingering around his lips.

“Indeed,” Piandao says, sounding amused. “I had a different set of dao in mind to reunite, Prince Zuko. But I suppose this will do as well.”

“It’s…not quite the same,” Zuko mutters after a moment, which means at least one of them has a clue.

Piandao raises an eyebrow. “I should hope not.”

Zuko chokes a little, flushing pink at the dry words. Sokka glances to Suki, who just shrugs, equally confused by the byplay. But Piandao is looking quietly amused and Zuko’s shoulders are relaxed, his face almost happy, so Sokka is content to wait on being let in on the joke and to appreciate the sight of Zuko looking so at ease and the way he tugs Sokka forward into the training ring without even seeming to think about it .

“You’ll never guess what Pakku said,” Katara bursts out as she strides into the tent, looking flushed and energized and a little bit ferocious still from her bending practice with the man. Sokka can still feel Toph and Bumi off somewhere rumbling the earth.

“That women belong in the kitchen?” Sokka guesses.

Katara snorts. “That he’s going to marry Gran Gran.”

Sokka blinks. “What?”

“Yeah. Apparently, after the White Lotus does its thing, he’s going to go South and ‘help his sister tribe reestablish itself.’”

Sokka slowly shuts his mouth. “…He does make a nice necklace.”

Katara grins, all teeth. “Gran Gran is going to boil his balls on day one.”

“Evocative.”

“But accurate.”

He rolls his eyes. “She would at least have the manners to skin him first. You’ve seen that woman with a whale-walrus,” he protests when Katara starts laughing. “Pakku doesn’t stand a chance.”
