Sokka wakes up in darkness. He’s confused for a moment—there’s no sound, no light—but then he feels the hot breath scalding his chest with each of Zuko’s exhales, the fine tremoring tension in his firebender’s body. “Zuko?”

Zuko’s words are hot enough to burn. “…The Comet is coming.”

“What?”

Zuko raises his head, and Sokka’s breath catches for a moment as he almost imagines the flash of moonlight filtering through the tent flap is Zuko’s eyes glowing gold instead. “Sozin’s Comet. It’s…it’s not here yet. But it’s close.”

Sokka frowns, hands coming up to Zuko’s waist, feeling the dryness of his skin compared to the sweat beading Sokka’s at every point they’re touching from the heat coming off him. “Are you okay?”

“Yes,” Zuko sighs, shuddering a little, shifting. “It feels…”

“Good?” Sokka can feel how *good* Zuko is feeling against his thigh, but Zuko isn’t focused on that right now, not that this is a private tent if he were.

“It’s like there’s another sun,” Zuko murmurs. “Just for me, just…” He shifts off Sokka’s body, cool air rushing in as Zuko rolls onto his side and tugs Sokka to mirror him. He raises a hand between them, twisting his fingers and a ball of flame comes easily, which isn’t a surprise in and of itself except this one is…

“Oh,” Sokka breathes, biting his lip against the urge to reach out to it. This one is like no fire Sokka has ever seen. Like all those flickering edges of Zuko’s flame ever since he got back from his trip with Aang have been concentrated down, reds and oranges and yellows and greens and purples and little flecks of blue.

Zuko extinguishes the flame after a moment, darkness sweeping back in except for the occasional errant spark on Zuko’s breath. Sokka blinks, willing his eyes to adjust as he reaches out to find Zuko’s arm, running his fingers over it, soothing and slow, matched to the rhythm of Zuko’s breaths. It’s just late enough to edge into early, the others still firmly asleep, but Sokka doesn’t think they’ll be getting back to sleep, not with the way Zuko is clearly adjusting to whatever the Comet is doing to him.

“Are you meditating with Iroh this morning?”

Zuko nods, his fingers skating up Sokka’s ribs. “Some katas, I think.”

“He’ll probably be awake soon too, then, if he isn’t already.” Sokka presses his hand to Zuko’s chest, feeling the sparrowkeet-fast beat of his heart, trying to imagine what it must be like to feel what Zuko is feeling right now, to feel a power like that inside his body.

“Probably,” Zuko agrees, the hot words drawing prickles of sweat against Sokka’s skin. So much banked heat, so much barely restrained fire…When does it become too much for one person to contain?

“Sit up, then,” Sokka says, shoving himself up and shivering as the night air touches his sweat-beaded skin. “I’ll do your hair.”

Zuko obligingly kneels up, but Sokka can see the questioning look even in the darkness.

“It’s been getting in your face when you train,” Sokka says, offering a little smile, aiming for levity. “I don’t want you to burn it off.”

Zuko exhales a laugh but turns to give Sokka his back, relaxing as Sokka takes a moment to indulge himself and just card his fingers through Zuko’s hair, finger-combing out the thick, silky strands. Then he gathers up a chunk from the front, fingers moving in familiar rhythms he doesn’t need to see to execute as he weaves a braid into Zuko’s hair, working slowly backward.

“I know you didn’t like all the Fire Lord talk yesterday,” Sokka murmurs. “But can I say something?” He needs to just…get this out there, when it’s just the two of them, before it’s other people and opinions and taking sides.

Zuko takes a long, deep, nearly meditative breath before whispering, “Yes,” a few sparks coming out along with the word.

“I know you want to go to help Azula, and if that’s what you think is best then I support you. You know way better than I do how all this political stuff goes. But I just want you to know that I think you’d be really good at it,” Sokka says softly, firmly. “I’m not saying you need to do it. But I think you would be good. You care so much, about all your people. And I think that maybe the Fire Nation hasn’t had someone like that in a long time. And loyalty and resources are supposed to flow up, and protection and care down, right?” Or something close enough to that, Sokka can dig the letter out if he needs to be sure. “It could be good for the Fire Nation to have that again.”

“…It’s not just about caring for people,” Zuko finally says, quiet, not fighting the issues, just…pointing it out, Sokka thinks.

“I think you’re better at the politics part than you give yourself credit for, too,” Sokka replies, refusing to think about Iroh’s words, about how much harder it would be to be with Zuko as Fire Lord than as a Prince trying to find his way in the world, which is all Zuko’s ever been as long as Sokka’s known him.

Zuko sighs, leaning back slightly into Sokka’s touch. “It scares me.”

Sokka’s fingers pause at the admission before he orders them back to work, waiting until he has the rhythm again before asking, “Why?”

“…I don’t want to be like my father.”

“Zuko.” Sokka stills again. “You could never be.” But he isn’t exactly surprised by the fear. He remembers how much that portrait of Ozai already looked like Zuko, like Sokka was looking at a template of what Zuko would become as he aged.

“He wasn’t supposed to have power and he took it,” Zuko whispers. “And I…how could I take it from Azula and not be like him? Even just a little? And then *being* Fire Lord, like he is…needing to be strong, and Sokka, I get so angry sometimes, it would be…easy.”

“Except you care, Zuko,” Sokka says quietly. “So much. And you have people who care about you back. He doesn’t.”

Zuko shifts, either in response to the words or to Sokka tying off the braid, but he doesn’t reply, breaths still steady and even as Sokka starts working on the other side, so Sokka carefully puts aside everything else he could say on that topic for later and gets back to the original point he wanted to make.

“Zuko, I want you to make the choice that’s right for you. But I don’t want you to put aside what *you* want just because you think you have to. Even though I know that’s your thing.”

Zuko huffs out a little laugh, which is good, hand briefly reaching back to brush against Sokka’s leg. “Yours, too.”

“Yeah, well, it’s a hard habit to kick,” Sokka says, pressing a quick kiss to the back of Zuko’s neck. “But I don’t want you regretting *not* doing something, either,” Sokka finishes, “Sometimes that’s just as hard, especially if you didn’t do it because of what someone else wanted for you, not what you wanted for yourself.”

Zuko sighs a gentle drift of sparks, though fewer this time. “I don’t want to betray my sister,” he finally says, low and tight and even hoarser than usual.

“I don’t want you to need to,” Sokka says softly. For Zuko’s sake, no matter how much the idea of Azula as Fire Lord quietly terrifies him. “I’d love nothing more than to leave it all to her and be able to take you South and build a nice house and have you as my own personal space heater for the rest of forever.”

Zuko actually laughs at that, muffling the sound against his hand when Katara stirs across the tent. “Is that all I am to you?”

“It would be a significant benefit during the winter,” Sokka says with mock seriousness. “And I’m sure I could find other uses for you.”

“I’m sure,” Zuko agrees, voice low with amusement.

Sokka takes a deep breath, giving Zuko’s hair a gentle tug as he gets serious again. “There are other ways to let your sister down, though. You told me back in the North that she was too much of a prodigy too young. That she probably wouldn’t make it to Fire Lord without you around.”

Zuko is still, wisps of his hair moving gently in the heat coming off his body.

“I don’t want you to be so worried about stepping on her toes that you leave her to drown. Because I think you would regret that even more.” Zuko’s nod is infinitesimal. “And again. I'm not saying you need to do anything. But if you see Azula, and the question comes up of who’s going to take the crown…just think before it happens about what you need to see from her to be comfortable with her taking it, okay? And also the choices you can make, so if you're there, and you do see something…you’re ready. Just in case.”

Sokka ties off the second braid, tracing his fingers back up over the familiar Water Tribe knots, gently shaking Zuko’s hair so the braids settle in among the loose strands. “It’s your choice, Zuko. I’ll do everything I can to make sure it’s your choice, if that’s what you need from me. I just want to make sure you feel prepared if you have to make it.” He can hear the echo of Katara’s voice from the streets of Ba Sing Se, urging him to think about the hard things that might be coming so they don’t paralyze him when they arrive.

Zuko nods slowly, a hand absently touching one of the braids as it swings forward. “Thank you.”

Sokka presses another chaste kiss to the nape of his neck, hugging him close until Zuko finally disentangles himself to leave for the day, knowing that Zuko isn’t thanking him for his hairstyling.

&#45;-

Uncle raises an eyebrow when he takes in Zuko’s hair in the gray early morning light but doesn’t otherwise offer a comment. The weight of them is odd, pulling on his scalp, brushing against his cheek. Zuko isn’t used to anything like this, having his hair loose but still held back, the slight tension so different than a topknot of phoenix tail.

It’s…nice, and for once Zuko wishes there was a mirror around. Sokka had been almost shy about it when he sent Zuko off to meet Uncle, which makes Zuko wonder if there’s a little more to it than just a hairstyle. He’s going to have to see how Katara reacts.

“Good morning, Nephew,” Uncle murmurs. “May Agni shine bright upon your day.”

“May she burn everlasting,” Zuko says, the rote reply coming easy, along with his bow, hands forming the eternal flame.

Uncle smiles, returning the gesture, equal to equal instead of teacher to student, and Zuko blinks, nonplussed as Uncle straightens and offers him a bland look. “Shall we run through some katas?”

Zuko nods, cautious during warmup of the wild edge to his fire. He has it pulled back toward his center, but it comes fast to his hands in an almost liquid rush, roiling under his skin, bigger than he should be able to contain for so long on his own. But it doesn’t feel like he’s overextending himself, it just feels like…a storm. One sitting right in his chest, gathering, slowly sliding lightning straight into his inner flame.

Agni’s balls, if this is what the Comet feels like, and it isn’t even here yet? Zuko glances over at Uncle, noting that he doesn’t show any outward signs of strain, feeling nothing but Uncle’s usual pool of calm control when he slides out a flicker of heat. Maybe he just isn’t good enough at governing his own inner flame to brush off the effects like Uncle clearly can, after so long without proper training. Or maybe his inner flame has just always burned a different way.

They flow together into their first kata after warming up, one that requires precision and timing more than power. It’s one of the basic forms, one of Uncle’s favorites that Zuko knows inside and out, and yet…this morning he can’t wholly get the feel of it. He’s off somehow, in a way he can’t quite pin down. He wants to flow where the form would have him rigid, wants to whip his fire where he’s supposed to punch it forward, wants to move when he’s supposed to root deep.

The second kata isn’t any better, even as Zuko feels his chi flowing more easily with his body fully warm and his mind more focused. This is one of the quieter, breath-control heavy forms. Despite the steady, even flow of his breaths, though, Zuko can feel that his edges aren’t as crisp as they should be, that his fire is dipping where it should rise, curling at the ends and rolling back over itself.

Zuko is fully aware of Uncle’s quick, neutral-but-concerned looks. He pointedly ignores them, though, and just moves into the third kata, letting his inner flame pull him this time, following where it gently tugs. His fire still feels bigger than it normally is, wilder than it should be. But it doesn’t have an aggressive edge, isn’t fighting him though, and when Zuko manages to find a lighter set of footwork that still matches the beats of the kata, his inner flame crests in response, settling easily into his hands.

“You have developed an…interesting style, Nephew,” Uncle observes as they begin cooling down once Agni is truly beginning to climb the sky, his pause somehow deliberate and encouraging at the same time.

Zuko shrugs, biting back a surprisingly fond smile. He never thought he’d miss all those neutral-but-not expressions and significant pauses and speaking silences, but there’s something comforting about them in their familiarity. “I guess.” Caldera Standard certainly doesn’t sit easily on him anymore, but Zuko’s known that for a while. Whatever he has now, something born of too long without proper instruction and too many days playing with his swords and the touch of dragon fire and copying Toph and Katara and Aang—Zuko finds his inner fire comes easily to whatever this is, where the bright-sparkling edges of it can’t find a place in the exacting angles of Caldera Standard. And he can be content with that.

“Perhaps you can share it with me one day,” Uncle suggests with so much neutrality that Zuko almost doesn’t register the words, nearly tripping out of his cooldown kata when he does.

“Um—I—” Zuko pulls up short and stares at Uncle. “You—What?”

“I would greatly enjoy learning from the Avatar’s firebending master,” Uncle says evenly, moving gracefully through the deliberate motions of the cooldown. “The opportunity to learn from someone who has studied the other elements so deeply—it is a rare thing, these days.”

“…Oh,” Zuko says, touching one of his braids. “I—should Aang be there?”

“That isn’t necessary,” Uncle says serenely. “Just yourself would be more than sufficient, Nephew.”

“Oh,” Zuko says again, not sure why he’s blushing except that his inner fire is suddenly turning and flipping in his throat, flaring high when it’s already so big, so much. “Sure, I— sure. That—yes. Sure.”

“Excellent,” Uncle says, smiling. “I look forward to it.”

“…Me, too,” Zuko says after a beat, a little part of him nearly surprised to realize that it’s true.

The second day of planning, the day before the Comet, is supposed to be all about logistics. The gritty details of what they’re actually going to do tomorrow, now that they’re all largely aligned around the four-part Caldera-Ba Sing Se-Airship-Hope-Aang-Shows-Up strategy.

Katara makes a little noise of surprise next to Sokka when Zuko walks in with Iroh, and Sokka is struck all over again seeing Zuko’s dark hair partially pulled back in a Water Tribe style, the braid brushing the pale skin of his cheek and neck as his head turns. All it needs are some beads, Sokka thinks. Blue, obviously. But maybe something gold, too? And that Fire Nation burgundy, of course. Or black, so you would barely even know it was in Zuko’s hair except when it catches the light and throws back the shine of Zuko’s own flames…

“Subtle,” Katara says dryly, pulling him out of his daydreaming.

“It kind of is,” Sokka points out. Braiding someone’s hair doesn’t necessarily have to be an intimate thing. Sokka’s done Katara’s hair before, and she’s done his, and Sokka used to sit patiently back home while the little kids practiced thick, clumsy plaits in his hair around the winter fires.

Though the braid Sokka put in Zuko’s hair…it’s not a lover’s twist, because Sokka wouldn’t do that without asking Zuko first, but his fingers must have had a life of their own because… it’s definitely reminiscent of one. Not that Sokka thinks that particular fact is in any way a secret, in this group, even if Pakku is looking like someone replaced his entire breakfast with bitter weed and Jeong Jeong is scowling enough for Sokka to think they must know a thing or two about Southern Water Tribe braids.

Or maybe that’s just their reaction to seeing something so clearly Water Tribe on their intended Fire Lord, and if so Sokka hopes they choke on it. Iroh at least seems blessedly neutral about it, an ease between him and Zuko that’s a relief to see, and Piandao just gives it a thoughtful look, glancing between Sokka and Zuko and seeming utterly unruffled, and that’s about the only Fire Nation opinion other than Zuko’s that Sokka wants to hear on the matter.

&#45;-

Sokka hates all Fire Nation opinions right now. All of them.

“What do you mean I can’t come! You can’t go *alone*!”

“Definitely not,” Iroh says immediately, all Grand Lotus immovable.

Zuko scowls at his uncle before returning his attention to Sokka. “You can’t come to Caldera with me.”

Katara frowns, face sympathetic. “I know you want to keep Sokka safe,” she starts, but Zuko is already shaking his head.

“It’s not about the danger.”

“It’s absolutely about the danger,” Sokka protests. The danger to *Zuko*, and Spirits, he hates that he’s needing to negotiate the space between tactical strategist and friend and lover in front of fucking *Pakku*.

Zuko hesitates, apology cracking his determination for a brief second, and in the gap Iroh speaks. “It’s about the laws.”

“It’s about *Azula* and the laws,” Zuko adds.

“It’s about *Azula*, full stop,” Sokka says, wondering how he can be the only one seeing this. Zuko *has* to be thinking this, right? “I know about the laws, I wouldn’t try to *do* anything. But Zuko, I don’t want you to have to face her alone.”

“What does everyone keep talking about,” Katara cuts in, casting a confused look around the table where Toph is wearing a look of dawning, grim comprehension and Jeong Jeong is rather pointedly looking at nothing, and Piandao is looking at Sokka with something like regret. “What laws?”

“Sozin made same-sex couples illegal in the Fire Nation,” Sokka says bluntly, setting aside Katara’s shock to deal with later and shifting to fully face Zuko. “But I’m not saying I’d be there as your boyfriend. Zuko, I really think you should have a friend with you for this.” Even if it’s not Sokka, Zuko should have someone there. None of them should be alone tomorrow.

Zuko fiddles with the fabric of his pants beneath the table. “If you come with me to Caldera, and I’m trying to challenge for the throne. It—I’m opening myself up to being challenged back.”

“Okay,” Sokka says slowly, frowning. “I get that this is one of those perception things. Is Azula not..?” Sokka isn’t quite sure how to finish the sentence—supportive? Because Zuko said only a week ago that this wouldn’t be a big deal compared to everything else he’s done.

“It’s not *that*,” Zuko says—which is a relief, actually—and Piandao speaks into his hesitation from across the table.

“If Zuko were to challenge for the throne and bring along…proof, if you will, of…”

“Dishonorable activity,” Jeong Jeong finishes bluntly. “According to the laws.”

“Yes,” Piandao agrees evenly. “It opens him up to having his claim invalidated.”

“But isn’t he already doing plenty of that?” Suki frowns. “No offense, but if we’re talking dishonorable activity, the whole the whole working with the Avatar, exile, price on your head thing seems like it would matter more.”

“If Fire Lord Ozai falls, then certain beliefs not based in law fall with him,” Iroh says softly.

Toph makes a considering sound. “Like the belief that Zuko is a traitor?”

Iroh nods. “If no one with enough…authority, I suppose, is around to maintain the perception, then everyone can decide to not act on it.”

Katara stares. “Everyone just pretends like it didn’t happen?”

“…Basically,” Zuko mutters. “The Fire Lord is never wrong.”

“Well, who would have enough authority,” Suki asks, clearly already in problem-solving mode, except this isn’t the problem Sokka is trying to solve right now.

“The royal family,” Zuko shrugs.

“The Fire Sages,” Iroh adds.

Zuko pulls a face. “Not lately.”

“Things might be different with a Fire Lord below the age of majority,” Iroh cautions.

Zuko snorts. “Don’t bet on it, with Azula. They know that cold fire so young hasn’t happened before, too.”

“Wait,” Sokka cuts in before Zuko and Iroh can really get into an argument on the balance of theological and secular power, which is fascinating and Sokka does in fact want to hear about, but later. “Can we just back up to Zuko being alone? Why can’t someone be there if people just pretend?”

Jeong Jeong sighs, giving Sokka a long-suffering look like he’s a particularly slow student who keeps failing to get the point, which maybe Sokka is but only because no one is answering his questions. “Because if the proof is walking around with the Crown Prince, before he can take the throne, then there are plenty of people in Caldera with more than enough standing to challenge his fitness.”

Zuko clears his throat. “Because of Azula,” he offers quietly, which Sokka is pretty sure isn’t the same answer Jeong Jeong just gave, but seems to be the one Zuko thinks is more relevant. “If you’re there, then you’re a threat to me.”

And Azula doesn’t tolerate threats to her brother, Sokka silently finishes, the answer no less jarring and unwelcome as it slithers down his spine for the fact that he saw it coming.

“Okay,” Sokka says slowly, trying to pivot, to shuffle between backup plans for the next best option. “But that’s just me. You still don't have to go alone. Not to face Azula.” Because she’s one of the most dangerous people Sokka has ever met, sure. But more because she’s dangerous to Zuko specifically, more about the fact that Zuko cares about his sister so deep and strong that Sokka doesn’t even want to imagine what it would do to him to feel like he’s been driven to a place of needing to actively pit himself against her. And mostly because Sokka is pretty sure that risk isn’t wholly out of the realm of possibility, and he desperately doesn’t want Zuko to have to face it without any support, no matter how much he can see Zuko getting ready to dig in his heels about it.

If Sokka didn’t know that Zuko can dig his heels in as deep as any earthbender, he would certainly be learning it now.

&#45;-

If Sokka didn’t know that Iroh can’t read his nephew as well as he thinks he can—Sokka wonders how far ahead Zuko was thinking with all those avoided pai sho games—then he would certainly have the proof of it after this.

“I don’t need anyone with me.”

“Nephew…” Iroh has cycled through Grand Lotus, General, Dragon of the West, and is trying again as Uncle.

“I’m not going to bring an *army* to talk to my own sister.”

“Not an army,” Sokka says, trying to give another Iroh a warning look. “Just a person or two to help. They don’t have to fight, or say anything to anyone other than you. But Zuko, regardless of how it goes with Azula, it’s going to be hard. You deserve to have someone there supporting you.”

“Just a few soldiers,” Iroh tries again, which is *not* what Sokka is trying to say, *fuck*. “A small squad used to covert operations.”

Oh, that was a misstep. Sokka winces as Zuko’s scowl ratchets up to a glare. “This is between me and her, and I am *not* bringing potentially hostile foreign nationals into—”

Jeong Jeong matches Zuko glare for glare. “The White Lotus is not *hostile—”*

“This is Fire Nation business, not—”

“What if I go?”

Sokka holds his breath as Zuko swings around to look at Katara, his glower freezing on the edge of something like surprise. Not an immediate rejection, and Iroh thankfully stays quiet and doesn't jump in to talk about soldiers and dig Zuko in even deeper.

“I can heal, and if I have to, I can fight. I know how to deal with lighting,” she says, eyes on Sokka, before transferring her gaze to Zuko. “And I’ve fought Azula before with neither of us getting hurt.” Thank the fucking Spirits she’s been listening. “And Zuko, you know I can work fast if it’s just the two of us. And if it’s just me, then it’s not an army, or a boyfriend. It’s just a friend. Even if that friend is a foreign national,” she adds, the last bit with more than a little tartness.

Sokka’s lungs are starting to feel tight from not breathing, but Zuko looks like he’s actually considering it, so Sokka isn’t going to do a single fucking thing that might disrupt that.

Finally Zuko shifts, casting Sokka a glance too quick to read before looking back at Katara. “You shouldn’t have to…”

Sunrise comes to a world on the edge of burning. The clouds are heavy above, the sky dark even though Zuko can feel that it’s well into morning. The pale light Agni should be shining even through the thick cloud cover in the east is gone, though. Overpowered, which sends a visceral kick through Zuko's chest that has his inner flame roiling in response. Instead, it’s like the entire sky is backlit, the beginnings of an inferno flickering through a paper screen, not yet caught but ready to flare to life.

“Can you feel it,” Uncle asks, stepping up beside him, face turned to the sky with something as close to awe on it as Zuko’s ever seen.

“Yes,” Zuko whispers, wondering if it’s possible for his very bones to turn to flame.

“I’ll see you on the other side,” Sokka finally says, grabbing Zuko’s hand and giving it a squeeze. Zuko’s gold eyes are molten as they flicker from the base of Sokka’s neck to his face before he leans in, resting his forehead against Sokka’s for a bare, burning moment before straightening and reluctantly pulling away.

“Be smart out there,” Zuko murmurs, bright sparks flickering on the words.

The city is dark, red-lit, some kind of twisted parody of a celebration. Limp flags line the street, bearing the Eternal Flame and the Rising Phoenix. Garlands drape across the streets, braziers burning at every crossroads in celebration of a new Fire Lord. Palace servants mingle with citizens and nobles, furtive, heads ducked, feet pointed toward the rim rather than Caldera’s center. The air is full of shouts—not the cheering of a crowd, or the enthusiasm of a festival, but brief, high, tight bursts that are quickly choked off.

It’s an atmosphere that Zuko instantly recognizes, even if he’s only experienced it once before, the morning he woke to find his Grandfather dead and his Father on the throne. A Fire Lord consolidating power can be a dangerous thing, especially unplanned, unforeseen. And Azula was already dangerous.

“We have to hurry,” Zuko interrupts, breaking into a jog, feeling his braids bouncing with the movement and suddenly achingly aware of the dao jostling against him with every step. He brought them because he felt naked without them, because he wanted something other than the fire boiling under his skin to rely on, but Agni, they suddenly feel less like a reassurance and more like an inevitable weight against his back.

His inner flame shudders, volatile against his emotions, and Zuko sends his fire sense spinning out around him, catching on to fires as he passes and seeking ahead and letting it pull him into a run.

She kneels, flanked by Fire Sages and nothing else. A statement—that Azula needs nothing but herself and Agni at her side in order to rule.

Or that she has nothing but herself. Depending on how you look at it.

The courtyard is largely untouched, but the palace Zuko walked through to get here was in shambles. Streaked with lightning scars, ash and dust across the walls, bodies that should be there missing, and he doesn’t know if it’s because they fled or were killed but either way it’s all a *waste*.

Zuko and Azula have always had rules. From the very beginning, there were the rules they needed to heed to survive—mind your father, don’t cling to your mother, chin up, shoulders straight, no weeping, no crying. But there were the rules they had for each other, too, the ones they handed down with no adult telling them what to do. For Zuko, things like don’t disagree too loud or you will get noticed, go down easy but never *stay* down, don’t let them know you’re still fighting. And for Azula, things like don’t let them realize what you are, better to put it back on the shelf unused than waste it, that a Fire Lord sees to the good of her people.

It’s been hard. Zuko got worse and worse at avoiding notice, and Azula doesn’t always have the same conception as Zuko does of value, of waste, of what’s hers. But it’s never been hard because she decided she didn’t need them anymore.

Taking in Azula’s ragged hair and smudged lipstick, the half-grin on her face that’s all snarl and no show, her expression raw and wild and burning—

Unused fire is dangerous. That’s one of the first lessons a firebender learns, the dangers of letting fire grow, letting too much build too fast, the risks that come when you can’t find a way to bleed off the edges and the urgency and the hunger, when you can't let it out as flame, or heat, or whatever way you can. And Zuko knows it’s a different kind of danger entirely when you don’t know how to take the fierce edges of something alien and let it skim along your inner flame, how to let your inner fire dance and twine with it until the wild thing becomes yours.

So Zuko knows, the moment he sees Azula, that he isn’t here to shore up her rule and help her consolidate power anymore. He knows that this is what that boiler engine looks like when it's stoked too high and finally breaks, the explosion that comes when the fire has never known how to be anything but contained.

He knows, he just doesn’t want to admit it. Not yet.

Azula twitches, raising her gaze, sweeping the courtyard, tawny eyes bright, bright, bright as they meet his without a shred of surprise.

“Zuzu.” His name almost like a sigh even as it carries across the courtyard. “So nice of you to finally join us.”

“Azula.”

Zuko knows, but he still has to try. After all, knowing when to stop has always been the one lesson—the one rule*—*Azula could never find a way to make stick.

Suki’s voice is quiet. “We aren’t going to make it.”

“I know,” Sokka says, grim. He can already see the fire pouring forth on that lead ship from what can only be Ozai’s hands. The blaze is bigger than anything Sokka has ever seen from a single man, sending bright spots dancing across his vision. But still not close enough, still too far away as it jets toward the earth below, trees nothing but kindling under the force and heat of it.

“Plan C?”

Sokka is reaching for the next contingency when an explosion of firebending suddenly rises up from the ground, meeting Ozai’s flames and sending fire sheeting outward.

“Aang!”

“What the fuck,” Toph snarls, grabbing at the console as the ship rocks beneath the force of the blast. “Aang is the plan?”

“Aang is here,” Suki shouts, turning to Sokka with a wide grin.

“What? Where?”

“Fighting the Fire Lord,” Sokka laughs, shoving his hands through his hair. Shit. *Shit*. Aang is actually *doing it*. The bet-it-all-on-hopes-and-prayers plan is actually *working*.

“Alright, Twinkletoes!” Toph grins, cracking her knuckles. “Are we helping him or what?”

Sokka freezes on the edge of relief, eyes cutting from the firebending tearing through the sky to the airships still moving forward, each with their own cone of Comet-powered flame beginning to touch down. A plan set in motion stays in motion. What had Zuko said? That the infrastructure is in place regardless of who is at its head? “We need to stop the airships.”

“So…Plan D?”

Sokka takes a deep breath and firmly, gently, decisively sets aside the foolish hope that this could ever have been done without sinking more soldiers into the Ocean’s grip. They’ll be in battle armor now. The naval ships are too far behind, and the shore is close, but…without a waterbender, not close enough. Spirits, he hopes Zuko can forgive him. He hopes he can forgive himself. “How do you guys feel about a controlled crash?”

Suki purses her lips. “Do they crash too?”

Toph raises her eyebrow. “Do we survive?”

“That’s the idea,” Sokka says, and gives the steering wheel a twist.

&#45;-

“Have you come to celebrate with me, Brother?” Azula drawls, still looking down at him from her knees. “On this momentous day of my coronation? Did you bring your *friend?”* Her eyes finally find Katara. “Or maybe you found yourself a new one. Really, Zuko, so fickle.”

Zuko ignores her searching barbs. “Can we talk?”

Azula’s head tilts, predatory, eyes glittering. “You want to talk, Zuzu? *Before* my coronation?”

Zuko wavers, trying to parse the truth, the lie, wondering if he needs to risk abandoning the attempt entirely. Can he dare to believe in the fear that she’s beyond the point of needing—or maybe remembering—codes and signals and the language of siblings that slides between and beneath and around the words everyone else hears?

“What could you possibly have to talk to me about?” Azula demands, surging to her feet, the Fire Sages stumbling back from her. “You should be groveling for my forgiveness.” Her voice turns venomous. “You should be begging me on your knees.”

“Azula, I just want to talk,” Zuko tries, snapping his mouth shut as he sees her mood swing again, anger giving away to exasperation. Agni, this is more open emotion than he’s seen from her in—years.

“Talk, talk, talk,” she says, flapping her hand through the air. “All you ever want to do is talk. All anyone ever wants to do is *talk*. Well, Zuko—” Her face twists. “—I am *tired* of *words*.”

Zuko can understand. He’s never had much talent for the kinds of words that are used in the palace. Still, if he can just get her off the dais, if he can just get her to him, sister to brother… “I’m just asking for this one—”

“Oh, you’re asking for more than just one simple *thing*, Brother,” she snarls, sparks crackling around her hands. Lightning, finding its way out. Leading her, when she doesn’t know how to be led. Zuko can feel it with his heat sense, can feel it charging the air, can feel it in her moods snapping and turning as fast as cold fire. “Why don’t you say what it is you really came here for.” The Fire Lord’s crown glints behind her.

He takes a deep breath, trying to be steady against her surging rage like she’s always been for him. “Will you talk with me?”

Her usual composure suddenly drops over her like a mask. “We are talking now, aren’t we?”

In public, then, if that’s how she wants to do it. “Azula, the power of Sozin’s Comet—”

Her laughter peals out, bright and high and hiccupping at the end. “Is it not glorious, Brother?”

Zuko stares. He doesn’t know if he’s ever heard her laugh, truly laugh, when it wasn’t an affectation, not since she lit her first sparks. And his inner fire seethes with uncertainty that he doesn’t know if she’s talking about her impending coronation, or the power of the Comet, or something else entirely.

“What we have done, here,” she continues, expression turning hard as she looks at him through the ragged fall of her bangs. “What *I* have done.”

“You broke,” he says carefully, “The rules.”

He can see the way that rocks her, the way it hits so hard she actually falls back a step before going tight and pulling herself up ramrod straight, denial and something like fear flashing over her face. “No.”

“Yes, Azula.”

“What rules?” She snarls, taking a step forward, then another, teetering on the edge of the stairs. “I didn’t break any of them. I’ve never—*what rules.”*

“The rules against wasting resources. Lives.” His eyes flick to the slow smoke he can see rising over her shoulder, some part of the palace smoldering. “The rules about a Fire Lord protecting her people.” There should be adulation, their Lightning Princess lifted up closer to Agni’s grace. That was always how it was going to be done.

Azula stares a moment, face frozen in a rictus of denial before it suddenly washes away under a jarring, mocking, teasing laugh. “You can be such a *Dumb Dumb*, Zuzu. I haven’t broken the *rules*,” she hisses, snapping right back into her bored drawl. “And even if I did—What would you do about it?”

“I can’t let you keep breaking them,” he warns, feeling his inner fire murmur with warning and regret and readiness. “That’s what we agreed.”

“*Let* me. Oh, Zuzu.” She steps forward, pushing off at the last moment to jump off the dais instead of falling. “As if you have ever *let* me do anything.”

Zuko shifts as she begins to move along the perimeter of the courtyard, keeping her solidly in his field of vision and trusting Katara to watch his back and his blind side. “I want to help, Azula. Please don’t make me try to stop you..”

She lets out a single bark of laughter, like she’s never heard a better joke in her life. “Oh, Zuko, what would you even *do*? Throw your Water Tribe peasant at me? Try to rally support for yourself? Challenge me to an Agni Kai?”

She giggles, but he can see the moment it hits, her laughter abruptly dying, face going tight and cold. The realization of a mistake, from someone who rarely makes any. That a taunt like that, delivered in front of an audience like this, an audience of Agni’s favored when Agni’s attention has already been called by her High Sage, can never be just a taunt. Not if Zuko doesn’t want to cede that he’s lost the favor of Agni. Not if he doesn’t want to leave and truly never be able to come back, which was never how it was supposed to be.

“Zuko,” Katara says somewhere behind him, dread and realization in her voice. “This is a bad idea. It’s a trick, she’s trying to—”

“It’s done, Katara,” Zuko says, taking a deliberate step forward, watching the way Azula’s eyes turn to ice. Challenged issued, challenge accepted, in the span of a few heartbeats.

The plan was to take out more than just a few other ships, in the initial pass, but Sokka will be happy with any he manages to knock out of the air—particularly when they’re still, just barely, over the water instead of the rocky, burning ground.

The plan was for their airship to last a little longer, too, but Sokka thinks it must be a newer, lighter, thinner design. Durability traded for speed, an easy decision when you don’t really expect anyone to be able to fight back.

The plan was to stay together. But Sokka has known since he was a child that a plan like ‘stay together’ is really more of a hope, a want, a wish, than anything that can be truly relied on.

&#45;-

“An Agni Kai it is, then,” Azula says softly, face going still. “And under our ancestor’s comet. Could we even call ourselves family, if we didn’t?”

One of the Fire Sages clears his throat from up on the dais. They’ve all shrunk toward the back, which Zuko doesn’t blame them for even as he feels a stab of resentment. They’ve all learned to flinch from the Crown’s power, instead of reflecting it and answering it, but that doesn’t mean Zuko can’t hate them a little bit for it. “We can choose either tomorrow’s sunrise or—”

“Now,” Azula says, not even bothering to look at them.

“But Your Majesty—Highness—Princess—Lady—”

“*Now.”*

“It won’t be an official Agni Kai, then,” Zuko warns, even as he moves to take his place across from her. They don’t have shawls, or armbands, or meditation, either. But if they’re going to do away with one, they might as well do away with all and not pretend that this could ever be something sacred.

Azula gives him a cold look, suddenly the picture of control again. “When has an official Agni Kai ever done anyone a bit of good, Zuko. You of all people should know what Agni’s *blessing* is worth in a duel.”

Zuko still tries, even though he’s known deep in his heart where he couldn’t look at it exactly where this was going to go since he woke up yesterday ahead of the sun with the Comet’s alien power sliding through him. “The Fire Sages—”

“Fuck the Fire Sages,” Azula says, words angry but tone distant. “The Fire Sages are useless. I banish the Fire Sages.”

Zuko doesn’t actually take his eyes off her to see if they obey. He has a sense they will, at least most of them. “Azula, we don’t have to do this.” Agni, he wonders if he'll ever be able to stop saying that to her. His inner fire coils at the ready, and he wonders if he wants to.

“It’s a little late for that, *Brother*,” Azula says as she sets herself across from him, the broad expanse of the courtyard between them. Neither of them make a move to take a knee or turn their backs or pause to pray for Agni’s guiding hand.

“I don’t want to have to do this,” Zuko corrects, throat tightening against the honesty even as the words hang between them.

“Empty words, Zuko,” Azula finally says, tone remote before her face twists. “I don’t trust words, not from people who call themselves friends and allies and family and then *leave*. I have no use for words when everybody lies.”

Zuko is thrown by the echo of his constant refrain. “You know I can’t lie,” he points out, mirroring her as she settles into a bending stance. “Not to you.”

“No,” she agrees with a harsh laugh. “You just pledge your words and then ignore them. Where is your precious honor when it comes to keeping your word, Zuko?”

“Azula—”

“You promised. Me and you to the end, you *promised.*”

Zuko meets her tawny eyes, feeling the weight of too many broken, twisted things between them, feeling the one last thread on the verge of fraying. “I’m here, aren’t I?”

Azula lets out a bark of laughter as her hands ignite. “And I guess this is the end.”

&#45;-

Some part of Sokka is frantic with worry over the fact that Suki isn’t with them, Suki isn’t here, the ship broke apart and Toph and Sokka fell one way and Suki didn’t fall with them, but she *fell* because there was nothing left to stand on, and—

Sokka shuts that part away, somewhere outside the battle calm he operates in as they sprint through this new airship. Toph peels away pieces of metal as Sokka calls out things that seem important, trying to destroy its functionality, and then just strips away pieces in general. To throw at soldiers, to barricade doors, to hurl as weapons. Binding and trapping and knocking back and knocking out—maybe, hopefully, there’s no time to check to be sure, and nothing to be done regardless.

Sokka’s sword is in hand, better in these tight quarters than his boomerang, and they’re making great time as they finally reach the back of the ship. Toph jams the rudder as easy as bending paper and the ship lurches, begins to gently list off course in a path that will force the others to maneuver, to break from their formation, to slow, and maybe they can do this, maybe—

Sokka dives before he consciously registers the need, tackling Toph down with a shout as a blaze of fire sheets over their heads where they’re pressed tight to the ground, intense enough to make Sokka’s skin feel dry and tight. It explodes against the metal wall, raining down sparks and embers that prick his skin, hot and angry and nothing like Zuko’s fire.

—Maybe they’ll finally be found. But Sokka’s been found by the Fire Nation before. And he’s pretty sure he understands physics and aerodynamics and ships better than any of these soldiers. And he and Toph are a sword Master in narrow quarters and a Master bender surrounded by her element. And Sokka will take those odds against the Fire Nation’s number any day.

After all, those odds are what they have.

&#45;-

Azula’s voice whips and roars like the fire they throw at each other, made wild and savage by the power of the Comet, ripping loose, cutting and incandescent and deadly.

“You could never just let it *be*, Zuko,” she snarls, blue flames erupting from her hands like two flowing waves. “You always have to *interfere*.”

Zuko kicks low and fast, slicing out his own red-orange-yellow fire. “I couldn’t just let this be.”

A lance of flame that nearly brings a pillar down on top of him, if Zuko hadn’t skipped out of the way. “Of course you could have, that was the *plan*.”

“The plan wasn’t supposed to happen like this,” Zuko snaps. “The plan was always supposed to adjust.”

“There was no need to—”

“The timing wasn’t *fine*, Azula,” Zuko shouts, punching quick balls of rapidly expanding fire.

“Nothing in the Fire Nation *changed*, Zuko, so whatever you’re telling yourself to justify—”

“The Fire Nation exists in the *world*, Azula,” Zuko says, voice breaking over the word. He dives out of the way of her instinctive punch at the evidence of his loss of breath control. “The Fire Nation can’t be fine if the world is burning.”

Azula stares, fire coiling in her hands, then lets out a shriek of rage, flames stabbing out around her. “It was never supposed to be about the world, Zuko! It was supposed to be about the Fire Nation. It was supposed to be about *us!* Did you even *think* about asking me to join you? Or did you just decide to throw me away, too?”

Zuko’s flames twist and writhe around his feet, visibly distressed as his breath dangerously freezes in his lungs for a moment. He didn’t, and he can tell that she can see it on his face. He didn’t mean to leave her out of it, thought he gave her opportunities to understand what he was doing and to reach out, but—maybe Zuko learned more from Uncle than he realized.

“I would have *never* thrown you away, Zuko. *Never.* The whole plan was so I could *keep* *you*.”

“Azula,” Zuko pleads, feeling dangerously off balance. “You still have me.”

Her jagged flames suck abruptly inward, coiling back into dense, tight, seething balls in her hands. “I’m not a fool, Zuko. Don’t treat me like one. You don’t have the right to change the terms and then be upset when you are called betrayer.”

“I’m not betraying you!”

“Look around you, Zuko,” Azula calls, arms flung wide, voice dripping scorn. “What would you call this, then?”

“*You asked for this!”*

“And you *forced my hand*,” Azula screams, hands swinging forward, sheeting flame. “What choice did you leave me with the way you *left?”*

Zuko falls back into a deep, solid block, body braced and face stinging from the heat of her fire as it breaks around him. “There are always choices, Azula,” he says, quiet, weary, low enough to almost be lost in the crackling fires beginning to ignite around them.

“Yes,” she agrees, cold, eyes flicking to the braids in his hair. “And you made yours. Water over blood.”

Zuko feels like his heart is breaking, like it’s been breaking ever since he stepped foot in Caldera. Maybe every day he’s ever spent in Caldera. “It’s not about him, Azula.”

Her flames coil, readying, terrifyingly steady as her face twists with rage. “Now you lie to yourself, Zuko. And to me.”

&#45;-

Sokka didn’t know how to account for Comet-powered bending, in his calculations. He’s still a sword Master, and Toph’s still a metalbender surrounded by metal. But that miscalculation just might be enough, to tip the scales. Not to swing them completely, but maybe enough to cause a stumble that slows them a bit too much, a misstep that means they have to cede ground, a flinch at the wrong moment, a railing peeled away to use as weaponry too early.

And then they’re falling instead of running, crashing instead of landing, and Sokka’s leg is breaking instead of holding, and Toph is desperately clinging to his hand, an earthbender swinging free in the alien, unfriendly air instead of rooted to the ground.

And suddenly they can’t run anymore, not like this. But Sokka can shift his grip so that he’s clasping Toph’s wrist, freeing her hand to cling back. And he can loosen his boomerang at his side and grab up his sword and level it in front of him and tense in readiness. Because they can’t run anymore, but they can still fight.

&#45;-

There are no words left between them, all their breath going to their fire. They’ve abandoned the semblance of an Agni Kai, with its hard boundaries and clear sides, darting around the courtyard, jumping rubble, spinning in and out of the covered walkways and around more fire than Zuko ever thought two people could ever possibly hold.

Only fire, though, and Zuko's on edge waiting for lightning, because he’s using his swords now, flames slinging from them in rhythms and patterns she’s never seen before, forcing her to pay attention, to think, to react instead of take the lead. And he’s using his heat, something she never knew he had, something he can see her trying to figure out. Boiling the air past his strikes, stealing the intensity from her blows, extending his stamina as he pulls power from around himself instead of from inside.

He can’t grab her inner flame with his heat sense when if he wanted to risk it, it’s too firmly in her grip even with her control this ragged. But Zuko can feel it, can find a pulse to the clash of her inner flame against his, can be a step ahead of its uncharacteristic flaring and ragged spikes.

Azula’s never known that, either. Being a step behind. Needing to keep up. Not when it comes to him, at least. He can feel the way her inner flame expands with her rage and whips his swords into a series of twisting, sliding blocks, redirecting, feeding off her fire, advancing even as she attacks, the balance between them shivering, like a wave on the verge of breaking.

He wonders, in a corner of his mind distant from their flames, how badly they’ll have to hurt each other to make the other yield. Wonders what if he’ll be able to bring himself to do that to her, how far necessity will drive him before he runs up against the limits of what he’s willing to do, of how like their father he’s willing to become. He would stop this, if he could —dangerous thoughts, for a duel like this—if only she said she wanted to talk. But he won’t hold out for the words. Even now, even after everything, he doesn’t think Azula has yet learned how to do anything but win.

&#45;-

“Sokka?” Toph cries out, high and tight, for the first time sounding like the twelve-year-old she is, the twelve-year-old who should never have been near this situation in the first place, if the world weren’t quite so awful as to ask it of her.

Sokka squeezes her wrist. “I’ve got you, Toph.” He has two hands to hold her now, after all.

“What’s happening?”

Sokka lets out an unsteady breath, chest fluttering with things he can’t feel right now. “I don’t think the boomerang’s coming back, this time,” he says, watching it spin away into the red-lit darkness. His mind is furiously calculating the time it’s bought him. A breath, but not enough to haul Toph back up when he’s laid out like this. Not enough.

“What does that mean,” Toph gasps, voice spiking with her fear as her fingers slip a half-inch. She whimpers, holding on hard enough that his wrist bones ache.

“I think it’s the end of the line, Toph,” Sokka says, fighting to keep his voice steady as the firebenders pace toward them. The last thing he wants is to make her any more scared than he can help. If that’s the last thing he does, is give her a piece of reassurance… “There are some things I regret—” Like Spirits, not getting to give Katara another hug, to see Aang, to kiss Zuko again and see him smile and laugh and know that he truly, actually understood how much Sokka loves him.

“Sokka, no.”

“—But it has been the honor of my life—”

“Sokka, no!”

“—to be able to call the greatest earthbender in the world my friend.”

“*No, no, no!”*

“And I want you to know—”

“*Fuck* this,” Toph screams, pure frustration and rage. “The greatest earthbender in the world does *not* die in the fucking *air*. And neither does her friend!”

Toph surges up, the grip around his wrist earthbender strong and sure, and Sokka cries out as the motion yanks on his broken leg, sending jagged, white-hot pain streaking up his body. But she’s ruthless in her determination, swinging again until his shoulder screams, then back, reaching, the fingers of her free hand just brushing the edge of the platform—

The metal *ripples*, surging up like a wave, crawling over the firebenders, the soldiers, suffocating, twisting, shrieking, and Sokka is shrieking too because his leg is *definitely* *fucking broken* and *moving* along with it, and—

“Hold on tight, Loverboy,” Toph snarls.

And Sokka doesn’t think he can hold on any tighter, until suddenly they’re falling again, metal folding out from beneath him, and it turns out he can hold on as tight as he needs to, except it’s too far, it’s not the ocean beneath them anymore, it’s—

Sokka *screams* as they land, as something else snaps and pops in his leg—fuck, fuck, *fuck*— his fall barely even half-cushioned by Toph, who’s already scrambling out from underneath him.

“What,” Sokka finally manages to grit out, vision blurred with pain as he looks wildly around to take in another airship. “How—”

“Your boomerang didn’t need to come back,” Toph says, cocking her head and slamming down her foot, the metal ringing from the blow. “Suki did.” Her grin is fierce, savage. “Can you still fight?”

“Always,” Sokka gasps out, boxing away the pain and reaching for his calm, casting around for something to make into a splint, for something to use as a crutch, a weapon. His heart is pounding, adrenaline singing through his veins, all his regret and longing and shuddering can’t-admit-it fear turning into fuel, into determination, into purpose.

“Good. Let’s finish this thing.” And Toph strides forward, hands raised, and starts tearing the airship apart from the inside out.

&#45;-

A cornered Azula is a dangerous Azula, and Zuko’s always known it. He expects her to finally draw on her best weapon now that the courtyard wall is getting closer and closer to her back, now that it’s taking more and more breath to maintain the intensity of her flames.

He doesn’t know why he’s surprised that instead of unleashing lightning, she turns to words. He has been waiting for her best weapon, after all.

“Sometimes I wonder how you became so unyielding,” she calls, darting between pillars, voice echoing crazed and wild off stone. “I never asked you for anything but this one thing.”

“You ask for more than that,” Zuko says, steady as he advances, swords glowing with heat in his hands beneath their coating of flame.

“Everything for the one reason, then,” she corrects, smirking before ducking away again, for a moment exactly as she should be. “And am I not reasonable? The *world* is going to ask you for more.”

“It’s not about how much, Azula.” Zuko’s always been willing to give her whatever he could. “It’s about what.”

“And your peasant is better?”

The words roll off him, for once blunt instead of sharp, like the raging flames between them are burning off the edges before they can strike. “It’s not a competition.”

“Everything is a competition, Zuko,” Azula says, trying to send a chunk of ceiling down onto his head as its support beams give out under a lance of her fire. “Only you would say otherwise in the middle of one.” She flips away from his attack, still as light on her feet as ever. “The thing about not realizing you’re playing the game, though, is that you never learn how to win.”

Zuko is silent, because they both know what’s happening now, no matter what she says. She might be stronger, better, but for once Zuko has more control, and with both of them overflowing with fire under the Comet’s power, strength isn’t as much of a differentiator as it once was.

She grins at his silence, teeth bared, something like triumph on her face even as she paces backward, running out of space. “Because even if you beat *me*—you still can’t win. Because it still can’t be you, Zuko.”

He almost falters, at that. Doesn’t, by a bare breath. He knows that she notices, though, her blue fire beginning to coil around her feet like snakes. He didn’t know she could do that, is horrified to think that maybe she doesn’t even realize it’s happening.

“A Fire Lord puts her people first? That’s the *rule*, right?”

“Yes,” Zuko says, casting his heat sense out in a wary flicker, stilling when he feels the energy coiling around her beneath the flame, the crackling concealed by the fire's roar.

Her face is all cool, amused triumph. “And how will you do that, dear Brother, when you can’t help but put the Water Tribe ahead of the Fire Nation.”

“I don’t,” Zuko says, slowly setting his feet, softening his knees, readying his arms. He’s never redirected lightning with his swords, before. Hopefully he can get the hang of it on the fly.

“No?” She grins before her face goes flat, hard. “Well then, in front of Agni and the Sages and what family you have left—Prove it.”

She pivots, lightning coming without her even needing to draw the tight circle, to call it, *fuck*, like it’s been at the ready this whole time, or maybe like she’s beyond that now. And Zuko is ready for it, he is. If only it were coming toward him. If only he hadn’t forgotten that Sokka isn’t the only member of the Water Tribe that Azula cares about.

Katara throws up a shield of water, which isn’t going to *help*, not with lightning, and Zuko doesn’t even think—he just proves Azula right, giving up his root and throwing himself forward, not even able to scream as the lightning hits and his whole world goes white with pain. It rages through him, ferocious and jagged and wild, and beneath it cold and uncaring and deadly. Just like Azula, beneath the Comet’s raging power. And just like Azula, lightning has always been Zuko’s friend, and his last thought before the full power of it crashes down to the heart of his already-overfull inner flame is to hope that there’s enough of Azula left in this Comet-fueled lightning to save him.
