## Chapter 31: All The Way To The End

### Notes

#### Chapter Notes

Warnings in this one for some brief mention of the aftermath of battle and medicinal pain killer use

### Text

When the realization—the relief—that it’s actually over hits Sokka it lands like a fist to the face. He distantly thinks it must be afternoon—not that anyone could tell with the thick, red-tinged cloud cover still lighting the sky in every direction—but the day has become such a blur of pain and exhaustion, punctuated by moments of sharp awareness, that he isn’t entirely sure.

Hauling themselves vaguely in the direction they think Aang must be in, Suki taking most of his weight even with the splint Toph’s cobbled together, Toph smoothing out the ash-thick, rocky ground as much as possible and Sokka still not being sure with each step if he’s going to be able to take another one.

Nearly crying when Suki sucks in a sharp breath and Sokka manages to gather himself enough to follow her gaze to see Momo winging down toward them.

The moment when Sokka just gives up on standing, when they finally see a familiar orange-clad figure. It’s less of a decision and more of a reality that Sokka abruptly becomes aware of as he lists against the pillar Toph scrambles to raise for him, Suki yelping as she tries to ease him into more of a lean than a collapse.

And then a blur of voices tumbling over each other, too fast for Sokka to keep track of on top of trying to keep from vomiting from the radiating pain in his leg, the way it simultaneously manages to be aching and sharp and throbbing and piercing all at the same time. When he breathes too fast or too deep or too freely he can feel something in his leg *grind*.

Suki is saying they’re fine and Toph is muttering that that’s debatable and Aang is lit with relief and happiness and a quiet kind of resolve and Sokka is just managing to focus enough to search Aang’s face, looking for the distress or anguish he expected to see there even if Aang had managed to kill Ozai through the distance of the Avatar state. Which—Sokka feels a stab of fear, deep and urgent sharper than the pain in his leg, that Aang *didn’t* kill Ozai. That maybe it *isn’t* actually done.

“Aang,” Sokka grits out, cutting into whatever Toph and Suki are saying about Katara and Zuko, or maybe where Aang went, or possibly Ba Sing Se. Sokka isn’t really following. Maybe they already covered it, and he missed it? “Is it done? Is the Fire Lord…?”

“He’s alive,” Aang says, face going serious and tone *far* too relaxed, and fuck, fuck *everything.* Toph was right to be skeptical of the sky energy thing, and Sokka has no idea where his impromptu spear got dropped, and at least Suki still has her knives, they can at least—“But it’s okay.”

“It’s *okay*?” Sokka repeats back, wondering if he’s mishearing, if the pain is impacting his senses. Toph and Suki look equally alarmed and Sokka isn’t sure if he should take comfort or not in that. Spirits, did Aang at least knock the Fire Lord unconscious before coming to find them? Do they need to hustle and find—restraints? Rope? Metal chains? “Where is he?”

“Back there.” Aang waves in some direction Sokka doesn’t have the wherewithal to keep track of right now—Suki has it—looking far too unconcerned about it even though the Comet is still raging in the sky above them. “I don’t think he’s a threat to anyone, though,” Aang says, expression settling into firm resolve. “I took his bending away and he can’t firebend anymore.”

A moment of silence, then, “Say that again, Twinkletoes. You took his *what*?”

“His firebending,” Aang repeats, face going serious. “I didn’t know what to do, so I prayed and meditated and I think I ended up in the Spirit world. I communicated with my past lives, and—well, the lion turtles showed me how,” he summarizes.

They all stare.

“The what now?” Suki finally asks.

“Let’s circle back to that,” Sokka cuts in before Aang can clarify even more. “So what, Ozai’s tied up somewhere?”

“Well. No,” Aang says, glancing back over his shoulder. “But he’s on a really tall rock. And he definitely can’t fly anymore, and his balance was a bit—” Aang makes a wobbly gesture. “—so climbing’s out too. So I don’t think he’s going anywhere. The rock is *really* tall.”

Flying—? Sokka…thinks the pain might be getting to him. Maybe he actually did get hit in the head, instead of just generally feeling like it.

“Okay,” Suki says after a beat. “So I’m hearing that we should just—”

Sokka accidentally vocalizes the oh-Spirits-please-no feeling stabbing him in the gut. Sokka and Aang and Toph and Suki *did their part*. If the Fire Lord can’t bend and is stuck on top of a rock, then *someone else can deal with it.* The rest of them need to *go.*

“—that the *White Lotus* should just…get some rope or something. And tie him up. Just to be sure. And while they do that we find ourselves a boat, and Iroh can deal with the rest.”

Aang blinks. “Why do we need a flower? And a boat?”

“We’ll fill you in once we’re on the boat,” Toph says firmly, cracking her knuckles. “We’ll have time to talk then.”

“Alright,” Aang agrees after a beat. “But why not take Appa?”

“Because Appa’s in the Fire Nation with Zuko and Katara,” Sokka says between his teeth, hearing the fear and worry bleeding into his voice and unable to care enough to hold them back. “We only have eel hounds, and they can’t swim that far and Toph tore all the airships apart, and if we could just—get this done. As fast as possible. And get over there. That would be great. Really great. Please.”

“Right,” Suki says briskly into the silence, taking charge even as she rubs a gentle circle over his back. “We make sure Ozai is nice and imprisoned, we make sure the White Lotus doesn’t have its head up its ass for cleanup here—”

“They definitely do,” Sokka mutters, mostly to himself, but that’s the White Lotus’ problem. At least until Sokka gets to the Fire Nation.

“—and then we get ourselves to the Fire Nation. Sound good?”

It sounds great, to Sokka. Except for the fact that traveling by boat instead of air bison means that it’s going to take more time than Sokka wants to think about for them to get there.

&#45;-

Sokka isn’t exactly sure how they managed to track down a boat, he’s just aware that they’re making progress in a boat-ward direction and that’s about as much as he can keep track of. He feels nauseated, lightheaded, restless, exhausted, the need to get to Katara and Zuko thrumming in his bones, which is *very* unpleasant when one of them is broken.

He can’t stop thinking about all the ways things could be going wrong in Caldera, ways that seem so much more likely than the way his own part of the plan fell apart. If Zuko had to fight Azula, or found his own people turned against him, or that Azula’s base of power isn’t as strong as either of them thought. If Katara had to fight too, a Water Tribeswoman in the Fire Nation, so clearly marked as an enemy. Or if they didn’t have to fight at all, if they talked to Azula and she just said no, or to arrest them, or some vicious lie, or—or fuck, if she wasn’t even there to find in the first place.

And Spirits, that’s just what could have gone wrong *today*. Sokka doesn’t know if he can handle thinking about all the things that could go wrong between now and when they finally reach Caldera’s shores. He doesn’t know if he can stop himself, though. Now that the fleet has been stopped and the immediate threat is at least contained, it’s far too easy to picture all the things that could happen to a Crown Prince involved in what amounts to a coup, and to the foreign national helping him.

&#45;-

Sokka definitely isn’t sure how they find their way onto the boat. He thinks he passes out a little, somewhere between needing to navigate the rocky sand and getting himself from the beach over the railing, and the way a sudden wave kicks the boat *up* when he expects it to go *down*, and—

Sokka finds himself on the deck half on his back, half on his side, fingers white-knuckled around the railing, head in Aang’s lap as Aang frets over him and Toph does something that feels reinforcing-y to his splint and Suki mutters something about tracking down the medical kit and seeing if it has any of the good stuff in it, whatever that means.

He doesn’t acknowledge any of that just yet, though. Partly because it’s taking the majority of his attention not to throw up over the side from the way the gentle rocking of the waves is lurching through his leg. Mostly because all the rest of his attention is fixed on the water below as they slowly pull away from the beach.

The ocean is little more than blackness—and maybe it’s the red-tinged clouds, but Sokka thinks he’s lost time somewhere in there, that it’s closer to night now—but he can still make out shapes in the water. Wreckage and scraps of machinery that they need to carefully maneuver around as they tack against the rising tide, pieces that used to be light and weightless and whole before they brought them down. And the shapes of things that seem much more organic—Sokka isn’t sure if they’re actually there, or if they’re just something he's imagining—remembering—to go along with the nagging sense of having been here and done this all before.

&#45;-

Suki finds the good stuff. Sokka doesn’t ask questions as she presses a steaming mug into his hands that somehow manages to smell both bitter and cloyingly sweet.

“I wouldn’t normally say to use it for more than a day,” Suki says quietly, gently bracing his shoulders up, Aang stretching his legs after Sokka has no idea how long of acting as his impromptu pillow. “But with the waves…”

“Yeah,” Sokka agrees tightly, pausing with the mug at his lips. “It’s not addictive, is it?”

She hesitates, which is…not exactly reassuring, but her voice is quietly confident as she replies, “If we only use it so you can sleep? Then it shouldn’t be, no.”

“Okay,” Sokka says, taking a testing sip before pulling a face and slugging the rest of it down. He fights the urge to cough or gag against the taste, because he’s already learned that both those things *hurt*, and Suki slips the mug from his hands once he has himself under control, settling cross-legged behind him and helping to ease him back down with his head in her lap.

“Sleep, Sokka,” Suki urges, running gentle fingers through his hair, slow and soothing. “I’ll keep an eye on things.”

And Sokka is more than happy in that moment to give everything over to her watchful eye, to close his own and let himself spiral down into darkness.

&#45;-

Sokka sleeps, but he doesn’t rest. He dreams of falling, of landing, of feeling his leg snap over and over. Of both his legs breaking, of his chest breaking instead, his heart, or his arm so he only has one left and needs to choose between Toph and being able to defend themselves, which amounts to the same thing. Of Toph slipping from his grip, and then Katara, Zuko, Aang and Suki, Hakoda and Bato and his mom, who’s more an idea than a face and somehow manages to slip away all the faster for it.

He wakes with a jolt that has him bracing against the accompanying wave of pain, eyes screwed tight until he can finally breathe through it enough to unclench his muscles limb by limb. He finally opens his eyes and realizes that it’s Toph with him now, her lap solid and warm and *present* beneath his head and shoulders, one hand surprisingly soft on his arm, the other bending little patterns and whorls into the metal of the railing. She doesn’t say anything, even though he knows she knows he’s awake. And after a while it’s enough just to have her here, stable and calm and in no need of the strength he doesn’t have in himself to give right now.

&#45;-

Sokka can’t quite find his way to sleep again, but he manages to doze, to find a place of half-awareness somewhere between awake and dreaming. It’s not necessarily a comfortable place. His thoughts are free to wander there, and it’s so hard not to linger over the memory of fear as he hauled Fire Nation bodies from the cold waters of the North, bracing for the next one to be familiar, or the next, or maybe the next.

But that’s almost better than thinking about how even if none of those Fire Nation soldiers were Zuko, they were still someone’s lover, child, parent, sibling before they sunk into the water. Someone’s friend, someone who just had a birthday, someone who will never have another. And yeah, maybe they were Fire Nation imperialists, maybe they were following their leaders to hurt the world, but they were still *people*. People who could change, and maybe do better, and now will never have the chance.

&#45;-

Sometimes Sokka thinks of other things, though. New things, rather than old ones, the kinds of things he never really allowed himself to think about before, because the idea of the war actually being *done*—Sokka has lived in war his entire life. He doesn’t truly know what it means, to be without it.

But he can start to imagine, in the hazy space between consciousness and sleep. His thoughts can drift to visiting Kyoshi and staying for a bit. Exploring the world with Katara and being able to wander wherever they want to go. Learning the Fire Nation through Zuko’s eyes. Showing Zuko the South through his own.

Sokka has so often struggled to picture Zuko alongside him when thinking of the future, or even the present. To imagine gold eyes glancing across a bowl of sea prune stew, the familiar tilt of Zuko’s head listening to Bato’s stories, the way Zuko’s scar would crinkle with laughter in some random village market. And maybe it’s just the lingering effects of whatever Suki gave him, or maybe it's the slowly settling reality that they might have actually *won,* but Sokka suddenly finds it’s as easy as breathing to spin out fantasies of the future suddenly ahead of him, and to picture Zuko at his side through all of it.

&#45;-

Sokka eventually manages to migrate to leaning against the wall of the cabin, his legs stretched out before him, which isn’t quite the ‘inside and on a bed’ that Suki was angling for, but it’s definitely a step up from the ‘vaguely passed out in the lap of whoever happens to be nearby’ that he’s been doing.

Aang brought food, which helps. Sokka doesn’t exactly want to eat, his stomach still half-queasy from pain, but he knows that eating is a thing he should be doing, especially if Suki is going to give him another dose tonight. And Aang’s face relaxes a little when Sokka starts picking at the bowl, like as long as Sokka still has his appetite then everything will be okay, so it’s not the worst thing to take another bite.

“Thanks, Aang,” Sokka says when he finishes, easing his head back to rest against the wall, staring up at the sky. It’s bright blue, nearly cloudless, a bright, calm day. He feels like it should be dark, overcast, ominous. Not because he particularly wants to experience a storm right now, he absolutely does not. But because the beautiful day is jarring, like a slap in the face after yesterday—and Spirits, yesterday somehow already feels like it was a lifetime ago.

“I was thinking,” Aang says as he carefully stacks their bowls together, “That the pain has to be really bad. And that it must be really hard for you.” His eyes flick up, assessing, but Sokka isn’t sure what exactly he’s supposed to say to that. “But if it’s more than just the pain. If things are hard for other reasons, too. You can talk about them, if you want. I can listen.”

Sokka stares.

“A heart-to-heart kind of thing,” Aang continues, fiddling with their chopsticks until they’re perfectly aligned on the bowls. “Only if you want to.” A pause, and Sokka still has no idea what to say. “Or not, we can just—watch the waves,” Aang says, shrugging, giving him a quick, searching look. “Or the sky. Or I can just keep you company while I meditate, that’s good too.”

“I have this math in my head,” Sokka says before he can second guess himself, almost before he even realizes he’s going to say it. “How many soldiers to crew an airship. And add in how troops an airship can hold as a transport, and how many engineers and cooks. And multiply by how many airships there are in a fleet. But don’t forget to factor in how many naval ships are there to support from the rear, and how many people they could hold, and how much faster an airship can travel. Or the weight of a set of armor, and how long the average person could tread water. And do all that and at the end, you get the number of people who are dead today because of me.”

Because of *them*, but—they couldn’t have done it without Sokka, just like Sokka couldn’t have done it without Toph or Suki. Does that distribute the guilt? Or concentrate it?

Aang inhales a slow breath, face going grave, but he waits for Sokka to find a way to say the rest of the words. Which Sokka appreciates, because his words might sound matter of fact, but he’s fully braced for Aang’s…what? Horror? Disgust? Aang was so against killing the Fire Lord even in combat that he went on a spirit quest for an alternative.

Sokka…didn’t. Sokka got his hands dirty in exactly the way Aang abhorred.

“I didn’t want to,” Sokka finally forces out. “But I did it. And we couldn’t *not* do it,” he adds, throwing the words down like a gauntlet. “The fleet—we needed the fleet to stop, and they weren’t going to, so then we needed them incapacitated and you can’t—you can’t just expect a whole fleet to get destroyed, things like that don’t just *happen*.” Not like discovering a way to take away a person’s bending, not everyone gets exactly what they’ve been looking for dropped into their lap right when they need it. “Someone had to *do* it, because even with the Fire Lord—it wasn’t just going to *stop.* And—” Sokka hitches, glaring, or maybe accusing. “—and there wasn’t anyone else but me.”

The silence stretches out except long enough for Sokka to finally register the sounds of the ocean against the hull and his own heavy breathing, until Aang eventually sets the bowls aside, the rattle of chopsticks against the ceramic rim overloud in the quiet.

“I’m not going to tell you you’re wrong,” Aang says, shifting to put his back to the cabin next to Sokka. “I’m not going to say I’d do it differently, either.” He sighs when Sokka shoots him a surprised look, staring out over the water. “I might *want* to, but…it’s not like wanting can make it so the North never happened.”

Another set of ships sunk into the ocean, and Sokka wonders if he and Aang are actually about to connect over their shared experiences with taking a Fire Nation fleet and leaving nothing behind but twists of metal and bodies.

“Thinking about it is still hard,” Aang confesses, hugging his arms over his knees. “I did, and I do, but sometimes I wonder if I avoid thinking about it too much still. Not just that it happened, but that I *let* it happen. I let myself be used like that, and it’s not…comfortable, knowing that I’m this *thing* that happened to someone.”

“No one used me though,” Sokka finally says, pushing through the absolutely surreal feeling of bonding with Aang over this. It’s not exactly how he had hoped they would go about it. “There wasn’t some spirit. Just…me.”

“Maybe it’s better that way.” Aang glances over when Sokka makes an immediate noise of disagreement. “It means you chose it,” Aang says, words low. “*You* decided what you were going to do. You weren’t just a tool in someone else’s hands.”

“Choosing though—it means knowing that all those people would be alive if I just…chose something else. If I just figured out a better way.” Sokka can see the appeal in having it all out of his hands, of being buffeted along by fate or some higher power even as he flinches from the idea of that kind of helplessness.

“You also saved people,” Aang points out. “That was a choice, too.”

Sokka gives him a sideways glance. “Weren’t you just saying that all lives are equal? That you can’t trade one for many? It shouldn’t matter if I saved people if that’s true.”

Aang doesn’t immediately reply, which Sokka appreciates, because if he’s basically going to ask the Avatar to judge him for his actions—and Sokka can’t believe he’s arguing against himself here, but he just can’t seem to pick up what Aang is offering, yet—he wants his thousand-year-old friend to give it some thought.

“I don’t think a person should *plan* to trade lives like that,” Aang finally says. “That’s an easy path to start walking down, and a hard one to leave. But sometimes, even when you try to do the right thing, it gets taken out of your hands.” He looks down at his own hands, turning them over, eyes briefly ancient. “Sometimes you try to extend your hand in friendship and people choose to turn away. You can’t *make* someone walk the path of peace. No matter how much you want them to.” Aang’s hands curl into fists.

“So it’s okay then?” Sokka frowns. “To hurt people? To kill them? As long as you don’t want to?”

“It should never be okay,” Aang says quietly, heavily. “Hurting someone like that—it hurts you, too.”

Sokka lets out a slow, shaky breath. Yes. It does.

“Especially if you were forced to it. It’s not fair for someone to bring that violence to you when you wanted peace,” Aang says, a flash of frustration before he takes a deep breath, finding calm in a gesture that makes Sokka’s heart trip with the way it reminds him of Zuko. “Some of the monks would say that if you don’t adhere fully to your ideals at all times then it doesn’t matter what ideals you hold, because you don’t live them.” Sounds like Zuko’s acid comments on situational morality, or whatever he called it. “They’d say that it just showed lack of conviction. Or lack of strength.

“But Monk Gyatso always said that we’re more than just individuals. We can’t just care about our own spiritual well-being, because we’re part of a community and everyone in a community is connected. And you can’t sacrifice someone else’s life to preserve your ideals and still say you’re part of that.”

Sokka hesitates, because…he *likes* that. That makes sense to him. Except, “That’s not quite what you were saying a few days ago,” he points out carefully. Or at least not the only thing, because Aang was saying…a lot of things. At very high volume, at times, when he and Zuko really got into it.

“Maybe not,” Aang admits, chewing on his lip. “It feels different to turn away when you’re the only one left to carry the knowledge of those ideas forward. It’s like there’s a whole community *in* me, too. Relying on me and needing me, and if I stray and lose my way, then they all get lost with me.”

“I don’t think ideas work that way,” Sokka says after a moment.

“No,” Aang agrees with a quick flicker of a smile. “Zuko would probably say you need to try a lot harder to kill them than that.” Sokka snorts and immediately regrets it as his leg throbs in warning. “It’ll be good to see then again,” Aang says quietly, voice going almost confessional. “Katara and Zuko.”

“Yeah,” Sokka says, hearing just the one word full to the brim with longing and worry and fear.

“I bet they’re waiting for us,” Aang says, somewhere between lovesick and eager. “I bet they have so much to tell us.”

“Yeah,” Sokka says again after a beat, trying to ignore the clench of anxiety around his ribs.

Aang visibly pauses, half-straightened in excitement as he turns concerned, confused eyes on Sokka. “Are you okay,” Aang asks, eyes darting down to Sokka’s splinted leg, flashing back up when Sokka sighs. “Did something happen when I was gone? More than what Toph and Suki said?”

“No, no,” Sokka says quickly before Aang starts thinking he and Toph need to play matchmaker again, or whatever’s going on in his head. Aang relaxes and gives him a patient, expectant look, and Sokka resists the urge to squirm.

“Aang, those weren’t just soldiers I killed,” Sokka finally says, fiddling with the end of his wrist wrap. “They were *Zuko*’s soldiers. He’s the Crown Prince and they were Fire Nation.” And Zuko cares so *much* about his people, even when they don’t seem to care back.

Aang’s gaze is thoughtful, neutral. “Do you think Zuko needs to forgive you, then? That he won’t?”

“I don’t know,” Sokka grumbles. “I just—it just *sucks*.” It’s not that he thinks Zuko wouldn’t, it's that Sokka so desperately wanted it to not even be an issue in the first place.

“It does,” Aang nods. “But Sokka—You tried, and I think it will matter a lot to Zuko that you did. And he was there for the planning, right?”

“…Zuko takes so much blame on himself,” Sokka mutters, fingers tight around his own wrist. Even when Zuko shouldn’t. *Especially* when Zuko shouldn’t.

“I don’t think that means he’ll put the blame on you,” Aang says gently, and Sokka blinks, wondering if that’s…what he’s been worrying about this whole time? “Zuko doesn’t seem the type to blame anyone else.”

“…Maybe he should,” Sokka sighs, setting that question aside for later. Because Aang is right, Zuko doesn’t do that, even when it seems like the people around him have more than earned it.

“I think the path that got us here started way before either of you,” Aang finally says. “Maybe even before me, too. And I don’t think Zuko’s going to need to, but Sokka? If you want Zuko to forgive you? It’s going to be hard if you haven’t forgiven yourself first.”

Sokka opens his mouth and promptly closes it again, nothing coming out as he struggles with the idea of just—what, letting himself off the hook?

“This kind of guilt is hard to let go of,” Aang says after a moment. “Trust me, I know. And maybe it’s the kind that you never *should* cast away entirely.” Aang glances down at his hands again, flexing his fingers briefly into claws. “But it doesn’t have to stay guilt. It doesn’t have to be something you punish yourself over forever. It can become something else.”

“…Like what?” Sokka asks, reluctantly aware that even if it doesn’t make him feel better— and Sokka isn’t quite sure yet that he should *want* to feel better—Aang has certainly had more time to think about the topic than he has.

Aang shrugs. “Motivation. Remembrance. A shared experience.” Though probably not one you’re proud to share. “You can turn it into lots of things without forgetting it.”

Sokka nods slowly, turning that over in his head and letting a thinking kind of silence fall between them. It definitely doesn’t make any part of yesterday more comfortable, but something about it makes things feel more…livable, maybe. Manageable. Like Sokka can believe a little more readily that in his own time, in his own way, he’ll find his way to some of Aang’s introspection and calm, or to a place where thinking about what he had to do is accompanied by something other than the sticky feeling of not having been good enough to stop it.

&#45;-

Toph says it blunter, later, as they begin to ease toward the coast. “Did you put them on the airship?”

“No, but—”

“Did you make the plan to invade the Earth Kingdom?”

“No, and that—”

“Did you make them attack you?”

“I mean, we did break in with—”

“Good on you for caring about saving lives,” she says, throwing herself down next to him. “But they brought the fight to us. And the way I see it? Any soldier who would strike down a child gets what’s coming to them when they find out *I’m* not a helpless kid.”

&#45;-

Sokka hears Katara shouting before Appa lands—which *hurts*, much as Suki and Aang try to brace him—and Spirits, he didn't know if he'd ever top how grateful he felt to see the familiar shape of Appa flying down from Caldera's rim to the harbor, but then he never thought he'd be e so relieved to hear his sister shrieking his name, either.

“Sokka! Aang!” She sprints to Appa’s side, looking like she isn’t sure whether to grin or sob. She lets out another cry of delight that breaks halfway through into something closer to an actual cry. Sokka can sympathize. She scrubs at her face, whirling toward the palace where Sokka notices a dark-clad servant hovering in the doorway.

“Li Ty, can you please find Zuko—” The woman twitches, somehow, without managing to move. “—and have him come here? But tell him *no running*.” And Katara might need to watch herself because the woman looks *really* put out by that.

“Are you sure you should be ordering her around?” Sokka mutters as he watches the woman stalk away with stiff propriety.

“It’s fine, I’ve been doing it all—” She breaks off as she finally catches sight of his leg. “Sokka!”

“It’s fine, I’m fine,” Sokka says, just on the wrong edge of too tight to totally sell it as Aang helps bend him down from Appa’s back to the courtyard before hopping down after. “Are *you* alright?”

“You guys,” Katara says wetly, then throws herself at Aang, and Toph and Suki after, and it’s a mess of hugs, everyone talking over each other as relief makes them giddy, and Katara is crying a little and covering it up by saying they all need baths, and *Spirits*, does Sokka ever want one of those.

“…Was that servant’s name Li Ty?” Sokka asks to distract himself when he gets his own hug, because he doesn’t think baths are on the immediate agenda.

“Shut up,” Katara hisses, gripping his hands tight enough to ache, tight enough that it’s like she never wants to let go.

Sokka squeezes back just as hard. “Zuko said Ty Lee had like, twelve sisters, are we sure she isn’t—"

“Don’t insult her—”

“Who says it’s an insult?”

“—and she’s fetching Zuko, so—”

Sokka’s head jerks away from whatever else Katara's saying as he feels a *tug* somewhere in his chest. He automatically turns toward it, already half a step forward, heart in his throat, as Zuko skids around the corner.

“*No running!”*

Zuko checks himself to something just this side of a run, straggling braids swing with his momentum, and Sokka’s heart leaps into his throat seeing them, seeing *him.* Fucking well enough to *run* and dressed in red and gold and looking at him with growing alarm and suddenly there’s nothing Sokka needs more than to hobble forward, to ignore Suki and Katara’s noises of worry and to trust in Toph’s splint and close the distance between them.

Sokka has a brief thought for the potential danger—Fire Nation, laws, perceptions—but then Zuko is grabbing him up, making a choked noise, and Sokka is more than happy to follow Zuko’s lead and fall into his arms. They hold onto each other, Zuko making another low sound of relief as Sokka tries to remember how to just breathe, both of them flinching away as they hit each other’s hurts and then clinging tight again because they can’t stand a bit of distance between them right now.

“You’re okay?” Zuko breathes.

“Fine, fine, it’s fine. You?”

Zuko shakes his head, once. “You’re hurt.”

“My leg might be broken,” Sokka allows, easing back just enough to sweep his eyes over Zuko. Spirits, he looks wan and tired and haggard and mussed and fucking beautiful. Sokka’s fingers already itch to redo the braids framing Zuko’s face, to smooth down the flyaways and make them neat and perfect again, even though the idea that Zuko kept them, that he clearly had the opportunity to bathe and change and still didn’t take them out—

Toph snorts behind them, breaking in before his thoughts truly start running. “There’s no *might* about it.”

“It’s fine,” Sokka insists as Zuko traces his fingers over the deep, mottled bruises around Sokka’s wrist from Toph’s grip. Katara’s here now, so it’s not even a lie. “You’re okay?”

“I’m fine,” Zuko says, flinching a little bit as Sokka runs his hands up his arms.

Katara purses her lips. “He isn’t going to keel over and die on the spot.”

“*Thank you*, Katara,” Zuko glares.

“You’re welcome, Your…?” Katara trails off, raising a pointed eyebrow, which makes Zuko huff and turn deliberately away from her, which Sokka doesn’t really get and is totally okay with because it means Zuko is turning back into him.

“Azula?” Sokka murmurs, anxiety tightening in his throat when Zuko stiffens a moment against him before sighing, deep and exhausted.

“She’s….” Another sigh, this time with a shake of his head. “Can I tell you later? When it’s just us?”

“Of course,” Sokka says, rubbing what he hopes is a soothing circle over a bit of Zuko’s shoulder that doesn’t draw a flinch, mind racing through the possibilities. Zuko here and using the present tense, sounding weighed down by it but not as much as Sokka expected, and not like he’s spiraling…

“Guys, what *happened?*” Aang explodes, rising a little in the air from the force of having kept the question in.

“No!” Katara shouts as everyone simultaneously opens their mouth to answer, scowling around at all of them and finishing with Sokka and Zuko. “Before we start this, we’re sitting. Everyone is sitting. And eating,” she adds, with an extra glare for Zuko. “Get them to bring us food. And you—” She transfers her glare to Sokka, who really doesn’t feel like he’s done anything to earn it yet. “Get him to eat it.”

Sokka blinks, sharing a bemused look with Suki and Aang.

“And where would you like the food?” Zuko asks with enough exasperated familiarity that Sokka can tell that Zuko has been introduced to the way Katara starts to micromanage everything around her when she’s feeling worried and insecure, which…raises a lot of questions about what’s been going on in the palace the past few days for them to be so stressed and worried and insecure about.

“It’s your palace,” Katara says. “Have it sent to the closest place we can sit.” She turns back to Sokka, eyes on his splint, a quick, brisk healer’s assessment. “Do you need to be carried?”

“…Not right now,” Sokka says, clearing his throat as Zuko lets out a little puff of breath, fingers tightening almost imperceptibly against him. Spirits, Sokka would love to just give himself over to Zuko’s arms right now and not have to think about anything else. But there’s so much they need to think about, and Sokka didn’t miss Zuko’s little winces every time Sokka pressed too hard in the wrong ways, or the fact that Katara doesn’t want Zuko exerting himself.

“It doesn’t have to be Zuko,” Suki says dryly, arms crossed. “I’m sure Aang can airbend you there.”

“It’s fine,” Sokka says quickly, easing himself a bit more upright to demonstrate and managing not to flinch as Toph helpfully sends his makeshift crutch flying in their direction, Zuko snatching it out of the air before it can hit Sokka in the face. “This works,” Sokka adds, taking the crutch in one hand and holding tight as Zuko tangles their fingers together on his other side. “This is good.”

“I’m sure,” Katara mutters, rolling her eyes but already striding off. “Come on. Sitting and food. In that order.”

&#45;-

Sokka gapes at the spread that is waiting for them when they finally straggle their way into some kind of parlor sitting room thing. It’s dominated by a huge table that would feel absurd for just six people and a lemur if it weren’t for the absolutely mind-boggling amount of food covering nearly every inch of the available surface area.

“What did you ask for, again?” Sokka mutters as he settles himself into a surprisingly comfortable chair, unable to keep in a little groan of relief.

“Just something for us to snack on while we talk,” Zuko frowns, poking at a tray of cakes piled seven layers deep.

Sokka cuts him a sideways look, then flicks a glance toward Katara. Apparently, she’s not the only one invested in Zuko eating. Or else the palace servants are eager to curry his favor, and is that a normal thing? Sokka doesn’t think so, judging by the way Zuko is glowering at the table.

Still, this seems…somewhat excessive. Though as Sokka considers the empty streets they flew over, the downed airships, Ozai in chains, and whatever happened here—he supposes they might be talking for quite a while.

&#45;-

Zuko and Sokka are matching each other bite for bite, apparently, and in between they manage to cover Ozai—Zuko is as reactive to the news as Sokka expects, which is to say not at all, but Sokka thinks that’s probably a good thing. Zuko would make his displeasure known, and the furrow of his brow doesn’t look like an upset one—and a brief outline of what happened in Caldera. Though Sokka thinks ‘there was an Agni Kai’ and ‘Azula didn’t quite follow the rules’ doesn’t really encompass the whole of it, but before he can really press there’s a polite rap on the door and another servant is bowing his way inside.

“A message,” the man murmurs, giving another neat bow and presenting a neat tray with an equally neat scroll for Zuko to pick up. Sokka raises his eyebrows, wondering if royalty are too fancy to get things handed to them, but the way Zuko immediately straightens in his chair has Sokka moving that question to the ‘when no one else is around’ list.

“Was there anything else?” Zuko asks, flipping the scroll over like there might be something on the back.

“Just this,” the servant bows again.

Zuko sighs, briefly pinching the bridge of his nose before his posture goes perfectly straight again. “My apologies,” he says, voice taking on a ring of formality as he tucks the scroll into his pocket. “I am being called away, but please, stay here as long as you want. When you are ready, Kaji will have rooms prepared for you. Near Lady Katara’s?” Kaji bows. “If you have any questions, please direct them to Lady Katara or Lady Beifong.”

“It will be done,” the man bows again, and Sokka wonders if he’s imagining the way the man’s shoulders relax a little. Sokka glances at Katara and mouths ‘Lady,’ earning himself an eyeroll.

“Thank you,” Zuko sighs, rising to his feet and ignoring—or missing—the way Kaji twitches. “I’ll see you all later.”

“Take a bun,” Sokka suggests, pulling one onto his plate so they can stay even and tossing one at Zuko, earning himself both his second eyeroll and a scandalized twitch. But Zuko takes it and grabs a napkin to put it into his pocket, so Sokka’s going to call it a win even if the fact that Zuko is walking away most definitely doesn’t feel like one.

“Has that been happening a lot?” Toph asks as she neatly grabs a roll from one of the trays with her chopsticks.

“Yeah,” Katara says, glowering at the door and looking supremely disgruntled by it. “Lots of notes.”

Suki grunts, eyeing Zuko’s empty chair. “So…this food is great,” she says, loading up her plate as if to demonstrate the point. “And I’m glad we have a place to stay. But what’s actually been going on? Are we safe here?”

Katara sighs, shoving her hair back from her face, her take-charge demeanor briefly cracking. “It’s…been weird. Tense. It’s just so *empty*,” she says, casting a quick look out the window at the beautiful, empty courtyard outside. “It’s not actively hostile. But I don’t think it’s welcoming, either. I don’t think they like me,” she adds, looking moodily at her plate, and Sokka tries to imagine how the Southern Water Tribe would react if he walked into a politically unstable Tribe after years of absence to challenge Katara for the chiefdom, with some foreign bender in tow who doles out at least half of the orders.

He's…pretty sure he gets it.

“It’s been a bit better since we got the messenger hawk that the fleet went down,” Katara says, and Sokka can’t stop a wince even though she says it like it’s a good thing. He supposes confirmation that an army wasn’t going to return to re-coup the place would help settle things. “Since then, we’ve just been waiting to see who came back.”

*Who* came back. Because the hawks would have just said *what* happened, the military details. And the fleet going down was no guarantee that any of them would have survived it, and in the scramble of finding the White Lotus troops and commandeering a boat, Sokka doesn’t remember any of them managing to come up with a hawk. Spirits, how long would Zuko and Katara have waited for news? How long before Iroh would have thought to send word?

“It’s still been hard, though,” Katara says quietly, eyes darting to the door like it’s a secret.

“That’s all fascinating,” Toph cuts in before Sokka can jump on that. “But I *meant* the lack of titles for Zuko. And using titles for you. Has that been happening?”

Katara hesitates, frowning. “I don’t—maybe? It’s not…” She sends Sokka a quick, worried look. Titles and honorifics aren’t something the Southern Water Tribe really does or thinks much about enough to notice their absence.

“Is that important?” Aang asks, voice low, glancing toward the door. There’s probably a servant right out there, Sokka realizes. Or—a guard?

“The Fire Nation is big into its hierarchy,” Toph says, ignoring Sokka’s snort at that particular understatement. “Were they bowing a ton?”

“Yeah,” Suki says when Katara hesitates. “Way more than I’ve ever seen.” She shrugs when Sokka shoots her a surprised look. “Kyoshi Island trades. You get a feel for what’s normal.”

Toph grunts, rapping her knuckles on the table before settling back. “They’re trying to make up for it, then. That’s something at least.”

“Make up for what?” Sokka presses, wondering if he should be trying to find himself a better weapon than a pair of chopsticks.

“The Fire Nation likes hierarchy, which means they like *titles*. And they aren’t giving Zuko any.”

Sokka hesitates. He can tell that’s important, that it’s probably a perception thing. But he doesn’t know enough about how things are supposed to be around royalty, or how the politics work, to see the potential problems that Toph clearly does.

“It means they don’t know where he stands and they’re too afraid to insult him,” Toph clarifies, catching his confusion. “They don’t *want* to insult him. But call him ‘majesty’ when it should be ‘highness’, or ‘Fire Lord’ when it should be ‘Crown Prince…’”

“Oh,” Sokka says, reconsidering all the servant’s twitches in a whole new light. Spirits, he’s going to need to get Toph to give him a crash course in this stuff. “But wait—does that mean Zuko isn’t—?”

“Azula is in one of the guest rooms,” Katara says quietly, and Sokka blows out a breath as relief and anxiety both hit him in the gut. “In the Western wing, I think.”

“A *guest* room,” Toph frowns.

“Yeah, her rooms are apparently pretty…” Katara trails off, and Sokka starts rapidly reassessing the reasons behind all the charred streaks and mostly-scrubbed-away lightning scars he saw on the way to this little room.

“Not prison?” Suki asks carefully, pitching her voice so it just reaches the other side of the table.

“No,” Katara replies slowly. “Zuko said the security wasn’t good—” Sokka is absolutely sure Zuko used very different words for that. “—and that he doesn’t want to go that far to visit her.”

“…Visit.”

“Yes.”

“Have *you* been to see her? When he visits?”

“No,” Katara says, sounding simultaneously upset and worried about it.

“Katara,” Sokka says slowly, a partial picture of what they’ve flown into starting to form. “How did Zuko get injured?” Because he clearly *was* injured. And still is, *with* Katara around, which…Spirits, Sokka doesn’t want to think about what that means. That she either felt the need to conserve her strength to fight, or that Zuko was in such a bad state that this is the best she could do with the days she had.

“Lightning,” she says, the word short and tight. Which means Azula.

“And that *ended* the Agni Kai?” Sokka presses. Which should be a simple answer, but Katara hesitates. Has Sokka missed some part of the timeline here? Someone challenged someone and Zuko went down, but he still has free rein of the palace and *Azula* is the one confined to a guest room? Did she attack him after losing?

Aang looks about as confused as Sokka feels. “If Ozai can’t bend anymore, and Azula is imprisoned…is Zuko going to be the Fire Lord?”

“I don’t know,” Katara says.

“*What?”* Toph snaps, head whipping toward Katara. “You don’t *know*? You were there for the Agni Kai! Who won?”

“Isn’t he already doing—” Sokka flaps a hand toward Zuko’s empty chair and the door and realizes he doesn’t actually know what Zuko’s doing. “—Fire Lord stuff?”

“I *thought* it was him,” Katara says, scrubbing her hands over her face. “He even set a coronation date. But no one is saying who’s being coronated. And they’re *definitely* doing that on purpose,” she adds before Toph even finishes opening her mouth.

“…Fuck,” Sokka mutters under his breath, slumping back.

“Who won the Agni Kai?” Toph asks again, face intense. “That should have sorted it. Even if they aren’t officially announcing anything yet, if the challenge happened here the palace at least would know.”

“Um,” Katara says, a response she definitely picked up from Zuko. Sokka wonders if he should be nervous about how much time they’re spending together. “It wasn’t wholly clear…”

“Winners and losers are clear, in a two-man battle,” Toph snaps. “Who won?”

“…*I* did?”

Sokka pauses with a fried roll halfway to his mouth before slowly, deliberately setting it back onto his plate.

“…Well, fuck,” Toph says, sitting back. “No wonder you’ve become ‘Lady Katara.’ Oma and fucking Shu, the Fire Lord missing and both claimants in the same palace and neither saying who it’s going to be? What a fucking mess. I wouldn’t be using any titles either.”

Zuko strides through the palace with his head high and his steps steady, projecting every bit of confidence he has, wearing the role of ‘power’ as close to his skin as he can. He knows he can’t keep this up for much longer, but he more than knows that there are always eyes in the palace, now more than ever. And hopefully with the Avatar and the rest of the crew here now, he won’t have to. Hopefully, Zuko can stop walking this fine, fine line he’s setting his feet along.

He and Katara have been in the palace for days, just the two of them, trying to slowly, carefully consolidate power—dangerous enough to begin with, before Zuko has to worry about doing it too openly. Because Zuko is acutely aware that he’s been trying to build a foundation of strength with the bulk of his firepower far from his back. That even needing to rely on outside firepower in the first place signals a dangerous lack of surety in his ability to rely on his own.

So Zuko can’t keep hidden, but he also can’t be too seen. He needs to be in charge of the recovery without preemptively assuming power. Tireless and available and firm and definitely not visibly injured. Zuko knows he’s pushing himself too hard, and Katara knows it too, and they both know that he can’t stop. Not yet at least.

He nods to the two guards posted on either side of the nondescript door, pausing to allow one of them to give a polite knock before opening the door for Zuko with a little bow. No one involved seems entirely sure if the guards are there for protection or confinement, Zuko included most of the time. Because Azula might be locked behind a door all day, but the lock is always thrown from the inside.

Her voice comes from the darkness, the room cold and unlit, heavy curtains drawn. “Come to gloat more, Brother?”

“I thought we didn’t need signals for truth and lies anymore,” Zuko says, lighting the candle nearest to him, letting the flame grow gradually instead of bursting to life.

“When will there ever *not* be a need,” she huffs, voice moving. “Fine then. Come to gloat, *Zuko*?”

Zuko hums and uses the candle to light another by hand, and then the fireplace. Together they’re something to see by, though not nearly enough to penetrate the darkness, to shine off the wary eyes he can feel on his back.

“Spiced bun?” He finally offers, pulling the napkin-wrapped bun out of his pocket and splitting it into two neat halves with an old deftness he’s pleased to see he hasn’t lost.

“…I don’t want your pocket snacks,” Azula snaps, stepping forward into the ring of light, looking at him like he’s some fascinating wild thing dragged off the streets and set in front of her.

“Suit yourself,” Zuko shrugs, setting her half on the table and making quick work of his own. She’ll eat it if he can manage to stay in the room for a degree or two and not be visibly poisoned by the time he walks out.

Azula folds her arms, eyes narrowed on the bun before flicking back to his face. She knows his game. “You didn’t come to bring me a snack, Zuko.”

“No,” Zuko agrees, trying to decide between sitting at the table or leaning against the wall or maybe leaning against the table, and then just standing in the middle of the room like he always does. “The Avatar arrived.”

Azula stills, tawny eyes narrowing with predatory intensity on his face.

“He brought word of Ozai.” Zuko doesn’t make her ask. “Alive—”

“*Fuck.”*

“—but imprisoned.”

“That’s something at least,” Azula snarls, her composure briefly cracking as she pinches the bridge of her nose. “Of all the useless, worthless, Air Nomad pacificist *stupid* things—”

“He can’t firebend anymore,” Zuko interrupts before she can really get going, watching the way Azula goes immediately still. “Apparently.”

The flame closest to her flickers a bare degree, like she can’t help but reach for it. “…Excuse me?”

“It turns out that the Avatar can take someone’s bending away,” Zuko says quietly, taking a slow breath, feeding his disquiet into his inner flame. It’s still twisting in a unique kind of horror at the thought of someone just…reaching in and extinguishing it, but Zuko takes comfort in the way it flares, pressing against the inside of his ribs, hot and vital and there.

“…Does he keep it?” Azula finally asks, taking her own stoking breath before a quick, lightning-fast grimace crosses her face. She flicks a sharp, tiny bolt of cold fire toward the hearth, neither of them flinching by this point as it bursts against the thick stones. “Is he increasing his own abilities? Reaping power?”

“No.” Zuko is already shaking his head. “I asked,” he adds when she raises an eyebrow, the picture of skepticism.

She pauses for a moment, considering, then snorts. “I’m sure he took that well,” she says sourly, shooting him a sideways look. “Good for you, Zuko.”

Zuko decides not to try to parse whether that was meant as an outright or backhanded compliment. “He called it mercy. To preserve a life.”

Azula stares, face totally neutral with shock. “A mercy, to live with your soul ripped away from Agni? For your blood to never again quicken from her touch? To never call forth a piece of her light from inside yourself and know that you’re holding a part of the divine?”

“He believes it,” Zuko says quietly, pretending not to notice the way the fire is pulsing in time with her breaths. “He isn’t just saying it.”

“…Well,” Azula finally says, something like satisfaction settling in her eyes. “I didn’t think the Air Nomad would have it in him. That’s my kind of mercy.”

“Yes.” It really is, and Zuko thinks part of Aang knows that he didn’t wholly do Ozai a kindness. Zuko hopes he knows, at least.

“You’re happy,” she observes, head tilted, like the sight is a foreign curiosity to be observed in a menagerie.

Zuko shrugs. ‘Happy’ feels too small to encompass all that he is. “Aren’t you?”

Azula hums, lips curling into a vicious little smile before her tawny eyes sharpen on his face again. “He can’t be allowed to do it to anyone else.”

“I know,” Zuko says, refusing to let himself respond to the way her frame coils with something close to her usual readiness along with the words.

“Not that I care if the Avatar makes himself into a monster to the world,” Azula adds, lest Zuko mistakenly think she cares about anything. “But the Fire Nation will not allow someone to walk around stealing Agni’s blessing at a whim.”

“I know,” Zuko repeats, because once, on the day of Sozin’s Comet, in semi-fated conflict? That can be looked away from if there’s reason enough to, even if it happened to a Child of Agni. But twice? Three times? Zuko fears the Avatar would be accused of committing his own genocide, then. “I’m going to talk to him.”

Azula studies his face. “And will you tell people? That it was the Avatar that did it?”

“Agni’s blessing is a gift, not a right.”

Azula scowls. “Don’t quote scripture at me. What Agni giveth can be taken away by *Agni*. And it’s not like it’s ever happened before.”

“It hasn’t,” Zuko agrees. “But it’s been written.”

“Which means the idea exists,” Azula finishes, shaking her head. “You’re walking a thin line, Zuko.”

He offers her a shrug. When is he not?

Azula huffs, her expression turning thoughtful as she begins to stroll around the room, slipping in and out of the light. Her words, when she speaks, are drawling and taunting, familiar and conspicuously without fire. “The Phoenix Emperor gone,” she muses. “A Fire Lord dethroned. Another Fire Lord uncrowned.” Her eyes flick to his bare topknot. “My, my, Zuko. You must be running yourself ragged.” Her eyes pointedly drift over his exhausted, tired state. “Just you and the peasant, trying to keep it all from falling apart.”

“Yes.” He catches a sliver of her face in the light as it seems to simultaneously tighten and relax at the admission.

“And I suppose our dear Uncle stayed in the Earth Kingdom, with his teashop and his secret club.”

“He did.” Which has made things at the same time so much easier, and so much harder.

“Hm.” She slips into the shadows, her voice the only thing marking her movement around the room now. “And how long do you think a Fire Nation can last without a Fire Lord?”

“Not long,” Zuko says softly. He’s honestly a little surprised it's lasted this long already. He doesn’t think it says good things about where the Nation was left that it has.

Azula nods as she steps back into the light, like he said something more profound than he did. “Then why,” she asks, face twisting into something like a snarl. “Are you *here*, Zuko. To gloat? To taunt? Or have you somehow still not managed to consolidate power, with the only other two viable claimants in the Earth Kingdom or imprisoned?” Zuko wants to protest that characterization but isn’t quite sure that he can. The lock might be thrown from the inside, but Azula hasn’t tried to leave yet. “Are you really that *weak*?”

Zuko refuses to rise to the bait, steadily meeting her glare. “I was never as weak as you thought I was, Azula.”

She shakes her head, glancing away first. “You were never strong enough to survive this on your own. To survive this without *me.*” The palace, the family, his banishment. Zuko doesn’t know which she means, but either way it’s true. For both of them, it’s true, and he knows she knows it.

“But things have changed,” he says, holding onto neutrality because he knows she won’t take gentleness. “You said it yourself—Ozai is gone. And in quite a crushing, internationally visible defeat.”

“And the airship fleet used most of the raw materials we had left,” Azula acknowledges, grudging.

“There’s barely enough to repair the factories,” Zuko agrees. Not after the recent spate of sabotages.

“So we can’t do that again, by air or by sea, even *if* we had enough soldiers who weren’t more than children,” Azula mutters, pulling a face.

“We might need to seize civilian vessels to pull troops out of the Colonies, if it comes to that.”

“Or ask the Water Tribe?” Azula says, with more than a little bite. Except they both know that’s true, too.

“And the Avatar has come into his power,” Zuko continues instead. “And he calls the Beifong heir his friend. And the Water Tribe heir. And the most powerful water and earthbender of their generation—”

“It doesn’t count if that’s the same pair of people twice,” Azula interrupts, wrinkling her nose.

“—And Kyoshi Island is behind him,” Zuko finishes, keeping his voice even. “And a Child of Agni.” He considers Uncle. “Maybe two.”

“What,” Azula bites out, back to pacing the perimeter. “Are you parading your newly discovered ability to make friends with something other than your dick?”

“There’s a chance to end the war, Azula,” Zuko says, words coming easily like they rarely do. “To really end it, like we always talked about.”

“If the Fire Nation surrenders, the other nations will—”

“It doesn’t have to be a surrender if we all want it to end! Azula, beating the others into submission isn’t the only way. Not anymore.”

“It’s still the best way,” she insists, sharp. “For the *Fire Nation*, which is what you’re *supposed* to care about.”

“And what cost does it come at?” Zuko pushes back. “You said it yourself, Azula—*we* *don’t* *have the resources* *to leave the islands*. We barely have the resources to get food and raw materials shipped *to* us at this point. How long before the other nations find out?”

Azula crosses her arms, glaring into the fire. “Peace doesn’t come without its costs, too. The war isn’t even technically done, and already the Earth Kingdom is talking reparations. You think that’s going to stop if suddenly *we* start asking for peace too?”

“No, it won’t,” Zuko sighs. The Fire Nation has long relied on its ingenuity to make what it has stretch beyond what it should, and reparations aren’t going to come easy when they’ve finally stretched themselves thin enough to break. “But isn’t it better to pay those costs knowing that it's building toward something? Because that sounds better to me than hoping we can grind out a victory before we collapse.”

Azula freezes, something like stunned disbelief on her face. “You better not be about to say something about the dual dao, Zuko,” she warns, expression going tight. “I think that’s well behind us by this point. You can’t actually be trying to get me to *support* your bid for the throne.”

Zuko doesn’t exactly say yes, but he doesn’t say no, either. “The Fire Nation needed you and your strength and all you are as Fire Lord when the only path we had was unilateral victory.”

Azula fixes him with an unblinking stare, eyes hooded. “Past tense,” she says softly. “Needed.”

Zuko sighs, rubbing the back of his neck. “Answer me honestly—is that what the Fire Nation needs from its Fire Lord now?”

“The Fire Nation is always going to need strength,” Azula snaps.

“Always,” Zuko agrees. “But its strength doesn’t have to be on the throne to be known.”

Azula’s face twists with disgust. “Fire flakes before the fist? Really, Zuko?” It’s a concept they had thoroughly beaten out of them a long time ago.

“We aren’t going to get a second chance at this,” Zuko says, quick and intense, leaning forward with the force of how much he wants her to *agree.* “Not us and not the nation. And you can’t start with the fist.” He waits for her to look at him again. “But you can always take away the fire flakes.”

Azula stills, all watchful focus as he reaches slowly into his pocket and takes out the Fire Lord’s headpiece. He tests the weight a moment before setting it gently down on the table next to the spiced bun and stepping back so they’re precisely equidistance from it.

“I’m not going to fight you for it,” Zuko says, ignoring her acid “*Again*.” “I’m not going to be like Father.”

Her words drip sarcasm. “You’re not going to steal my throne while I’m trying to find myself after an emotional break before I'm crowned?”

“If you truly believe you are still best for this, then I will support you like we always planned,” Zuko says, ignoring the jab and feeling the echo of that conversation that happened so long ago. “If you can genuinely say that you think you’re better than me with the way things are now.” Not the way they were all those years ago, the first time he and Azula faced each other across a headpiece and talked about what needed to be done to make themselves and their nation safe.

“Still interested in being my conscious, Zuko?” She gives him a guarded, assessing look, maybe remembering the same thing. “What do you want, agreement?”

“It’s how we did it the first time,” Zuko says quietly.

“Except your mind is already made up,” Azula snaps, folding her arms, face tight.

Zuko just raises his eyebrow. “Isn’t yours?”

Azula doesn’t answer for a long moment and then neatly dodges the question, which Zuko of all people knows how to recognize. “You didn’t care about my agreement when you showed up to stop my *coronation*.”

Zuko winces. “Now that you aren’t…”

“Fire mad?”

Zuko doesn’t say yes, but only because they both know that’s another true thing, and in the silence she finally steps forward, picking up the headpiece, turning it in her hand, admiring it in the firelight. Zuko watches her eyes instead of the flashing gold.

“Brother,” Azula finally says, voice so low Zuko can barely hear it. “You are too good for this place.” Then she tosses the headpiece down with a clatter, sending it skidding over the table so that Zuko needs to lunge to catch it before it hits the floor. “You are going to get eaten alive, Zuko,” she says with all her usual bite and disdain. “I have no need to rush. I can wait.”

&#45;-

Katara finally pins Sokka down for a healing when they run out of things to debrief on and Toph and Aang start looking itchy to explore—or case the perimeter, as Toph puts it. Sokka makes a half-hearted effort at protest—it’s not that he doesn’t *want* the healing, he just wants to make sure that no one else needs it more—before Katara pins him with a glare and asks rather pointedly if he would like another crutch or to be carried or maybe risk his permanent well-being to punish himself?

Since walking unassisted isn’t an option, Sokka shuts up and accepts Suki’s help to the room Katara directs them to—a servant twitching as Katara breezes past. It seems to be part bedroom, part study, part armory, light streaming in from the courtyard-facing windows and glinting off the blades around the room. Sokka immediately recognizes Zuko’s swords on the dresser and relaxes, and then tenses right up again at the idea of Zuko walking around without them.

“This is going to hurt,” Katara warns once she gets eyes on his leg, like taking the splint off and cutting away the fabric of his pants didn’t already. “Worse,” she adds, catching his expression.

She’s right.

Her blue-glow water is cool and familiar and goes right to the pain but *Spirits*, it’s like a dull, persistent throbbing in his bones that makes his *teeth* ache, interspersed with zinging pinpricks of pain somewhere on the border of hot and cold. Sokka would normally complain about it, vocally and at length, except Katara’s expression is a little too grim, a little too exhausted, like the fact that she’s causing him pain is hitting a little too close.

“I’m sorry,” she says after it’s done, flopping down next to him on the bed, careful not to jostle too much even though in the aftermath of her healing his leg feels…actually pretty great. “Some things were healing wrong, and there was a lot of tendon damage, and I’m just…”

“Tired?”

“Yeah,” she sighs into the covers.

Sokka eyes her, face-down, hair wisping out of her braids, and weighs the benefits of letting her just pass out against his itching need to *know*.

Knowing wins.

“Katara,” he asks, carefully easing down so their heads are level. “How bad was Zuko hurt?” She freezes, burying her face a little deeper into the covers when Sokka pokes her gently in the side. “Katara…”

“I don’t know how he survived it long enough for me to get to him,” she finally says, quiet and clear even through the bedspread. “I don’t—Tui and Lai, Sokka, it was some kind of miracle.”

Sokka exhales hard, closing his stinging eyes at the confirmation, delayed fear beating frantically against his ribs, only the fact that Zuko was holding him and smiling at him just before this keeping Sokka from panic. “Are you still healing him?”

“When I can,” she says, which puts her frustration at Zuko being called away so often, and her demands of ‘*no running,’* into a bit more context.

Sokka takes a deep breath, bracing himself for a fight. “He’s the priority over me. If you have to choose.”

Katara finally pulls her face out of the covers, shoving her hair back, expression already set in protest.

“Katara, he is,” Sokka insists before she can find her words. “This—” He wiggles his leg a little, which doesn’t even really hurt. “—can keep. We need him, okay?” And not just that Sokka needs him. He hates the idea of needing to be coldly practical about it, but in the palace, in the Fire Nation, having just taken down the Fire Lord and an entire fleet—they *need* Zuko.

“…I know,” Katara finally says, grim in a way that makes him pause. “I already—I know. I…rushed his healing,” she admits, guilt flashing over her face. “It’s made it harder for him, now. And it’s not how a proper healer would have acted, but Azula was in chains and Zuko was down and it was just me. And I needed him to wake up.”

Spirits, Sokka can picture it all too well. A lone waterbender standing over the two downed royals, her only ally unconscious at her feet. Fuck, he has no idea how the lot of them managed to all make it through this, but he will be grateful for it every day of his life.

“You did the right thing, Katara,” Sokka says, reaching out and fumbling for her hand, gripping back when she squeezes tight. “It’s okay. It’s going to be okay. You saved him and got yourself the time to help him. And he’s going to be fine in the long run, right?”

“If he stops *running* everywhere and *eats*,” Katara mutters, waspish and more than a little watery.

“We can make him do that,” Sokka says, already starting to line up every way he can think of to make Zuko slow down and eat and probably sleep while they’re at it, too. “Don’t feel bad about what you had to do, okay?” He rolls into his side when she makes a noise in the back of her throat, trying to put every bit of feeling he has into his words. “Katara, I’m *so* happy that you were here with him. To heal him and to help him after. I couldn’t have done half of what you’ve been doing.”

“I don’t know why I rushed it so much,” Katara says, voice tight and muffled by the blankets again. “I could have just taken five more minutes. Tui and La, I should have talked him out of the Agni Kai in the first place, it was a terrible idea!”

“Maybe,” Sokka says, thinking that their collective grasp of the politics around imperial Agni Kai probably doesn’t amount to even a quarter of what was going on at the time. “But it was Zuko’s decision, not yours.” And Sokka suspects that if fighting Azula is where it ended up, there was very little that Zuko felt could have gone differently.

Katara makes a low, aggrieved noise, reluctantly nodding when he gives her hand another squeeze. “I just keep going back over the whole thing,” she admits, finally pulling her face out of the covers to look at him. “The healing and the fight and the Agni Kai and running through the city, just—if I hadn’t faced Azula before, if I hadn’t had that experience healing Aang—”

“But you did. You do,” Sokka cuts in quietly. “And yeah, you made choices. But so did everyone else. There were probably a thousand choices we all made just in the past few days.”

“…And you’re not beating yourself up for all of yours?”

“There are things I *wish* had been different,” Sokka admits, glancing away and fully aware that she knows exactly how his mind works. “But we’re here, right? All of us. And how can we know that things would still turn out okay if any one of us had chosen differently?”

“Is that what you do these days?” she asks quietly, genuinely, maybe a little skeptically. “Focus on the big picture and not all the pieces on the way?”

“I’m giving it a shot,” Sokka sighs, scrubbing his free hand over his face and holding back that it has *not* been easy, or natural. She knows exactly how his mind works, after all. “But we can’t change the past, right? And we’re here now and we’re okay, and every step you took got us there.”

“…Yours too,” Katara says after a moment, pale eyes serious as she finally meets his gaze. “All of your steps, too.”

“All of ours,” Sokka agrees quietly. “So don’t second-guess the ones you had to make.” Regardless of how much he might want there to have been another way.

Sokka awakes to darkness and panic. There’s a soft bed under his back, which is briefly, sharply disorienting—shouldn’t it be sand, or grass, or stone?—and he can hear Katara and Aang breathing next to him, Suki’s almost-snores by the door to the hall, Toph on the floor by the door to the courtyard. But Sokka’s expected steady, even breaths, firebender controlled even in sleep, and there *aren’t* any, where—

“It’s fine, Sokka,” Toph whispers, blankets quietly rustling as she shifts.

“What?” His vision is adjusting enough to the moonlight filtering in that he can see the shape of the room. Paper screens, tall thin windows, and—Fire Nation. This is Fire Nation.

Toph gently taps her bare foot onto the floor. “I have his heartbeat. He’s fine. As much as he ever is.”

That’s…not wholly reassuring.

“He’s not actively fighting,” Toph clarifies. “Just up early.”

Sokka drops back down onto the bed as relief slams into him, his heart still pounding. Zuko is up *very* early, then. Or maybe never went to sleep? Sokka doesn’t remember dozing off with Katara, just briefly surfacing as the others trickled into the room. If it’s early, it’s still ahead of dawn enough to be totally black. Maybe that’s just how it is in the center of Caldera, though, at the bottom of the crater? Though Sokka doesn’t hear any birds or the quiet movement of servants he learned to associate with pre-dawn hours in Ba Sing Se.

Still, now that his adrenaline is fading, Toph’s reassurance is spreading through his chest, along with exhaustion and the tiredness that always comes on the heels of a hard healing. And Sokka trusts Toph to keep a watch over things, so he counts his people again one last time and lets sleep drag him back down.
